en: Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.

May the wise ones of the earth daily drink this [work], which was brought forth by my own words, standing far removed from the many contradictions of the well-guarded doctrines of former teachers. || 2 ||

Although the status of the inquiry as having the "object" (karman) as its referent is established by its requirement for an object even when the relationship is understood in a general sense, nevertheless, because that which is expressed directly (ābhidhānika) must be accepted over that which is obtained through implication (ākṣepataḥ), the genitive case is taken in the sense of the "object."

The desire to know is "jijñāsā. Since desire has that which is desired as its primary object, it is knowledge itself that is enjoined here as the object of desire. Because the ritual action (karma) known from the first part of the Mīmāṃsā yields results that are limited and impermanent, whereas the knowledge of Brahman determined by the subsequent part yields infinite and inexhaustible results, it follows that after the prior knowledge of ritual action—and for that very reason—Brahman is to be known. Thus says the author of the Vṛtti:
"After the acquisition of the knowledge of ritual action, there arises the desire to know Brahman."
Thus [he says]. And he will state the unity of the two treatises on ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*) and Brahman (*brahma-mīmāṃsā*):

"This *Śārīraka* is conjoined with the sixteen-chaptered [work] of Jaimini; thus is the establishment of the unity of the scripture" (*śāstraikatvasiddhi*). Therefore, the distinction between the *Pūrva* and *Uttara* Mīmāṃsās is like the distinction between the six books (*ṣaṭka*) or the distinction between the chapters (*adhyāya*), based on the difference in the objects intended to be explained. The Mīmāṃsā-śāstra begins: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*).

Beginning with this and ending with "no return, on account of the word; no return, on account of the word," [the text] follows a specific sequence characterized by a particular connection. For instance, first of all:
"One's own Veda is to be studied."

By the word "I" (*iti*), the acquisition of the collection of syllables known as the Veda— which is denoted by the term *svādhyāya*— is enjoined through the act of study itself. Thus, the injunction for study culminates merely in the acquisition of the collection of syllables, accompanied by the rules [of recitation] as in the case of a mantra.
"By those who bathe [only] in water, [the goal] is not attained," and "Those forms of sacrifice are perishable.

If that is so, then one should not even engage in the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* (the inquiry into the nature of the Self), since everything would already be known through the mere study of the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*).

True, there is indeed an initial impression (*āpātapratīti*); nevertheless, because a sentence assisted by logic (*nyāya*) is what determines the true meaning, one might argue: "Even an initially perceived meaning does not transcend doubt and error; therefore, for the sake of its definitive determination, an inquiry into the Vedānta texts must be undertaken. If you think thus, then please consider that an inquiry into Dharma must likewise be undertaken!
For ritual acts, such as the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, are investigated "right here" [in the Mīmāṃsā].
If it is argued that [liberation] cannot be achieved [by action],

then how could action— which has not been mastered— be the means for the cessation of ignorance, which consists in the cessation of all desire for rewards? Furthermore, the Śruti texts demonstrate that actions have impermanent fruits and are thus opposed to liberation, and that knowledge alone is the means to liberation.
Thus, when the desire to know [Brahman] arises in one whose impurities have been worn away by specific actions performed over hundreds of previous births without aiming for their particular fruits,
[the Upanishad declares]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite";
"partless and actionless," "peaceful";
"this Self is Brahman"; "That thou art."
From the knowledge produced by such statements as these, ignorance is removed.

Establishment (*pratiṣṭhāpana*) is reflection (*manana*). For the sake of dispelling the beginningless impressions of duality that are contrary to this, there is the continuous meditation (*nididhyāsana*) on this very same meaning.

Regarding the phrase "thus it has been said": therefore, since knowledge of ritual action (*karmajñāna*) is of no use [for liberation], one must state that the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) alone is what precedes [the inquiry into Brahman].

Nor should it be argued: "As long as the latent impression of duality (*bhedavāsanā*) has not been discarded, the sentence does not produce the knowledge that sublates ignorance (*avidyā*); even when such knowledge has arisen, the fact that the cognition of duality does not immediately cease for everyone is no fault. It is like the non-cessation of the cognition of two moons even after the oneness of the moon is known. Furthermore, even if it does not cease, it cannot lead to bondage because its root has been severed."

Because it is impossible for knowledge not to arise when the causal complex is present; and because, even when contrary latent impressions are present, the arising of subverting knowledge is observed through authoritative instruction, inferential signs, and so forth.

Nor can you maintain that even when there is knowledge of the meaning of a sentence, a cognition of difference persists to some degree due to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*); for since those latent impressions, which constitute the causal complex for the cognition of difference, are themselves false in nature, they must cease upon the very arising of [true] knowledge. If that false impression were not removed even when knowledge has arisen, it could never be removed, as there would be no other means to effect its cessation.

To say that the cognition of difference—the effect of latent impressions (vāsanā)—has had its root cut yet persists is the talk of a fool. In cases such as the cognition of two moons, however, even when a sublater (bādhaka) is present, the persistence of false cognition is not contradictory because the cause of that false cognition—namely, the ultimate defect of ophthalmia or the like—is not destroyed, since it cannot be sublated by cognition. Nevertheless, effects such as fear cease because they have been sublated by a stronger means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).

Moreover, for those who maintain that the arising of knowledge occurs by means of the eradication of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality, the production of such knowledge will never be established; for the latent impressions of duality have been accumulated since beginningless time and are thus immeasurable,
whereas the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) opposed to them is slight, and it is impossible to eradicate the former by means of the latter.

By means of such passages as "one should form a firm conviction" (*prajñāṃ kuryāt*), meditation (*dhyāna*) is enjoined—following upon the statements "having understood" (*anuvidya*) and "having known" (*vijñāya*) which refer to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences—as in "one should form a firm conviction" and "he knows," because the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences is an aid to meditation.

The statement "it is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*); for since the Veda studied for its own sake is seen to lead to the comprehension of a purposeful meaning, a person who has studied the Veda spontaneously engages in hearing (*śravaṇa*) in order to determine that meaning, and thus hearing is already established. Furthermore, since reflection (*manana*) is for the sake of establishing what has been heard, the statement "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*) is also a restatement. Therefore, it is meditation (*dhyāna*) alone that is enjoined. And the author will state later: "Repetition [is required], because of the repeated instruction."
Regarding the statement, "He who knows what he knows has been told this by me," [Nārada said]:
"Venerable sir, instruct me further regarding that deity whom you worship."
Thus [it is said].

And meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of an uninterrupted continuum of mindfulness, like a stream of oil. This is because it is heard in scripture that constant mindfulness is the means to liberation: "Mindfulness becomes firm; when mindfulness is attained, there is the loosening of all knots. Furthermore, that mindfulness has a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*): "The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted—when He, who is both high and low, is seen."
Because of this and other such passages, they share a single purpose (*aikārthya*).

This being the case, by the statement "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," the state of meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) having a form identical to direct perception (*darśana*) is enjoined. And through the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), recollection (*smṛti*) indeed attains the nature of perception. All of this has been elaborated upon by the author of the *Vākya* [Brahmasūtrabhāṣya].

"Upāsanā should be [understood as] meditation (*dhyāna*), because it is heard in that context"—here, "uninterruptedness" means being unseparated by any other cognition of a different kind. If the word *dhyāna* refers to a continuum of memory in general, even when interrupted, then its specific application is defined as "meditation. If, however, it refers specifically to an uninterrupted continuum of memory, then the explanation of the word *dhyāna* is "meditation," and so forth.
"Vipramokṣaḥ" means liberation through separation, that is, absolute release.
"Having a form identical to perception"—this means that the similarity is not merely due to the identity of the object, but also because of its immediacy (*āparokṣya*).

Thus, in all the Upaniṣads, it is stated that "knowledge" (*vedana*), which is enjoined as the means to liberation, is actually "meditation" (*upāsana*). Having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "one should perform the cognition only once, since the purpose of the word has been accomplished, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings," etc., [the sūtra refutes this].

Regarding the sūtra, "But meditation is established on account of the word," it has been determined that knowledge (vedana), when repeated, is the means to liberation. Furthermore, "Meditation must be constant remembrance, because of the etymological derivation from the root meaning 'to see'."

Thus, it has been described that this very meditation (*upāsana*), when repeated and performed continuously, constitutes "constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛti*). This remembrance is established as being of the nature of direct vision (*darśana*); and its nature as vision is the attainment of direct perceptual immediacy (*pratyakṣatā*).
"To those who are constantly disciplined and who worship Me with love,
I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me.
Thus [it is said].
"For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me.

Therefore, one for whom the remembrance in the form of direct realization—being remembered as something exceedingly dear—is itself "exceedingly dear," is alone to be chosen by the Supreme Self; thus it is said that the Supreme Self is attained by that very person.

This very constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) of such a nature is designated by the word "devotion" (*bhakti*), because the word *bhakti* is a synonym for "meditative worship" (*upāsana*). For this very reason, it is stated thus by the Śrutis and Smṛtis:
"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death."

"One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here; there is no other path for going. "Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen Me."
"O Arjuna, scorcher of foes, it is possible to know Me as I am, to see Me in truth, and to enter into Me, only through unswerving devotion.
O Pārtha, that Supreme Person is attained through unswerving devotion."
Thus [it is said].

It will be stated [in the Sūtras] that "sacrifices and other rites are the means for this kind of constant mindfulness (dhruvānusmṛti), because of the scriptural mention of sacrifices and so forth, as in the case of the horse. Although sacrifices and the like are enjoined for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)—as in the phrase "they desire to know"—nevertheless, since that very knowledge, which consists of meditation, is a means for attaining Brahman when it is practiced daily, its excellence is enhanced through repetition, and it continues until death, all duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) must be performed throughout one's life for its production. And the author will say:

This is seen in such passages as "Even there, up to the vital breath," "But the Agnihotra and so forth are for that very purpose, because of the scriptural vision," and "And by way of being auxiliary causes."
Thus it is said.
Herein is the explanation: "When food is pure..."
"Purity; in purity of truth, there is constant mindfulness.
Thus:
"Liberation is non-attachment to desires."
Thus:
"One should meditate while being tranquil" is the definition.
"Ārambhaṇa is repeated cultivation, that is, practice.
And the etymological definition was cited by the Commentator from the Smṛti:
"Always permeated by that state."
Thus:
"The performance of the five great sacrifices and so forth according to one's capacity is action (kriyā).
This is the etymological definition.
"He is an active performer of rites, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman"; and,
"The Brāhmaṇas seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting."
And thus:
"Truthfulness, straightforwardness, gentleness, self-restraint, non-violence, and lack of covetousness are auspicious.
This is the etymological definition.
"He is to be attained through truth," "This dustless world of Brahman belongs to them alone," and so forth.
"Due to defects in place and time, and from the recollection of objects of grief and so forth, there arises a dejection and lack of luster in the mind; this is despondency (avasāda).
Its opposite is non-despondency (anavasāda). This is the etymological definition.
"This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength.
"Exultation (uddharṣa) is the contentment born from the opposite of that [weakness]."
Thus [it is said]. Its opposite is "lack of elation" (anuddharṣa). And "excessive contentment" is its contradictory—this is the meaning. There is also an etymological derivation:
"Peaceful and self-controlled. "He too, relying on knowledge, performed very many sacrifices."
"Having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman, one may cross over death by means of ignorance.

Furthermore, action—whether in the form of merit or demerit—is opposed to knowledge. Because both obstruct the arising of the knowledge of Brahman and result in undesirable fruits, both are designated by the term "demerit" (pāpa).
[This occurs] by way of the increase of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are opposed to the pure *sattva* that serves as the cause [of knowledge].
Furthermore, its opposition to knowledge consists in the fact that sin is opposed to the arising of knowledge.
This is understood from the Śruti: "It is this very [Self] which causes him to perform evil deeds, whom it desires to lead downwards."

Knowledge [of the self], as well as the knowledge that actions performed solely for their own sake yield results that are meager and unstable—this must be understood through the *Karmamīmāṃsā*; therefore, that very [knowledge] which is required for the "inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*) should be stated as having preceded it.

Moreover, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, and so forth, cannot be accomplished without hearing the Mīmāṃsā; for it is difficult to comprehend the nature of ritual action, its results, and their permanence (or impermanence), as well as the specific determination of the fruit, the instrument, the procedure, and the qualified agent. Furthermore, the status of these as means is to be understood through application (*viniyoga*), and application is determined by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so on. And that [application] is based on the Tarka [section].

Furthermore, meditations such as that on the *udgītha*, although intended for the successful completion of ritual acts (*karma*), take the form of viewing [the object] as Brahman and thus depend upon the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, they should be considered right here [in this section]. Moreover, since those very rituals—when performed without desire for their fruits—generate the knowledge of Brahman, these meditations, which bring about the perfection of those rituals, are all the more appropriately connected right here. And it is universally accepted that these meditations depend upon the comprehension of the essential nature of the rituals themselves.
Thus concludes the *Laghusiddhānta*.
Now, the Great Purvapaksha:

"Now, as for the higher [knowledge], how that Imperishable is attained—that which is unutterable, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, undecaying, which the wise behold as the source of all beings;
[and] 'Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.'"
"Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless. "He by whom It is not thought, by him It is thought; he who knows It does not know.
It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know."
"Do not seek to see the seer of seeing... do not seek to think the thinker of thinking. "Bliss is Brahman.
"All this is that which is the Self."

‘There is no diversity whatsoever here. He goes from death to death who perceives any kind of diversity here. ‘For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another... But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what should he know whom? ‘A modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the clay alone is real. ‘For when he makes even a slight distinction within this [Self], then fear comes upon him.’

"Even from the standpoint of place, there is no dual characteristic for the Supreme Being, for it exists everywhere! But [the world] is mere illusion (māyāmātra), because its true nature is not fully manifested.

And this defect is beginningless ignorance (avidyā), which conceals the true nature [of reality], produces various and manifold distractions, and is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent.
"For they are veiled by untruth."

"For those who exist as truths, untruth is a covering": "Then there was neither non-existence nor existence; there was only darkness hidden by darkness, unperceived in the beginning. "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā."
"Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (*māyā*). "My *māyā* is difficult to overcome.
"When the individual soul (*jīva*), sleeping through beginningless *māyā*, awakens..."

By such statements as these, it is shown that Brahman alone—which is non-dual pure consciousness—has its true nature concealed by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), which is indefinable as being either real or unreal; and this [ignorance] is the defect. The manifoldness (or diversity) of the projection (*vikṣepa*)—which is to say, superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—is due to "I-ness," "this-ness," and their various sub-divisions. Regarding the dilemma of whether that [ignorance] is ultimately real or not ultimately real, the term "indefinable as real or unreal" accepts its lack of ultimate reality. The word "beginningless" avoids the fault of infinite regress. The phrase "of various kinds" indicates that the manifold superimpositions have a single defect as their root. This is what is meant by "ignorance."

It is intended that there are two states of this very same ignorance: the concealing (*ācchādikā*) and the distracting (*vikṣepikā*), because it is stated [in the *Śrutiprakāśikā*] that they are the causes of concealment and distraction.
It is understood that one perceives the diversity inherent within oneself, as it has been said:

"Thus, O Bhava, I have declared the true nature of existence; knowledge is the truth, while everything else is unreal. Furthermore, regarding that which pertains to worldly transaction, I have also explained to you its dependence upon the universe."

"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path," and so forth—these are the scriptural texts (*śruti*). Here, by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is denoted. As stated in the words of Sanatsujāta:
"I declare that negligence indeed is death; I declare that constant vigilance is immortality."
Thus [it is said].
For this is precisely stated: "One should meditate upon him as the Self alone."

This is established by such scriptural statements as "That thou art," "I am indeed you, O venerable deity; you are indeed me, O venerable deity," and "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he am I. And the author will state this very point later:
"But they acknowledge [the self] as 'Self' and cause others to grasp it as such. And so says the author of the *Vākya*:

"But surely, the cessation of all distinctions is contradicted by perception; how then can it be effected by the cognition produced by the *śāstra*? Or how is the cessation of the snake, which is contradicted by perception, effected by the cognition: 'This is a rope, not a snake'?"
If it is argued that there is a contradiction between two types of perception, whereas here there is a contradiction between scripture— which is rooted in perception— and perception itself—
then how can there be a relationship of sublation and sublated when the two are equal?
If it is replied that this is due to the former and the latter being produced by defective causes and lacking such causes respectively:
This same principle applies to scripture and perception as well:
in the relationship between the sublated and the sublator,
there exists equality, dependence, independence, and so forth.

This is what is meant by "nanu ceti" (if it be objected). The intention of the objection is that, like the inferences and scriptural statements such as "fire is not hot" or "the sacrificial post is the sun," the Śruti lacks the capacity to establish an object that contradicts perception. It is replied: [The Śruti] is made the subject; how so? In no way [is it possible for it to contradict perception]. This very scripture, when confronted with what is contradicted by perception, must be interpreted as having its primary meaning sublated and being taken in a figurative sense.

Or how so? The word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers merely to that which is not indirect (*aparokṣa-mātra*). The point is that before sublation there is the conceit of non-appearance as illusory, and sublation is the same for both the world-appearance (*prapañca*) and the delusion of a snake in a rope (as stated in the *Tattva-ṭīkā*). The cessation of the [illusory] snake is brought about; the absence of the snake is made the object. Being perceptible is not the determinant for being unsublated. It is "not the cause," because perception cannot be set aside by the inference of the difference in flames; for in that case, the identity of the flame is apprehended by perception.

"And this being the case, when there is a contradiction between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that one whose validity could be established otherwise is the sublated (*bādhya*); the other, which is not established otherwise and has no [other] scope, is the sublator (*bādhaka*)—such is the determination of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator everywhere."

[Objection: But surely, even for a scripture that is faultless because its tradition has been uninterrupted, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," which relies upon duality, would the consequence follow that it is sublated? [Reply:
True; just as in the case of a prior scriptural injunction when there is a subsequent contradiction, so it is with the scripture concerning liberation.

Even among the Vedānta passages, those devoted to the meditation on Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahmopāsana) are set aside by it, because they have no scope [in relation to the ultimate reality];
this same principle applies to all scriptures, since the supreme Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirguṇa).

"Is it not so," and so forth. The intention of the objection is that since perception and other means of knowledge which apprehend difference are contradicted by the Śruti texts on non-duality (*advaita*), they have been declared to be sublated; however, in that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*). The word "api" has the sense of contradiction. The mention of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth is intended to clarify that [perception] relies upon difference, which is the very reason for its sublation. "Sublation" means that because it is produced by the defect known as the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference, sublation would follow as a consequence. Nor is this an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it has been established that [the Veda] is free from defects due to its being of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*); such is the meaning.

"It is true" means that there is no admission [of validity] when [the cognition] is produced by a defective cause (*duṣṭakāraṇa*). For it is precisely the states of being "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) or "not established otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddha*) that serve as the determining factors in the relationship between the sublated (*bādhya*) and the sublator (*bādhaka*). Indeed, the previously mentioned state of being produced by a defective cause is itself a specific mode of being "established otherwise. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the prior and subsequent removals" (*pūrvāparāpacchede*):

In the *Karmamīmāṃsā*, it is stated: "When two [rules] apply in succession, the earlier one is weaker, as in the case of the archetypal (*prakṛti*) rite. This means that since there is no opposing factor at the time of the earlier [rule's] origination, its origination is possible without subverting the later; however, for the later [rule], because an opposing factor exists at the time of its own origination, its origination is untenable without subverting the earlier. Thus, having subverted the earlier, the later arises; and because it is not established otherwise, the later is stronger.
It is accepted that that which relies upon difference is sublated.
The earlier arises without subverting the later, precisely because it has not yet been produced when the later arises.
"For the arising of the subsequent [teaching] is established without sublation of the prior.

This refers to the scripture on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*)—that is, the statement that reveals the cessation of the distinctions consisting of bondage. Because it is "without scope" (*niravakāśatva*), meaning there is no opportunity for its arising without sublation of the prior; and because the scripture concerning the attributeless (*nirguṇa-śāstra*) is stronger by virtue of the principle of the "successive annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*), while the scripture concerning the qualified (*saguṇa-śāstra*) has scope as having meditation as its object, the sense is that the qualified scripture is what is to be sublated.
But is it not said: "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving," and "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, as are His innate knowledge, strength, and action"?
How can the authority of those scriptural passages—such as "His desires are true, His resolves are true"—which are intent on establishing the nature of Brahman, be sublated?
We reply: by the force of the passages concerning the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.
This is what is meant:
"Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long; Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite";
it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).

Statements such as "stainless" (*nirañjana*) and so forth establish that Brahman is the eternally immutable consciousness from which all distinctions have been eliminated; other statements, however, describe it as possessing attributes (*saguṇa*). When there is a conflict between these two types of statements, by the very principle of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*), the statements concerning the absence of attributes are more authoritative because they are subsequent and do not depend on [the prior acceptance of] attributes. Thus, nothing is lost.
This is not so; for through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is the cognition of a single referent.

If it is argued that even when denoting multiple qualities, a single referent is not contradictory, then the "beloved of the gods" (the opponent) is ignorant of the nature of denotation. Single referentiality means the identity of meaning among all words. When denoting qualified objects, a difference in the meanings of the words is unavoidable due to the difference in their qualifiers. [Your position] is not established.
Consequently, there is a single referent;
that is, all words possess meaning by virtue of referring to a single object as being the opposite of its respective contrary term. Thus, there is both a single referent and non-synonymy.

Thus, the three words—*arthavattaram*, *ekārtham*, and *aparyāyam*—signify that a single entity alone possesses forms that are mutually exclusive; they are therefore more meaningful, have a single referent, and are not synonyms.

Therefore, it is stated that Brahman alone is self-luminous and devoid of all distinctions. Only when the meaning of the sentence is established in this way does its identity of purport with such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second" become evident.

Thus, according to the principle of the "cognition of all branches" (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya*), Brahman—excluded from all things of its own class and of other classes and non-dual—is understood from all causal statements. The true nature of this non-dual Brahman, which is indicated as the cause of the world, must be explained in a manner consistent with that [non-duality]. The scriptural teaching of non-duality does not tolerate even a second entity by way of attributes (*guṇataḥ*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such passages as "stainless" (*nirañjana*) and "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇaḥ*). Therefore, this defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) establishes Brahman as indeed an undivided, single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*).

But is it not the case that metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) for all words has never been observed? Even if there were metaphorical indication for all words, it would not be a fault; therefore, the Vedāntas are authoritative precisely because they establish this very collection of meanings.

In the statement "the jar exists," both existence (*astitva*) and its distinction (*tadbheda*) are being expressed. However, it is not possible for both of these two usages to have perception as their basis; for they are the results of cognitions occurring at different times, whereas perceptual cognition exists only for a single moment. Therefore, one must investigate whether it is the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) or the distinction (*bheda*) that is the object of perception.

Since the apprehension of difference necessarily depends upon the apprehension of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) and the recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it must be admitted that difference has its own nature as its object; therefore, difference is not grasped by perception. Consequently, the conventional usage of "difference" is rooted solely in error.

For those who maintain that difference is merely the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*), even the "dependence on a counter-correlative" (*pratiyogyapekṣā*) cannot be imagined; for there is no distinction between the thing's own nature and its difference, as both are equally the thing's own nature. Just as the linguistic usage of "own nature" does not depend on a counter-correlative, the linguistic usage of "difference" would likewise be independent of one. Consequently, "pot" and "different" would be synonyms, just like "hand" and "arm. Nor is difference a "property" (*dharma*).
It would have to be its very own nature (*svarūpa*).

If it were a property (*dharma*), a distinction from its own nature would necessarily have to be admitted. Otherwise, if there were a distinction, that [distinction] too would have a further distinction as its property, and that too another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

All categories of objects are seen to be permeated by existence (*sattā*) and persistence (*anubhūti*); since this [existence] is seen to persist through all things, that alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
"In all cognitions," here [the question is]: "In the case of 'the jar exists,' is there the non-existence of the cloth and so forth?

It is established, then, that by the statement "the jar exists," the cloth and other things are sublated (*bādhitatvam*). Therefore, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is the cessation of the object which results from the sublation; that exclusion proves the non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthyam*) of those things being excluded. Like a rope, the pure Being (*sanmātra*) alone persists uncontradicted. Consequently, everything other than pure Being is "non-ultimate. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Existence is the ultimate reality (paramārtha), because it persists, like the rope in the case of the rope-snake and similar illusions; whereas jars and other objects are not the ultimate reality, because they are subject to exclusion, like the snake superimposed upon its substrate, the rope.

This being so, experience (*anubhūti*) alone, as that which persists, is the "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*); it alone is existent. [Objection: But surely "pure existence" (*sanmātra*) is distinct from experience, since it is the object (*viṣaya*) of experience. [Response: Is it not like the absence of a cloth? For if one cannot state the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of a cloth except through its absence, then one must accept that the exclusion is indeed the absence itself; such is the meaning.

"Then it is established," and so forth: just as there is a sublation (*bādha*) of silver by the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" even in the absence of an explicit negation such as "it is not silver," so too there is the sublation of cloth and the like by the cognition "the jar exists" even in the absence of a negation such as "it is not cloth. Sublation is the result of sublation; that is to say, it is a negative cognition produced by non-defective causes, such as "cloth does not exist," which is established by such a cognition. The cessation of the object is the non-existence of those things (like cloth) that were cognized by the previous cognition.

Exclusion (*vyāvṹtti*): What is the nature of this exclusion when it is conceptually constructed? It persists as pure existence (*sanmātra*). However, the statement that even pure existence is sublated by the reasoning of the Mādhyamikas is untenable, because an error without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna-bhrama*) is impossible.

This being the case, "experience itself" is the reason (*hetu*). The word "itself" (*eva*) indicates the unreality of the object of experience. That very thing is existent—experience alone is the referent of the word "existent."

It is not so; for difference has already been refuted previously, both because it is not an object of perception and because it is difficult to define. For this very reason, the status of the existent as an object of experience also does not enter the path of valid means of knowledge. Therefore, the existent is indeed experience itself. And that is self-established, because it is experience. If it were established by something else, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its being "non-experience," just like a jar or other such objects.

"It is experienced. For no one experiences even that experience which has become "this is a jar" as something devoid of its own nature. Just as the contact of the sense organs such as the eye [with their objects] is the cause for the very existence of experience, experience is inferred by the mark (liṅga) of the excellence of the light of consciousness.

Knowing this, at that very moment, when the manifestation of the jar and so forth is accomplished, there subsequently arises the cognition of the object as "this. If it is argued, "In that case, since experience is non-inert (ajaḍa), it would follow that it possesses inertness (jaḍatva) just like the object," we ask: what is this so-called "non-inertness"?

First of all, there is no non-deviation from manifestation for its own existence, because that [non-deviation] is possible even in the case of pleasure and so forth. For pleasure and the like are never found not to be perceived while they exist. Therefore, cognition is not experienced by itself, because it is impossible—just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself while touching another object.

Since the property of manifestation (*prakāśa*) belonging to the object is not perceived—just like color and other qualities—and since all worldly transactions are established by the very experience admitted by both parties, it is illogical to postulate a further property called "manifestation. Therefore, experience is neither inferred nor established by another cognition; rather, experience, while establishing everything else, is itself established by its own nature. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Experience (*anubhūti*) has its own properties established independently of anything else, because it is the cause for the application of those properties to other objects through its relation with them. Whatever is the cause for the application of a certain property to another object through its relation with that object is observed to have that property in itself independently of anything else; as, for example, color and so forth in regard to visibility and the like.

For color and so forth, while producing visibility and the like in earth and other substances through their relation with them, do not depend upon a relation with color and so forth themselves for that visibility and the like in themselves. Therefore, experience, in its state of being manifest to the self, [is expressed as] "it is manifest."
And thus, in common usage, it is itself the reason.

Precisely because it is self-established (*svatasiddha*). For the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of experience, which is self-established, cannot be apprehended either by itself or by anything else.

If "experience," while existing, were to make its own non-existence known, it could not do so because of the contradiction involved in its existence; since its non-existence is impossible when it exists, how could it make its own non-existence known?
Likewise, it does not make it known even when it is non-existent; for how could experience, being itself non-existent, serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its own non-existence?

Nor can it be understood from anything else, because experience (*anubhūti*) has no other object. A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that seeks to establish its prior non-existence must do so by making "this experience" its object; however, since it is self-established (*svatassiddha*), it is incapable of being made an object in the form of "this" or "that. Therefore, its prior non-existence cannot be apprehended from anything else.

This experience, being unarisen, does not tolerate even multiplicity within itself, because of the perception of something contradictory to its pervasiveness. Indeed, that which is unarisen is never seen to be manifold. Furthermore, since difference and the like are themselves objects of experience, it is impossible for them to be attributes of experience itself, just as color and other qualities cannot belong to the nature of experience. Therefore, because experience has the very nature of experiencing, there can be no other object of experience that is an attribute of this [experience].
And because it is non-inert: since inertness is pervaded by non-selfhood, its exclusion from consciousness also excludes non-selfhood from consciousness.

Regarding the status of being an object (*gocaratva*): if it were admitted that the Self is the agent and the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), then the unavoidable consequence would follow that it shares the body's qualities of insentience, externality, and non-selfhood. It is well known among authoritative persons that the Self, as the enjoyer of the fruits of actions such as heaven resulting from those deeds, is distinct from the body—which is established as the agent and the object of the "I"-notion. Likewise, it must be understood that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is the witness (*sākṣin*), which is entirely different even from the knower who constitutes the referent of "I."

Do not speak thus; for it is observed that the palm of the hand, though manifested by the mass of the sun’s rays, acts as their manifestor. Indeed, it is commonly seen that the rays of the sun emerging through the lattice-work are made even more clearly visible by the very palm they manifest.
This is the great conclusion (*mahāsiddhānta*):

for those who maintain that reality is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣavastuvādibhiḥ*), it is impossible to say, "this is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a reality devoid of attributes"; because all means of valid knowledge have as their object reality possessed of attributes (*saviśeṣavastuviṣayatvāt*). As for the convention established within one's own circle—that [reality] is "established by one's own experience" (*svānubhavasiddha*)—that too is refuted precisely by the fact that experience, which has the self as its witness, is itself characterized by attributes; for all experiences have as their object something qualified by some particular attribute, such as, "I saw this."
Since other specific qualities of that very same entity are excluded by means of two specific qualities, a qualityless entity is never established anywhere.

What is called *nirvikalpaka* (indeterminate cognition) is the apprehension of an object devoid of any particularity (*viśeṣa*). It is not [the apprehension] of something entirely devoid of all particularities, because such a thing is never observed to be apprehended and is logically impossible.

For every cognition arises in the form "this is thus" by means of some particularity; for it is impossible to apprehend any object whatsoever without particularities such as its triangular shape, dewlap, or other configurations. Therefore, among objects of the same class, the apprehension of the first individual is called *nirvikalpaka*, while the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals is called *savikalpaka* (determinate cognition).

Since configuration (*saṃsthāna*), color, genus, and so forth are equally perceptible by the senses, and since it is impossible to cognize the possessor of configuration (*saṃsthānin*) without the configuration itself, even at the apprehension of the first individual, the object is grasped as "thus" precisely as possessing its configuration.

Therefore, in the apprehensions of the second and subsequent individuals, the fact that the cow-nature (*gotva*) and so forth are qualified by the property of persistence is always grasped—just like the configuration and the possessor of configuration—and thus these [cognitions] are exclusively determinate (*savikalpa*). Consequently, perception never has an indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*) object.

And there is exclusion [of others] because of the cognition "it is thus" as qualified by a specific configuration such as "cowness" (*gotva*). In every case where the relationship between qualifier and qualified is apprehended, their absolute difference is very clearly manifest through that very cognition.

In that regard, objects such as sticks and earrings, being established in their own distinct configurations and residing in themselves, occasionally and in certain instances exist as qualifiers of another substance. Cowness and the like, however, being themselves entities consisting of the very configuration of the substance, exist as qualifiers of that substance.
In both cases, the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is the same;
however, this is the distinction: [only] those things capable of existing separately are subject to the cognition of their difference.
But "cowness" and so forth are, by necessity, unworthy of that [status as a cause],
such as the staff and so forth.

Therefore, the claim that "there is a contradiction with reality" is stated solely on the basis of denying the very mode of cognition; for the mode of cognition is universally accepted as being precisely "this is thus. This point has been clearly established by the author of the Sūtras in the aphorism: "Because [these qualities] cannot exist in one [substratum]."
Inference, too, has only qualified objects as its domain.

Even though there may be disputes regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this very same domain belongs to all those means of valid cognition that are universally accepted; thus, the existence of an unqualified entity (*nirviśeṣavastu*) cannot be established by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.

By asserting that the very same entity is "without distinction" despite its actual specificities of intrinsic nature, he does not even realize his own contradiction in speech, like one who claims his mother is barren.

For this very reason, there is neither an infinite regress nor mutual dependence. Even though perceptual cognition exists for only a single moment, within that very moment the specific nature of the object as well as its configuration, such as "cowness" and so forth, are apprehended; since they are apprehended, nothing remains here to be grasped in a subsequent moment.

Furthermore, if the two cognitions regarding the horse and the elephant had the same object, then because the subsequent cognition would be grasping what has already been grasped (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), and because there would be no distinction [between them], it would not differ from memory.

If one were to admit a distinction for each successive cognition, then it would follow that perception itself has as its object a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭārtha*). If all cognitions had a single object, then since the entirety would be grasped by a single cognition, the consequence would follow that there would be no such things as the blind or the deaf.

It would merely be a restatement (*anuvādaka*), and the Brahmin [subject] would become an object of cognition (*prameya*). Consequently, you yourself have stated that [the subject] would suffer from such defects as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and perishability (*nāśitva*). Therefore, perception has as its object precisely that which is qualified by distinctions characterized by genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which consist in the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of things.

But surely, if difference is nothing other than genus (*jāti*) and so forth, then once that [genus] is apprehended, there should be a linguistic usage of "difference" just as there is a linguistic usage of it [the genus].

True; difference is indeed expressed through the linguistic usage of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. For cowness and the like are themselves the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from everything else; for when cowness and so forth are apprehended, there occurs the cessation of both the cognition and the linguistic usage of things belonging to the same class as those other than it. Indeed, by the very apprehension of difference, non-difference is excluded.

However, regarding the conventional usage "this is different from that," since the mention of the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is dependent upon that [correlate], it has been stated that the usage "different" occurs in dependence upon the counter-correlative.

In this regard, there is no contradiction at all among things such as jars and cloths due to differences in place and time. When the existence of something is established in a particular place and at a particular time, then, because of that contradiction, the stronger [cognition] acts as a sublater and the sublated [cognition] ceases. If, however, its non-existence is established in a different place or time—

There is no contradiction in the cognition of the non-existence of an object experienced as being connected with another place and time when it is perceived to be absent in those other place and time; so how can there be a relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva*) here? Or how can it be said that what has ceased in one place ceases in another? In the case of the rope-snake and the like, however, because the cognition of non-existence occurs precisely through its connection with that [specific] place and time, there is contradiction, sublation, and exclusion. Since "being excluded from another place and time" is not observed to be pervaded by falsity (*mithyātva*), the mere fact of being excluded is not a valid reason for unreality.

As for the argument that "Being (sat) is the ultimate reality because it persists," that is already established and thus does not require further proof; therefore, the entity is not merely Being alone.

In this context, "due to contradiction" (*virodhāt*) means: because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence, when one of the two must be sublated, that which is stronger possesses the power of sublation, while the other, being sublated, ceases to exist. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "only. "Cessation" (*nivṛtti*) refers to a specific exclusion as intended by you.
It is the cognition of negation. "Contradiction" (*virodha*) is the absence of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Non-defective causal origination is sublation; the nature of being a sublater consists in having the form of a negation while being produced by non-defective causes.
Cessation (*nivṛtti*) means non-existence in that which stands before one;
or, for that which has ceased elsewhere— namely, in a case of contradiction or sublation— it means either non-appearance or the absence of the appearance of reality.

The argument that "consciousness itself is the existent, because the difference between consciousness and the particular existent is established by perception through their relationship as object and subject, and because this is uncontradicted," is also refuted.
There would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of linguistic usage. Furthermore, one infers the teacher’s possession of knowledge and proceeds to attend upon him;
yet that [inference] would not be possible.
If it is argued that if experience were itself an object of experience, it would follow—just as it does for a jar—that it is not opposed to ignorance; [we reply:

even if it were not an object of experience, it would likewise follow—just as it does for a sky-flower—that it is not opposed to ignorance. Therefore, the claim that "if it is an object of experience, it is not experience" is laughable.

Now, if you think that since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of experience and so forth is established, there is a rule that it exists at the same time as that [experience]—have you ever seen such a thing anywhere, by virtue of which you state this rule? Alas! In that case, since the prior non-existence and so forth are established from that very perception, there can be no denial of it. Furthermore, what sane person would say that its prior non-existence exists simultaneously with it?

For this is the inherent restriction of sensory perception (*indriyajanya-pratyakṣa*): namely, that it apprehends only an object existing at the same time as itself. This is not so for all cognitions or means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since in cases such as memory, inference, verbal testimony, and the yogic perception of practitioners, we observe the apprehension of objects belonging to other times as well.

Therefore, this [objection] is also refuted: "Memory does not have an external object, because memory is observed even when the object has perished. For it is observed that [memory] makes known existence; however, the prior and subsequent existence of a jar or similar object is not perceived. And that non-perception is due to the fact that consciousness is perceived as being delimited by time.

If consciousness, which has objects such as a jar as its content, were itself perceived as unconditioned by time, then the jar and other objects that are the contents of that consciousness would also be perceived as conditioned by time [only in relation to it], and thus they would be eternal.
If consciousness were eternal and self-established, it would be perceived simply as "eternal.
But it is not so.
It is perceived.

Furthermore, there is no consciousness whatsoever that is devoid of an object, because such a thing is not apprehended. Indeed, it is precisely through its apprehension as the illumination of an object that the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatā*) of consciousness is established. For if consciousness were to lack the nature of illuminating an object, its self-luminosity could not be proven; moreover, since an experience cannot be experienced by another experience, consciousness would otherwise be a mere nothingness.

It is said: even in the absence of powerful causes such as the departure of the body—which would otherwise cause the obliteration of all mental impressions—the rule of non-recollection establishes precisely the absence of experience.
It is not only from the rule of non-recollection that the absence of experience is established.
If it is argued that, like the certainty "I knew something," there is for one who has just awakened from sleep the realization: "For all this time,
my self-experience was not merely consciousness alone."
"No; for it will be demonstrated that it [the cognition] has a basis."

If it is argued that all its modifications (*vikāra*) are unreal, do you maintain that there exists even a single modification that is ultimately real (*paramārthabhūta*), by virtue of which that qualification would be meaningful? For such a thing is not admitted.

If there were no division from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then in fact the Self would be nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*). By establishing the distinction between the visible world through uncontradicted cognition, the distinction between the modes of seeing is likewise established; it is like the distinction between the act of cutting based on the distinction between the objects to be cut.
For "presentness" is indeed eternity (*nityatva*). "Oneness" (*ekatva*) is the delimitation by the number one.

Even if these [qualities] consist in the absence of insentience (*jaḍatva*) and so forth, there remains the unavoidable fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) because of those very qualities which are attributes of consciousness (*caitanya*). However, in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), if one does not admit an attribute—whether of the nature of an absence or a positive entity—that consists in being the opposite of insentience and so forth as distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then nothing at all would be stated by the negation of those [attributes].
But has it not been said that consciousness itself [is that opposite]?
For instance—someone has spoken something that is true regarding a certain matter; yet, "that was poorly expressed.
With respect to what has arisen, that [speech], being related to it as a form of establishment (*siddhi*), is itself accumulated (*saṃcita*); how indeed could it [then] become its own nature?
You yourself have established that luminosity belongs to this specific attribute of the agent of the transitive verb "to experience," just as [luminosity] belongs to its object.
Even agency is difficult to establish.
Furthermore, recognition in the form "I saw [it]" would not be possible. The occurrence of recognition is impossible;
for what was experienced by one cannot be apprehended by another. Moreover, the conclusion that "the mere experience itself is the ultimate reality" is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
They have been refuted.
Furthermore:

If the referent of "I" were not the Self, then subjectivity would not belong to the Self; for it is by means of the cognition of "I" that the subjective referent is distinguished from the objective referent. (1)

That whose existence, cognition, and so forth, depend upon its own relation [to a subject], cannot even be established as cognition when separated from that relation. (5) Just as cutting and the like are not established in the absence of both the cutter and the object to be cut, it is certain that the "I-sense" is indeed the cognizing inner self. (6)

"The knower [is not slain]—by what could he be slain? and "He indeed knows"—so says the Śruti. And the Smṛti says: "Him who knows this, they call the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). (7) Beginning with the Sūtra "The Self [is eternal], because of the Śruti," the author of the Sūtras will also state:
"[The Self] is a knower for that very reason. Therefore, it is established that the Self is not mere consciousness (jñaptimātra). (8)
The statement that "the knower established by the thought 'I know' is the referent of the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmad-artha*)" is contradictory in meaning, like saying "my mother is barren.

Furthermore, this knower who is the referent of "I" does not have its manifestation dependent on another, because it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*). Indeed, self-luminosity consists in having consciousness as one's essential nature (*caitanya-svabhāvatā*). Whatever has manifestation as its essential nature does not depend on anything else for its manifestation, just like a lamp.

This is what is meant: just as a single substance of light exists in the form of both radiance (*prabhā*) and that which possesses radiance (*prabhāvaddravya*), even though radiance is a quality (*guṇa*) belonging to the substance that possesses it, it is nevertheless the substance of light itself and not a quality like whiteness and so forth. This is because it exists elsewhere than its own substratum, because it possesses color (*rūpavat*), and because it differs from qualities such as whiteness. Furthermore, because it possesses luminosity (*prakāśavattva*), it is indeed a substance of light and not a separate entity. And its possession of luminosity consists in its capacity to illuminate both its own nature and other things.

The conventional designation of this [light] as a quality, however, is based on its being eternally dependent upon that [substance], being subordinate to it, and having it as its substrate. Nor can it be said that the light consists merely of the disintegrated parts of the substrate circulating outward; for if that were so, it would follow that gems, sun-crystals, and the like would perish [as their substrates would be consumed].

Furthermore, there could never be a cognition of a whole (*avayavin*) even in the case of a lamp. For it cannot be said that lamps—whose parts are by nature disintegrating—necessarily arise as a mass measuring only four finger-breadths, ascend upwards, and subsequently disperse simultaneously in all directions—sideways, upwards, and downwards—in a uniform manner. Thus, a lamp arises and perishes at every moment due to the successive occurrence of its full set of causes;
therefore, [the lamp] is with radiance (*saprabhāka*).

It is understood from its destruction as well. The greater intensity of illumination and the greater intensity of heat in the vicinity of light’s own substratum are established by perception, just like the heat of fire and other such things. Thus, the self is of the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), having consciousness as its quality (*caitanyaguṇaka*).
"For this person— the self of consciousness— is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower,
and the doer"; "O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the Knower?"
"This person indeed knows:
'The seer sees neither death nor disease, nor even suffering; not remembering this body, he does not see rebirth.'"

"He is the Supreme Person. "In this very same way, these sixteen parts of the observer here go toward the Person and, having reached the Person, they vanish. "Now, different from this self consisting of mind is another inner self consisting of consciousness."
And so forth. Furthermore, he will state:
"The knower [is established] for this very reason.
Therefore, this self is self-luminous and is indeed a knower, not mere luminosity.
Because it is luminous by its very nature, consciousness (saṃvit) would be the illumination of only some [object], like the light of a lamp or similar things.

Therefore, consciousness cannot be the Self. For those who know the meaning of words, in both common usage and the Veda, terms such as "consciousness," "experience," and "knowledge" are "relational" terms; indeed, they do not recognize a verb like "to know" (jānāti) as being intransitive or devoid of an agent.
The application has already been observed.

The state of having an existence whose manifestation is non-deviant (*avyabhicaritaprakāśasattākatva*) is also refuted because it is inconsistent in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and the like. If it should be argued: "Pleasure and the like, though their manifestation is non-deviant, are 'non-self' (*anātman*) because they manifest to another, and thus are insentient (*jaḍa*) like a jar or similar objects"—then [we reply]: Does consciousness (*jñāna*) manifest to itself? For even that manifests only to another, namely the knower who is the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), as in "I am happy" and likewise "I know. Therefore, [the definition of self] as "manifesting to oneself"— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical flow of the argument up to this point.)
The quality of "non-inertness" is unestablished in the case of form (rūpa) with respect to consciousness;
therefore, that which is established for its own self solely by its own existence and is non-inert is the "I-sense" (ahamartha) alone, which is the Self.
It is manifest to its own substrate-consciousness and unmanifest to others; therefore, the self is not mere consciousness, but rather the object of "I," which is the knower itself.

Just as there is the cognition "Devadatta is without a staff" even when only the staff is present, how could it be asserted that [the self] has as its object only the experienced particularity which serves as its qualification?

Therefore, the state of being a knower is of the nature of modification, insentient, and situated within the knot of the ego (ahaṅkāra), which is a transformation of the unmanifest (avyakta) that serves as the locus for insentient changes; thus, the state of being a knower does not belong to the Self (ātman), but rather to the ego in its form as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). For agency and the like are attributes of the object of perception, just like color and other qualities. If agency and being the object of the notion of "I" were admitted to belong to the Self, it would follow—just as in the case of the body—that the Self would be non-self, external, and insentient.

Just as [the Self] is distinguished from inwardness and so forth, so too the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is distinguished from that [Self] by those very same reasons, precisely because it is a substance.

Therefore, due to this contradiction alone, the ego-sense cannot possess the status of a knower, just like the status of being an object of vision (*dṛśitva*). Just as the status of being an object of vision is not admitted for the ego-sense—which is its own object—likewise the status of being a knower must also not be admitted for it.
It has been stated that for this very one whose nature is knowledge, the status of being the locus of knowledge is not contradictory, just as gems and the like are the loci of their own radiance.

If it is argued that the manifestation of egoism— which is by nature insentient— is possible through the proximity of consciousness and the reflection of its shadow upon it, then what is this "falling of the shadow of consciousness"?
Is it that consciousness (saṃvit) undergoes the reflection of the ego (ahaṅkāra), or that the ego undergoes the reflection of consciousness?

It cannot be the former, because consciousness is not admitted to possess the status of a knower (jñātṛtva). Nor can it be the latter, because, as stated previously, it is impossible for that insentient (jaḍa) entity to be a knower, and because both are invisible (acākṣuṣa); for the reflection of invisible things is never observed.

"This is not [the case] in consciousness (*saṃvit*). Because knowership (*jñātṛtva*) is not admitted [in consciousness] from the standpoint of reality (*vastutaḥ*), there is no knowership in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) through contact with it, nor is there the perception thereof.
