Thus, O Maitreya, this great word *Bhagavān* [is used]."

"This word [Vāsudeva] does not apply to anyone other than Vāsudeva, who has become the Supreme Brahman; for this term is endowed with the technical definition used to denote the object of worship there, and it is not applied elsewhere even figuratively. "O King, that Great Form of Hari, which is different from the universal form (Viśvarūpa), is that wherein all these powers are established."
O Lord of Men, He who is the embodiment of all powers performs,
by His own sport, the various activities designated as those of gods, animals, and humans.
"For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the Immeasurable One is not born of karma; it is all-pervading and unimpeded in nature.
"In this manner, the entire [universe] is eternal, pervasive, and undecaying."

"The supreme state called Viṣṇu is devoid of all that is to be abandoned. [This is] the word *mahat*; it is so because it contains a great meaning (*mahārtha*). "The expression of the parts of the object to be honored" means the expression of the constituent meanings of those things worthy of worship. "Technical convention" (*paribhāṣā*) means conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). "In other cases, by way of metaphorical application" (*upacārataḥ*): where knowledge and the rest are unrestrained, that alone is the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). Since usage is possible even through a connection with a mere fraction of the qualities, the function in other cases is metaphorical. For when a usage is established otherwise, it is not proper to postulate a primary power (*śakti*). By the phrase "the dissimilarity of the universal form," the difference in configuration (*saṃniveśa*) is stated.

"Great" means immeasurable. "By His own sport" (svalīlayā): since sport is the purpose, the intention for that [sport] is the cause; the meaning is that it is not by means of karma. "For the benefit of others," not for the sake of enjoying the fruits of His own karma. "Conforming to the incarnations. "Unimpeded in nature" means free from obstructions caused by place, time, or substance. "The Supreme among the supreme, the Highest Self, established in the Self; devoid of specific designations such as form, color, and so forth."
That which is devoid of diminution, destruction, transformation, increase,
and birth can be described as simply "existing always."
Since he indeed dwells everywhere and in everything,
for that reason he is recited by the wise as Vāsudeva.
That Brahman is supreme, eternal, unborn, imperishable, and immutable;
it is always of a single nature and stainless because of the absence of anything to be discarded.

"That very [reality] is indeed all this," consisting of the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest; likewise, it exists in the form of the Puruṣa and in the form of Time. "I have thus explained Prakṛti, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest."
And both of these, including the Puruṣa, dissolve into the Supreme Self.
"The Supreme Self, the support of all, the Supreme Lord, is celebrated in the Vedas and the Vedāntas by the name Viṣṇu.
That Brahman has two forms, indeed both the manifest and the unmanifest; these are the natures of the perishable and the imperishable, abiding within all beings."
That syllable is the supreme Brahman; this entire world is that syllable.
Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so too does it pervade all.
"The power of the Supreme Brahman is this entire universe. "The power of Viṣṇu is declared to be supreme; likewise, that called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the inferior [power];
and another, known as ignorance (avidyā) and action (karman), is held to be the third power."
Just as that all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), O King, when enveloped [by ignorance],
undergoes all the incessant torments of saṃsāra.
"Just as the wind, clinging to the water, sustains hundreds of droplets,
so too is that power of Viṣṇu, whose self consists of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa. Therefore, O best of sages, this entire world is imperishable and eternal.

By such passages as, "possessing the conceptualizations of manifestation and disappearance, birth and destruction," [the text] establishes that the Supreme Brahman is by its very nature free from even a trace of all defects, consists of all auspicious qualities, and has as its divine play (līlā) the creation, maintenance, dissolution, internal entry, and governance of the universe. Furthermore, it teaches that the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient entities, existing in all their various states, is the body of the Supreme Brahman—which is itself the ultimate reality—using terms such as "body" (śarīra), "form" (rūpa), "limb" (tanu), "part" (aṃśa), "power" (śakti), and "manifestation" (vibhūti), as well as through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with those respective terms.

Having stated that the conscious reality, which is the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of that [Brahman], exists both in its own essential nature and in the form of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) through its association with the non-conscious, it is established that in the state of being the knower of the field, there is a lack of awareness of its own innate nature as knowledge due to being enveloped by ignorance in the form of karma consisting of merit and demerit, while there is an awareness [of itself] in the form of objects of the non-conscious nature. Thus, it is understood that the Supreme Brahman is "with attributes" (*saviśeṣa*), and that the world, which is its manifestation, is also ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

It is said that [reality], characterized solely by the existence of consciousness and self-cognizable, is not within the range of the mind of one engaged in yoga; by this, there is no denial of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
If it is asked, "How is this understood?"—

Regarding the second [aspect], known as *karman* (action): for one devoid of *vidyā* (knowledge), who is separated from the insentient (*acid*), whose form is solely consciousness (*jñānaikākāra*), and who is the immaterial (*amūrta*) portion designated as *ujjūrti*; since this is the object of meditation for perfected yogins, it serves as a non-support for the mind of one engaged in yoga (*yogayuṅmanas*). Furthermore, because it lacks inherent purity (*svataśśuddhi*), its status as a "pure substratum" (*śubhāśrayatva*) is denied. This [aspect] consists of the supreme power (*paraśakti*) in its immaterial form, and the subordinate power (*aparaśakti*) in its material form known as the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). And there is the ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of action (*karma*) called the third power (*tṛtīyaśakti*), which is the cause for the Self—which is of the nature of the supreme power—to assume the state of being the knower of the field (*kṣetrajñatā*).

This is said to be the "auspicious substratum" (*śubhāśraya*), which is the basis for these three powers; it is the unique form of the Lord (*bhagavat*)—established in the Vedānta as "having the color of the sun" (*ādityavarṇam*) and so forth—which is called the "embodied nature" (*mūrtasvarūpa*). In this context, it is described as "completely pure. For it is said:
"O King, because that [form] cannot be conceived by one engaged in yoga;
it is the second [aspect], the supreme state of the one named Viṣṇu, which is to be meditated upon by the yogi."
And all these powers, O King, are established in Him.
And it also says: "That other great form of Hari is different from that universal form."

"From Brahma down to a blade of grass, all living beings situated within the world are subject to the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) produced by their own karma. Therefore, they are of no benefit to those who meditate;
for they are all enveloped in ignorance and remain within the sphere of worldly existence."
Furthermore, those whose awakening arises subsequently are of no benefit regarding meditative absorption (dhyāna),
because even their awakening is not innate, since it too must come from another source.

Therefore, by such statements as "that stainless Brahman is, by its very nature, endowed with consciousness," it is declared that the unique essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu alone is the auspicious refuge (*śubhāśraya*). Consequently, no denial of difference (*bhedāpalāpa*) is perceived here.

If it is argued that because the world and Brahman are perceived as identical through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and since it has been stated that the appearance of objects in Brahman—which is by nature pure consciousness—is an illusion (*bhrānti*), it follows that the entire aggregate of objects must be false; this is incorrect. For in this scripture, the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu is established as being free from even a trace of defects such as ignorance, as consisting of all auspicious qualities, and as possessing great majesty (*mahāvibhūti*); therefore, the possibility of His perceiving anything through delusion is impossible.

Furthermore, the demonstration of identity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is both incapable of being sublated and non-contradictory, as will be demonstrated immediately hereafter. Therefore, this verse also does not contradict the true nature of the object. For instance, when it has been concluded that "Brahman is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world"—based on the passage: "That from which indeed these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at death; desire to know That; That is Brahman"—one should then "strengthen the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
"The Veda is afraid of one who has little learning [thinking], 'This man will deceive me,'" according to the scripture;

thus it is understood that the meaning [of the Veda] must be supplemented by the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. "Supplementation" (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) means the clarification of the meaning of the Vedic sentences as they have been understood by oneself, through the words of those who have mastered all the Vedas and their meanings, or who have directly realized the true essence of the Vedas through the power of their own yoga. Since the meaning of a sentence understood from an entire recensional branch (*śākhā*) is difficult to grasp due to hearing only a small portion of it, and since certainty regarding it is impossible without such supplementation, supplementation must indeed be performed.

Thereupon Maitreya—who had been granted the knowledge of the supreme reality of the Divine by virtue of the boon bestowed upon him by Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha, and who, having understood the meaning of the Vedas from the Blessed Parāśara, desired to know more—questioned him:
"O Knower of Dharma, O Illustrious One! I wish to hear from you how this world came into being and how it will come to be again."
"O Brahman! That by which this world exists, from which this world of moving and non-moving beings arises,
wherein it was dissolved, how it was so, and where it will go to dissolution"—
and so forth.

Thus [is derived] the suffix *mayaṭ*. And the entire world, by virtue of being His body, is indeed full of Him (*tatpracura*). Therefore, the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the response "the world is He" with the question "consisting of what? is determined to be based on the relationship of body and self between the world and Brahman.

Otherwise, if a scripture intended solely to propound a featureless reality were accepted, all these questions and answers would not be consistent; indeed, the entire scripture, which consists of their exposition, would not be coherent. For if that were the case, there would be only a single answer—namely, "nothing but featureless consciousness"—to a single question such as, "What is the substratum of the delusion of phenomenal diversity?"

Having first prostrated with this verse, he likewise pays homage to that very Hiraṇyagarbha, who exists in the form of the triad of deities—Śiva being one of his own incarnations—as well as in the collective and individual forms of Kāla (Time) and Kṣetrajña (the Knower of the Field). Among these, the verse beginning with "jñānasvarūpam" declares the essential nature of the Supreme Self existing as the individual Kṣetrajña; therefore, there is no perception of a featureless reality here.

The objection is as follows: Since effects such as origination are observed in those things that are endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, and are subject to the influence of complete karma, how can the status of being the creator of creation and so forth be accepted for one who is devoid of the qualities of *sattva* and so forth, who is perfect, who is not subject to karma, and who is unfit for connection with karma? The resolution is this: For Brahman, whose nature is exactly as described and who is entirely dissimilar to all perceived things, the possession of all powers is not contradictory—just as fire and other elements, which are dissimilar to water and the like, possess powers such as heat.

Furthermore, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of such words as "O Lord of the world" (*jagataḥ pate*), which would contradict the context of the praise of the Blessed One, Mahāvarāha.

Regarding Him who lifted up the earth through His divine play, [the Lord] says, "That which is seen here," meaning: since the entire world is pervaded by You—who are the Self of knowledge—as Your very self, therefore the world is Your form; yet those devoid of yoga, the means for experiencing that identity with You, perceive it through erroneous cognition, thinking, "This is merely the form of gods, humans, and so forth."

"Not only is the view that the world—which consists of gods, humans, and so forth—is in reality identical with you a delusion; even the perception that the selves, whose nature is consciousness, take on the forms of objects such as gods and humans is a delusion. Thus he says: "The entire [universe] has the nature of consciousness."

"Furthermore, those who are wise—those who know the Self whose nature is knowledge, whose minds are purified by being fit for the yoga that is the means for experiencing that everything has the Blessed Lord as its essence, and who perceive this entire world and even Your own body as having the form of a specific body resulting from the transformation of *prakṛti* (primordial matter) consisting of gods, humans, and so forth, yet as being the Self whose nature is knowledge distinct from the body"—this is what is meant by the words "But those who know through wisdom. Otherwise, there would be redundancy of verses, figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*) of words, contradiction of meaning, contradiction of context, and contradiction of the purport of the scripture.

In this context, the word *para* (other) denotes a self distinct from oneself, while the word *anya* (different) serves to negate having a different form, since that [self] also possesses only the single form of cognition (*jñāna*). What is meant is this: if there were some self distinct from me whose form were other than the form of the cognition that constitutes my own form, then it would be possible to designate, "I am of such a form, and this one is of a different form. But this is not the case; for all [selves] are identical precisely because they possess only the single form of cognition.

In the phrase "by the distinction of the holes of the flute" (*veṇurandhravibhedena*), it is also taught that the difference in form among the selves (*ātman*) is not caused by their essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather by their entry into the physical bodies (*piṇḍa*) of gods and so forth; it does not imply the identity of the selves. Furthermore, in the illustration, the various portions of air residing in the multiple holes do not possess identity of essence, but only similarity of form. For those [portions of air], which are of a single form as air, the distinction of names such as *ṣaḍja* and so on is indeed caused by their emergence through different holes. In the same way, there is a distinction of names for the selves, such as "god" and so forth.

Just as even fiery objects, which consist of portions of non-earthly substances, possess unity only in terms of their respective substantiality and not in terms of identity of essence; likewise, a difference in essential nature among the aerial portions is unavoidable.

Concluding with the word "ākāraḥ" (form), he says, "Abandon the delusion of difference among the selves caused by the distinction of forms such as gods and others. Otherwise, the designation of difference in the form of "I am you; all this is the nature of the Self"—which teaches that the Self's true nature is distinct from the body—would not be possible. Furthermore, because the words "I," "you," and so forth stand in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "all this is the nature of the Self" as its implied referent (*upalakṣya*), their status as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) is also inconsistent.
He states that "he too acted according to the instruction," concluding with: "He abandoned [the sense of] difference, possessing the vision of ultimate reality."

Regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*): "identity of essential nature" (*ātmasvarūpaikya*) has been refuted according to the method stated above. Furthermore, identity of essential nature between the individual soul and the Supreme is as impossible as it is between the body and the self. Thus says the Śruti:
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating."
"Drinking the *ṛta* in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest upper realm,
those who know Brahman call them shadow and light— those who maintain the five fires and those who have thrice performed the *Nāciketa* sacrifice.
"He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all."
And so forth. In this scripture as well:

"O Sage, He has transcended the creation of all beings, their transformations, and the defects such as the *guṇas*; having transcended all veils, He is the Self of all, who dwells within the interior of the universe. "He consists of all auspicious qualities."
"He is the highest of the high, in whom no afflictions or the like exist, the Lord of the high and the low. "Ignorance (avidyā), known as karma, is held to be another, a third power;
by which [power], O King, the all-pervading power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is enveloped"—because of such declarations of difference.
"For both [schools] indeed study this [text] with a distinction:
'And because of the designation of difference, [the Self] is other,' and 'But it is superior because of the mention of difference.'"
And in such sūtras as these:
"He who, dwelling in the self, is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within";
and "Embraced by the conscious self (prājña-ātman)."
By such passages as "mounted by the intelligent Self" (*prājñenātmanānvārūḍhaḥ*), the essential nature of both is determined through their mutual opposition.

Nor is the identity of the liberated one who possesses knowledge with the Supreme possible through the performance of spiritual means; for that which is capable of being the locus of ignorance cannot possibly be unfit for it [to cease]. As it has been said:

The scriptural passages (*viṣayavākya*) for the two sūtras beginning with "ubhaye'pi" are "ya ātmani... and so forth. The scriptural passage for "adhikaṃ tu... is "prājñena... and so forth. Regarding the term "nirṇayāt": the meaning is that the determination of this matter is made by these scriptural citations within the sūtras.
"The union of the supreme self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality;
for this [union] is false, since one substance does not become the nature of another substance."
Thus [it is said].
"Because there is a mark [indicative] of equality in respect of mere enjoyment," and "Because of the designation of being approached by the released.
The commentary also says:
"Except for the activities of the world, he is equal to the light.
And the author of the Dramiḍa-bhāṣya states:
"Through union with the deity, even though bodiless, there shall be the accomplishment of all purposes, just as for the deity."
Thus he says; and the Śruti texts also state:
"Those who depart from here having discovered the Self here, and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds."
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme";

"He, together with the all-knowing Brahman, attains all desires"; "Having reached this Self consisting of bliss, moving through these worlds, eating what he desires, and assuming forms at will, he moves about there."

"He is indeed the essence (rasa). For having obtained that very essence, he becomes blissful. "Just as rivers flowing along reach the ocean and disappear, casting off name and form, so the knower, freed from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high.
"Then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, stainless, attains supreme equality," and so forth.
In the passage, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," it is likewise stated:
"Freed from name and form, he attains the divine Person, higher than the high."

Because of the identity of meaning in such passages as "The stainless one attains supreme equality" and "Having reached the highest light, he manifests in his own true form," it is stated that for one who is liberated from natural name and form and whose distinctions caused by them have been eliminated, there is a state of being a mode (*prakāratā*) of Brahman due to having knowledge as its sole form. And when there is identity of mode, the usage of the term "thatness" (*tattva*) is indeed primary, just as in the expression, "This is that cow. This is also the case here.
"O twice-born one, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has knowledge as its instrument;
having accomplished the task of liberation, it should indeed cease once it has fulfilled its purpose.

Since this statement declares the cessation of the instrument—which consists of meditation on the Supreme Brahman—upon the attainment of its own nature, wherein all residual mental impressions have been utterly destroyed through the fulfillment of its purpose, it follows that [meditation] must be practiced until such perfection is achieved. Thus it is said.
"Having attained the state of being that [very essence], he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
and any difference of his would be caused by ignorance."

Thus he describes the nature of the liberated one. "Tadbhāvaḥ" means the state of Brahman—its own nature (svabhāva). It is not identity of essence (*svarūpa-ekya*), because that would contradict the second occurrence of the word *bhāva* in the phrase "having attained the state of being that state" (*tadbhāvabhāvam āpannaḥ*), and it would also contradict the meaning previously stated. "The state of Brahman" is the condition in which all mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) have been entirely destroyed; "attaining that" is the attainment of that state. At that time, "he becomes non-different from the Supreme Self"—that is, he becomes free from duality.
When he has thus attained this state...

Because it possesses the single form of knowledge (*jñāna*), this [individual soul] is of one nature with the Supreme Self; its differentiation into the forms of gods and so forth is merely from that [Supreme Self]. This [differentiation] is rooted in action (*karman*) which is itself rooted in ignorance (*ajñāna*), and is not produced by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). However, when that action—which constitutes the root—has been destroyed through meditation on the Supreme Brahman, that differentiation into gods and so forth ceases due to the absence of its cause, and thus the soul becomes non-differentiated (*abhedin*).
As it has been said:
"But the distinction of having a single nature arises from external action and mental fluctuations;
when the distinctions such as 'god' and so forth are destroyed, that [nature] exists indeed without obstruction.
He explains this very point:
"When the knowledge that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction,
who will create the non-existent distinction between the Self and Brahman?
As it has been said:
Thus: "Vibheda" means manifold differentiation—consisting of gods, animals, humans, and immobile beings. Śaunaka also says:
"This fourfold differentiation is based upon false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*).

When ignorance, known as karma—which is the cause of the manifold differentiations such as the forms of gods and so forth within the Self whose nature is knowledge—is utterly destroyed through meditation on the Supreme Brahman, then, due to the absence of a cause, [the Self] becomes non-distinct from the Supreme Brahman.
The meaning is: "Who will create the distinction of forms such as gods and so forth? For it has been stated in this very context: "Ignorance is known by another name as karma."
"There is nothing that could exist without it. This is a summary of the Lord's manifestations (vibhūti), and it must be accepted as such.
Therefore, this is said:
Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), there are seven types of logical impossibilities:
"If ignorance, which is of the nature of non-knowledge and illusory in essence, were to conceal the Supreme Brahman which is of the nature of knowledge, who would be capable of removing it?"
If it is argued that knowledge is Brahman, then since knowledge is the remover of ignorance,
it too must be a remover [of itself], because like Brahman, it is self-luminous.
If there were a cognition that "Brahman is knowledge," then Brahman would be an object of knowledge;
by your own statement, it would follow that Brahman lacks the nature of self-experience.

If it is argued that the cognition "Brahman has the nature of knowledge" is the sublater of that ignorance, and not the knowledge that constitutes its very nature, we say no; for since both are equally the manifestation of the nature of Brahman, there is no basis for discerning a distinction such that one is opposed to ignorance while the other is not.

This is what is meant: by the cognition "Brahman is of the nature of knowledge," that intrinsic nature of Brahman which is apprehended is itself manifested by virtue of Brahman’s self-luminosity; thus, there is no distinction between the essential nature [of Brahman] and the cognition having that as its object, insofar as both are opposed to ignorance.

If it is argued that the ignorance regarding the nature of Brahman is simply its state of having a second (*sadvitīyatva*), which is removed by the knowledge of falsity (*mithyātva-jñāna*), while its true nature (*svarūpa*) is established by one's own experience— this is not so. For while it may be true that Brahman’s non-duality (*advitīyatva*) as its nature is established by self-experience, that [state of] having a second, which is opposed to it,
must belong to something distinct from it.
There would be neither ignorance regarding form (*rūpa*) nor its sublation.

If it is argued that non-duality (*advitīyatva*) is an attribute (*dharma*), we say no; for you yourself have established that Brahman, whose nature is pure experience (*anubhava-svarūpa*), is devoid of any attribute that is an object of experience (*anubhāvya-dharma*). Therefore, because it is contradictory for Brahman, whose nature is knowledge (*jñāna-svarūpa*), to be the locus of ignorance, it cannot be its substratum.
[Objection: It is not ultimately real (*paramārtha*), because it is not admitted [as such].
Nor is it unreal (*aparamārtha*); for if that were the case, it would have to exist either as the seer (*draṣṭṛ*), or as the seen (*dṛśya*), or as the act of seeing (*dṛśi*).

Or it must be accepted as [the locus of] error; yet it cannot be the act of seeing (*dṛśi*), because no difference in the nature of the act of seeing is admitted, and because, if it were the direct seeing itself, it would follow that the Madhyamaka position is correct, which is not admitted as being non-ultimate. However, if it is the seeing delimited by the seer and the seen—which serve as the substratum for the illusion—then, since these are conceptual constructs, there would be an infinite regress due to the requirement of further underlying defects.
Now, if it is argued that experience (*anubhūti*) itself—which is ultimately real and of the nature of Brahman—is the defect, [we reply:

if Brahman itself were the defect, then that would be the very root of the perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); what, then, is the use of postulating another ignorance (*avidyā*) equal to the phenomenal world? Furthermore, if Brahman were the defect, because of its eternity, there would be no liberation. Therefore, as long as a real defect distinct from Brahman is not admitted, error cannot be established.
And what is intended by "indefinability"?
If it means "being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent," then such an entity would simply be indefinable due to its lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And every cognition—by which it is meant that the entire range of entities is established by means of cognition—is of the nature of both existence and non-existence. If it were admitted that the object of a cognition characterized by the forms of both existence and non-existence is something distinct from both existence and non-existence, then everything would become the object of every cognition.
Furthermore, it is understood through the force of reasoning that since an object is false, its material cause must necessarily be false as well.
If it exists, then due to that very contradiction, the experience of the absence of knowledge is impossible;
if it does not exist, then the experience of the absence of knowledge— which necessarily depends upon the cognition of the locus and the counter-positive— is all the more impossible.
This is possible.

This same inconsistency applies equally if ignorance is considered inferable or if it is the object of the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*abhāva*). However, since there is no contradiction even when the knowledge of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) exists if this ignorance is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), one must accept that this experience has positive ignorance as its very object.

But surely, even though this ignorance is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), it becomes an object of the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) only as distinguished from its specific objects. Since the establishment of such an object depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how indeed can ignorance—which is distinguished from the "I-sense" (*asmadartha*)—be made an object by the witnessing consciousness?

This is not a fault; for the entire range of objects, whether known or unknown, is the object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*). Among these, that which is insentient is established as "known" only through the mediation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, for the non-insentient inner reality (*pratyagvastu*), which is self-established, there is no dependence on the mediation of a means of valid cognition. Therefore, it is logical that the manifestation of ignorance occurs at all times through perception (*pratyakṣa*) reinforced by reasoning, as the "excluder" (*vyāvartaka*) of that [ignorance].
Ignorance is perceived as having a positive (bhāva) nature.

If it is argued: "Darkness is either merely the absence of light or merely the absence of the perception of form; it is not a distinct substance. Therefore, how can it be put forward as an illustrative example for proving that ignorance is a positive entity (bhāvarūpa)?"—it is replied:
Because it is perceived as possessing color and because it is experienced through states such as density and rarity, it is faultless to conclude that darkness is indeed a distinct substance.
If it has not been apprehended, how could ignorance—which is devoid of knowledge regarding its own substrate and object—be experienced?

Now, if you argue that the manifestation of a clear nature is opposed to ignorance, whereas an unclear nature is what is actually perceived, and thus there is no contradiction in experiencing ignorance even when there is knowledge of the substrate and the object—well then, the prior absence (prāgabhāva) of knowledge would also have a clear nature as its object. There is no difference [between the two cases] except for your personal bias.

However, the knowledge of its locus (*āśraya*) and its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) does indeed involve dependence. To explain: "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is either the absence of knowledge, something other than it, or its opposite. In all three cases, a dependence upon the knowledge of its own nature must necessarily be admitted. Although there is no requirement for light (*prakāśa*) in the apprehension of the essential nature of darkness (*tamas*), nevertheless, in the apprehension of it in the form of "that which is opposed to light," there is certainly a requirement for the apprehension of light. At times it is established in its own nature, but [it is always established] precisely as "ignorance."
If that were the case, your preferred "ignorance" would not be so; for, like the absence of knowledge,
its dependence on that [knowledge] is the same.
If it is argued that [the self] experiences ignorance, whose nature is concealed even though its own nature is self-evident,
then what is this "concealed nature"?
If it is said to be "a non-manifested nature," then...
How can that whose very nature is self-experience have an unmanifested nature?

If it is argued that even for that which has self-experience as its nature, an unmanifested nature may be established by means of something else, then in that case—since light itself is the nature [of consciousness] due to the non-acceptance of a property called "illumination"—there would simply be the destruction of its own nature by something else; this has already been stated previously.
Furthermore: Is the experience of ignorance by Brahman "self-evident" (*svataḥ*) or from another source?

If it were self-evident, then because the experience of ignorance would be inherent to its own nature, there would be no liberation; for Brahman, whose very nature is consciousness, would have the experience of ignorance as its essential form, and thus—just as the experience of silver is removed even by the subverting cognition of false silver—the nature of Brahman, which consists in the experience of ignorance, would be removed by the sublating cognition.
If, on the other hand, it were from another source, what is that "other"?
If it is argued that [ignorance exists] subsequent to ignorance, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that ignorance itself becomes an object of experience only by setting aside Brahman, then in that case, this ignorance would set aside Brahman by its very existence, like a piece of glass or the like; consequently, ignorance could not be sublated by knowledge.

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "This ignorance, being itself beginningless, simultaneously effects its own status as the witness of Brahman and the concealment of Brahman's true nature; therefore, defects such as infinite regress do not apply.
This is not so; for it is impossible to establish the status of Brahman—which is by nature self-evident—as a witness without first concealing its own nature.
If it is argued that [Brahman's nature] is concealed by some other cause, [we reply:]...
In that case, its beginninglessness is discarded, and the previously mentioned infinite regress (anavasthā) follows. Furthermore,
if the status of being a witness were attributed to Brahman only when its own nature is not obscured, then Brahman’s exclusive devotion to its own self-experience would be impossible.

In a reality that is partless, devoid of distinctions, and pure luminosity, concealment and manifestation cannot coexist simultaneously, as it is impossible for two forms to exist therein. Now, if it is argued that Brahman— which is of the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss— has its nature obscured by ignorance and thus appears as if indistinct,
then what could the nature of "distinctness" or "indistinctness" possibly be for that which is pure luminosity?

This is what is meant: that which possesses parts (*sāṃśa*) and specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*), being an object of illumination, has a complete manifestation (*sakalāvabhāsa*), which is a clear manifestation (*viśadāvabhāsa*). A manifestation devoid of some specific qualities, however, is an unclear manifestation (*aviśadāvabhāsa*). In that regard, concerning the aspect (*ākāra*) that is not apprehended, because there is simply an absence of illumination in that part, no lack of clarity in the illumination exists; and as for the part that is apprehended, the illumination regarding that object is indeed clear.

Therefore, lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*) is impossible in every case regarding the aspect of manifestation. Even with respect to an object, when its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is being cognized, "lack of clarity" consists solely in the non-cognition of certain specific attributes (*viśeṣa*) inherent therein. Consequently, in the case of Brahman—which is not an [empirical] object, is devoid of specific attributes, and is pure manifestation—when its essential nature is manifesting, that which is called "lack of clarity," consisting in the non-apprehension of certain inherent specific attributes, cannot possibly be an effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Furthermore, when there is cessation, one must discern what the nature of the object is:
if you say it is its "distinct nature," does that distinct nature exist prior [to the cessation], or not?
If it exists, then the lack of clarity which is the effect of ignorance and its cessation would not occur!
If it does not exist, then liberation, being an effect, would be non-eternal!
As for what was stated—that even by means of inference, ignorance in the form of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) is established—[that is refuted].
That is incorrect; because inference is impossible.
But was it not stated that there is an inference?

It is true that you have spoken, but what you have said is poorly stated; for even in the case of ignorance, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory because it establishes another form of ignorance that is not intended. In that regard, if another ignorance is not established, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*). If it is established, however, that ignorance precludes the very nature of being a witness to ignorance.
Consequently, the postulation of ignorance would be fruitless.

Even for the sense organs, their status is solely that of being causes for the arising of cognition, not that of being illuminators. As for the light of a lamp, however, its role is merely to be an auxiliary factor for the visual sense organ as it produces cognition, by means of dispelling the obstructing darkness. It is with reference to the lamp’s status as a cause that assists the visual sense organ while it is engaged in producing cognition that the conventional usage of "illuminator" (*prakāśaka*) is applied to the lamp. Furthermore, the applications of the term "illumination" (*prakāśa*)— [The text ends here.]

6. Brahman: Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not that which is removable by knowledge (*jñāna*); because it is not an object of knowledge (*jñāna*). Whatever ignorance is removable by knowledge is an object of knowledge, such as a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. 7. The valid cognition under dispute does not have for its antecedent an ignorance distinct from its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); because it is a valid cognition, like the valid cognition that serves as the means of proving the ignorance you yourself accept.

8. Knowledge does not destroy an object; because, in the absence of being augmented by a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣa*), it is knowledge. That which destroys an object is seen to be either knowledge augmented by a specific power, as in the case of the knowledge of the Lord, yogis, and so forth, or non-knowledge (*ajñāna*), as in the case of a mallet and the like. 9. Nescience (*ajñāna*) is positive in nature (*bhāvarūpa*); it is not destroyed by knowledge, because it is positive in nature, like a jar or similar objects.

The non-establishment of ignorance through scripture (*śruti*) and presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) will be explained immediately hereafter. Furthermore, the claim that "the material cause of a false object must itself be false" is refuted by the logic of the section beginning with "Not so, because of the difference in nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*). Therefore, there is no cognition whatsoever whose object is an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) ignorance.

If it is argued that, since it is impossible for one thing to appear as another, one must instead postulate that "this silver, which is neither existent nor non-existent and is indefinable (anirvacanīya), is perceived as something entirely new due to the influence of a defect," [we reply:

even in the view that the object does not exist, there would still be the attribution of a qualifier belonging to one thing to another thing, and the perception of two cognitions as being one, all while treating them as if they were present.

Now, as for the objection that the defect resides in the sense organs and so forth—that is not so; because, since those defects reside in the person (the self), they cannot produce an effect that resides in the object. Nor can the sense organs be the locus of the defect, because they are merely the instruments of cognition.
Nor are the sense organs themselves defective, for their capacity to produce a distinction exists only with respect to the cognition that constitutes their own specific effect.
Furthermore, the claim that they have beginningless false cognition as their material cause has already been refuted.

If you say, "Because of its similarity to silver and so forth," then the cognition and the word should be simply "that which is similar to it"! If you say, "Because of its connection with the universal (jāti) 'silver' and so forth," is that [universal] ultimately real or not ultimately real?
It is not, first of all, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it is impossible for that [ultimate] to possess a connection with the non-ultimate (*aparamārtha*).

Nor is it the non-ultimate reality, because it is impossible for it to possess a connection with the ultimate, and because it is impossible for it to serve as the basis for the application of the concepts and words "ultimate" to what is non-ultimate. Enough, then, of this refutation of immature sophistry.
The view of those who know the Veda is that all cognition is in accordance with reality, because through the Śruti and Smṛti there is the realization of the selfhood of everything in everything. (1)
"At the commencement of creation and so forth, preceded by the resolve 'May I be many,' it was enjoined by the Śruti itself: 'Of these, each one became threefold. (2)
For this very process of triplication is perceived through direct observation:
"That which is the red form of fire belongs also to water. (3)
If the white and black [qualities] of the earth are indeed threefold by their very nature, this has been shown by the scripture itself; therefore, all [elements] are present everywhere.
And it is likewise stated in the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa at the beginning of the account of creation: "Possessing diverse powers and existing separately, they [the elements], being without cohesion... (5).
They were unable to create living beings without coming together entirely; having met in mutual union, they became dependent upon one another.

From the passage beginning with "The Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa), constitute the Egg," the author of the Sūtras likewise stated that the elements possess a threefold nature [in Sūtra 3.1.2]: "But because they consist of the three [guṇas] and because of their abundance. Therefore, there is a distinction in terminology. Experts in logic know that when *soma* is unavailable, the use of *pūtīka* plants is enjoined by the Śruti because of the presence of parts of the *soma* within them; and when rice (*śrī*) is unavailable, the use of wild rice (*nīvāra*) is prescribed because of its being a form of rice.

That alone is similar to it which partakes of a portion of that substance; the existence of silver and so forth in mother-of-pearl and the like has been taught by the scripture itself. (10) The difference in designation, such as "silver" or "mother-of-pearl," is caused by their relative abundance; furthermore, this mother-of-pearl and the like is perceived as being similar to silver and the like. (11)
Therefore, its existence here is established by perception as well; however, due to some defect in the eyes or other senses, it may at times appear devoid of the "silver" portion.

Therefore, one who desires silver acts because the silver-portion is apprehended; however, when the defect is removed and the nacre-portion is apprehended, that [activity] ceases. Thus, the cognition of silver and the like regarding mother-of-pearl and such is indeed "as-it-is" (yathārtha); moreover, the relationship of sublated and sublator is also logically established on the basis of frequency.
The distinction between having a false object and having a true object does not depend on whether there is an apprehension of the shell's abundance, its non-deficiency, or its totality.
Thus, when everything is everything, there is the establishment of conventional usage. || 15 ||
Objects are created as they are, appearing at their respective times;
for thus says the Śruti concerning the subject of dreams:

"There are no chariots there, no yoke-horses, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, yoke-horses, and roads. There are no joys, delights, or pleasures there; yet he creates joys, delights, and pleasures. There are no pools, lotus-pools, or rivers there; yet he creates pools, lotus-pools, and rivers. For he is the creator. Thus it is said: "In him all worlds are supported; no one ever transcends him."
And so it is said. The author of the Sūtras also states:
"The creation in the intermediate state [is real], for so scripture declares";
and "Some [mention] a creator, as well as sons and so forth."
Thus, by means of these two Sūtras, having raised the objection regarding the individual soul's (*jīva*) status as a creator of objects within dreams, [the text] states:
"But it is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), because its true nature is not fully manifested.

By this and other arguments, it is established that the individual soul’s capacity to create through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) is not tenable; for its innate qualities, such as the power of true resolve, remain entirely unmanifest during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). This creation, which is experienced solely by each particular person and is thus a marvel, belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*) alone.
He offers this rebuttal: "In that [ether], all worlds are supported, and no one transcends it"—from this, it is understood that the Supreme Self alone is the creator therein.

Furthermore, [experiences] such as the decapitation of the head, which are the fruits of merit and demerit, are possible through the creation of another body whose form and configuration correspond to that of the body lying [in the womb].

Even in the cognition of water in a mirage, there is correspondence with reality (yathārthatva), because both fire and earth are present, and due to a defect, fire and earth are not perceived, while by the power of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), water is perceived.

Regarding the fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) as well: due to the extremely rapid movement of the fire-brand, it comes into contact with all points in space; because the intervening spaces are not perceived, such a cognition arises. Even in the perception of a circle, it is simply the perception of various objects in contact with those respective locations, preceded by the non-perception of the intervening spaces. The distinction is this: in some cases there is no perception of intervening spaces because they do not exist, while in other cases there is no perception because of extreme speed. Therefore, that too is real. Regarding mirrors and the like, even the perception of one's own face and so forth is real. [The sense organs...]

For the visual rays, having their course reflected by a mirror or similar object, first apprehend the location of the mirror and then apprehend one's own face and so forth. Even in that case, because of extreme rapidity, the intermediate space is not perceived, and thus such a cognition arises.

As for the perception of another direction—since another direction exists in this very direction—it is by the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that a portion of another direction, separated from this directional part, is apprehended. Therefore, the cognition of another direction is indeed real.

Regarding the term *marīcika* (mirage): this is an explanation establishing the correspondence (*yāthārthya*) of the cognition of mirage-water. Regarding *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen merit/demerit): the fact that the *adṛṣṭa* acts as a regulator must be accepted by all proponents of other theories of manifestation (*khyāti*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everyone would experience erroneous cognitions (*bhrama*) regarding every object, at all times, and in all places; and furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that no erroneous cognition would ever occur. Regarding "due to the non-perception of the interval" (*antarālāgrahaṇāt*): because of the non-perception of the intermediate time between the prior and posterior conjunctions of the fire-brand (*alāta*) with its respective locations—that is, due to the non-perception of the sequence (*krama*). "The perception of a circle" (*cakrapratītiḥ*): refers to the perception of a [real] circle.

Regarding the phrase "in mirrors and the like": if it is asked how there is a reversal of left and right in mirrors and such objects, [the answer is that] the status of being left or right is indeed relative. In this case, because the mirror faces oneself, its left and right sides appear reversed; thus, the very non-perception of the space between the face and the mirror—which has itself undergone a reversal of left and right—is what constitutes the "reversal" located at the site of the mirror. Consequently, the face is perceived as having no intervening space [between it and the observer]. Because the space between the mirror facing oneself and the face is not perceived, the perception of the face's orientation toward oneself is consistent with reality. This also applies to [perceptions of] one's own smallness and so forth.

Even in cases such as the cognition of two moons, due to a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*)—such as the pressing of a finger or ophthalmia (*timira*)—two mutually independent causal complexes become the cause for the apprehension of two moons. Each causal complex apprehends the moon as qualified by its own location; one [complex] does so through a particular movement of the visual rays (*nāyana-tejas*).

The second [instance], however, involves a slightly curved motion; having first grasped a location near the moon, it grasps the moon as separated from its own [original] location. Thus, when the moon is simultaneously grasped as qualified by two locations due to the two sets of causal conditions, a specific cognition arises—namely, "there are two moons"—because the form of the object differs according to the difference in grasping and because there is no grasping of unity.

The status of the other location as a qualifier [of the moon] arises from the continuous perception of the other location and of the moon whose own location is not being perceived. In that case, the duality of the causal complex is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Consequently, the two perceptions of the moon qualified by the two locations are also ultimately real, and the duality of the form is also ultimately real.
Through the duality of the perception, the moon itself is the object of apprehension.

In that case, regarding the apprehension of two moons qualified by two distinct attributes, there is the thought, "Only one moon is to be grasped. Just as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), because the visual organ alone lacks the capacity [to grasp both], visual cognition remains fixed in that very same way with respect to the two.

Even when the two eyes arise from a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the visual light becomes two distinct causal complexes due to defects such as *timira* (ophthalmia); this is to be inferred from the effect. However, when the defect has departed, because the moon—qualified by its own location—is cognized through a single act of perception, the cognition arises: "The moon is one. Thus, it is faultless to conclude that the duality of the causal complex is caused by the defect, the duality of the acts of perception is caused by that, and the duality of the apprehended forms is caused by that.

Therefore, it is established that all cognitions are in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*). Since these [views] have already been elaborated upon by various disputants themselves, no further effort is made here.
Alternatively, what is the use of this extensive method of demonstration? [The following are] the refutations of other theories of manifestation (*khyāti*).

For those who accept the collection of means of valid knowledge known as perception, inference, and scripture—and who acknowledge the Supreme Brahman, who is accessible through scripture, who is free from even a trace of all defects, who possesses an infinite, immeasurable, and innumerable multitude of auspicious qualities, who is omniscient, and whose will is ever-true—what could not be accomplished? What would not be logically possible?

For by the Blessed One—who, as the Supreme Brahman, creates the entire universe for the sake of its enjoyment by the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) in accordance with their merits and demerits—the objects of experience, which result in the fruits of pleasure, pain, and indifference, are created such that some are objects of universal experience, while others are objects of experience for specific individuals alone, limited to specific times, and are to be experienced accordingly. The sense is that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of the two eyes consists of duality; likewise, there is duality of form, meaning the state of being qualified by one's own location.

There is one form (*ākāra*). A distinct spatial location whose intervening space is not perceived constitutes a single form. Its "form-ness" consists in its being a qualifier. Due to extreme rapidity, two cognitions—which are produced by two sets of causal conditions consisting of the movement and the difference in the visual light—are not perceived as having a sequence nor as having a difference; they grasp the moon as having unperceived unity and the other location as having an unperceived interval, thereby grasping them as continuous. Consequently, there is the conventional usage of "two moons. This is the meaning. Thus, it is "flawless," which means it is a demonstration of the theory of *yathārthakhyāti* (the correspondence theory of truth).

Alternatively, the reading beginning with "atha vā kim anena" is seen in many manuscripts and has been commented upon by the commentators. In that context, regarding the statement "parāgarthaviṣayā parokṣam eṣu," the refutation is accomplished by the latter [verse] alone.
Therein, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is established both by being the object of universal experience and by being devoid of that [relationship]; thus, everything is consistent.
"Because of the statement: 'They do not find this world of Brahman, for they are veiled by untruth,' and [the mantra]:
'There was neither non-existence nor existence.'"

In this passage as well, the words "sat" (existent) and "asat" (non-existent) refer to the individual manifestations of consciousness and matter respectively; for this sentence is intended to demonstrate the dissolution at the time of reabsorption of those two entities—designated by the words "sat" and "tyat" at the time of their origination—which consist of the individual manifestations of consciousness and matter, into the entity designated by the word "tamas," which constitutes the collective totality of non-conscious matter (*acitsamaṣṭi*). Here, the indefinability (*anirvacanīyatā*) of anything is not being asserted, because the statement merely expresses the temporary non-existence of the existent and the non-existent at a particular time. It is true that by the word "tamas," the subtle state of *prakṛti* in the form of the collective totality of non-conscious matter is denoted;
however, its...

If it is argued that [the world] possesses indeterminability because it is designated by the word "māyā" in the passage, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," this is not so; for the word "māyā" is not observed to have the sense of "indeterminable."

If it is argued that the word *māyā* signifies "the indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*) because it is a synonym for "false" (*mithyā*), that too is not the case. For the word *māyā* does not everywhere have "the false" as its object; since the word *māyā* is employed even in reference to real things such as demons (*āsura*), Rākṣasas, and weapons. As it has been said:
"By that swift-moving [missile], he [Indra] destroyed the thousand *māyās* of Śambara."
"While protecting the body of the fool, it was destroyed one by one.
Thus [it is said].

Therefore, the word *māyā* denotes that which produces a manifold creation; and it is precisely because it produces a manifold creation that *prakṛti* is designated by the term *māyā*. This is shown by the passage: "From this, the wielder of *māyā* (māyī) creates this universe, and another is confined within it by *māyā*," which demonstrates that *prakṛti*, denoted by the word *māyā*, is the producer of a manifold creation.

And the Supreme Person is said to possess the nature of an illusionist (*māyin*) merely by virtue of possessing that [power], not by virtue of being ignorant. For it is heard in scripture that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is subject to obstruction through *māyā*:
"And in him, another is completely obstructed by *māyā*."
Thus it is said: "When the individual soul (jīva), asleep through beginningless illusion (māyā), awakens."
In the verse, "Indra moves in manifold forms through his magical powers" (*indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate*), it is likewise these diverse powers that are being denoted;
for this very reason:

Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*): since it is precisely the followers (*anuyāyin*) that constitute the ground for the application of the term, the common factor (*anugata*) running through all objects to which the word *māyā* is applied is simply its nature as a marvel (*āścaryatva*). And this "marvelousness" consists in being worthy of wonder; and that [wonderfulness] arises from the capacity to produce a manifold creation of objects. Furthermore, the word "manifold" (*vicitra*) signifies "of various kinds," and because it produces diverse effects, even primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is worthy of wonder.

The meaning is that since the quality of being wonderful exists even in things real or unreal that are objects for the application of the word *māyā*, the very fact of being wonderful is the basis for employing the term *māyā* in the present context (*Śrutiprakāśikā*).

Regarding the term "māyitvam" (the state of being possessed of *māyā*): what is expressed by the word "māyī" is the connection with *māyā*, not the state of being concealed by it; rather, it signifies being presided over by it (*taccheṣitvam*). However, the state of being concealed belongs to the *jīva* alone, because it is heard in scripture that it is the *jīva* who is thus [concealed]. Regarding the phrase "śvanādīti": the meaning is that this statement cited from another source serves precisely to show that the subjugation by *māyā* belongs to the *jīva* alone. Regarding the phrase "śaktayaḥ": from the use of the plural in "māyābhiḥ," it is understood that it denotes many diverse powers.

This is a restatement of that very point: there is no multiplicity in the ignorance (avidyā) accepted by him, because its unity is admitted. "He shines forth manifold like Tvaṣṭṛ," for no one who is overcome by falsehood shines forth.
It is said, "My māyā is difficult to cross.

Even here, because of the statement that it is "composed of the guṇas," it is that very Prakṛti consisting of the three guṇas which is being referred to; thus, there is no presentation by the Śrutis of an ignorance (ajñāna) that is indefinable as either existent or non-existent.

"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"—by this, it is stated that everything down to the ultimate limit of the Supreme Self indeed possesses the state of having "name and form. This is a conceptual construction based on knowledge.

Thus, having established by means of two verses beginning with "Therefore, it is not Brahman" that the distinctness of entities is unreal even according to the manner in which the world is perceived, and having concluded the previously asserted "unreality of everything other than Brahman" with the verse "Therefore, nothing exists apart from consciousness," [the text declares] "consciousness is one."

Thus, having clarified that "one's own karma alone is the root of ignorance, which causes the perception of difference in Brahman, whose true nature is knowledge," and having purified the nature of Brahman—which is the very essence of knowledge—by stating "knowledge is pure," [the Lord] says, "In this way, my teaching on the true state of being has been declared to you. This instruction is indeed observed to show that the reality belongs only to Brahman, whose nature is knowledge, and not to anything else; furthermore, it teaches the truth that everything else is indeed unreal, and that the apparent reality of the world and so forth is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
"Listen to the summary."
Beginning with these words, it is explained as follows.

He says that the basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which will be explained starting from the passage "The luminaries are Viṣṇu," is precisely the relationship of body and self;
this has also been stated repeatedly previously in this treatise: "All those are His body."
"Indeed, all that is the body of Hari;

he alone is the self of all beings, the universal form, because he is imperishable. This identity, which depends on the relationship between body and self, is designated through grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), as in: "The luminaries are Viṣṇu."

For the Blessed One, who exists as the self of all knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) without exception, knowledge alone is His natural form, not the form of entities such as gods or humans. Precisely because this is so, insentient things such as "gods," "humans," mountains, oceans, and the earth are the manifestations of His consciousness; that is to say, while He exists as having the single form of knowledge, these [entities] are rooted in the contemplation of His own manifold nature through the forms of gods and so forth—meaning they are rooted in karma which itself is rooted in the contemplation of the forms of gods and so forth.

And since non-intelligent matter (*acidvastu*) is the locus of transformations according to the karma of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), it follows by implication that it is denoted by the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*), while the other [the intelligent self] is denoted by the word "existent" (*asti*). He explains this very point with the words: "But when it is pure, possessing its own nature.

When this reality of the Self, whose sole form is knowledge, becomes free from defects and completely purified—possessing its own nature through the destruction of all karma rooted in the mental construction of diversity within itself in the forms of gods and so forth—then [the notions of] gods and so forth...

By unifying [all things] through this process, the distinctions between objects within entities—which are rooted in the conceptualization of a self and are the results of karma for the sake of experiencing it—do not exist.

The meaning is as follows: those various objects—such as gods, humans, mountains, oceans, and so forth—which exist as objects of enjoyment within entities like the gods that are conceived of as the Self, do not exist once the karmas that are their root have perished. Thus, because non-conscious matter (*acidvastu*) possesses occasional specific states, it is denoted by the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*). Conversely, the other [the conscious principle] is always established in its own nature as having the single form of knowledge; therefore, it is denoted by the word "existent" (*asti*).

He says, "What substance exists? because that which is insentient (*acidvastu*), by virtue of changing at every moment and being subject to occasional states, can only be designated by the word "non-existent.

For that entity which is denoted by the word "exists" is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and is eternally of one uniform nature; it is never fit to be the object of the cognition "it does not exist. No insentient thing has ever been seen anywhere to be of such a nature. What follows from this? To this he replies:
Regarding the phrase "and that which is alteration":

when a thing undergoes alteration at every moment, it abandons its preceding state by attaining each successive subsequent state; thus, there is no reconnection (*pratisandhāna*) of that preceding state within the subsequent state. Therefore, it is always denotable only by the word "non-existent. To illustrate this, he says: "the earth becomes a pot."

By their own karma, through states such as gods or humans, [beings] perceive—that is, experience—the insentient object that constitutes their own sphere of enjoyment as changing at every moment, despite being fixed by their own certainties. This being the case, is there any insentient object whatsoever worthy of being designated by the word "is" (asti)—something devoid of beginning, middle, or end, and perceived as eternally uniform? The intended meaning is: no, there is not.

Since this is so, he says, "Therefore, nothing other than the Self whose nature is consciousness ever exists anywhere as something denotable by the word 'is' alone," meaning that insentient matter, being distinct from the Self whose essence is knowledge, is never at any time or place expressible by the term "existence" in isolation.

The Self, however, because its sole form is knowledge, has a nature that is the opposite of the distinctions such as "god" and so forth; yet, although it is thus, it is conceived in many ways through various forms by means of self-conceptions of the Self as divided by the distinctions of "god" and so forth—which are rooted in the diverse karmas performed by oneself and which serve as the cause for entering bodies such as those of gods. Thus, he says, "Consciousness is one," to show that this perception of distinction is not prompted by the true nature of the Self.

The nature of the Self, however, is devoid of action; for that very reason, it is untouched by *prakṛti* in its form as impurity (*mala*). Consequently, it is unattached to all qualities to be abandoned, such as sorrow, delusion, and greed, which are caused by that [impurity]. Because it is incapable of increase or decrease, it is one; for that same reason, it is eternally of a single form. And since that is the body of Vāsudeva, it consists of Him, because there is nothing whatsoever that does not consist of Him; thus he says, "pure knowledge."

He states that the true nature of the world has been correctly explained by saying, "The world, consisting of both consciousness and unconsciousness, is the body of Vāsudeva and has Him as its essence," with the words "Such is its true being" (*sadbhāva evam*). Here, the conclusion of what was introduced as "the real" and "the unreal," or "that which exists" and "that which does not exist," is reached. He says, "But this which... to explain that the cause for this—which exists as a mixture of the conscious and the insentient, resting upon the worlds in the forms of gods, humans, and so forth, appearing as a diversity fit for practical usage despite being essentially uniform in its nature as pure consciousness and devoid of distinctions accessible to speech—is indeed *karma* alone.
Thus [it is said]. He explains that very point:
"The sacrifice is the animal."
He states that the purpose of "knowledge of the true nature of the world" is the application of the means to liberation, saying: "And this which... and so forth.

In this regard, not even a single word is seen that is consistent with the view that the world is imagined (*kalpita*) within the attributeless Supreme Brahman and the ignorance (*ajñāna*)— which is both existent and non-existent yet indefinable— that serves as its substrate. Rather, the entire world, consisting of consciousness and matter and denoted by the words "is" and "is not," is of the nature of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman, as it constitutes His body (*kāya*).

The cause for the experience of various forms such as gods by the Self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, and for the transformation of insentient matter, is the very *karma* of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), which is opposed to the knowledge of the true nature of reality; this is what is established. Furthermore, because words such as "non-existent" (*nāsti*) and "unreal" (*asatya*) lack the capacity to denote an object that is "indefinable as being or non-being" (*sadasadanirvacanīya*), the terms "non-existent" and "unreal" are opposites of the terms "existent" (*asti*) and "real" (*satya*). Consequently, through these two [terms], "non-existence" (*asattva*) is indeed understood, not "indefinability."

And here, regarding non-sentient objects (*acidvastu*), the words "is not" (*nāsti*) and "is" (*asti*) are not employed in the sense of being void (*tucchatva*) or false (*mithyātva*), but rather in the sense of perishability (*vināśitva*). Even in the cases of "Does the object exist? and "The earth [attains] the state of a pot," it is indeed perishability that is established; neither lack of evidence nor sublation by cognition is intended. For non-existence is established through the perception of something otherwise at a later time due to a specific transformation, even though it was experienced with one form at one time. Voidness (*tucchatva*), indeed, is the unfitness for connection with any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for sublation (*bādha*), it pertains to a particular place, time, and so forth—

The perception that "it does not exist" with respect to a thing previously perceived as "existing" by virtue of its connection to a particular place, time, and so forth, is [the perception of non-existence] through its connection to that same place, time, and so forth; it is not, however, the perception that "it does not exist" due to transformation or other changes at a different time regarding something experienced at another time, because there is no contradiction between different times. Therefore, there is no falsity.

This is what is meant: the reality of the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is devoid of beginning, middle, and end; it is eternally of one and the same nature, and thus by its very self it is always denoted by the word "exists. The insentient, however, which is the object of experience for the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), undergoes transformation according to that [knower's] karma and is subject to destruction; therefore, it always contains within it the sense of non-existence, and is thus denoted by the words "does not exist" and "unreal.
As it has been said: "That which, even after the lapse of time, does not indeed assume another name..."
"O King, what indeed is that object which arises from transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth?

Regarding the phrase "by transformation and so forth": the word *pariṇāma* refers both to transformation in general and to its specific instances. Just as the word *vāda* (discourse) is common to all types of talk yet specifically refers only to the discourse of those free from passion (*vītarāga*), so too is this word *pariṇāma* here used to denote a state of growth, as seen in the usage "by transformations, decay, and birth. Regarding the phrase "by the difference of time": this is the answer to the question, "How is it not a sublation (*bādha*) when there is no perception at a later time of that which was experienced at a different time?"
For the meaning is that sublation occurs when there is contradiction. "Therefore" [means]: the intention is that being subject to sublation is indeed falsity.
"The wise accept that which is imperishable and the ultimate reality..."
Regarding that, it is said: "There is no doubt that it does not exist [as such], for it is established as a perishable substance.

Thus, it is stated that with respect to an object characterized by existence and non-existence depending on specific place, time, and action, its being cognizable by a cognition of mere existence (*kevalāstibuddhi*) is the non-ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*). On the other hand, its being cognizable by a cognition of mere existence in the very absence [of those conditions] is called the "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*).

In sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not aim at the identity of a single, attributeless reality; for the two words "that" (*tat*) and "thou" (*tvam*) denote Brahman as possessing attributes. Indeed, the word "that" refers to Brahman—the omniscient, whose will is true, and who is the cause of the world—since it is that very [Brahman] which is the subject under discussion in passages such as, "It thought: May I be many."

And the term ‘thou’ (tvam), being in grammatical apposition with that [term ‘that’], conveys Brahman as having the individual soul—qualified by non-sentient matter—as its body; for grammatical apposition has as its purport a single entity existing in two modes. If those two modes were abandoned, grammatical apposition itself would be abandoned due to the impossibility of a difference in the grounds for application (pravṛttinimitta), and there would be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of both words.

In the case of the statement, "This is that Devadatta," there is likewise no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for there is no contradiction in the cognition of identity through the connection with both past and present times. And the contradiction regarding difference of place is resolved by the difference of time. [Objection: No; because before the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) has been manifested, the error and its subsequent sublation—which depend upon that substrate—would be impossible. [Reply: If it is argued that the substrate, which is the locus of the error, is not concealed [at the time of the error];

That very nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is what contradicts the error; therefore, when that [nature] is revealed, there can by no means be either the occurrence of the error or its sublation (*bādha*) based upon it. Consequently, if one does not admit the concealment (*tirodhāna*) of a real attribute that is distinct from the substratum, then error and sublation are difficult to establish. For, only when the substratum is perceived in its mere human form while its real, superadded royal status remains concealed is there the error of being a hunter.

And its cessation occurs through the instruction regarding kingship, not through the instruction regarding the substrate alone; for since that [substrate] is self-luminous, it cannot be an object of instruction, and because error has not yet arisen there.

Through the presentation of a single, qualified entity, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also established. Furthermore, the sovereignty consisting in Brahman’s being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul—Brahman who is devoid of all defects and whose nature consists of all auspicious qualities—is demonstrated, as is conformity with the opening statement (*upakrama*). There is also the justification for the promise that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all; for Brahman, whose body is the subtle sentient and non-sentient reality, is the effect [of creation] by virtue of having the gross sentient and non-sentient reality as His body. "Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7).
"His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold;
he is one whose desires are true and whose resolves are true;
he is free from evil."
And there is contradiction with other scriptural passages such as these.

Because this [fact] has already been established by this very [statement]. For a scripture is purposeful only regarding what has not yet been established. Having pointed out "all this" as the world together with the living soul (*sajīva*), it was demonstrated by the words "this is its Self" (*aitadātmyam*) that "this is its Self.
And the reason for that has been stated.

"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. "All this, indeed, is Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him—therefore, be at peace."
Thus it is said.
"Having entered within, the Teacher is the Self of all beings," and "He became both the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat)," and so forth. Here too— in the passage,

"Entering with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"— it is established that the reality and the expressibility by words of all things occur precisely through the entry of the living being whose essence is Brahman.

Because of its identity of meaning with the passage, "Having entered into that, it became both the existent (sat) and the non-existent (tyat)," it is understood that even the individual soul (jīva) possesses the nature of Brahman precisely through the entry into Brahman.
"This whole world has that as its self"—
this is the meaning of the proposition [established by] "That thou art."
Thus, by way of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), there is a summary in the particular.

If it is argued that this is understood by its own statement alone and there is nothing to be determined through the teaching of identity (*tādātmya*), [we reply: that would merely be the negation of an imagined difference; however, it has already been stated that such negation is not to be determined by the teaching of identity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
