Furthermore, coreferentiality in the case of Brahman, by presenting two distinct modes, would only bring about contradiction. Coreferentiality...

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of absolute difference, because an identity between two absolutely distinct things is impossible in any way whatsoever, the teachings regarding the state of Brahman as the Self would be untenable; thus, there would be a total abandonment of all Vedānta.

Regarding the claim that "co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is present everywhere," it is precisely the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) that is the basis for co-referentiality, not mutually exclusive universals (*jāti*) and so forth. For it is only when substances established in themselves are at some time or place qualifiers of another substance that possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) are observed, as in "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) or "earring-wearer" (*kuṇḍalin*); this is not the case for substances that are incapable of being apprehended or existing separately. Their status as qualifiers is to be understood solely through co-referentiality.

It is understood that [the body] has the Self as its sole purpose, because its very existence is for the sake of experiencing the fruits of that [Self's] karma; and it is also of the nature of that [Self], since it is perceived as a mere qualification of the Self, as in "a god" or "a human."

This indeed is the reason why words such as "cow" and others extend to the individual (vyakti). When [attributes] such as a staff or an earring serve as qualifiers, there occurs the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) in forms such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer") and *kuṇḍalī* ("wearer of earrings"). Because bodies such as those of gods and humans have the nature of having the Self as their sole substratum, having that alone as their purpose, and being of the form of that [Self], there is usage in common parlance and in the Veda through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "god," "human," and "Self. There is a necessary co-perception of the universal (*jāti*) and the individual; for both are perceptible by the eye.

Since the self is not visible to the eye, it is not perceived by the eye at the time of perceiving the body. For that which is capable of being perceived separately, it is impossible for its nature to be identical with [the body], precisely because it lacks such a nature.

Do not speak thus; for, just as in the case of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, the body also has the nature of being a mode of that [Self] alone—this being understood through its having the same substratum, the same purpose, and being its qualifier. As for the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*), it is based on the fact of being cognizable by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*);
the meaning is that it is a qualifier that is not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*). Regarding the phrase "it is also a mode of that":
what is intended by the term "being a mode of that" is the absence of cognition as an independently established entity (*siddhatvena pratītyabhāva*).
The use of the ablative case in the statement "because its cognition occurs separately once the cognition of the qualificand has been established" is merely figurative.

Just as, for example, the connection of earth and so forth with smell, taste, and so on—which is inherent—is not grasped by the eye, so too the body, though being grasped by the eye and having as its sole nature the mode of being the self, is not grasped as such; for the eye lacks the capacity to grasp the self.

By this much, there is no absence of the body’s own nature as having that [Self] as its mode; rather, the very fact of having that as its sole mode is the basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). A word, however, which is capable of conveying [the object] as having the Self as its mode, conveys it as having everything as its mode.
Thus it has been stated.
Therefore, like words such as "cow" and so forth, words such as "god" and "human" have the self (ātman) as their ultimate referent.

In this regard, the truth is as follows: certain Śruti texts declare the distinction between the essential natures of the non-sentient (acidvastu), the sentient (cidvastu), and the "Supreme" (para) Brahman, in terms of their being the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the Ruler respectively: "From Him [the Māyin] the magician creates this universe; and another, bound by Māyā, resides within it. "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the possessor of Māyā (Māyin). "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara. The one God rules over both the perishable and the self (Ātman). [And: "Pradhāna is the object of enjoyment for the Self... ...and so forth. Thus, they state the differentiation of the essential forms of these three.
In the passage, "The imperishable syllable is Hara," the enjoyer is indicated. He is called "Hara" because he takes away (*harati*).
"He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him"; "the Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the master of the guṇas";
"the Lord of the universe, the self-ruling, eternal, auspicious, and infallible."
"The two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord"; "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many";
"Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller."

"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one thereafter attains immortality. "The unborn one, delighting in her, lies beside the single unborn female who is red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form; but another unborn one leaves her after she has been enjoyed.
"On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by his own powerlessness."
"When he perceives the other, the Lord, as the one who is cherished, and [perceives] His greatness, he is freed from sorrow"—thus [it is said] in such passages. Also in the Smṛti:
"This eightfold nature of Mine is called the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)"; "This is the lower; know now My other, higher nature."

"O mighty-armed one, she is the life-force by which this world is sustained. "O son of Kuntī! At the end of a kalpa, all beings go to my own nature; at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth again."

"Taking hold of My own nature, I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature. Under Me as the supervisor, nature produces the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the world revolves.
Know both nature and the person (puruṣa) to be indeed beginningless. My womb is the Great One; in that I place the seed."
"From that, O Bhārata, the origin of all beings occurs" (9.8).

The meaning is this: when I unite the "embryo" known as consciousness with that which is my own "Great One"—the subtle element of being called *prakṛti*, which is insentient matter and the source of the world—then, from that union of consciousness and matter brought about by Me, the origin of all beings, mixed with the insentient, ranging from gods down to stationary objects, comes to be.

Thus, regarding the sentient and the insentient which exist in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed and abide in all states, certain Śrutis declare their non-separateness from the Supreme Person by virtue of being His body and being subject to His control, and they declare the Supreme Person to be the Self: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, and who controls the earth from within."
Beginning with these words, it continues:
"He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who controls the self from within— he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal."
Likewise:

"He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth, whom the earth does not know"—beginning thus, and continuing until—"He who moves within the Imperishable (akṣara), whose body is the Imperishable, whom the Imperishable does not know; he who moves within Death, whose body is Death, whom Death does not know—he is the one divine Lord Nārāyaṇa, dwelling within all beings, free from evil."

Here, by the word "death" (mṛtyu), the subtle state of the insentient entity denoted by the word "darkness" (tamas) is expressed; for in this very Upaniṣad it is stated: "The unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable (akṣara); the Imperishable dissolves into darkness."
And: "The Teacher, the Self of all, has entered within people."

Thus, in order to make known this truth—that the Supreme Person alone, having the non-sentient and sentient entities in all their states as His body, exists as the mode (prakāra) of that [body] in the form of the world in both its effected and causal states—certain Śruti passages declare that "the world in its effected state and its causal state is He alone," beginning with: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It emitted heat. And so forth.

"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. All this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; thou art That, O Śvetaketu. Likewise: "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate. He created all this. He performed austerity; having performed austerity," and so forth.
Beginning from this point up to "Both truth and falsehood became truth," here too,
the distinction between the essential natures of the conscious and the unconscious, as well as the Supreme Person, is established by other scriptural passages.
And so forth. It is recalled [in scripture]:
"Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms."

Thus, because the effect is non-different from the cause, the knowledge of the effect is [already] known through the knowledge of the cause; therefore, the intended "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is more appropriately established.
[This is shown by the statement: "Having entered these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms."

Thus, having pointed out all insentient entities (acidvastu) by saying "the three deities," the text declares that through the entry of the individual soul (jīva), which is His own self, into them, there occurs the differentiation of names and forms (nāmarūpavyākaraṇa). Consequently, all words denoting [entities] denote the Supreme Self alone as qualified by the insentient and the individual soul. Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between a word denoting the Supreme Self in His causal state and a word denoting the effect is primary (mukhyavṛtta).
Hence, Brahman alone—characterized by the gross and subtle sentient and insentient modes—is both the effect and the cause; thus, the world has Brahman as its material cause (upādāna).

Even with respect to their status as material causes (*upādānatva*), the non-confusion of the natures of consciousness (*cit*), unconsciousness (*acit*), and Brahman is more appropriately established. Just as a multicolored cloth, though having as its material cause a collection of white, black, and red threads, possesses its respective qualities such as whiteness only in the specific regions occupied by those particular threads—and thus there is no confusion of colors anywhere even in the state of the effect—so too, although the world has as its material cause the aggregate of consciousness, unconsciousness, and the Lord, there is no confusion of the states of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*), and the controller (*niyantṛtva*) even in the state of the effect.

In the case of threads that are capable of existing separately, they may—by the will of a person—sometimes become combined, thereby possessing both causality and effectuality. Here, however, the distinction is this: since both consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*) in all their states constitute categories of existence only as modes of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) by virtue of being His body, the Supreme Person, as the substrate of those modes, is always denoted by every word. Thus, the difference in intrinsic nature and the non-confusion between them are equal in that [Vaiśeṣika] system and here [in Vedānta].
Furthermore, the declarations regarding the Supreme Brahman as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) are justified because of its lack of connection with qualities to be abandoned (*heyaguṇa*).
Having negated qualities to be abandoned by stating, "He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst," [the text then continues]:
"He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true."
Thus, this very Śruti, while establishing auspicious qualities, restricts the negation of qualities understood in a general sense to the domain of qualities that are to be abandoned (*heya-guṇa*).

Furthermore, the doctrine that "Brahman is of the nature of knowledge" is more logically consistent, because it is accepted that the nature of Brahman—who is omniscient, omnipotent, and the source of all auspicious qualities that are the opposite of everything to be abandoned—is defined as consisting solely of knowledge, being self-luminous and of the very essence of knowledge.
As it is said: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

"His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, and [his] knowledge, strength, and action are innate"; "By what, my dear, could one know the Knower?"—such passages proclaim the quality of being a knower; as does "Truth, Knowledge... [and so forth].
And such [entities] possess the nature of knowledge, because they are definable solely by means of knowledge and because they are self-luminous.

The manifold nature of Brahman—which arises from its own volition and is established by such scriptural passages as "He thought, 'May I be many,'" and which appears through various names and forms—is likewise negated.
This is established in the context of the negating statements, such as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone," and so forth.
"He who knows all as other than the Self has been excluded from all that";
and "Of this great Being, verily, this is the breath— namely, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda," and so forth.

Thus, there is seen no possibility whatsoever for the doctrine of ignorance regarding Brahman (*brahmājñānavāda*), the doctrine of Brahman’s difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikabrahmabhedavāda*), or any other doctrine rooted in fallacious reasoning that contradicts all the Śrutis.

For it is not contradictory that while the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord—whose distinct natures are established by their respective Śrutis—are understood by the Śrutis themselves as being related as the body and the self (*śarīrātma-bhāva*) in the relation of the mode and the possessor of the mode (*prakāra-prakāritva*), another Śruti may establish the relationship of cause and effect between them, as well as the identity of the cause and the effect.

Just as the two "injunctions of the collection" (*samudāyānuvāda*)— which take the six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya, which have arisen separately through their originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), and which have attained the status of two groups— lead to the injunctive statement of qualification (*adhikāravākya*),

"By means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa," enjoining them as duties for one who possesses a desire; in the same way, [the scripture teaches] the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, whose forms and natures are distinct from one another.
"The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara. The one God rules over both the perishable and the Self.
"The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self"; "The Self is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme."

Having established [the distinction] as "separate" through such statements, there is indeed no contradiction in denoting it; just as when a specific self, which is embodied within a human body, is denoted by the word "self" in the expression "this self is happy. Enough of this excessive detail.
"This is false, because another substance does not attain the nature of that substance," according to the scripture; and [as stated in the Gītā]: "But the Supreme Person is indeed other."

Furthermore, from the teaching that "having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct," the knowledge of Brahman— the inner ruler who is of a different nature from the individual soul— is the means for liberation, which is characterized as the supreme human goal. Moreover, since even the "knowledge that removes [ignorance]" favored by you is itself of a false nature, another remover must be sought for it.
If it is argued that this subverting knowledge, being opposed to space, "subverts" the entire collection of differences and, due to its momentariness, "perishes" by itself—this is not so;

because since its own nature, its origination, and its destruction are all conceptual, another subverter must be sought for the ignorance that consists of that destruction, its conceptualization, and the conceptualizer.
If it is argued that its destruction is simply the very nature of Brahman—

If that were the case, the very production of the knowledge that brings about cessation would not occur, because while that [ignorance] persists, its destruction remains and the production of that [knowledge] is impossible.
If Brahman, whose very nature is that of pure consciousness, were the knower, then our own position would have been accepted.

The statement that the nature of the subverting knowledge (*nivartakajñāna*) and its "knower" (*jñātā*) are included within what is to be subverted by it—because they are distinct from Brahman—is laughable; it is like saying, in reference to the very act of cutting, "the entire ground other than [Devadatta] was cut by Devadatta," which implies that this cutter and this act of cutting have entered into the object to be cut. Furthermore, the superimposed knower cannot himself be the agent in the subverting knowledge that is the cause of his own destruction.

Because one's own destruction is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). If the destruction of that [duality] were admitted to be the very nature of Brahman, then there would be no possibility of even the conceptualization of "perception of difference" or of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest rooted therein! Enough, then, with this blow of the mallet of ill-fated fate.

It arises from knowledge alone; and its production is obtained through the performance of duties appropriate to one's caste and stage of life, which have been refined by a specific understanding of the true nature of the self as a mode of worshipping the Supreme Person day after day.

In this regard, the fact that purely ritual acts (*kevalakarman*) yield results that are meager and unstable, whereas those acts performed as a mode of propitiating the Supreme Person with a view toward the fruit [of liberation]—by means of generating knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*)—yield infinite and stable fruits in the form of the experience of the true nature of Brahman, cannot be known without knowing the true nature of action itself. Furthermore, the adoption of action in its aforementioned form, preceded by the abandonment of its mere external form, is not possible [without such knowledge]. Therefore, after the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*), for that very reason, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) must be undertaken; thus it was said: "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*).
Thus is the great established conclusion (*mahāsiddhānta*). Now begins the application of the meaning intended by the author of the Sūtras.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers as follows: since the capacity of a word to convey meaning is determined only through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and since such usage is preceded by the cognition of something to be done (*kārya*), the authority of a word pertains only to that which is to be accomplished; therefore, the meaning of the Veda consists solely in what is to be performed (*kāryarūpa*). Consequently, the Vedāntas cannot function as a means of valid knowledge regarding the "supreme" Brahman, which is already an accomplished reality (*pariniṣpanna*).

Furthermore, in the case of sentences concerning established entities such as the birth of a son, because the causes of joy— objects existing in the three periods of time— are infinite, and because there is the possibility of the occurrence of other objects that cause joy, such as an easy delivery (*sulabha*), the determination that [the sentence] is the cause of the cognition of a specific meaning is made through signs such as the expansion of the face, which serves as the means for perceiving the beloved object.

In this context—"*prapañcasatyatve sthite sati*"—the word "therein" (*tatra*) is connected with the word "established" (*sthitam*), which stands within the body of the section (*adhikaraṇa*). The meaning is that, since the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is established, the structure of the section as formulated by the proponent of falsity (*mṛṣāvādin*) is untenable; thus, the structure of the section remains as it was [previously]. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) is the Prābhākara, who holds that the object characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*) alone is what is propounded by the Veda. Or, according to the school of Jaimini, the injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that impels one toward action. The "conduct" (*vyavahāra*) of these two consists of both speech and physical action. The elder [who is the authority] is one whose nature is [to perform] the task (*kārya*).
[The speaker is] one who is proficient, the one to be prompted, and the prompter.

Nor is there a determination of a word’s power to denote an established entity (siddhavastu) through the ascertainment of the meaning of another word or the ascertainment of the meaning of the verbal root (prakṛti) regarding the meaning of the case-ending of a word other than [the one in question]; for that [ascertainment] consists in the determination of a specific part of a collection of words denoting a known effect.

It has been accepted that a word conveys its meaning as something that prompts action by virtue of its pervasion with the cognition of an effect to be accomplished; for all words have the effect as their ultimate purpose, since it is the effect itself, as qualified [by other factors], that is communicated by all words. Thus, there is no determination of a word’s power to denote merely its own meaning as related to another.

Therefore, since the cognition of something to be accomplished (*kārya*) alone is the cause of activity, and because only that which impels action is denotable by words— given that the Vedas do not reveal what is already established— and because the attainment of Brahman, characterized as an infinite and stable fruit, is understood through such texts as "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes indeed inexhaustible," which demonstrate that ritual actions themselves possess stable fruits; thus, it is argued that the commencement of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) is not justified, as it would be based on the knowledge that the fruits of action are insignificant and unstable, while the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is infinite and stable.

Thus, it is said, children grasp the relationship between word and meaning: their parents and others, with the intention of saying, "Learn this one" and "Understand this one," repeatedly point with their fingers at various objects—such as mother, father, maternal uncle, and so forth, or moon, animal, human, deer, bird, snake, and so forth—while using those respective words. Gradually, seeing that a cognition arises within themselves regarding those very objects through those very words, [they come to understand the connection].

Because no other relationship between word and meaning is observed, and because the person who established the convention is unknown, they conclude that the employment of those words for those meanings is based solely on their capacity to convey understanding. Furthermore, having been instructed by elders in the same manner regarding words whose meanings are already known— namely, "this is the meaning of this word"—
they comprehend the meaning of all words and employ various collections of sentences capable of conveying specific meanings in order to inform others.
Even if the Veda has action as its purpose, the inquiry into Brahman must indeed be undertaken;

for by such statements, the attainment of Brahman is heard of in scripture. Thus, the nature of Brahman and its attributes are established solely for the sake of utility toward an action—just as heaven and other specific locations are established as being unmixed with suffering, just as "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, and just as the relationship between means and end is established in cases such as the threat of a hundred strokes of a whip (*apagoraṇa-śatayātanā*).
For you, an effect (*kārya*) is that which arises from volitional effort (*kṛti*) and is the objective of that effort.

"Being the objective of an effort" means "being the object of volitional effort. And "being the object of volitional effort" means "being that which is most desired to be attained through volitional effort. Furthermore, that which is most desired is either pleasure or the cessation of present suffering.

In this regard, if it is perceived that a desired object such as pleasure cannot be accomplished by a person without his own effort, then the person, desiring [the result], exerts effort; for nowhere is there found anything called "being the objective of effort" apart from the fact that the object of desire has its accomplishment dependent upon effort, since it is precisely this dependence on effort for its accomplishment that constitutes the motivating force of the object of desire, as it is from this alone that activity arises. Nor is "being the objective of effort" equivalent to being favorable to the person, because only pleasure itself is favorable to the person.

Furthermore, the cessation of suffering does not possess the quality of being "conducive to the person" (*puruṣānukūlatva*). For the distinction between the natures of pleasure and pain is as follows: "Pleasure is that which is conducive to the person; pain is that which is contrary to it. Because pain is contrary to the person, its cessation is desired, not because it is conducive to the person. Indeed, the cessation of suffering is simply abiding in one's own nature, free from association with both the conducive and the contrary. Therefore, it is impossible for action and so forth, which are distinct from pleasure, to possess the quality of being conducive to the person.

It is not because it serves the purpose of pleasure that [the primary cause] is favorable to it, for that [pleasure] is essentially of the nature of suffering. Even by way of being "for the sake of pleasure," there arises merely a desire to acquire it. This is because [pleasure] is something to be experienced, and because we observe that even a master acts with the servant's objective in mind when supporting him. If it is argued that the master acts "with his own objective" even while supporting the servant, we say no; for the servant also acts "with his own objective" alone when supporting the master.

Since the very nature of the "task" (*kārya*) cannot be defined, the claim that "the subordinate (*śeṣa*) is that which is related to the task, and the principal (*śeṣin*) is that which is related to it" is also incoherent. Furthermore, being the purpose of an effort (*kṛti*) does not mean being the objective of an effort; for the purpose of a person’s undertaking an effort is simply the motive for that effort, and that is the object of desire (*icchā-viṣaya*).

Therefore, since the state of being the objective of an effort—which would have to exceed mere desirability—cannot be defined, the "task," characterized as "that which is to be accomplished by effort" (*kṛti-sādhya*) and "that which is dependent on effort" (*kṛti-adhīna*), is indeed impossible to define.

Since even *niyoga* (the mandate) is distinct from pleasure and the cessation of pain—which are the direct objects of desire—it is desired and capable of being accomplished through action (*kṛtisādhya*) solely by virtue of being a means to those ends. For this very reason, it is distinct from mere action; otherwise, the "thing-to-be-done" (*kārya*) would be nothing but the action itself.

In accordance with its syntactic connection with the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), the "thing-to-be-done" expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth must be a means to heaven. Therefore, the "thing-to-be-done" is precisely the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), which is stable, enduring, and distinct from momentary actions. Indeed, the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding the *apūrva* arises solely from its status as a means to heaven.

Therefore, it is laughable [to claim] that an action (*kārya*), which is first understood as having no other purpose, subsequently becomes the means for attaining heaven (*svarga*) by means of the *apūrva*—solely for the sake of fulfilling its lack of another purpose; for this would contradict the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), which denotes an action connected to that desire (*iṣiḥ* = wish). This is because even the mandate (*niyoga*) is distinct [from the desire]. Here, "being desired in itself" (*svata iṣṭatvam*) is intended to mean being desired without being a means to any other object that is the focus of that desire.
This is the same [for both]. Both of these possess "being desired in itself" and "being achievable through an effort prompted by that [desire]."
Therefore, neither pleasure nor the cessation of suffering [is the object] of the injunction; rather,
it is action alone— the meaning of the verbal root itself.
The meaning is "it is established. Otherwise—that is, if one does not accept its establishment as a means (*sādhana*).

Therefore—because prior to the syntactic connection with the word *svargakāma* (one desiring heaven), the status of being the object to be accomplished (*kāryatā*) is understood to belong solely to the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), and because upon that connection, [the root-meaning] would be subordinate to that [heaven]; furthermore, since it has not been stated that [the root-meaning] is for no other purpose even initially, it is impossible for that which is for no other purpose to be perceived as something to be accomplished by volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*).

If it is argued that, because the scripture teaches that the *niyoga* (injunction) other than the cessation of pleasure and pain and their means constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), one will experience [the fruit] "later on," then what is that scripture which expresses that the *niyoga* is the human goal?
First of all, it is not a worldly statement,
because its object is an action whose nature is suffering; for by that [worldly statement],
there is merely the communication of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*) precisely as a means to pleasure and so forth.
Nor can it be the Vedic [injunction], because even that establishes the "task" (kārya) solely as a means to [attaining] heaven and so forth.

Nor can it be the scripture concerning obligatory and occasional rites, for its denotation of that [task] is likewise preceded by the acquisition of the understanding of the "unseen potency" (apūrva) from the sentence "one desiring heaven," and thus, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it too inevitably denotes a task whose means are the mouth and other such [organs].

Furthermore, since no experience of a pleasure consisting of a mandate (*niyoga*) is observed—apart from the food, health, and so forth being experienced at that time as the fruit of a performed action whose result is restricted to this life—we find no evidence whatsoever for the claim that "the mandate is pleasure.

Even in the *arthavādas* and similar passages, you have never seen a description of the nature of pleasure consisting of a mandate, any more than there is a description of the nature of pleasure such as heaven and the like.

It is determined that the denotation of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is indeed established as follows: that the sacrifice and other such acts are of the nature of propitiating the Supreme Person who dwells within deities such as Agni; and that the accomplishment of the fruit proceeds from the Supreme Person once He has been propitiated, as well as the accomplishment of the "meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvartha*), namely the sacrifice and so forth.

Therefore, since the fruits of mere ritual actions are limited and unstable, whereas the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman is infinite and stable, it is established that the commencement of the inquiry into Brahman—which results in its definitive determination—is appropriate. || 1 ||

The meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman is that Supreme Person from whom—possessing infinite auspicious qualities such as knowledge and bliss, being omniscient, omnipotent, and supremely compassionate—the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world proceed.

To begin with, birth and the other [characteristics] do not define Brahman as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*); for, by virtue of being excluded from multiple qualifiers, it would follow that Brahman is manifold. For "being a qualifier" indeed means "that which distinguishes. Now, one might object: "In the case of [the description], 'Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, red-eyed, and of medium stature,' even though there are many qualifiers, only a single Devadatta is perceived; likewise here too, Brahman must be one! This is not so; because in that case, oneness is perceived through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the qualifiers are subsumed within that very single entity.

Thus, by the phrase "Śrībhāḥ," it is shown that the one denoted by the word *sat* alone functions as both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, having established its status as the material cause through the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed Being, one only," and having excluded any other presiding agent by stating it was "without a second" (*advitīya*), [the text proceeds].
"Then It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat.

Since this establishes that there is only one [source], it follows that "That from which the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of the world proceed—that is Brahman. Thus, birth, subsistence, and dissolution define Brahman as the entity that serves as both its own efficient cause (*nimitta*) and its material cause (*upādāna*).

Thus, the essential nature of Brahman—the cause of the world’s birth and so forth, which has been established as the cause—is described as being excluded from everything else: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite.

In this context, the word "Truth" (satya) denotes Brahman as that which possesses existence unconditioned by limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika-sattā). By this, [it is distinguished from] that which is the locus of modification.

The term *acetanam* (the insentient) excludes the sentient being conjoined with it; they are distinct because, by virtue of possessing different states that require different designations, the two lack the possession of unconditioned existence (*nirupādhika-sattā*). The term *jñāna* (knowledge) denotes that which has the single form of eternally contracted knowledge; by this, the liberated ones are excluded, as they are characterized by contracted knowledge only occasionally. The term *ananta* (infinite) denotes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) devoid of limitations of space, time, and substance. Since the essential nature possesses qualities, its infinity consists in both its own nature and its qualities. By this, [the Lord] is distinguished from the two poles excluded by the preceding two terms.
The specific natures and qualities [of substances] are eternal and distinct, because qualifiers have the function of differentiating. Therefore, [the following applies]:

The reality [of Brahman] is established; for it is accepted that "ignorance is the root of error, and Brahman is the witness of ignorance. Witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) is indeed predicated precisely by way of being a "revealer" (*prakāśaka*). Furthermore, luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is what distinguishes [Brahman] from the insentient; it exists by virtue of having a nature that brings about the capacity for practical activity (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*) for both itself and others. This being so, [Brahman] possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*). In the absence of that, there would be no luminosity at all; it would be a mere nothingness (*tucchatā*). || 2 ||

Since Brahman, being absolutely beyond the senses, is not an object of perception or other means of valid cognition, it has scripture as its sole authority; thus, Brahman, whose nature has been described,
is that "from which indeed these beings are born."
The meaning is that such statements indeed convey this very point.
Nor is there inference, whether of the "seen through particulars" (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*) or the "seen through generalities" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) variety.
Because there is an absence of the determination of a relation regarding a supersensible object (*atīndriya-vastu*), it is not *viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*.
Nor is it *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*, as that is restricted to a specific person capable of directly perceiving all things and creating them.
The indicative mark is perceived.

First of all, it is not the case that [the world] has its origin and subsistence dependent upon Him; for the illustrative example would then be devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala). For one's own healthy body is not dependent on a single conscious being for its origin and subsistence, because the origin and subsistence of that body are produced by the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) of all conscious beings who experience it, such as one's wife and others.

Furthermore, the persistence of a whole body (*śarīra*), consisting in its inherence in its own parts, does not require a conscious being (*cetana*) apart from a specific conjunction of those parts. However, persistence characterized by vital breath (*prāṇana*) is not possible in the earth, oceans, mountains, and so forth, which are intended as the subject of the inference (*pakṣa*); thus, we do not perceive a uniform persistence common to both the subject and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). If it is argued that "dependence upon that" means "subordination to that," [we respond:]...

There is a deviation [in the argument] regarding heavy chariots, stones, trees, and so forth, which are accomplished by many conscious beings. If [the reason] were "dependence on mere consciousness," it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Nor is it the case that agency is impossible for living beings due to their lack of knowledge regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth; for all conscious beings possess the capacity for the direct perception of the earth and other material causes, as well as the instruments such as sacrifices. Just as the earth and sacrifices are perceived directly at present, so too do conscious beings—through the power of sacrifices and other instruments, which are denoted by terms such as "merit" (*apūrva*) and consist of the potency of those sacrifices—even in the absence of the direct perception of the visible [result], [possess the required knowledge].

There is no impossibility of agency, because the commencement of an action does not depend upon the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of that [agency]. Indeed, it is the direct perception of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) alone that is useful for the commencement of an action. However, with respect to power itself, mere knowledge (*jñānamātra*) is what is required, not direct perception. For potters and others do not begin the production of effects such as jars or bowls only after they have directly perceived the power [of their tools], in the same way that they perceive the staff, the wheel, and other implements used for the task. In this case, however, the commencement of action by conscious beings who have understood through scripture the specific powers of sacrifice and so forth is not untenable.

Furthermore, since it is observed that effects such as jars are produced by one who is not the Lord (anīśvara), who possesses limited knowledge and power, who has a body, who is subject to grasping, and whose desires are unfulfilled, this reason of "being an effect" (kāryatva) would be contradictory (*viruddha*) if it were to establish a conscious agent of that very same nature, because it would prove the opposite of the desired attributes of the person's omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.

However, this does not entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference; for when the subject possessing the mark (*liṅgin*) is within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), those "contrary" particulars presented by the force of the mark (*liṅga-bala*) are set aside, their movement being obstructed by that other means of cognition.

But here, regarding the subject of all other vital breaths (*prāṇa*), which is the possessor of marks (*liṅgin*) and is capable of creating everything, all properties whose rules of invariable concomitance have been understood through positive and negative induction apply without distinction. Since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), they remain exactly as they are.
Therefore, how can God be established except through scripture (*āgama*)?
1. The earth, mountains, and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, are effects; because they possess parts, like a jar.

Similarly, when jars, water-pots, and the like have been made, a person who has inferred the knowledge of the maker’s power to produce them from the observation of those effects, upon seeing for the first time a royal palace with its manifold structure, determines its status as an effect by means of its specific arrangement of parts, and at that very moment infers the variety of the maker’s knowledge and power.

To include the seed, sprout, and so forth within the subject (*pakṣa*) and thereby to charge them with the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) is the manifestation of ignorance on the part of those who are like *śrotriya*-zombies. For that very same reason, the statement regarding inconclusiveness by means of pleasure (*sukha*) and the like is likewise [invalid].

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate such a presiding agent for the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*)—who is accepted by both disputants—on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*); for it is certain that they lack the capacity to perceive the subtle, the concealed, and the remote. Indeed, every postulation must be consistent with what is actually perceived. And there is no certainty regarding the Lord’s (*Īśvara*) incapacity, as there is for the field-knower.

Therefore, there is no impossibility of establishing that [the Creator] through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Being established by the reason of "being an effect determined by a capable agent," He is established as being endowed precisely with the innate direct perception of all objects and the power to govern them.

As for the claim that "by establishing [the Creator's] lack of sovereignty and so forth, there is a proof of the opposite of the specific property [of the subject]"—this is based on an ignorance of the functioning of inference. For it is not the case that all properties observed together in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), nor properties of the effect that are not its causes, necessarily apply to the object of inference (*liṅgin*). What is meant is this: when something is being produced by someone, it requires the agent’s capacity for its own production and knowledge of its own material causes and instruments; however, it does not require the agent’s lack of other capacities or lack of other knowledge, because those are not causes [for the effect].

Since one's own capacity for creation is established by the very knowledge of one's own material cause (*upādāna*) and instruments (*upakaraṇa*) at the time of its own arising, it is illogical to postulate that something else—such as the ignorance of other objects—which is irrelevant and does nothing more than being perceived as related, can be the cause.
Furthermore, regarding the ignorance of objects other than the thing being produced: does this ignorance of other objects pertain to all things, or only to a few?
It cannot be universal; for a potter or the like does not fail to know anything whatsoever other than what is being produced.

Nor does it apply to only a few subjects, because among all agents there is no restriction regarding their respective ignorance or capacity; thus, since [qualities such as] ignorance and the like are found to deviate from all [agents], the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) does not fail to reach the subject (*liṅgin*)— namely, those who lack the capacity for lordship (*anīśvaratva*) and so forth— and therefore it does not constitute a proof of the opposite.

Therefore, since the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*), being subject to merit and demerit and possessing limited power and knowledge, is not capable of creating effects such as the body and the world—which consist of a specific arrangement of diverse parts—it follows that God (*īśvara*) alone is established by inference. He is the Supreme Person, skilled in the creation of the entire universe, possessing inconceivable, unlimited knowledge, power, and sovereignty; he is bodiless, and the infinite, vast, and diverse array of his manifold creation is accomplished solely through the instrument of his mere volition.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for partless substances such as space to be effects, one cannot establish that Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the entire universe.

Because there is a lack of evidence. It is not the case that all things possess a single commonality of being effects—like a jar made by Caraka—such that, by observing differences in time and agent among individual effects, one could infer a single agent through the identity of time and agent. For no such rule is observed.

Nor can it be argued that because individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) lack the power to create the diverse world, one must postulate a creator distinct from them on the strength of the fact that the world is an effect; for such a postulation would involve the logical fault of assuming multiple unknown entities when a single agent suffices. This is because we observe a diversity of powers among those very souls who have accumulated specific merits, and since it is possible for them alone—through the presence of extraordinary *adṛṣṭa* (unseen moral force)—to be the causes of their respective distinct bodies, it is illogical to postulate an entirely unseen person beyond them.

Furthermore, the simultaneous arising and destruction of all things do not ascend to the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for the arising and destruction of all things are postulated as being imperceptible effects, and because arising and destruction are observed only in a sequential manner. Moreover, there is no contradiction in postulating [the nature of things] in accordance with what is actually observed.
[Establishing the contradiction by another method through the effect-reason:

Furthermore, since all effects—such as the body and so forth—are observed to be permeated by pleasure and the like, which are themselves effects of the qualities such as *sattva*, it must necessarily be accepted that they have *sattva* and the other qualities as their root. The specificities residing in the cause, which serve as the reason for the diversity of effects, are *sattva* and the rest. The establishment of those effects as having that [triple nature] as their root occurs through the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the Puruṣa endowed with them.

And since the connection of the person with that [activity] is rooted in karma, the agent's relation to karma must necessarily be accepted as being for the sake of initiating specific effects, just like the power of knowledge; for the diversity of the power of knowledge is itself rooted in karma. Even though desire is a cause for the initiation of activity, its connection to karma is unavoidable, because that desire—when qualified by a specific object—is rooted in the *sattva* and other guṇas.

Therefore, the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) alone are the agents; no one distinct from them is established by inference. And there are indeed formal arguments (*prayoga*) [to this effect]: [The formal arguments follow.]
1. "The body, the world, and so forth, have the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) as their agent, because they are effects, like a jar.
Nor is he possessed of a body, for that [position] cannot withstand analysis. Is that body eternal or non-eternal?
It cannot be eternal; for if that [body], which possesses parts, were eternal, there would be no contradiction in the eternity of the world, and thus God (*īśvara*) would not be established.
Nor is it impermanent, because at that time there is no cause for its body other than itself;
if it is argued that the cause is the self,
we say no, because that is impossible for one who is bodiless.
If it is argued that he is "embodied" by means of another body, we say no, because it would lead to an infinite regress.
Nor does an agent devoid of activity produce an effect, like a liberated soul.

If it is asserted that the world, which is the effect, has as its agent an activity consisting of mere will, then the subject (pakṣa) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva), and the example (dṛṣṭānta) is deficient in the property to be proven (sādhyahīnatā).

The *Miśrā* [commentary], which possesses ninefold superior excellence, establishes that [the Lord] is an ocean of immeasurable and noble qualities and is by nature the adversary of all that is to be abandoned; thus, there is no possibility of even a trace of the defect arising from the application of similarity to an object already determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to remove a possible doubt. That is to say, it is indeed possible for Brahman to have the scripture as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

This is because of "coherence" (*samanvaya*); "coherence" means connection by way of being the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). This is because Brahman, which constitutes the supreme human goal, is connected [to the scriptures] as their subject matter (*abhidheya*).
"From this very Self, indeed, space was produced";
"In the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed";
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"; "Bliss is Brahman."
And so forth.

Because they are devoid of any purpose consisting of engagement or cessation with respect to Brahman—which is the cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the entire world, free from all defects, an ocean of immeasurable and noble qualities, and whose nature is unsurpassed and infinite bliss—scriptures that are focused on it would appear to have no other intent; for all means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) terminate in the comprehension of their own respective objects, and the operation of a pramāṇa does not conform to a purpose, but rather, the purpose conforms to the pramāṇa.

Nor is there a lack of purpose for [statements] devoid of connection with engagement or withdrawal, because they are perceived as being connected to human goals. Likewise, even in cases where the primary focus is on the thing-in-itself, such as "A son is born to you" or "This is not a snake," we observe that they possess a purpose consisting of joy or the cessation of fear.

The meaning is: "because of its being the means of knowledge. Regarding the word *akhila* (entirety), he states the object as understood from the causal texts (*kāraṇavākya*) in order to exclude the possibility that [the Upanishads] have another purpose due to being within the scope of other means of knowledge. Regarding the word *aśeṣa* (without remainder), he states the object as established by the causal texts and understood from the purificatory texts (*śodhakavākya*). The intention is that it is difficult to maintain that they have as their ultimate purpose the *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* favored by the Sāṅkhyas. Regarding the phrase *ānandasvarūpa* (of the nature of bliss), this is for the purpose of excluding the charge that they have another purpose because they do not have the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) as their ultimate aim.

"Being intent on something else" (*anyaparatvam*) means the absence of *tātparya* (purport) and the absence of authority regarding Brahman. For the meaning is that the various means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) culminate in the cognition of their respective objects, but not in [prompting] engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). Regarding the phrase "and not for the sake of a purpose" (*na ca prayojana*): here, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin the negation of two pervading factors (*vyāpaka*). The sense is that it is improper to claim that the connection with withdrawal (*nivṛtty-anvaya*) is a pervader of authority (*prāmāṇya*), and likewise, it is improper to claim the same for a purpose (*prayojana*).

"Just as [validity] does not have pervasion by activity, nor is it [activity] itself"—the word "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*) is to be supplied. Regarding "puruṣārtha": the meaning is that even in the absence of the nature of activity or cessation, there is the cognition of a connection because Brahman, which is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is the very thing expressed. In the phrase "na ca" (nor), the word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the two negations of pervasion. Just as validity does not have the pervasion of being connected with activity and cessation, so too the purpose (*prayojana*) does not have the pervasion of being connected with activity and cessation.
"In such [injunctions] as 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' 'One should not eat kalañja,' and so forth."
How so?

Brahman, whose sole essence is knowledge—though appearing as having a manifold world due to beginningless ignorance—is to be made free from the manifold world; thus, Brahman becomes the object of an injunction by way of the dissolution of the phenomenal world.
"Free from phenomenal manifestation," "without a second.
What is this injunction whose object is Brahman— the single essence of the knowledge to be accomplished— by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world consisting of the seer and the seen?

That is incorrect; for by one who maintains that the meaning of a sentence is *niyoga* (an injunction), the following must be stated: the *niyoga*, its object (*viṣaya*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and the instigator (*prayoktṛ*). Furthermore, the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) must be stated, for therein resides the person to be enjoined.
The qualification is not to be adopted; and that [qualification] is the cause,
which is twofold.
In this regard, it must be discerned: what is the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*), and what is its cause—is it a fruit or something else?
If it is the realization of the true nature of the essence of Brahman, then that is the qualification of the person to be enjoined.
In that case, it cannot be the cause [of the action], because— like the desire for life— it is unestablished [as a constant].

Furthermore, if it were the cause, then because it would be eternal, there would follow the consequence of its performance being obligatory even after liberation, just as the Agnihotra and other rites performed for the sake of life are obligatory.

Nor is it a fruit; for, as a fruit resulting from a mandate (*naiyogika*), it would follow that it is non-eternal, like heaven and so forth. If it is argued that Brahman alone is the object of the mandate here, we say no; because Brahman, being eternal, is not of the nature of something to be accomplished (*abhāvya*), and because it is not an action (*abhāvārtha*).

If it is argued that "Brahman," being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), is the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), [we reply: even if it is something to be accomplished, it is nonetheless a fruit (*phala*). Because it is not a positive entity (*abhāvārthatvāt*), it cannot be the object of an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, of what is there the state of being "to be accomplished"? Is it of Brahman, or of the cessation of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañcanivṛtti*)?

It cannot be Brahman [the object of the injunction], because it is already established and because it would follow that it is non-eternal. If you say it is the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then Brahman is not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). If it is argued that the cessation of the phenomenal world itself is the object of the injunction, we say no; for since that cessation is the fruit (*phala*), it cannot be the object of an injunction. Indeed, the cessation of the phenomenal world is liberation (*mokṣa*), and that is the fruit. If this [cessation] were the object of a mandate (*niyoga*), there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the cessation of the phenomenal world would result from the mandate, and the mandate would depend upon the cessation of the phenomenal world.

If it is argued that the *niyoga* (the injunction) brings about the knowledge that causes cessation, and by means of that knowledge becomes the remover of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then since that [knowledge] arises from the very sentence itself, there is no need for a *niyoga*. This is because the entire phenomenal world, which is false and distinct from Brahman, is sublated by the very knowledge of the meaning of the sentence; furthermore, the *niyoga*, along with its accessories, would remain unestablished. If the phenomenal world is to be removed—whether the *niyoga* that removes the world is the very nature of Brahman or something distinct from it—[in either case, the *niyoga* is redundant].

If the very nature of Brahman is indeed the "non-remover," then, due to its eternity, the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which is to be removed—is impossible; and because of that eternity, it is also untenable for the injunction (*niyoga*) to be accomplished through the performance of its object.

Now, if [it is argued that] the agent—who is distinct from the nature of Brahman—is destroyed because the performance of the object consisting in the cessation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is what must be accomplished, then [the injunction] fails due to the absence of a substratum (*āśraya*). Since by the very performance of the object consisting in the cessation of the phenomenal world, everything distinct from the nature of Brahman has already ceased to exist, there is no fruit called liberation (*mokṣa*) to be produced by an "injunction" (*niyoga*). Furthermore, since the cessation of the phenomenal world lacks the "manner of performance" (*itikartavyatā*) required for an instrument (*karaṇa*), and since that which is unaided cannot function as an instrument, it cannot possess the status of an instrument.
If it is asked, "How can there be an absence of *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance)?"—it is replied:
In this case, its *itikartavyatā* must be either positive (*bhāvarūpā*) or negative (*abhāvarūpā*).

And if it is positive, it is possible that it is divided according to the accomplishment of the body of the instrument (*karaṇa-śarīra-niṣpatti*) and the various distinct functions that assist it (*tadanugrāhaka-kārya-bheda*).
Nor is it of both kinds;

for, as in the case of a blow from a mallet or similar means, no agent whatsoever is observed that can bring about the cessation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and thus it cannot have a perceptible purpose.

Nor is it possible for it to assist an already accomplished instrument in the production of its effect; because, due to the presence of an "assisting portion," the very nature of the instrument—which consists in the cessation of the entire phenomenal world—would remain unestablished.

If it is argued that the knowledge of the non-duality of Brahman produces a body-instrument (*karaṇa-śarīra*) consisting of the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then by that very fact liberation—consisting of the cessation of the phenomenal world—is established; thus, nothing remains to be produced by instruments and the like, as has already been stated previously.

Furthermore, if [Brahman] were of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-rūpa*), then because it is non-existent, it would not produce a body-instrument, nor would it be a benefactor (*anugrāhaka*). Therefore, an injunction (*vidhi*) whose object is the non-phenomenal Brahman is impossible.

"One should meditate [upon him] as the Self," and "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world. Here, the injunction has meditation as its object; since that meditation must be defined solely by its object, it implies the object of meditation. And that object of meditation is the Self specified in its own scriptural passage. When the question arises as to what its nature is, [the text proceeds] by way of imparting the specific details of its essential nature—

Regarding such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" and "In the beginning, my dear, this was that alone," their authority is derived from being supplementary to the injunction for meditation; thus, they indeed possess a purport regarding the very nature of Brahman as it enters into the body of the meditation that constitutes the object of the injunction. Therefore...
"One alone, without a second";
"That is the Truth, That is the Self, That art thou, O Śvetaketu";
"There is not any diversity here whatsoever."
From such passages as these, it is understood that "Brahman" alone is the one true reality, and everything other than that is false.

Now, it might be argued: since we observe the cessation of the fear of a snake through the instruction, "This is a rope, not a snake," liberation—being false in nature like the snake-in-the-rope and thus sublatable by knowledge—is rightly brought about by the very knowledge produced by the [Vedic] sentence, and not by a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). For if liberation were something to be accomplished by an injunction, it would be non-eternal, like heaven and so forth; yet the eternity of liberation is accepted by all disputants.
Because bodilessness (*aśarīratva*) is one's very nature (*svarūpa*), it cannot be something to be accomplished (*asādhya*).
Bodilessness is to be accomplished through the mandate (*niyoga*),
as the Śrutis say:

Furthermore, liberation cannot be something to be accomplished (sādhya) in any of the four ways—namely, by way of origination, attainment, modification, or purification. Nor can it be "something to be purified" (saṃskārya) through rubbing, as in the case of a mirror and the like. The Self is not purified by acts such as bathing while residing in the body; rather, it is the ego-maker (ahaṅkartā) who is grasped by ignorance and associated with it. The experience of the fruits of those acts belongs to that [ego-maker] alone. And the ego-maker is not the Self, because the Self is its witness. Thus says a Vedic mantra:
"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating."
Thus:
"The wise say that the Self, when joined with the body, the senses, and the mind, is the enjoyer";
and: "The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings."

"The overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, absolute, and devoid of qualities. "He has pervaded all—bright, bodiless, woundless, without sinews, pure, and untouched by evil. From the ego-maker (ahaṅkartṛ) who is seized by ignorance, the "Self" (ātman)—whose nature is incapable of receiving any addition, eternally pure, changeless—is extracted. Therefore, because it is the very nature of the Self, liberation (mokṣa) is not something to be accomplished.
And thus it is said.
If this is so, one might ask: "What is accomplished by the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence?
We reply: "It is merely the cessation of the obstacles to liberation. And so the Śruti texts state:

"You indeed are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore beyond ignorance. "Venerable sir, I am that very person. For I have heard from those of your venerable lineage that 'the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
Yet I am in sorrow. May your venerable self carry me across to the further shore of this sorrow."

"To him whose impurities have been wiped away, the Blessed Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness," and so forth. Therefore, by the knowledge of the meaning of the [Vedic] statement, there is brought about the cessation of the obstruction to liberation itself, which is eternal. Although this cessation is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), being of the nature of a non-existence following destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), it does not perish.

Statements such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" establish that liberation occurs immediately after knowledge; thus, they preclude the intervention of a ritual injunction (*niyoga*).
Nor is there entry into the sphere of action by being the object of the act of seeing (*vidi*) or the object of the act of meditation (*dhyāna*),
because both kinds of objecthood are prohibited;

nor does the cessation of bondage result from knowledge alone— thus, the injunctions for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are not purposeless, because they serve as the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence by way of turning one away from all other mental constructs that proceed from one's own nature.

Nor should it be argued that the cessation of bondage is not observed to result from mere knowledge alone; for since bondage is illusory in nature, its continued existence after the dawn of knowledge is logically untenable. For this very reason, it is not correct to say that the cessation of bondage occurs only after the fall of the body, as if the cessation of the fear of a snake superimposed upon a rope required the destruction of the snake itself beyond the realization of the rope’s true nature. [In such a case,] one would require the destruction of the snake in addition to knowledge.

If the connection with the body were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), then indeed there would be a dependence upon its destruction. However, that [connection] is not ultimately real because it is distinct from Brahman.

On the other hand, it is understood that for one whose bondage has not ceased, knowledge itself has simply "not arisen," because the effects of knowledge are observed [to be absent]. Therefore, whether the persistence of the body continues or not, immediately following the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, that person is indeed liberated.

Therefore, liberation is not something to be accomplished through the practice of meditation; thus, Brahman is not established as a subordinate element of an injunction for meditation. Rather, [it is established by such texts as]:
"Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."
This is established by the very collection of words "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman."
That is incorrect; for the cessation of bondage cannot result from the mere knowledge of the meaning of a sentence.

Even though bondage, being illusory in nature, is sublated by knowledge, nevertheless, because bondage is directly perceived, it is not [sublated] as in the case of the perception of a snake in a rope—wherein one thinks, "I am bound"—[only after the snake has been removed].
It is sublated by the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence in a non-perceptual form; for instance,
when there is a non-perceptual erroneous cognition of a snake produced by the instruction of a reliable person, [it is sublated] by the statement, "This is not a snake, this is a rope."

For it is observed that fear does not cease through mere [instruction]; however, the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) is the cause for the cessation of fear, by virtue of being the cause for the activity that results in the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of the true nature of reality (*vastuyāthātmya*).

For instance, a person who has turned away out of fear upon seeing a snake in a rope, when prompted by the instruction of a trustworthy person that "this is not a snake, this is a rope," proceeds toward the perception of the object as it truly is; having seen that very thing through direct perception, he turns away from his fear. Nor is it reasonable to say that the word itself generates perceptual knowledge, because it is not a sense organ. Indeed, among the causal factors for knowledge, the sense organs alone are the means for producing immediate (aparokṣa) cognition.

Furthermore, for a person whose impurities have been washed away by the performance of actions without regard for their fruits, and who has turned away from external objects through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the sentence alone does not produce immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*); for even in such a person who is intent on that goal and whose obstacles have ceased, it is observed that the specific causal factors of knowledge—the senses and so forth—do not transcend the restriction of their respective objects, and thus [the sentence alone] is incapable of producing it.

"Because they are not sense organs (*anindriyatvāt*). Nor is there a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason, on the grounds that light and so forth—though not sense organs—are observed to produce cognition; for what is intended [by the reason] is their non-inclusion in the causal complex of cognition (*jñānasāmagrī*) which has the sense organ as its primary factor. This is indicated by the phrase "in the causal complexes of cognition. Within the causal complexes of cognition, along with their accessories—namely, the sense organs, inferential marks (*liṅga*), words (*śabda*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*)—it is the sense organs themselves [that are meant]. The ellipsis to be supplied is "accompanied by light and so forth."

Furthermore, meditation cannot be the means for knowing the meaning of a sentence, because of mutual dependence: meditation would have that [meaning] as its object once the knowledge of the sentence-meaning has arisen, yet the knowledge of the sentence-meaning would arise only when meditation has been accomplished.

Furthermore, there is no difference in the object of meditation (*dhyāna*) and the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthajñāna*); for if that were the case, meditation would not be a means to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. Indeed, meditation upon one thing does not produce an orientation toward another. Since meditation consists of a continuous stream of recollection of a known object, it necessarily presupposes the prior knowledge of the meaning of the sentence; this is because there can be no other cause for the knowledge whose object is Brahman, the thing to be meditated upon.

Nor is it tenable to say that knowledge rooted in meditation (*dhyāna*) is produced by another statement, while the knowledge that brings about cessation is produced by statements such as "Thou art That" (*tattvamasi*). For is this knowledge rooted in meditation—which is produced by another statement—identical in object with the knowledge produced by the statement "Thou art That," or is it of a different object?
[In the former case] it is contradicted by those scriptures:
"When one has awakened, the marketplace is here; one would not experience suffering right here"; and "By this, the other is explained."
Thus, by this [statement], liberation through mere knowledge is refuted. Therefore, liberation in the form of the cessation of all distinctions is not possible for one who is still living.
If you say it is "by way of the purity of the mind," then it is exactly the same for me as well.
For me, however, knowledge arises through the scripture when the mind is pure.
If you argue that the causal complex for knowledge must be stated as being present in a pure mind, [I reply:]...
"But by your command, we say that for the mind, 'meditation'— the mind itself purified by the practice— is the means. If it is asked, 'By what is this understood?'"

Or rather, it is by your own actions that the mind becomes pure; and when the mind is pure, the scripture produces the knowledge that leads to liberation for one who has indeed turned away from all other objects through hearing, reflection, and meditation—how is this understood? [It is known] from such texts as: "They desire to know [Brahman] by means of sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting," and "It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
If you argue that this is established by such scriptural passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," then it is the same for me as well.
"It is to be heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon";
"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme";
"It is not grasped by the eye, nor even by speech."

"By means of a purified mind," "With the heart, with wisdom, and with the mind, one should conceive [Brahman]," and so forth— through such scriptural passages, it is understood that the mind becomes stainless through the application of meditation (*dhyāna-niyoga*), and the stainless mind generates direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman; thus, [the position] is faultless.

The meaning of the statement is: "That which is not expressed by speech, that by which speech is expressed. Otherwise, it would contradict the passage, "Know that very thing to be Brahman," and the injunction for meditation would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, through the very mandate of meditation, which has the direct realization of Brahman as its fruit, there occurs the cessation of the entire bondage consisting of the phenomenal world of the seer, the seen, and so forth, which is ultimately unreal.
It is perceived, for example, as in "this clay is a pot," or "the cow is spotted," or "the cow is hornless.

Furthermore, not a single entity of a uniform nature has ever been observed in the world. Nor is it seen that non-difference, like fire [consuming] grass and the like, annihilates difference; thus, there is no contradiction in the nature of things, because that which exists in the form of clay, gold, a cow, a horse, and so forth, likewise exists in the form of a pot, a crown, a fragment, a mare, and so forth. Nor is it the command of the Lord that the non-difference and difference of an object—whether non-distinct or distinct—are one and the same mode of being.

In an object standing before one, a difference in form is perceived, such that "this persists" and "this changes. Just as a cognition of unity arises regarding an effect and a particularity whose identity is already established, so too does an undifferentiated cognition of unity arise regarding that which possesses a cause and that which possesses a universal. In this very way, even among objects that are absolutely distinct in terms of place, time, and form, there arises the recognition: "This is that very same thing."

Therefore, since an object is perceived as consisting of all three aspects [universal, quality, and substance], the attempt to establish an absolute difference between cause and effect, or between genus and individual, is contradicted by direct experience.

This is incorrect. For indeed, only an uncontradicted cognition establishes the object in all cases. However, the notion "the self is the body of the gods and so forth," being contradicted by all means of valid knowledge whose scope is the true nature of the self—just like the cognition of a snake in a rope—it does not establish non-difference between the self and the body. In the case of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) such as "the spotted cow" or "the hornless cow," no contradiction is observed anywhere by anyone. Therefore, there is no over-extension of the principle.

Thus, because non-difference is heard in the *Brahmasūkta* within the *Saṃhitopaniṣad* of the Atharvaṇikas: "The eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many"; "The two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord";

"Another [cause] is seen as the cause of their conjunction through actions, qualities, and the qualities of the self"; "He is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the Lord, the master of the qualities, the cause of bondage, existence, and liberation from *saṃsāra*"; "He is the cause, the Lord of the lords of the senses."

Furthermore, because of scriptural declarations of difference such as: "One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6); "He who dwells in the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22); "Embraced by the conscious Self, one knows nothing that is external" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21); "Mounted by the conscious Self, he goes forth emitting [breath]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35); and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7), both difference and non-difference must necessarily be accepted for the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). In this regard:

From such scriptural passages as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," which declare that at the time of liberation the individual soul attains the very nature of Brahman, and from the prohibition of perceiving the Lord through duality at that time— namely, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"— it is understood that non-difference is innate.
From the scriptural statement, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," a distinction is perceived even then by virtue of the word "together" (*saha*). And the author will state later:
"Except for the activity of governing the world, because of the context and because of being non-proximate," and "Because of the indicative mark of equality in enjoyment alone."
Thus [it may be argued]. This is not so;
for [the scripture says], "There is no other seer but this."
