Because the difference between selves is prohibited by hundreds of such scriptural passages;

for the statement, "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," means that he enjoys Brahman along with all desires—that is, he enjoys Brahman endowed with all attributes. Otherwise, by the phrase "together with Brahman," the subordination of Brahman would result.

Regarding the phrase "except for the activity of governing the world," it will be stated that if the liberated one were to remain in a state of distinction [from Brahman], there would be the undesirable consequence of a deficiency in his sovereignty. Otherwise, [it is said]:
"Having attained [union], he emerges [in his own form], because of the scriptural statement."

Because of contradictions [with scripture] due to such [statements as these], therefore non-difference alone is natural. The difference among individual souls (jīvas) from the supreme Brahman and among themselves, however, is caused by the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the intellect, the senses, and the body.

Although Brahman is partless and all-pervading, nevertheless, just as space appears divided by jars and other objects, so too does difference occur in Brahman through the limiting adjuncts of the intellect and so forth.

Because there would be no further limiting adjuncts for the adjuncts themselves, and because an infinite regress would result if such were admitted; therefore, it is held that the limiting adjuncts arise from Brahman as being of a nature both different and non-different [from it].

Therefore, in accordance with the karma of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is stated here: the collection of Vedāntic statements is intended for the injunction of meditating upon Brahman, which is non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). Through these Vedāntic statements, non-duality (*abheda*) is perceived. Duality is perceived through the ritual scriptures (*karmaśāstra*) which rely on difference, as well as by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge. Since duality and non-duality are mutually contradictory, and because the perception of duality can be accounted for as being rooted in beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*), it has been stated that non-duality alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Regarding what was stated there—that because both difference and non-difference are established by perception, there is no contradiction—that is incorrect. For, indeed, the state of being distinct from something is difference; its opposite is non-difference. Who that is not insane would assert the possibility of these two, which consist of being such and not being such, existing in one and the same thing?

If it is argued that there is no contradiction due to the difference in aspects—namely, non-difference in the form of the cause and the genus, and difference in the form of the effect and the individual—then [the response follows].

No; because it cannot withstand analysis. For one who asserts "non-contradiction" on the grounds of a difference in aspects (*ākāra*), does the intention mean that there is difference in one aspect and non-difference in another aspect? Or rather, that both [difference and non-difference] pertain to the entity itself as it possesses those two aspects?

"Distinctness" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) means "otherness. For the cognition regarding difference and non-difference takes the form: "This is not that," and "This is that. Regarding the phrase "of those two": the term "difference-and-non-difference" (*bhedābheda*) is not the name of any single property. If the meaning of the word "difference-and-non-difference" is accepted as being in accordance with worldly convention, then the contradiction between existence and non-existence is unavoidable—this is the sense. Furthermore, by this [position], it cannot be asserted that there is no contradiction anywhere.

This is because the three types of contradiction—namely, having different substrates (*bhinnādhāratva*), non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), and the relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer (*nāśyanāśakabhāva*)—are observed [in this case]. If there were no contradiction between existence and non-existence, then there would likewise be no contradiction even between one's own words and the words of others, such as when it is said, "It is both different and not different. By the phrase "in the form of the cause" (*kāraṇātmanā*), he restates the opponent’s claim that the difference and non-difference between two lumps [of clay] are not contradictory due to the difference in their forms (*ākāra*). In the expression "in a single form," the word *ākāra* refers to an entity (*padārtha*). In the former alternative—that there is difference residing in the individual (*vyakti*) and non-difference residing in the genus (*jāti*)—it does not belong to a single [entity].
If it is argued that the threefold nature—
consisting of the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*)— would result in the abandonment of the restriction [of these being distinct],
then [we reply]: no, because of the difference in their forms (*ākāra-bheda*).
And it has been stated that in the first case, being distinct from one another and its opposite are contradictory.

In the second alternative, however—namely, that there are two forms mutually distinct from each other and an object which is their substratum remains unperceived—even if the third position is accepted, only the mutual distinctness of the three would be established; how then could there be non-difference?

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the two forms are being superimposed upon the underlying substance (*vastu*), which serves as their substratum, such that the substance is both different and non-different [from them]—then how can the two forms, which are distinct from themselves and reside in their own substratum, serve as the means for reconciling the coexistence of two contradictory attributes within that same [substance] according to the first alternative? In this regard, there are three possible alternatives concerning the relationship between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*): are they mutually different, non-different, or both different and non-different? Regarding the first alternative—that [the universal] resides in the individual—he refutes the first of these options.

"Regarding the word *ekasmin* (in one), he refutes the third [alternative]. The meaning is that the contradiction between existence and non-existence—namely, that "the universal is both the individual and not the individual"—remains precisely as it was. Furthermore, regarding the phrase *apratipannaṃ ca* (and unperceived): here, the fact that a third entity distinct from the universal and the individual is unperceived constitutes an additional defect. This is what is intended by the expression *apratipannaṃ ca*. The phrase *na punar* (but not) means that otherwise, there would be an absence of a triad."

Regarding the phrase "by means of two aspects": here, with respect to the third entity, he raises the objection that there is no contradiction because difference and non-difference can be established through two aspects. These two aspects involve three alternatives: is this [entity] different from its own substratum, or non-different, or both different and non-different? He refutes the first alternative, beginning with "from itself."

For contradiction exists by virtue of having a single substratum (*ekāśrayatva*). Indeed, the two forms that serve as the mediators of non-contradiction cannot themselves be the substrata of difference and non-difference; therefore, they do not mediate non-contradiction. [Otherwise] the two forms residing in fire—tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) and brilliance (*aujjvalya*)—would become cold and hot within the fire! How much more so in the case of that which is non-distinct?
Furthermore, if one accepts a threefold nature (*tryātmakatva*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement for further mediators.

Nor does a cognition of a single form arise regarding an object that possesses a universal, in the same way as there is a cognition of a single individual that is commonly recognized; for every cognition everywhere occurs precisely as a relation between a qualifier (*prakāra*) and a qualified (*prakārin*), in the form "this is such-and-such. In that case, the aspect of the qualifier is the universal (*jāti*), while the aspect of the qualified is the individual (*vyakti*); thus, there is no cognition of a single form.

For this very reason, it is also impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be both different and non-different from Brahman. Therefore, since non-difference is rooted in scripture that cannot be explained otherwise, the cognition of difference has its source solely in beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*).

[Objection: If this is so, then Brahman itself would possess "ignorance," and defects such as birth, old age, and death—which are rooted in that [ignorance]—would belong to the two-fold form and its possessor.
It is evident;
and therefore:
"He who is omniscient is all-knowing."
Otherwise, scriptural passages such as "This Self is free from evil" would be contradicted.

For one who does not admit any entity other than Brahman, the association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) within Brahman itself, and the defects resulting therefrom—such as being a transmigrating soul (*jīva*) or being subject to death—would exist in reality. Indeed, limiting adjuncts associated with the partless and indivisible Brahman do not associate with it by cutting or piercing it; rather, having joined with the very nature of Brahman, they perform their respective functions within that very [Brahman].

If one should think: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). It is of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), and its atomicity is due to the atomicity of the mind (*manas*), which serves as the limiting adjunct. Furthermore, this limitation is beginningless (*anādi*). Thus, defects that attach to the 'portion' (*aṃśa*)—which is Brahman as conditioned by adjuncts—do not attach to the supreme Brahman, which is unconditioned."

One must ask: Is the individual soul (*jīva*) a fragment of Brahman cut off by a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), resembling an atom? Or is it a specific portion of Brahman that remains uncut but is joined with an atomic-sized adjunct? Or is it the very nature of Brahman itself as joined with an adjunct? Or is it a distinct conscious entity joined with an adjunct? Or is it the adjunct alone?
Since Brahman is indivisible, the first alternative is not tenable.

It might be argued: "Cutting is indeed the making twofold of that which was one. Furthermore, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is partless (*niravayava*), cutting—such as that of a finger—is impossible; thus, Brahman is indivisible (*acchedya*), and its cause is partlessness. [The text says] "as if divided" (*bhittveva*); this means that even though it is not actually cut, there is a distinction according to specific locations, like the hands and feet. The meaning is that limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not affect Brahman through either spatial division or actual cutting, because of its partlessness and its indivisibility.

If one were to think thus, there might arise the suspicion that—like space—the existence of both faultiness and faultlessness is possible through the distinction between the conditioned and unconditioned aspects. To avoid the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—namely, that the state of being a *jīva* arises from the limitation by adjuncts (*upādhi*), while the limitation by adjuncts arises from the state of being a *jīva*, and that the state of being a *jīva* arises from karma, and karma [arises] from that [state of being a *jīva*]—it is stated that [the *jīva*] is "beginningless" (*anādi*).
*J* [end of fragment].

"This is what must be asked. The third alternative arises because the word *aṇu* (atomic) in the Śruti can possibly intend the sense of "subtle" (*sūkṣma*). The fourth and fifth alternatives were formulated with the intention that there is no other way [to resolve the difficulty] than through these two; they are not based on the opponent's own admission. The fourth alternative is based on the fact that the word *brahman* is used figuratively (*upacāra*) even for the individual soul (*jīva*). The fifth alternative is based on the admission that the individual soul and Brahman are both different and non-different (*bhedābheda*).

In the second alternative, however, all defects would belong to Brahman alone due to its connection with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) at a specific location. Since it is impossible for the limiting adjunct, as it moves, to pull along that portion of Brahman with which it is conjoined, there would be a difference in the portions of Brahman conjoined with the adjunct at every moment; thus, bondage and liberation would occur moment by moment. Furthermore, if there were such a pulling, since Brahman is indivisible, the entire Brahman would have to be pulled.
If it is argued that pulling is not possible for that which is partless and all-pervading— [The response follows: ... [the text continues with the refutation of this objection].

In that case, if it is the adjunct (*upādhi*) itself that moves, the very same fault mentioned previously would arise. Furthermore, since all adjuncts are in contact with unbroken regions of Brahman—and since all individual souls (*jīvas*) are portions of Brahman itself—there would be a recognition [of identity] among them due to their oneness. Conversely, if there were no such recognition because of the difference in spatial locations, then even for a single soul, there would be no recognition when its own adjunct moves.

In the third alternative, however, because the very nature of Brahman would descend to the state of being a *jīva* through its connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there would be no establishment of an unconditioned Brahman distinct from that [jīva]. Furthermore, there would be only one single *jīva* in all bodies.
In the fourth alternative, however—that the *jīva* is indeed other than Brahman—the conditioned nature of the distinction between *jīvas* would have to be abandoned.
And in the final case, the position of the Cārvākas alone would be accepted.

Therefore, although the authority of a scripture resides solely in its purpose of enjoining activity or cessation from activity, it is nonetheless established that the Vedānta passages possess authority regarding the nature of Brahman as being supplementary to the injunction for meditation.

That too is incorrect; for even if the Vedānta passages were subordinate to an injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*), it would be impossible for them to lack authority regarding the reality of their meaning.

What is meant is this: do the sentences whose scope is the nature of Brahman attain authority regarding the nature of Brahman by entering into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with an injunction for meditation, or are they independent?

If they constitute a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*), it is impossible for there to be an intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the nature of Brahman, because the focus would be on the injunction to meditate (*dhyāna-vidhi*). If they are separate sentences (*bhinnavākyatva*), then due to the absence of any purpose consisting of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), they would simply lack the capacity to produce knowledge. Nor should it be argued: "Meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of a continuous flow of memory (*smṛti-santati*); and since that is defined solely by the object to be remembered, when the injunction to meditate requires a specific object to be remembered, [the texts provide it]:
'That which is this Self,' 'Brahman, the experiencer of all,' and 'Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite.'"

"That too is incorrect" means that not only is this theory of an injunction for the removal of the manifold (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa-vidhi*) untenable, but this view as well is untenable; such is the sense of the word "also" (*api*). Regarding the phrase "this has been stated": if [the Upanishads] were subordinate to an injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*), how could there be an incompatibility with their having the reality of the object as their purport? Or, setting aside subordination to an injunction, would they possess authority regarding Brahman independently? To this, the answer is: "unity of statement"—that is, unity of statement within the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).
[The objection is that the Upanishads] lack the capacity to produce understanding; for it would be impossible to engage in hearing [the texts] and so forth if they were difficult to accomplish.

Nor should it be argued—anticipating the objection that Brahman might be established as a subordinate element of an injunction under the view that [the Upanishads] form a single syntactical unit—with regard to the injunction for meditation. In injunctions of "seeing" such as "One should meditate on Name as Brahman," even though the substantive (the object of meditation) is real, the unreality of the qualifying attribute makes the unreality of the qualified whole unavoidable.

Passages such as these establish the essential nature and specific attributes of Brahman. Consequently, having attained syntactic unity with them, they serve as authoritative means for the existence of that reality—
even though the injunction to meditate requires a specific object to be remembered—
such as "Brahman" by name.

Thus, according to the rule for such modes of viewing, since the accomplishment of meditation is possible even through an unreal specific object, there is no dependence upon the reality of the object of meditation.

Therefore—the Vedānta passages being devoid of the purpose of instigating activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation from activity (*nivṛtti*); even if they were subordinate to injunctions for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*), they would terminate merely in presenting the essential nature of the object to be meditated upon; and even if they were independent, like sentences used to console one afflicted by illness, their capacity to culminate in the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) would be established through knowledge alone—[it follows that] since they lack the scope of the reality of an already accomplished entity (*pariniṣpanna-vastu-satyatā*), it is not possible for Brahman to have the scripture as its means of valid cognition (*śāstra-pramāṇaka*). This is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*).

Regarding this, it is stated: "But that [is established] because of the concordance" (*tattu samanvayāt*). "Concordance" (*samanvaya*) means "perfect concordance," which signifies "concordance by way of being the goal of human endeavor. Since Brahman—which is the supreme goal of human endeavor and whose nature is unsurpassed, unsurpassable bliss—is concordant as the subject matter [of the scripture], the meaning is that its status as being established by the authority of the scripture is indeed proven.

One who asserts that a collection of sentences does not culminate in a purpose because it lacks the intent to prompt engagement or desist from action, states that for a person living in the royal court, there is a lack of purpose in entering the lairs of hunting dogs.

This is what is meant: for all those beginningless knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*)—whether gods, asuras, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, kiṃnaras, kiṃpuruṣas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, humans, beasts, birds, reptiles, trees, shrubs, creepers, or *dūrvā* grass—who are distinguished by gender (female, male, or neuter), whose true nature as the higher and lower principles is concealed and enveloped by ignorance in the form of beginningless karma, who possess specific objects of experience characterized as "fixed, sustaining, and nourishing," and for whom there is no distinction from the liberated ones and from oneself.

A statement that brings about the realization—"The Supreme Brahman exists"—which generates an unsurpassed and infinite bliss through its own nature, its qualities, its majesty, and its activities, is indeed effective in achieving its purpose. However, a statement centered on engagement or avoidance does not achieve its purpose until it conveys a connection with the goals of human life.
In response to the inquiry, "How is such supreme Brahman attained?"—
one who dwells in the royal palace, is born into the royal family, or is an intimate of the royal household;
*kauleyakas* are dogs.

This refers to those who live off dogs or to the Mlecchas. Regarding the phrase "the vow is devoid of purpose": the meaning is that it is untenable to state that a statement directed toward the supreme human goal—which is inherently infinite—is devoid of purpose.

Regarding the phrase "beginningless karma": the intention is that because experience is obstructed by karmas, the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) lack knowledge of that [nature] as being for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), and not due to any deficiency in that [nature] itself. The enumeration of gods, asuras, and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating their fixed states of experience. The expression "the possibility of experience" is stated to dispel the doubt regarding non-perception of the capable; for the suitability of an object for cognition would not be possible without its suitability for that [cognition].

Therefore, by the statement that [Brahman] generates an unsurpassed and infinite bliss, it is established that Brahman possesses an unsurpassed and infinite suitability [for being an end]. By the phrase "consisting of its own nature" (*svarūparūpa*) and so forth, its state of being an object of enjoyment in every respect is shown; thereby, its status as the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is established. By the phrase "in activity" (*pravṛtti*) and so forth, the deficiency of activity and cessation as human goals is stated; for [activity] is to be adopted only because it is a means to a small portion of desired pleasure, and because, being of the nature of suffering, it lacks inherent enjoyability.

"Of such a nature" means that even indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is of the nature of bliss; therefore, sentences whose primary purpose is to describe the essential nature of reality (*svarūpa*) necessarily culminate in the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Consequently, for one who desires the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of that [nature], even those sentences enjoining meditation (*dhyāna*)—which make known the means to that realization—are not fruitless. As for the phrase "just as," etc.: although it is thus the case that even a sentence producing indirect knowledge culminates in the human goal—as in "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world"—[the subsequent texts serve a specific purpose].

Thus, by means of words such as "feeling" (*vedanā*) and so forth, meditation is enjoined as a means for attaining Brahman. This is just as when, upon hearing the statement "There is a treasure in your own house," one learns of the existence of the treasure and, being satisfied, subsequently exerts effort toward its acquisition; or as when a certain prince, addicted to childish play, having departed from the royal palace, strayed from the path and was declared "lost" by the king, yet remained unaware of his own father and was raised by a certain eminent brāhmaṇa.

Having mastered the Vedas and the Shastras, you remain at sixteen years of age, a mine of all auspicious virtues. Your father, the sovereign of all the world, endowed with the qualities of profundity, magnanimity, affection, good conduct, heroism, valor, and prowess, desires to see only you, his lost son. Therefore, it is appropriate for him to engage in meditation with a view toward a specific result, just as it is said: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darsha-Purnamasa."

The intention is as follows: in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," although each individual rite—such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa—is a means to heaven, the commencement of another action and the repetition of the same action are both justified by the expectation of a specific result; just as, for example, even one who has experienced joy upon hearing of the birth of a son may subsequently act out of a desire for the pleasure of beholding his face, so too is it here.

The two analogies of the treasure-trove (*nidhi*) and the prince (*rājakumāra*) are stated to demonstrate that, through the distinction between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the quality of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) residing in both is present in Brahman. This is based on the Śruti text: "Just as [one finds] a treasure-trove of gold... The term "prince" indicates kingship in the Lord and sonship in sentient beings; here, the analogy of Kuśa and Lava applies. "Addicted to play" refers to the inclination of sentient beings toward external objects. "Departed" refers to [the departure from] the Lord’s...

"Being outside the ether" refers to the attainment of the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*). "One who has strayed from the path" indicates the absence of connection with the means such as ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). "Nurtured by the best of the twice-born" refers to the relationship with a teacher (*ācārya*) who brings about the completion of study and other practices that serve as the cause for achieving the fitness for the perfection of knowledge of the Lord. "Sixteen years old" refers to the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). "A mine of virtues" refers to being filled with those qualities favored by the Lord. By the words "your father," and so forth, [the text refers to] the multitude of the Lord's qualities.

"Profundity and so forth" refers to the qualities conducive to accessibility (*saulabhya*) with respect to the devotee (*upāsaka*). "Valour and so forth" are included within "otherness" (*paratva*). Profundity (*gāmbhīrya*) is the disregard for the lightness of the gift and the weightiness of what is being given. Magnanimity (*audārya*) is the state of possessing the realization that "the gift has been made," devoid of the conceptual distinction between giver and recipient; or it is the disposition of thinking, even after giving away one's own self and possessions, "my debt has increased like a friend. Affection (*vātsalya*) is the perception of faults as virtues, as in a mother toward her calf.

Good character (*suśīlatva*) indeed consists in having a nature of close intimacy with the great even when they are dull-witted; possessing that quality is *sauśīlya*. Heroism (*śaurya*) is the capacity to enter into the midst of enemies as if in one’s own home; for heroism is the opposite of cowardice. Prowess (*vīrya*) is tirelessness. Valor (*parākrama*) is valorous exertion. Although not explicitly mentioned here, fortitude (*dhairya*) is also included—the regarding of oneself as mere straw even when being assailed by enemies.

If he hears a statement uttered by some most eminent person, "He resides in the best of cities," then at that very moment, he becomes filled with unsurpassed joy, thinking, "I have a living son, and my father possesses all wealth.

And the king, having heard that his son is alive, healthy, of exceedingly beautiful appearance, and one who has mastered everything to be known, feels as though he has attained all human goals; thereafter, he strives to recover him, and finally, the two are reunited. Thus it is.

Furthermore, as for the claim that a statement concerning an established reality possesses validity regarding the existence of its object—even if the fulfillment of human purpose occurs through mere knowledge of it, like a statement used to entice children or the sick—that is incorrect. For when the non-existence of an object is ascertained, even an object known [by such a statement] does not lead to human purpose. Even in the case of children, the sick, and others, the arising of joy and so forth is due to the delusion regarding the existence of the object. If, while that very cognition exists for them, an ascertainment of the non-existence of the object were to arise, then at that very moment their joy and other emotions would cease.

Furthermore, if it were certain that even the Upaniṣadic statements lack the intent to establish the existence of Brahman, then even when knowledge of Brahman were attained, there would be no culmination in the supreme human goal.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "That from which these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1) should be contemplated as referring to the sole cause of the entire universe, which is free from even a trace of all defects and possesses attributes such as omniscience and the realization of true intentions. The Lord’s intention is expressed by the words "desirous of seeing" and "that great-souled one is very difficult to find. By the term "in the best of cities," his dwelling within the body known as the City of Brahman is indicated. By the word "most proficient," the Guru who imparts the knowledge of the Lord is meant. Through the phrase "he becomes one who has attained... [the text] establishes that the purpose of the statement is fully realized.
Therefore, the rule that the purpose must culminate solely in being directed toward an object that prompts action is refuted.

Regarding the phrase "the existence or non-existence of the object": this statement refers to the subject (*pakṣa*), or it applies commonly to both the subject and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The nature of being a reason (*hetutva*) is implied. The meaning is that when there is no certainty regarding the existence or non-existence of the object, there is no culmination in the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). The word "entire" (*nikhila*) expresses the meaning of the causal statements; the word "entire" is intended to indicate that even ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, which are considered eternal by opponents, are actually effects. The word "one" (*eka*) in the phrase "single cause" indicates the identity of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*).

It is thus established that [the scripture] teaches that Brahman exists, which is a mine of infinite auspicious qualities and is characterized by unsurpassed, limitless bliss. [Thus ends the section of four aphorisms in the first chapter of the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad-Rāmānuja.

[The definition of validity consists in] being the producer of a valid cognition regarding the Supreme Brahman, the sublation of its contrary, and the removal of invalidity which opposes validity; [and] the enjoyment of the fruit—that is, the fruit resulting from—that very meditation.

*Saṃrādhana*—the worship of the Lord in the form of knowledge, and the attainment of the experience of Brahman; these four objects of knowledge (*prameya*), consisting of reality (*tattva*), welfare (*hita*), and the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), have been thoroughly and skillfully reflected upon—that is, investigated and determined.

By the third—that is, by the third chapter—(in due order) the following have been investigated and determined: the state of being possessed of defects (*sadoṣatva*) on the part of the individual soul (*jīva*), that is, the embodied self, meaning its susceptibility to what is not the goal of man (*apuruṣārtha*); the state of being free from defects (*adoṣatva*) on the part of the Supreme (*para*), the Supreme Self, meaning the absence of any connection with what is not the goal of man; the worship of the Supreme (*paropāsti*), which is meditation on the Supreme Person in the form of knowledge (*vidyā*); and also the "how-to" (*itikartavyatā*), consisting of the duties pertaining to caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) and so forth, which are to be performed as auxiliary parts of that knowledge. || 5 ||

I swear—that is, I make a solemn oath—by the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Mahālakṣmī. I consider this manifestation of power like my own—the public display of a strength such as ours in the world—to be merely the flapping of mosquitoes; I know it for certain to be equivalent to the power of gnats.

The splendor of the words of the best of ascetics, Rāmānuja—the lord of self-restraint—is ever vigilant; it remains constantly active and unwearied. It is exceedingly capable of unimpededly dispelling the masses of people who speak in opposition to the true meaning, being skillful in the unobstructed destruction of the host of adversaries. While I am utterly incapable, this splendor of his speech brings glory—spreading the renown of victory—and remains perpetually awake. || 2 ||

Indeed, what loss is there to us on the path of poetry, O Gautama? Nor do we possess familiarity with the system of Kaṇāda or the philosophy of Kumārila, nor even with the scriptures of the Guru’s school or other such treatises; nevertheless, the effortless speech of the illustrious Yatīśvara brings us victory everywhere. Adhikaraṇasārāvali,
composed by the venerable Great Teacher Nigamānta Mahādeśika.
This work was composed by Veṅkaṭeśa, whose intellect is sharpened by his capacity to endure all things, and who possesses right vision through the grace of the venerable Varadācārya and Rāmānuja;

it is to be served with the faculty of hearing by those of peaceful mind or those seeking the attainment of peace—a mass of *sragdharā* verses, naturally endowed with many virtues, which has proven effective in its bodily task. || 2 ||

In this Śārīraka-śāstra, there are [the faults of] redundancy and contradiction of what has already been stated—redundancy being the fruitless restatement of a matter already expressed, and contradiction being the statement of something contrary to a matter determined by logic; as well as dullness and incoherence—meaning meager utility and weakness of reasoning—and likewise, lack of consistency between preceding and succeeding parts.

And [the dawn] dispels the absence of a subject-matter—the failure to resolve doubts already encountered—and fruitlessness, which consists in the lack of purpose or the pursuit of an unintended purpose; as well as sublation by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and contradiction by other authorities. It uplifts those seekers who are distressed by mental exhaustion caused by the inability to distinguish between the primary matter to be determined and its supporting details, who are bewildered regarding the directions like those suffering from disorientation, and whose hearts are withered; rising at dawn, it shines forth like the rays of the sun.

Like a row of rays from the sun, the lord of the Śreṇikas, it stands as if having entered the heart—touching the heart rather than merely reaching the ears; this delightful garland of verses (*padyāvalī*), existing in the intellect as something yet to be composed, shall gladden those who have been made attentive and free from negligence. || 3 ||

Regarding the meaning of the Vedas, which is to be investigated through reasoning, the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) was first understood by means of the instruments of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
then, [the section on knowledge] was treated by means of application (*prayukti*), sequential arrangement (*kramaviracana*), subordination (*adhikāra*), and extended application (*atideśa*).
Therein, subsequently, by means of all its specific attributes following after it, and by means of the limbs obtained through differentiation according to their respective applications.
Then, by means of the Tantra and through its application, there follows the fourfold definition concerning the meaning of the deity.

In the *Nyāyacintya*—that which is to be determined after first establishing the principles of logic—concerning the threefold subject matter expounded by the Veda, consisting of ritual action (*karman*), deities (*devatā*), and Brahman: first, at the outset, the category of ritual action—the collection of activities such as sacrifice—is [established] through the means of proof (*pramāṇa*), that is, through the distinctions such as "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth, which indicate the differences in the essential nature of the rituals.

By means of the authorities that establish the Dharma, such as injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like; by means of the application (*viniyoga*), which consists of the relationship between the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*), serving as the motivator for the performance of ritual acts, and consisting of *śruti* and other forms that determine the sequence of actions; furthermore, by means of qualification (*adhikāra*), which is denoted by the term "entitlement" and consists of the desire for results and so forth; and by means of extended application (*atideśa*), which is the principle known as extension that causes what is prescribed in one place to apply elsewhere—even in that case of extended application.

With all [its] specificities—in their entirety, including every intermediate division; thereafter—that is, subsequently, in the ninth [book]; by means of that which follows it—the one called *ūha*, whose nature is obtained through extended application (*atideśa*); by means of exceptions (*prāptabādha*)—those which set aside meanings obtained through extended application; by means of *tantra*—in the form of a single performance suitable for two types of benefit; and then by means of *prasaṅga*—in the form of the accomplishment of another through incidental occurrence due to a necessary performance—he has been understood—his nature having been determined.

Following that—occurring immediately thereafter—is the *Catur-lakṣaṇī*, consisting of four chapters, which concerns the deity (*devatārthā*). It is useful for determining the true nature of the deity who is to be propitiated through ritual action, the non-difference [of the self] from that deity, the method of worshiping that deity, and the fruits thereof;
it employs the "limbs" (*aṅgaiḥ*), namely *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth.
Mīmāṃsā arises through the loss of purpose and other such factors.

Since unrighteousness is slight, the goal is stable, the objects of the senses have been pacified, and one is engaged with such a venerable teacher—therefore, from this point on, Brahman, which possesses manifold greatness, must be investigated in the section concerning the embodied soul (*śārīraka*). Why should one not first abandon ritual action and undertake the inquiry into Brahman by means of the understanding attained through the complete study of the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs? To that, we reply: because it would be contradicted by the scriptural injunction for the simultaneous performance of both. (Verse 6)
Regarding the *trivarga*— the group consisting of *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*— there is *prāvaṇya*, which is attachment;
this is because [these acts] are also limbs of worship (*upāsanā*),
[occurring] first, that is, prior to [other rites].
Also because it brings about the practice of Brahman-worship for those belonging to the [four] castes and [four] stages of life,
it serves as an exposition of the entire meaning of the Veda.

The fruitfulness of the undertaking: for those qualified [to study], there is success in their initial engagement with this scripture—in this form of exposition, in this Mīmāṃsā-śāstra. This fixed order of sequence, this arrangement of priority and posteriority, should occur precisely by following the primary order—that is, the order existing within the Veda which is to be explained. In this Mīmāṃsā-śāstra, first of all, the subject matter consisting of validity (*prāmāṇya*) and so forth must be investigated and determined through reasoning; likewise, before the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is known—[as in the passage] "That very [Ātman]... [and so on].

Prior even to the meaning consisting of meditation, which is propounded by such sentences as "They desire to know," the subject matter—the meaning in the form of rituals such as sacrifice, which is expressed by words contained within those very sentences, such as "by sacrifice" and "by charity"—is to be investigated; likewise, prior to the illustrative examples (dṛṣṭānta) cited in various places as the objects of comparison (upameya), that is, as the subjects of the analogy (dāṣṭantika) according to the *Śārīraka-sūtras*, and prior to the meanings stated in the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā* which serve as the points of comparison (upamāna), the "honey" (madhu) is to be investigated.
If a sweet and essential object were to be found right nearby in one's own garden, why would one go toward a mountain situated far from the house— for what purpose would one go?

Some have explained that the *Karmamīmāṃsā* itself is the prerequisite for the *Śārīraka*; others [have explained] that the destruction of the three-fold suffering is the prerequisite. However, the Veda declares that the fourfold means of attainment are the prerequisite for this section (*kāṇḍa*), as they are the fruit of the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*).
For the study of the scripture together with its auxiliary branches gives rise to the subject matter; what occasion is there here for other treatises?
This sequence is established by propriety, and is not further constrained by an explicit injunction.

Certain [commentators]—namely the followers of Yādavaprakāśa—have explained the "destruction of the threefold affliction" (the impact of the three types of suffering mentioned in Sāṃkhya) as the subject matter established at the outset in this *Śārīraka-kāṇḍa*, which is to be commenced; they have specifically propounded that the meaning of the word *atha* (*then*) is the object that serves as the antecedent to its logical sequence (*ānantarya*). Others—the Advaitins—[propound] the fourfold means: discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, the perfection of the means such as tranquility and self-restraint, and so forth.

Dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, and the desire for liberation—this is the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). The *Nigama*, that is, the Śruti, declares through such statements as "having examined the worlds" (*parīkṣya lokān*) that both of these aforementioned pairs are the fruit of reflection on action—that is, they are dependent upon the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*). For indeed, the study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅgādhyayana*)—meaning study accompanied by the auxiliaries such as phonetics (*śikṣā*)—produces a superficial knowledge (*viṣaya*) of the subject matter;
[only after this] is there an occasion or scope for the study of other systems (*tantrāntara*), such as the Sāṃkhya and others.

Where?—that is, in what respect? This sequence—the prior and posterior relationship between the Mīmāṃsā of Action (Karma) and the Mīmāṃsā of Brahman—is established by propriety—that is, conceived merely by considering their fitness—and not, however, joined with an injunction; it is certainly not scriptural (vaidha). || 8 ||

The attainment of that which is eternally present and indistinguishable from the golden necklace already around one's neck occurs by removing what is false through the perception of its source in the fragments of scripture; where, then, is action of any use? Even the mention of its being the "opponent" [of knowledge] is merely a figurative description of my own view.
The manner of responding to the chatter "It has been attained here" has been explained in detail. || 9 ||
Some accepted the Mīmāṃsā; others—those who maintain the non-dualism of Brahman devoid of distinctions—held it to be such.

They considered the *Rāhukalpa*—which is like the planet denoted by the word *rāhu*—to be the very *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā*, which consists of the investigation into the head (*śiras*) of the three Vedas. [This was done] by those whose intellects were robbed of clarity by internal contradictions—that is, by those whose wisdom was destroyed by contradictions imagined by their own fancy between the two scriptures—and who, for that very reason, were wandering about with erroneous understandings; and along with both kinds of those who consider themselves Mīmāṃsakas, who are slightly less than being outside the Veda (*bāhya*), what is the use of such a futile effort?

What is the purpose? Since it is established without dispute that the entire Veda is to be studied, let aside for a moment the impulsion of one's own injunctions or the injunctions of others; whether the study of the Veda is prompted by the injunction for study itself, or whether it is prompted by the injunction for teaching—let it be whatever it may be.

When there is a comprehension of the entire surface-level meaning—that is, when a superficial knowledge of the whole meaning of the Veda has been established—why would those of perfected intellect, who are discerning, not undertake a comprehensive reflection—that is, a thorough investigation of the entire meaning of the Veda? Why indeed would they not do so? They certainly would. || 10 ||

If it is argued that because of the various distinctions of specific qualities (*vaiśiṣṭya*) and so forth, the deities mentioned in the first section are distinct, then how can such a mere discrepancy in nomenclature lead to the destruction of what has been studied as being to be sacrificed?
For here, in a ritual application where the offerings are different, this difference in the form of the object to be designated (*uddeśya*) is indeed [the cause].
But weakness [is established] on the basis of substance (dravyataḥ) because of the deity's finality in the sequence of the [sacrificial] materials. 12.

And so forth; since this has been demonstrated in many ways—that is, in numerous manners—therefore, for that very reason, *atra*—in the case of the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*) and the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-mīmāṃsā*)—there is *aikaśāstryam*: a unity of composition based on their being a single field of knowledge (*vidyā-sthāna*). The phrase "forced" (*haṭhakṛtam*) means that [this unity] is merely imagined through dogmatic insistence and is not natural; such is the intention [of the opponent]. But this is not incorrect. (Why? Because of the dialogue with Brahmā regarding the existence of Brahman, there is a consensus of opinion (*abhiprāyaikyam*) on that matter, as Jaimini says: "The highest [is the goal], according to Jaimini."

Because [the meaning] is firm in such passages, the removal of contradiction—the resolution of apparent contradictions—is indeed established even between the two sections, namely the *Karmakāṇḍa* and the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, just as it is within the six chapters and so forth contained in the *Karmakāṇḍa*. This is because there is the attainment of the removal of the delusion produced by statements with hidden intentions intended to refute outsiders, and the attainment of knowledge according to reality;
thus, it would be like [the consistency within] a single section.
The state of having a single ruler is free from obstruction. || 13 ||

In the *Vṛtti* text, the *Saṅkarṣa* is presented as having been composed by Jaimini as part of the sixteen-chapter work; yet how can the statement in the *Tattvaratnākara*—that it originated from Kāśakṛtsna—be justified? To this we reply: we do not intend here to pointlessly refute a well-stated claim. Rather, a reconciliation through figurative usage (*upacāra*) is possible in some cases, for there is indeed a unity of intent (*ekatātparya*) in the connection [between the two]. || 17 ||

In the Vṛtti-grantha—that is, in the Vṛtti on the two Mīmāṃsās of Bodhāyana—the portion consisting of sixteen chapters, which takes the form of an inquiry into ritual action (*karma*) and deities (*devatā*), is recorded as having been composed by Jaimini; that is, it is mentioned as being authored by the sage Jaimini. (This being the case,) [there is] the Saṅkarṣa.

"The section concerning the investigation of deities (*devatā-vicāra-bhāga*), consisting of four chapters, is of the origin of Kāśakṛtsna"—meaning it was composed by the sage Kāśakṛtsna—such is the statement from the *Tattvaratnākara*, the words of Bhaṭṭa Parāśarapāda. How, or in what manner, could this be correct? When such an objection arises, we reply: we declare there is no contradiction between the two statements; for among these two authoritative utterances of experts, one or the other might be "vain" (i.e., erroneous) only in the absence of a decisive, powerful means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to determine the truth.

"To refute"—that is, to declare [the other] invalid—persons such as we are are not capable. "To determine"—we are not entitled to do so, because we are contemporaries of neither of those two authors. However, as for the "resolution"—the establishment of the validity of both statements—it occurs in some cases by way of "metaphorical usage" (*upacāra*), that is, by considering the sense to be secondary (*gauṇa*). There is a "conjunction of a single intention," meaning that their underlying purports are non-contradictory; for indeed, this is consistent and appropriate. || 15 ||

The intention of the experts (*tāntrika*) is that, provided they serve the purpose of the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇārtha-upayogitva*) and are immediately subsequent (*anantaratva*—that is, occurring without an intervening interval), one should not postulate a division of sections (*adhikaraṇabheda*)—that is, a multiplicity of sections—on account of minor purposes (*alpasārair atyalpaiḥ prayojanair nimittabhūtaiḥ*), just as in the case of dice (*akṣaiḥ*).

—by the number eleven through the *indriyas* (senses); by the waves (*ūrmibhiḥ*)—through the sixfold number consisting of hunger and so forth; by the directions (*āśābhiḥ*)—through the tenfold number residing in the quarters; by the serpents (*ahibhiḥ*)—through the eightfold number residing in the snakes; by the quarters (*kāṣṭhābhiḥ*)—through the tenfold number established in the directions; by the elephants (*dviradaiḥ*)—through the eightfold number residing in the world-elephants of the directions; by the sages (*munibhiḥ*)—through the sevenfold number perceived by the seven seers (*saptarṣi*); by the Vasus (*vasubhiḥ*)—through the eightfold number consisting of the eight Vasus; and by the waves (*ūrmibhiḥ*)—through the sixfold number consisting of the six waves (*ṣaḍūrmi*).

By the number six; by the "stones" (*adribhiḥ*), meaning by the number eight residing in the principal mountains such as Himavat and others; by the "principles" (*tattrais*), meaning by the number twenty-six residing in the *tattvas*; by the "Atiśakvarī," meaning by the number fifteen residing in the position of the meter named Atiśakvarī; by the "senses" (*akṣaiḥ*), meaning by the number eleven residing in the eleven senses; by the "five offerings" (*pañcaprayājas*), meaning by the number five residing in the *jagatī* [meter]; and likewise, according to the rule of the feet (*pādanīti*), there is the composition of the *prayājas* residing in sixteen feet, respectively.
The composition of the subjects has been arranged according to the six flavors and by way of the number six. || 16 ||

This treatise, however, consists of sixteen chapters divided into two groups of eight, according to the principle of the sixfold classification and so forth; these chapters primarily concern the investigation of consistency, non-contradiction, and attainment.
Among them, the first pair declares the established subject matter, while the subsequent opposing pair addresses its antithesis.
And since it is the Self that is the means for attaining the Self, the Supreme Brahman must likewise be contemplated therein. 17.

This treatise, namely the Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā-śāstra, consists of four chapters (*adhyāyas*)—namely, those primarily concerned with the investigation of *samanvaya* (harmony), *avirodha* (non-contradiction), *sādhana* (means), and *bhagavat-prāpti* (attainment of the Lord)—each bearing its respective name, like the sixteen limbs (*ṣoḍaśāṅghri*) or sixteen feet (*ṣoḍaśapāda*), and likewise divided into six sections (*ṣaṭka*).

According to the method of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), by means of the logic of the distinctions between direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*) found in the six chapters (*ṣaṭka*), it is divided into two pairs (*dvikayugabhidura*). Within those two pairs, the first pair—the initial pair—declares, that is, establishes through investigation, the reality that is Brahman in its perfected form and as the nature of the object (*siddha-viṣaya*).

"Param"—the second pair that follows, which is its counterpart: the "sādhya" (the goal to be accomplished) as the counter-correlate of the "siddha" (the already accomplished), and the "viṣayin" (the subject) as the counter-correlate of the "viṣaya" (the object); this dyad, consisting of the fruit of knowledge, he "vakti"—that is, he establishes through inquiry. Even there—in that second pair—"param brahma ca"—the Supreme Brahman alone is the "sādhana"—the means—toward one's own attainment and one's own absorption; for it is indeed "svayam"—by itself alone—that must be "cintyam"—contemplated. Therefore, the entire scripture is simply the inquiry into Brahman. || 17 ||

The refutation—namely, that [space] and so forth are not effects—is addressed respectively in the third and fourth quarters [of the second chapter]: in the third chapter, which primarily establishes the means of proof, the fact that space, vital breath, and so forth are created; and in the case of the two [categories] consisting of those who bear existence and others, the presence or absence of defects.

In the first and second quarters [of the first chapter], there is the faulty nature of the bound conscious being (*baddha-cetana*) and the absence of any connection with defects in the eternally liberated Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Devotion (*bhakti*)—in the third quarter—is the meditation (*upāsana*) that serves as the means to liberation. And "the limbs" (*aṅgāni*)—in the fourth quarter—are the duties pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) and so forth, which constitute the limbs of that meditation. Now, in the final, concluding fourth chapter, which primarily concerns the fruit [of the practice]:

The powers of the meditations (*upāsāroha-prabhāva*), the departure from the body (*utkrama*), the path (*saraṇi*), and the fruits (*phalāni*)—[these are located] respectively in the [four] quarters. These objects of knowledge—the power resulting from the perfection of knowledge, the departure from the body, the journey beginning with the rays of light (*arcirādi-gati*), and the fruit consisting of the experience of the complete Brahman—have been reflected upon, deliberated, and determined.

Having studied the Vedas according to the injunctions, and having desisted from ritual acts by the power of those very injunctions, they cross over to the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman through the inquiry, "What [is the goal]?"— thinking, "Let us act. However, in this present fourth age (Kali Yuga), because of the perception that the strength of the vital breath and the intellect are limited,
and due to an inability to endure the waste of time, a few fortunate ones find delight immediately in the End (the Final Goal).

It has been accumulated for the sake of attaining the knowledge of Brahman—that is, for the acquisition of the knowledge of Brahman—because the rule of approaching a teacher is prescribed in the passage, "He should approach a teacher" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 2.23.1), which enjoins the service of a teacher; likewise, because of the instruction by him, as the Śrutis show that the teaching of reality is given by the teacher alone; and also because of the *Sadvidyā*, namely the Śruti contained within the *Sadvidyā* section, "A man who has a teacher knows," which [shows] the attainment of the knowledge concerning the Supreme Self (*parabrahmavitti*) upon having a teacher.

It clarifies—that is, makes explicit—the connection with a true teacher (*sadācārya*). Likewise, in that very same manner, another *śruti* as well—another Vedic text—is heard [to say]: "From the teacher [comes] knowledge; knowledge is learned from the teacher. This *śruti*, "He should approach the Guru alone," is not contradictory when understood by those who know the principles of conduct (*nītividbhiḥ*)—those who contemplate logic—as an indicator of a restrictive rule (*niyamāṃśa*) for what was previously unknown. || 21 ||
Since this is indeed the case, this is therefore a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).
Thus [it is].

It is certain and established [that, therefore, although it is obtained through passion (*rāga-prāpta*) and not through injunction (*vaidhatva*), and although there is an absence of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding its being a fruit— just as in the case of heaven— and although it is obtainable even when the primary meaning is set aside (*lakṣaṇā-bhaṅge*) by the statement of Brahman’s existence, and although it is cognized by inference (*anumāna-pramita*), it is nonetheless partially knowable through scripture (*śāstra-vedya*).]
Even if it were intended as an injunction, since there is no contradiction, the statement concerning another object would be a valid means of knowledge regarding its own meaning;
for the straight-forward and eloquent author of the Sūtras does not tolerate anything other than what is stated in the *anvāra* (concomitant) expression. // 23 //

The apprehension of futility—the delusion that [the inquiry] is fruitless—is set aside, meaning it is removed (by virtue of its being *apūrva* and its being the supreme human goal). This method of describing how even the four aphorisms (*catuḥsūtrī*) serve as an introduction (*upoddhāta*) is both consistent with the natural inclination of numerous portions of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) through its propriety in the form of the existence of the characteristics of an introduction, and is justified by reflection on the inherent consistency of many parts constituting the Commentary; furthermore, it is "prior," having acquired its established form through the traditional succession of ancient commentaries. — [Thus says] Eke-meghanāda and others.

The commentators named Sūri, however, have stated—that is, they have propounded—that the first [sūtra] alone is the single initial sūtra for the purpose of commencing the treatise, meaning it is useful for the commencement of the Śārīraka-śāstra; and that the subsequent three sūtras constitute the "treatise" itself, meaning they are the Śārīraka-śāstra itself. || 24 ||

Some [teachers], bypassing the first and fourth systems here, propound [the second and third]; this is untenable, for how could one consider the fruit of that [system] here as established when its awakening is not yet accomplished?
Furthermore, what they know regarding the two middle systems—the domains of form, name, and procreation—is itself deficient.

Pointing with their fingers—such as the index finger and so forth—to something related, like their mother and others, or something unrelated, like the moon or a cow, and directing the eyes of children toward the object, they cause the children—who desire to learn—to acquire proficiency by means of specific words employed that signify those respective objects; thus, those collections of words are put to use.

In certain specific usages, such as "a son has been born to you," words produce a cognition regarding a particular object that is already established (*siddha*)—that is, one that is accomplished and endowed with universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth. We accept that it is "productive of harm" (*anarthakṛt*) in accordance with the prohibition, and thus [this quality] applies to the object of the prohibition.

Likewise—in the same manner as stated—regarding the object of prohibition, namely *apagoraṇa* (threatening) in the injunction "one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa," we accept that its quality of being a source of harm (*anarthakṛttva*)—that is, its capacity to produce hellish injury such as being struck by a hundred spears—is conducive to the prohibition; in other words, it serves to effect the censure of the censurable act. By means of such statements as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth, it is established without restriction that the cognition of Brahman—a consciousness whose object is the already-existent Brahman—arises indeed with a non-erroneous object, that is, with an object that is fit for realization. || 34 ||

"Birth and so forth"—the collection of effects consisting of the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of the world—would lead to the contingency of a difference in the substantive (*viśeṣya*) caused by a difference in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). In the Bhṛguvallī, which contains the use of the word "imāni" (these), the Supreme Person—the Lord of all and the Controller of everything—is reckoned as the one characterized by the birth and so forth of the universe; that is, by those unique attributes consisting of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world. By this fact—that He is made known through His own unique nature—it is clearly demonstrated (*adarśi*) that the universe to be created belongs to the Blessed One.

By this very world-variety that has been described, the qualities of the Creator Brahmā—the Supreme Self who fashions the universe—which serve as reasons for His being an object of inquiry (*jijñāsyatā*) by establishing the necessity of investigation, have been shown to be radiant—that is, accessible through the Vedas because they are non-contradictory and unrefuted. These are His natural attributes conducive to creation, such as omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
Furthermore, the very variety of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of its inconceivable, absolutely distinct, and wonderful forms, has also been demonstrated.
These have indeed been made clear. || 8 ||

The logicians (*nyāyavṛddha*), who are experts in words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), state: regarding the sentence "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*), for each individual word—namely the words *satya*, *jñāna*, *ananta*, and *brahma*—there are specific grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) such as truthfulness, knowability, infinity, and being Brahman, which must necessarily be expressed through their respective fixed etymological causes (*nimitta*) associated with each word. All things, beginning with the earth, possess parts—that is, they are composed of constituent parts—therefore they are effects; and being effects, they possess a cause characterized by being produced by an agent. That conscious being who is established as the agent is the Lord, known as Bhagavān, established by the force of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the principle of corollary establishment, which is the establishment of another thing by implication when one thing is being proved). Thus, the conscious Lord is established.

This—that is, such an investigation into the proof of God through inference and other means—would not be possible, nor would it be at all tenable; because, in the production of the universe—the creation of the world as an effect—when it is to be proven that the agent and time are one and the same, i.e., that they were created by a single being simultaneously, there arises the consideration of a "deviation from the nature of being an effect" (kāryatvavyabhicāri), which is a specific inconclusive fault (*anaikāntika*) of the reason, whether it be the defect of being too common (*sādhāraṇa*) or too uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), or else a contradiction (*viruddha*) regarding vast effects.

Because we observe both long durations of time and multiple agents, the reason "being an effect" (kāryatva) either proves its own probandum or else proves something that is not contradictory to it. || 10 ||

This [liberation] is not seen here as the simultaneous abandonment of all [defilements] through the path of logic; since conceptual construction is merely an accessory, the "other" (the supreme self) is not to be inferred. || 12 ||

He is capable—able—to create; even a living being, though embodied and situated far from the effect, may create the world—may produce the effect known as the universe—or else, let the body of the world-creator, even if it were possible, remain invisible—that is, beyond the reach of the senses. || 13 ||

Thus, because of his lightness upon ascending by the power of inference, he manifested here the all-pervading Lord— who is endowed with sovereignty born of karma according to the conduct of Viśvāmitra and others— as one to be known through the scriptures.

The fact of having an origin (*utpattimattā*), or being produced by an agent (*kṛtisādhyatā*), which is intended as the indicator of "having an agent" through its nature as an effect—possessing a fixed sequence of application through positive and negative concomitance (*vītāvīta-prayoga-krama-niyatimatī*), characterized by both positive (*anvaya*) and negative (*vyatireka*) pervasion with the probandum—makes it known that this entire universe, the world consisting of the earth, mountains, and so forth, which is the subject of dispute, was fashioned by an omniscient being—a specific person who is fully cognizant of all the materials, instruments, and other requirements. That is to say, it leads to the inference.

In this regard—concerning the subject of God established through inference—the investigation by means of scriptures, such as the Upaniṣads and the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras], is fruitless; indeed, it is as useless as grinding what has already been ground. Thus, when the Naiyāyika has raised this objection based on the force of inference—

Due to its dependence upon inference—according to the principle of Viśvāmitra and others, that is, by way of specific conscious beings such as seers (*ṛṣis*) who possess extraordinary power and are endowed with the capacity for creation observed in passages like "another Indra"—it manifests only in a particular individual soul (*jīva*) who possesses sovereignty born of action and is endowed with distinguished capability dependent on specific ascetic practices (*tapas*). Once [the Lord] is established as the creator of the world (and thus a different entity is reached), then by the force of the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava*), in this *Śārīraka* treatise, the omnipresent one—

Bādarāyaṇa set forth—established by means of the aphorism "Because [the Lord] has the scripture as His source" (Śāstrayonitvāt)—the Lord who is capable of creation and who is to be known through the scripture, being accessible solely through the scripture. || 41 ||

The earth and so forth are preceded by an agent, like a bracelet, because they possess the nature of being effects; thus, that agent is established as one who perceives atoms, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and other causes, and as being omnipotent. This is not so. Just as the ear has no desire to perceive fragrance and the like due to the absence of such a capacity, he too would not perceive every cause; yet, the mere fact that he does not perceive everything does not imply his lack of agency regarding the potter here.

And he would possess all powers. Such a description of the Naiyāyika is improper; for this kind of reflection—this desire for the apprehension of fragrance and so forth by means of the senses such as hearing, which do not grasp objects like odor—is similar to the longing to perceive objects such as scents. Why? Because of the absence of such pervasion (*vyāpti*); that is, because the pervasion consisting of the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between being an effect and having an omniscient creator as its cause is unestablished even in this instance of the example.

A potter, the maker of a jar, such as a potter and so forth, does not perceive every cause—the general category of causal agents that produces all effects—for he indeed does not perceive them. Nevertheless, by the mere fact of not perceiving all causal agents, one cannot say that this potter lacks agency—that is, that he lacks the status of being the maker of the jar. || 42 ||

Although the inference of another self and so forth is faultless through various types of logical marks (*liṅga*), nevertheless, the method of universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) established by perception is certainly not relaxed in any variation of the subject (*pakṣa*).
For, according to the principle that "the speech of such a reliable person (*āpta*) is not false," even a marvelous statement in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) does not become untrue.

Due to the equality regarding the absence of sublation and other factors, there would be figurative usage and so forth in that which possesses contradiction, as in the case of worldly [convention]. (44)

The inference—the valid cognition consisting of an inferential judgment—of other selves, that is, of the selves who preside over other bodies, as well as their knowledge, volition, and so forth, is accomplished through various logical marks (*liṅga*) such as possession of vital breath (*saprāṇatva*) and the like;
and although this [inference] is indeed faultless and free from defects.

It is established. Indeed, it is not weakened, nor is it destroyed. (In the case of the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*), however, there is a disparity because [God], who possesses eternal knowledge and so forth and is unestablished through perception, is known through inference. But in the *Āmnāya*—that is, in the Veda—there is "marvelous speech" (*adbhutokti*), which is the expression of an extremely unseen and wondrous matter (to be understood as an *arthavāda*). According to the principle of such authoritative speech—that is, by analogy with the words of an authority who has come from another land and whose words have never been seen before—it is not false; it does not become a non-valid means of knowledge. (Why?)

Because of the equality regarding the absence of sublation and so forth—that is, because the quality of having an unsublated meaning is common to both cases—in a case involving contradiction (*vihati*), such as in the specific instance "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*) which is opposed by other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), there would be figurative status (*gauṇatādi*)—that is, a metaphorical meaning (*aupacārikārthakatva*) resulting from the sublation of the primary sense—just as in worldly usage (*lokavat*); this must be accepted. || 44 ||

Nevertheless—even that being so—in certain instances involving the inference of another's self (*parātmanumana*) based on a difference of position, there exists the method of establishing pervasion through perception (*pratyakṣavyāptiśailī*), that is, the limit of pervasion established by direct observation.

Indeed, those for whom the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is paramount sometimes relate that the Supreme Creator is to be inferred from effects impossible for beings such as ourselves; it is this that the *Janmādi-sūtra* intends to convey.
If it is argued that, therefore, it is improper for a follower of the Veda to abandon inference, we say no;
for [the Veda] teaches propriety in every instance, and because [inference] is merely a restatement of what is already established by such arguments as "existence" (sattva) and so forth. || 45 ||

"Mayas prevail"—thus they recount, making it known by following the very system of the logicians (*tārkika*). The statement regarding birth and so forth—the passage beginning with "From which indeed these [beings arise]"—intends that very inference; it takes inference alone as its primary purport. Therefore, since the inference of God (*īśvarānumāna*) is evident within the Śrutis and their supporting expositions (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), the rejection of the inference of God—that is, the non-acceptance of the inference of God—is improper, that is, unreasonable, for a follower of the Vedas, one who maintains the authority of the Veda.

If this is argued, it is not so; such a thought is not correct, because in certain portions of the Purāṇas, due to the instruction on propriety (*aucitya*), there is the demonstration of the portion stating that the Supreme Self can also be an object of inference (*anumeya*). Furthermore, the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) found in the sentence "from which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*) is appropriate as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what is established by the manifestation of Being (*sat*), since it is of the nature of a restatement of the meaning established by sentences in the Knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*) such as "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning. (It is not, however, appropriate as a means of producing inferential knowledge. || 45 ||

Fie upon those addicted to the Kaumārilas’ system, who—even though they have triumphed over the Prābhākara method—alas! prattle on as if the world were bereft of its Lord!

Far removed from any suspicion of causal defects or sublation, how is it that the statements of injunctions, mantras, and explanatory passages (arthavādas) do not possess intrinsic validity regarding human goals, just like [the validity of] prescriptions? (15)

Alas! We utter a cry of "Fie, fie! against those who, out of a lack of discernment, shamelessly proclaim—without contradiction—that the entire universe, the whole range of created things, is devoid of a Lord (*nirīśvara*); [we speak thus] regarding those addicted to the system of the Kaumārilas—the followers of the Bhaṭṭa-Mīmāṃsā—as well as those who have mastered the Prābhākara method, even those who consider themselves experts in the Prābhākara-Mīmāṃsā system.

(They are to be pitied) because they remain far from the cognition of defects in the cause and from subverting cognitions—that is, outside the scope of both knowledge dependent on defects and subverting knowledge; and because they are indifferent toward the Lord, who is the self-evident goal of persons, whose nature is the supreme human end (*puruṣārtha*), who bestows desired objects, and who is the refuge and master of all the world—toward Him, the Vedic utterances consisting of mantras and *arthavādas* proceed spontaneously, just like injunctions (*vidhi*).

Validity—that is, the quality of producing a cognition of an object that is not sublated independently—how could they not possess it? By what reason would they not attain it? They certainly attain it in every respect. || 15 ||
Regarding the matter to be performed— that is, with respect to the entity in the form of the goal— the purpose of hearing the statement by the listener would be accomplished.
For it has been said: when that which is to be established is indeed stated in its accomplished form, the result for the listener is achieved; as in the statement: "The crow has eight teeth."

Just as in such cases, when an already established fact is communicated that is of no use for engagement or withdrawal, there would be no further purpose—nor would there be pleasure—as in sentences such as "There is a mango tree in your house," which produce mere joy; for that purpose, why has one not seen even a false statement—a sentence that does not correspond to reality—employed by untrustworthy persons in the world? (Indeed, such a thing certainly does not deserve the status of a valid means of knowledge.)

If the statements concerning Brahman were for the sake of knowledge—that is, if they served as qualifications for specific forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of being auxiliary to them—then, just as in the case of a perceived object, when one perceives Brahmanhood and so forth in the mind through the meditation "The mind is Brahman," Brahmanhood and the like would be merely superimposed upon the mind, which is the object of that perception. Consequently, even that reality which is to be known through the Vedāntas would be unreal (*anṛta*). That unreal Brahman would not be something to be investigated; it would not be fit to be the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). (And therefore, the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā] should not be commenced.)

When an objection—an apprehension—is raised, [the author] states the purport of the scripture regarding the reality of Brahman, which consists of infinite bliss (*niravadhika-sukha*), as being *ananya-śeṣa*—that is, without being subordinate to any other sentence. By means of this section (*adhikaraṇa*), it shall be established that the author of the Sūtras has demonstrated the final conclusion of the Vedānta scriptures, which is their ultimate subject matter. This is done in order to establish its fruitfulness—that is, to conceive of its purposefulness (*sāphalya*).

Even if there were no contradiction regarding the *tātparya* (intended purport) with respect to the reality of Brahman, even under the view that [the Upanishadic texts] form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions (*vidhi*), there would still be a similarity to the statement regarding the number of teeth of a meat-eater (*śvapaca*)—which is established through its own internal consistency despite being distinct [from the injunction].

For it is not possible to maintain that [the Upanishads] have the purpose of providing pleasure while simultaneously accepting their falsity; thus, the hypothesis that they are false is untenable because it lacks the capacity to produce delight.
Even in cases such as deceiving children and the like, joy arises solely from the cognition that the object exists in that very way.

Even in the view that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the injunction (*vidhi*) through the injunctive sentence, and even in the view that the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) convey meaning by forming a single syntactical unit (*vākyaikavākyatā*) when combined, the *tātparya*—the finality of the subject matter—remains unimpaired and uncontradicted even regarding the reality of Brahman, that is, the nature of the Supreme Brahman. Even in the case of difference—that is, when they constitute separate sentences—their own respective meanings are established.

Because the attainment of the fruit in the form of pleasure exists, there is no similarity to the counting of a crow’s teeth—that is, a resemblance to the enumeration of a crow’s teeth—it does not occur, it certainly does not happen. [The opponent's claim that] "having a purpose for one's own enjoyment" means "having pleasure as its motive" is not tenable; the intention that what is false can be fit for a purpose, whereas only what is true can be so, is incorrect.
