When Brahman, which is pure consciousness without distinction, becomes free from the perception of difference caused by ignorance upon the complete destruction of karmas, and is no longer touched by afflictions and the like caused by karma, then all those worldly, non-ultimate differences—which appear as real entities, which are the fruits of the tree of ignorance that serves as the cause for all kinds of conceptualization—no longer appear at all.

When all karma—which is the cause for the soul's contemplation of the manifold forms of gods and others within itself—comes to an end, then the reality of the self becomes a single form of pure knowledge, with all bonds cast off, and its innate essential nature and qualities become manifest. Likewise, the distinctions such as being a god and so forth, which are objects of experience resulting from karma rooted in the misconception of the body as the self, no longer remain at all within the reality of the self.

Therefore, cast away the ignorance-based knowledge which causes one to perceive division within the single nature of the Self, appearing as the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge! Thus urged by Ādibharata, that King of Sauvīra, having attained the state of being focused on the One as his true goal, abandoned the cognition of duality.

Urged by him with the words, "Abandon the delusion of diversity in the Self—caused by the differences in forms such as those of gods and others residing in the body—regarding everything that is conventionally treated as mutually distinct in the form of 'I,' 'he,' 'you,' and so forth, because its true nature is the single form of pure consciousness," he [the disciple], through the conviction of reality directed toward the actual nature of the Self which consists solely of the form of knowledge, dispelled his former delusion.

"That by which something is perceived—being free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single nature—is either seen or realized; that is knowledge, and anything other than that is said to be ignorance."

That which is unworthy of contact with defects (*doṣa*), the adversary of defects, and untouched by defects; likewise, immutable by nature and essence, or bound by a vow to protect those who have taken refuge in it—the Supreme Brahman known as Viṣṇu—is that which is first made an object of cognition through knowledge dependent on scripture (*āgama*), which is then made directly perceptible through meditation (*dhyāna*), and which is experienced after its attainment through that knowledge designated by the term "supreme devotion" (*parabhakti*). This very reality, possessing these three forms, is in truth to be understood by the term "non-figurative knowledge" (*anupacaritajñāna*); anything else is determined to be merely ignorance (*ajñāna*).

Prakaraṇa-saṃgraha: The Means of Valid Cognition with Explanations, Part 2.1.2.103–104. The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are two: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Among these, perception is that which is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Conceptual construction is the association of a name (*nāman*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or substance (*dravya*) with a thing. That [perception] is devoid of such [conceptual construction]. Furthermore, it is non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). For example, the cognition of a person suffering from jaundice as yellow is not perception because it is erroneous. Therefore, by being both free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous, the definition of perception is established. Inference is the cognition of an object through its mark (*liṅga*). The mark is that which possesses three characteristics (*trirūpa*): (1) it must be present in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), (2) it must be present in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and (3) it must be absent in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣāsattva*). Based on such a mark, the cognition of the object to be inferred (*sādhya*) is inference. It is of two kinds: inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) and inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). Inference for oneself is the cognition arising from the mark itself. Inference for others is the communication of the three characteristics of the mark through words so that another may understand. Thus, the means of valid cognition are established as two.

The relationship of mutual manifestation between the self, whose nature is pure experience, and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is not tenable, because their natures are mutually contradictory. If the self were something to be manifested, then—just as in the case of a jar or other objects manifested by a lamp—one would have to admit that the self lacks the quality of being experience (*anubhūtitva*), which is accepted by the Advaitins.

Truthfulness, straightforwardness, compassion, charity, non-violence, and freedom from covetousness are the "virtues" (*kalyāṇa*). These consist of: speech that brings benefit to all beings; equanimity of the three organs (body, speech, and mind); the inability to endure the suffering of others regardless of one's own interest; the renunciation of one's own wealth and so forth—righteously acquired—according to rule to a worthy recipient; the avoidance of harming others through body, speech, and mind; and the avoidance of fruitless anxiety. These are the things denoted by the term "virtue" within the group of seven means [to liberation].

"This *Śārīraka* [system] is connected with Jaimini’s *Ṣoḍaśalakṣaṇa* [work], and thus the unity of the scripture is established. This means that this treatise on the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*) composed by Bādarāyaṇa, known as the *Śārīraka*, is connected to the treatise on the inquiry into ritual action and deities (*karmadevatāmīmāṃsā*) composed by Jaimini—which consists of sixteen chapters—by virtue of being a commentary whose subject matter is to be explained as a single whole in a fixed sequence of priority. Statements expressing the established conclusion (*siddhānta*)— four such passages from the *Śrībhāṣya*—
show that because other attributes are negated only of an entity already qualified by certain specific attributes, there is nowhere any establishment of a featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) reality.
Therefore, an "entity" must be described as being indeed qualified by specific attributes recognized through valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika-viśeṣa*).

Consequently, indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is the apprehension of the first individual among objects belonging to a single class; the apprehension of the second and subsequent individuals is called determinate perception (*savikalpaka*).
Thus, perception never has an entity devoid of specific attributes as its object.

Therefore, since perception has as its object that which possesses qualifiers (*saviśeṣa*), and because inference also has as its object that which is qualified by a relation perceived through perception and other means, inference too has only that which possesses qualifiers as its object. No means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishes a thing devoid of qualifiers (*nirviśeṣa*).

Consequently, perception has as its object only that which is distinguished by differences characterized by genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which consist of the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of the thing itself. ...
Configuration itself is the genus. Configuration is that which is the unique form of a thing.

Therefore, it cannot be said that "experience is self-established. Consequently, the claim that "if it were an object of experience, it would not be experience" is laughable. Experience—otherwise known as cognition (*jñāna*), realization (*avagati*), consciousness (*saṃvit*), and so forth—is a specific attribute of the experiencing self; its nature is to render some object suitable for practical discourse by its very existence to its own substrate, and it is transitive (having an object).

Thus, the self (ātman) is indeed of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa) and possesses consciousness as its quality. For the state of being of the nature of consciousness is self-luminosity (svayaṃprakāśatā). Therefore, this self, being self-luminous, is necessarily a knower (jñātṛ), not mere luminosity.
Consequently, the self cannot be consciousness (saṃvit) itself.

Therefore, that which is established for its own self by its very existence as the non-insentient "I-sense" (ahamartha) is the Self (ātman). Consequently, the Self is not mere consciousness (jñaptimātra); rather, it is the knower (jñātṛ), the "I-sense. 93. Therefore, due to contradiction alone, the "I-maker" (ahaṅkāra) cannot possess the quality of being a knower; for [the "I-maker"] is like the faculty of seeing. Indeed, the state of being a knower consists in the quality of knowledge—
[It possesses] the state of being a substratum. And the knowledge of this eternal [Self] is eternal, by virtue of being its inherent attribute.
Therefore, in no way is there a manifestation of experience through the ego (ahaṅkāra).
In both worldly and Vedic usage, it is designated as the "Witness" (sākṣin); it is not mere knowledge alone.

Therefore, since it is the "I-sense" (ahamartha) alone that is established as the knower, it possesses the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman). Consequently, the notion of "I," being free from sublation, has the Self itself as its direct object; whereas the notion of "I" directed toward the body is merely ignorance (avidyā). Thus, it is difficult to justify the realization of the true Brahman from an unreal scripture. For grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) consists in the application of words to a single referent through different bases of application (pravṛttinimitta)—as in the rule: "Coreferentiality belongs to words with different bases of application... Therefore, even by virtue of the nature of the causal statements, it is understood that Brahman is presented as possessing attributes precisely by the text, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite.
Consequently, all the Śruti texts enjoin the very realization of Brahman as the means to liberation (*apavarga*).
Brahman is not merely bliss; rather, it is blissful. For knowledge itself, when it is favorable, is called bliss. Indeed, the state of being a knower is itself the state of being blissful. 134.

Since the contemplation that the world—divided into the various categories of gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings as they actually exist—is essentially Brahman serves as a cause for peace and a cause for attaining fearlessness, there is no possibility of it being a cause of fear. Furthermore, it is understood that the Supreme Brahman, along with its differentiated attributes and the world that constitutes its manifestation, is indeed ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Therefore, [there is no fear].
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu is indeed unique and is the auspicious refuge (*śubhāśraya*).

Although all selves (*ātman*) are identical insofar as they possess the single form of pure consciousness (*jñānaikākāratā*), the perception of duality among the selves in the form of gods and so forth—caused by association with the physical bodies (*piṇḍa*) which are specific transformations of *prakṛti* such as those of gods and humans—is said to be unreal (*atathya*). Duality pertaining to the body is not denied even when it pertains to the self; however, the entire reality of the self existing within the bodies of gods and others is equal.

Furthermore, an identity of essential nature between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is not possible in the same way that an identity between the body and the self is impossible.
In all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), it is Brahman with attributes alone that is to be meditated upon, and the fruit is likewise of a single nature.

Therefore, in the scriptures there is no teaching of a featureless reality; nor is there any teaching regarding the illusoriness of the multitude of objects; nor is there a denial of the essential distinction between consciousness, matter, and the Lord.
Therefore, because of this very contradiction, Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, cannot be the locus of ignorance.
This is established by both ordinary perception and by perception supported by reasoning in the form: "I am ignorant; I know myself and others.
Consequently, the word *māyā* denotes that which produces a manifold creation. And it is for this reason that the term *māyā* is applied to *prakṛti*.
Precisely because it brings about the creation of diverse objects,
the Vedas do not establish a knowledge of that which is existent, non-existent, or indefinable.
Therefore, there is no postulation of ignorance regarding Brahman.
Even in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, the doctrine of Brahman’s ignorance is nowhere to be seen.

In this world, which is a mixture of the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the conscious element possesses a nature that is distinct from its own self-awareness and is beyond the reach of speech and mind; being of the single form of knowledge, it is untouched by the distinctions of material nature (*prakṛti*).
Due to its imperishability, it is denoted by the word "exists" (*asti*).
But the non-conscious portion (acid-aṃśa), which is a specific transformation caused by the activity of the conscious portion (cid-aṃśa) and is subject to destruction,
is denoted by the word "non-existent" (nāsti).
Both [the sentient and the insentient], however, are identical with that [Brahman] because they constitute the body of Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, it is understood that the identity of the entire aggregate of things—consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious—with Brahman arises solely from the relationship of self and body. Consequently, since everything other than Brahman possesses reality only as His body, even the word that denotes such a thing expresses its own meaning only as culminating in Him. Thus, it is established that all words denote Brahman as qualified by the meanings of their constituent parts, which are understood through worldly linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*).

Therefore, just like words such as "cow" and so forth, words such as "god" and "human" terminate in the Self (*ātman*). Thus, because individual souls (*jīva*)—distinguished by their bodies as gods, humans, and so on—are modes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by virtue of being His body, words denoting the individual soul terminate in the Supreme Self. Consequently, since both the conscious and unconscious entities constitute objects of reference only as modes of the Supreme Brahman, they are used in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Him.

Therefore, since the Supreme Person alone possesses the gross and subtle sentient and insentient entities as His body—both in His causal state and His effected state—and because the effect is non-different from the cause, it is most appropriately established that by knowing the cause, the effect is known; thus, the intended "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is fully justified.

Therefore, Brahman alone—characterized by the modes of gross and subtle consciousness and unconsciousness—is both the effect and the cause; thus, the world has Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*). This being so, even though Brahman enters into the effect, there is no alteration in its essential nature (*svarūpa*); hence, it remains unmodified (*avikṛta*). For the gross state consists in the subsistence of the entities of consciousness and unconsciousness—which were previously divided by a distinction of forms—as the very self of Brahman. Furthermore, its status as an effect is more appropriately established, for "being an effect" is simply the attainment of another state.

Therefore, since bondage has its root in ignorance in the form of a beginningless stream of karma, its eradication occurs only through knowledge characterized as previously described. And the arising of that [knowledge] is attainable through the performance of duties appropriate to one’s caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), which have been refined by a specific understanding of the self’s true nature (*ātma-yāthātmya-buddhi*)—an understanding manifested as the worship of the Supreme Person (*parama-puruṣa*) performed day after day.

Consequently, because the Vedāntas teach the perfectly established Supreme Brahman and its worship, which yields immeasurable fruit, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-vicāra*), which results in the definitive determination of that [Brahman], must be undertaken.

Therefore, even in injunctive sentences, it is determined that the suffix *liṅ* and others denote merely the state of being accomplished through the agent's activity. Furthermore, the meaning of the verbal root, such as sacrifice (*yāga*), consists in the propitiation of the Supreme Person who dwells within the deities such as Agni; and from that Supreme Person, thus propitiated, the attainment of the fruit results.
This is indeed established by the grammatical instruction on words (śabdānuśāsana).

For example, suppose a certain prince, while engaged in childhood play, were to depart from the royal palace and stray from the path; the king, believing him lost, would remain unaware that his son was still alive. Meanwhile, the prince, having no knowledge of his father, would be raised by an eminent brahmin. Having mastered the Vedas and the Shastras, he would stand at the age of sixteen, endowed with every auspicious quality. [His father would think: "Your father is the sovereign of all the world, possessed of such qualities as profundity, magnanimity, affection, virtuous conduct, heroism, valor, and prowess; he seeks only you..."

If one hears a statement uttered by a most authoritative person—“He stands at the city gate, desiring to see his lost son”—then at that very moment, one becomes filled with unsurpassed joy, thinking, "I am indeed the son of one who lives, and my father is enriched with every prosperity.

176. The ignorance under discussion does not have Brahman, which is pure consciousness, as its substrate; because it is ignorance, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects. 187. The ignorance under discussion does not conceal Brahman, which is pure consciousness; because it is ignorance, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects. 187. The ignorance under discussion is not removable by knowledge; because it does not conceal the object of that knowledge. That ignorance which is removable by knowledge necessarily conceals the object of that knowledge, as is the case with the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects.

Brahman is not the locus of ignorance, because it lacks the status of being a knower, like a jar or similar objects. Brahman is not veiled by ignorance, because it is not an object of knowledge. Whatever is veiled by ignorance is an object of knowledge, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like. Ignorance is not that which is removable by knowledge in Brahman, because Brahman is not an object of knowledge. Whatever ignorance is removable by knowledge is an object of knowledge, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like.

The knowledge that is the subject of dispute is not preceded by an ignorance distinct from its own prior non-existence; because it is a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*), like the valid cognition that serves as the means of proving the ignorance you yourself accept. Ignorance is of a positive nature—it is not to be destroyed by knowledge—because it is of a positive nature, like a jar or similar objects.

10. On account of merging into itself. Because of the scriptural statement that at the time of deep sleep the individual soul (jīva) merges into its own cause denoted by the word "Being" (sat), the Pradhāna—which is "non-scriptural" (aśabda) in the sense that it is unfit to be connected with the status of being the cause of the soul—cannot be what is denoted by the word "Being."

11. On account of the uniformity of approach (*gatisāmānyāt*): because it must necessarily be stated that the manner of propounding the reality which serves as the cause of the world—whether pertaining to this Upaniṣad or to other various Upaniṣads—is identical (*sāmānyāt*), that is, possesses a single form; [therefore, even though it is being propounded here as the cause of the world, it is indeed the Supreme Brahman].

12. And because it is heard [in scripture], and because it is heard—since it is heard in this very Upaniṣad that "all this is indeed from the Self" (*ātmata eva idam sarvam*), which serves as a proof that the world originates from a conscious being alone—the *pradhāna* favored by the Sāṃkhyas, being non-scriptural (*aśabda*) insofar as it is accessible only through inference, is not what is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*) which teaches the cause of the world; rather, it is the Supreme Brahman alone.
The Section on the One Consisting of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa) 13:

"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition. The object denoted by the term *ānandamaya* occurring in the *Ānandavallī* of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad is not something other than Brahman—namely, the individual soul (*jīva*) distinct from Brahman—but is indeed Brahman itself; this is because of "repetition," that is, because of the fitness [of the context] characterized by the repeated mention of unsurpassed bliss.

14. "If it be argued that [the Supreme Self] is not [meant here] because of the word denoting a modification—since in the term *ānandamaya* we hear the suffix *mayaṭ*, which denotes a modification, this serves as an indicator that the unmodified Supreme Self is not what is signified by the word *ānandamaya*—such an assertion is not tenable; for [the suffix] *mayaṭ* signifies abundance (*prācurya*), meaning that the Supreme Self, who is full of bliss (*ānandabahula*), is indeed what is expressed by the term *ānandamaya*."

18. And because of the designation of difference—because of the designation of the difference between the one to be ruled, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the ruler, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); or (alternatively) because of the designation of the difference between the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and the individual soul consisting of knowledge (*vijñānamaya*), through its explicit statement in the Śruti—the other, the individual soul, cannot possibly be the referent of the term "consisting of bliss."

19. And because of the desire, there is no dependence on inference; and because of the desire—since it is understood from the Śruti text, "Let me be many," that the creation of the world has the Supreme Self as its agent, there is no dependence on inference; that is, in the creation whose agent is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), there is no dependence on *pradhāna* (primordial matter). (Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is not the individual soul.)
10. The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa):

"The Light [is Brahman], because of the mention of its feet" (1.1.25). The entity designated by the word "Light" in the scriptural passage, "The light beyond heaven shines," is Brahman—the Supreme Brahman intended as the object of inquiry—because of the mention of its "feet," that is, because of the clear exposition in the scripture, "All beings are one foot of Him," which describes the possession of all beings as feet, a characteristic unique to the Supreme Self.

25–26. If it be argued that [the light] is not the Supreme Brahman because of the mention of a *chandas* (metre), we say no; for there is a scriptural injunction regarding the fixing of the mind [on it], and such is seen [in scripture]. Because of the mention of the *chandas* called Gāyatrī—which was the subject under discussion immediately preceding—as being "this whole world" (*gāyatrī vā idaṃ sarvam*), and because it is described in the Śruti as having all beings as its feet, [the opponent argues] that what is indicated by the word "light" cannot be the Supreme Brahman. However, this statement is not correct.

Likewise, by taking as the basis the similarity of attributes residing in the Gāyatrī, there is the scriptural teaching—meaning the instruction for the sake of a result—of the meditation upon Brahman, which is the fixing of the mind; for thus, when a word denoting a meter is applied to something other than that [meter], it is indeed by prioritizing its similarity to it, as is observed in other instances such as the usage "This is Virāj" and so forth.

If it be argued that [the Supreme Self is not the one taught here] because of the instruction regarding the self of the speaker—since the meaning indicated by the two words "Indra" and "Prāṇa" in this context is the individual self (adhyātma) and not the Supreme Self to be meditated upon, because of the instruction given by the speaker Indra—who is well-known to be in the state of a living being—to the effect that "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self," and because of the scriptural declaration "Meditate on me"—then such an assertion is indeed improper; for, in this [context]...

In this section (from the beginning up to the conclusion), only the abundance—the multiplicity—of the unique attributes of the Supreme Self, which is distinct from the individual self, is perceived in relation to the inner self.

However, from the perspective of the scriptures (*śāstradṛṣṭyā*), the instruction—such as "Worship Me"—is an instruction given by the Lord of beings (*jīvabhūtendrakartṛka*) regarding one's own self as the object of worship; it is like the case of Vāmadeva, where Vāmadeva engaged in the practice of non-difference between himself and the Supreme Self. But from the perspective of the scriptures, such as "You are That" (*tattvam asi*) and "The Self of All," this instruction proceeds precisely through the contemplation of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), which is established by their relationship as body and Self (*śarīrātmabhāva*). This is based on the meaning perceived in the scriptures.

31. 32. "If it be argued that [the passage refers to the individual soul] because of the marks of the individual soul and the chief vital breath, we say no, because of the threefold nature of meditation; for that [threefold nature] is resorted to here, as it is appropriate in this context. If it be argued: "Because of the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—namely, the mention in the scripture of the killing of Tvaṣṭṛ's son, which is a characteristic unique to the individual soul, and of dwelling in the body which is the cause of longevity, which is a characteristic unique to the chief vital breath—it is not necessary to determine that the Supreme Self is meant, on account of the abundance of internal (spiritual) connections"—such a doubt is indeed not tenable, because of the threefold nature of meditation.

In order to teach the threefold meditation upon the Supreme Self—namely, [meditation] on His essential nature, on His being the body of the class of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ*), and on His being the body of the objects of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment—it is because the Supreme Self is denoted by words expressive of the individual soul (*jīva*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*); because this very sequence is adopted elsewhere in various Upaniṣads; and because, due to its applicability here as well—in this *Pratardana-vidyā*—the threefold nature of the meditation remains uncontradicted.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter.

34. And because of the possibility of the intended qualities—namely, the qualities about to be mentioned, such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, including the attributes ending with "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—and because of their possibility in the Supreme Self alone, that is, because they can exist there without contradiction, for this reason also, "everywhere"—Brahman, which is well-known as the cause of the world and which stands as the correlate to identity with all—is indeed Brahman; (not the individual soul).

Śārīraḥ—the individual soul (jīva) which possesses a connection with a body produced by karma; 35. "But on account of impossibility, it cannot be the embodied one"—that is, it cannot be the counter-correlative of the identity with all things stated in the passage "All this, indeed," because of impossibility—that is, for the reason that the intended qualities are impossible in the case of the embodied individual soul.

36. And because of the designation of [the Self] as both object and agent of action, the embodied one—the individual soul (jīva) connected with the body—is not the counter-correlative of universal identity; this is also because of the designation of [the Self] as both object and agent of action, for it is clearly established in the Śruti by the statement "this" (*etam*), which indicates the Supreme Self as the object of attainment, and "I shall attain" (*abhisaṃbhavitāsmi*), which indicates the individual soul as the agent of attainment.

37. On account of the distinction in words, the embodied one—the individual soul (jīva)—is not [the subject]; it is not the counter-correlative of universal identity; rather, it is the Supreme Brahman alone. This is because of the distinction between the two words—those denoting the object of meditation and the meditator—namely, the words "this Self" (eṣa ātmā) and "of me" (me). This distinction consists in the difference in grammatical form: "this" (eṣaḥ) being in the nominative case as the object of meditation, and "of me" (me) being in the genitive case as the individual soul who is the meditator.

38. And on account of Smṛti, the one residing in the body is the individual soul (jīva); it is not the object of worship as the correlate of universal identity; rather, it is the Supreme Self alone, different from that [jīva], because of Smṛti—namely, because in the Smṛti passage "And I am in the heart of all," there is the perception of the difference between the one abiding in the heart as the object of worship and the individual soul.

39. "On account of its being of small size and because of the designation of that [smallness], it is not [the Supreme Brahman]; if this is argued, we say no, because it is to be perceived as such, and because it is like space. On account of its being of small size—that is, because it resides in a limited place within the heart—and because of the designation of that [smallness]—that is, because its small dimension is clearly stated in the phrase 'smaller than the minute'—if it is argued that it is not the Supreme Brahman, since it is described as an object of meditation through identity with all things, [we reply: this statement is not correct. It is not so, because it is to be perceived as such; that is, by virtue of its residing in the heart."

Because the Supreme Self is to be meditated upon, it does not possess a limited nature; for just as with space—even though space is vast, it may appear as if delimited by the hole of a needle—so too the Supreme Self, though infinite, appears as if delimited by the location of the heart.

40. "If it be argued that [the Supreme Self] would attain enjoyment (*sambhoga-prāpti*), we say no, because of distinction (*vaiśeṣyāt*). If it is argued that—given the Supreme Self’s residence in a specific part of the body called the heart—it follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that He too, like the individual soul (*jīva*), would experience pleasure and so forth, and thus attain enjoyment—if such a doubt is raised, it is not tenable; for there is a distinction (*vaiśeṣya*). This is because [the Supreme Self], though residing in the body, is distinct from the state of being subject to karma [which characterizes the individual soul]. (Sūtra 13: *attra-adhikaraṇam*)

The Self is the subject under discussion because of the mention of "the moving and the unmoving. In the *Kaṭhavallī*, the meaning expressed by the passage, "Of whom Brahman and Kṣatra are the rice-porridge" (*yasya brahma-kṣatre odanau*), refers to the one who is the agent of eating, with Brahman and Kṣatra as the rice-porridge and Death as the condiment; it cannot be the embodied soul—the individual *jīva*. This is because of the mention of "the moving and the unmoving," since Brahman and Kṣatra serve as indicators for the entire universe consisting of both the mobile and the immobile.

Also because of the context, the "Eater" is the one previously mentioned who possesses the agency of the act of eating (and is not the individual soul, but rather the Supreme Self who withdraws the world); for this reason, as well as because of the context—since the discourse begins with the Supreme Self alone in such passages as "the great, all-pervading Self"—(for indeed, having introduced one subject, another cannot be described). 43.

"Because those two selves have entered the cave"—that is, because the two selves, namely the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), both of whom are conscious, have entered and abide within the cave of the heart; for it is from the observation of their entry into the cave of the heart that the Śruti has introduced them in such passages as "The ancient one hidden in the cave, dwelling in the deep recess" and "Entering the cave, they abide. (Therefore, the Eater here is the Supreme Self alone, having the individual soul as its companion; it is not the individual soul having the internal organ as its companion.)

44. And because of the specific qualification—the "Eater" mentioned in this context is the Supreme Self alone; for He is specifically designated in the Śruti by means of two unique attributes belonging to both the individual soul and the Supreme: namely, the state of being the seeker and the sought, and the state of being the attainer and the attained.

14. The Section on the Intermediate State (Antarādhikaraṇa). 45. [The person] within is the Supreme Self, because of the logical possibility. Regarding the person spoken of as existing within the eye in the passage, "This person who is in the eye," it is the Supreme Self alone; because of the logical possibility—that is, because the qualities to be mentioned later, such as being the center of blessings (*saṃyadvāmatva*), are possible only in the Supreme Self without contradiction.

And because of the designation of abode and so forth—namely, because of the designation of the abodes and so forth, such as the eye, its stability, and its governance—as clearly stated in scriptural passages like, "He who dwells in the eye" and "He who controls the eye from within," the Person spoken of as being "within"—that is, existing inside the eye—is the Supreme Self alone; not the individual soul (jīva).

47. Furthermore, because of the very mention of one distinguished by bliss—namely, because of the mention of the Supreme Brahman itself as taught by the Fires, being distinguished by unlimited bliss—and also because of the statement in the passage "This person who is in the eye" that "this one" is spoken of as the object of meditation, the "inner one"—the person within the eye—is the Supreme Brahman alone, not the individual soul (jīva). 48.

And for this very reason, and for this very reason—that it is designated as Brahman because it is unlimited bliss—for these same reasons, that person within the eye is of the nature of unlimited bliss; he is Brahman, the Supreme Brahman itself, and not the individual soul (jīva).

49. And because of the mention of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads—of the wise man who has understood the true nature of the Supreme Person, the "path" being the path beginning with light (arcirādi) as established in another scriptural text—and because of the teaching by the Teacher to Upakosala, who had heard about the Person in the eye, it is indicated that the Person within the eye is indeed the Supreme Brahman, not the individual soul (jīva). 50.

"And because of non-abiding and impossibility, it is not the other. Because of non-abiding—since it is impossible for [the Self] to abide invariably within the eye in the case of a reflection and so forth—and because of impossibility—due to the contradiction of attributes such as immortality being without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*) and others—the "other," meaning something different from Brahman such as a reflection, cannot be the person within the eye.

Furthermore, because of its presentation as having a form connected to the Imperishable which is the source of beings—as stated in the passage beginning with "Fire is his head, the eyes..."—[it follows that] the Imperishable which is the source of beings is the Supreme Self alone; it is neither Pradhāna nor Puruṣa.
17. The Section on Vaiśvānara.

57. Vaiśvānara is [the Supreme Self] because of the distinction of the common term. Regarding the term *vaiśvānara* mentioned in the passage, "One should meditate upon this very Self as Vaiśvānara," it refers to [the Supreme Self], and not to the triad beginning with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*).

However, it is the Supreme Self alone [that is meant], because the word "Vaiśvānara"—which is generally applicable to four possible meanings, namely the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), the elemental fire (*bhūta-tṛtīyāgni*), a specific deity, and the Supreme Self—is here specifically qualified by attributes exclusive to the Supreme Self, such as the epithets of being the "Self of all" (*sarvātmakatva*) and so forth, as well as by the word "Brahman" and others; thus, it is made known through its capacity to convey a unique meaning.

58. "That which is being remembered would be an inference"—that is to say, in the manner of [the verse] "Fire is the head, the eyes... and so forth, that which is being remembered—that is, being recognized—would be an inference; it would serve as a mark (*liṅga*) for the fact that the one denoted by the word Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self.

59. [Objection: It cannot be so, because of the mention of sound and other qualities, and because of its being established within. [Reply: This is not so, because there is instruction based on such a perception, because [such qualities] are impossible [in the primary sense], and because they study this very one as a Person (*puruṣa*). This is because of the word "fire" (*agni*) which stands in grammatical apposition with the word "Vaiśvānara" in the passage, "This is indeed that Vaiśvānara fire"; likewise, because of the imaginative attribution of having enemies to Vaiśvānara who resides in locations such as the heart; and similarly, because he is the locus for the offering of breath (*prāṇāhuti*); and because of his being established within, as in: "He knows him as established within the person."

If it is argued that, because of the scriptural statement that Vaiśvānara is established within the person, the one denoted by the word "Vaiśvānara" cannot be the Supreme Self—[we reply: such a reflection is not tenable; for it is so with Vaiśvānara, who is Brahman.

Because of the teaching based on perception and because of the injunction for meditation upon him as the body of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), that which is denoted by the word *vaiśvānara* is indeed the Supreme Self qualified by the digestive fire, and not the digestive fire alone. (The understanding of this meaning follows) from impossibility—since it is impossible for the digestive fire alone to have the three worlds as its body. Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins study and recite [this text], "Vaiśvānara who is the person" (*puruṣa*), thus regarding him as the Person without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*).

60. For this very reason, Vaiśvānara cannot be a deity or an elemental being; because Vaiśvānara has the three worlds as his body, and because he is designated by the word "Puruṣa," he cannot be a deity called Agni, nor an elemental being—the third element, fire—denotable by the term Vaiśvānara.

61. Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even in the direct [sense]; that is, Jaimini—the teacher named Jaimini—considers that there is no contradiction, meaning the absence of the contradiction consisting in describing a word denoting a specific meaning as denoting something other than that, even when words such as "Agni" and others directly denote the Supreme Self through their own constituent powers (*avayava-śakti*) without any mediation.

62. "On account of manifestation," says Āśmarathya—(this refers to the statement that the all-pervading Supreme Self, Vaiśvānara, is limited by the measure of a span)—it is for the sake of facilitating the meditation of practitioners. This is the meaning held by Āśmarathya—the teacher named Āśmarathya.

63. Bādari [holds that the Puruṣa-form of the Supreme Self is] for the sake of recollection—(that is, the conceptualization of the form of the Supreme Self through such passages as "The sky is His head," etc.)—for the purpose of perfecting the meditation which is the cause of attaining Brahman; this is the view of the teacher named Bādari.

64. "Because of the identification; for so [the scripture] shows," says Jaimini. (Regarding the conceptualization of the sacrificial altar and other elements within the limbs of the worshiper of Vaiśvānara, who is the Supreme Self: "Because of the identification"—that is, for the purpose of identifying the oblation of breath offered by that worshiper with the Agnihotra sacrifice—so says Jaimini, the teacher named Jaimini.

It is so considered; for indeed, the scripture clarifies that very mode, which consists in the perfection of the Agnihotra, by stating: "He who, knowing thus, performs the Agnihotra. (65) And they declare Him in this [body]—the scriptures declare that the Supreme Self, Vaiśvānara, whose body is the earth and so forth, exists in this—namely, in the body belonging to the worshipper—by means of contemplation at the time of meditation, describing Him as possessing a form similar to that [of the worshipper's body].
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter.

69. Because of the designation of difference—that is, because of the explicit teaching of His distinction from the individual soul (*jīva*) in the Śruti text, "Another Lord" (*anyam īśam*), [it follows that this support of the earth and other elements is the Supreme Self alone, not the individual soul].

70. On account of the context—because, by the passage beginning with "Now, the higher [knowledge]," the Supreme Self alone is the subject under discussion, [it follows that] this support of the earth and so forth is the Supreme Self itself, and not some other entity not under discussion.

71. And because of "abiding" and "eating"—by "abiding," meaning it exists as one who does not eat, being devoid of the enjoyment of the fruits of karma, and existing as one who shines; and by "eating," meaning it eats what is sweet, being subject to karma and tasting its fruits—there is a mutual distinction based on the scriptural statements [of the Śruti]. (Therefore, this support of earth and so forth, and the attainer of immortality, is the Supreme Self alone; it is not the individual soul. 19. The Section on the Plenum (Bhūmādhikaraṇa).

72. *Bhūmā*—the Supreme Self alone, not the individual soul (*jīva*)—is the subject, characterized by the quality of abundance (*bhūman*, i.e., greatness), meaning its essential nature is bliss distinguished by unsurpassed vastness. This is known because it is taught as being "above" (*adhi*) the state of perfect serenity (*saṃprasāda*), that is, in comparison to the individual soul; for the scripture, in the passage, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly through Truth," makes known the superiority [of the one who speaks surpassingly through the Truth-form of the Supreme Self] over the speaker who surpasses the individual soul designated as *prāṇa*.

73. And because of the possibility of [certain] attributes—namely, because attributes such as natural immortality, which have been described as being connected with the referent denoted by the word "much" (bhūman), are possible only in the Supreme Self, since they exist there without contradiction; therefore, it is the Supreme Self alone, characterized by the quality of "muchness," and not the individual soul (jīva).

20. Section on the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). 74. The Imperishable (is Brahman), because it supports everything up to the ether. The term "Imperishable" (*akṣara*)—designated by the word *akṣara* in the scriptural passage, "This indeed is that Imperishable, O Gārgī"—refers to the Supreme Brahman alone. This is because it supports everything up to the ether—that is, the primary cause denoted by the term "undifferentiated ether" (*avyākṛtākāśa*), which is the material cause of the air-filled space—as indicated by the scriptural inquiry: "In what, then, is this space woven like warp and woof? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7). It is known [to be Brahman] through its supporting of all things.

And that [support]—namely, the support of the Pradhāna denoted by the term "the end of space," which was mentioned previously—is due to "praśāsanāt" (from governance), that is, from a preeminent governance consisting of an unimpeded command; [therefore, such an Imperishable is the Supreme Brahman alone, not the individual soul].

76. And because of the exclusion of other states—namely, the non-difference from the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) in the entity denoted by the word "imperishable" (*akṣara*), and the exclusion [of that same non-difference] from the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) (since those which possess difference from the Supreme Person cannot possibly possess the quality of being the Seer, and this is established in the supplementary passage by the fact that such a state has never been seen by anyone).
21. The Section Concerning the Object of the Act of Seeing (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*).

77. "Because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of seeing. The object of the act of seeing—referred to in the statement, "He sees the Person dwelling in the city"—and the object of the meditation referred to in the statement, "One should meditate upon the Person," is that very Being, the Supreme Self. This is because of the designation; that is, because the attributes of the Supreme Self, such as tranquility and immortality, are explicitly stated in the Śruti with reference to the entity that is the object of the acts of seeing and meditating.

22. The Section on the Subtle (Daharādhikaraṇa). 78. The Subtle One [is Brahman] because of the subsequent [statements]. "The subtle one" refers to that which is denoted by the word *dahara* (the small) as being in grammatical apposition with the word *ākāśa* (ether). That is indeed the Supreme Self, because of the subsequent [statements], namely, those characteristics common to the Supreme Self which serve as indicators and are set forth in the subsequent passage beginning with, "This Self is free from sin... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

79. By both movement and scriptural statement; for it is seen through the movement—that all creatures, day after day, go to the small ether (dahara-ākāśa) preceded by a departure due to their lack of knowledge—and by the scriptural statement, namely the word "Brahma-world" (brahma-loka) applied to that very subject which serves as an indicator, it is known that the "small" (dahara)—the referent denoted by the word "small"—is the Supreme Self (paramātman).

For—since such a form of going and the state of the world of Brahman (brahmaloka) are seen [to apply] to the Supreme Brahman alone, as established in the Śruti—and this very point is sufficient evidence.

80. "And because this greatness of support is perceived in this"—(1-3-15). Because this—namely, the greatness (*mahiman*) consisting of the support of the universe, which is characteristic of the Supreme Self—is perceived in this object denoted by the term "small ether" (*daharākāśa*), as evidenced by the scriptural statement, "This is the bridge, the supporter" (*eṣa seturvidharaṇaḥ*), [it follows that the small ether is the Supreme Brahman]. 81. "And because of its well-known usage. (*prasiddheśca daharaḥ*).

(Ākāśa)—The referent denoted by the term "daharākāśa" (the small ether) is the Supreme Brahman; this is because of its well-known usage—since the word "ākāśa" is understood in the sense of Brahman in such passages as "All these indeed... from Ākāśa alone," where the particle "ha vai" indicates that it is a very well-known fact.

82. If it be argued that "He" refers to the individual soul because of a reference to it—on account of the observation of the teaching, "The serene one, having risen up from this body," [and] because the term "small ether" denotes the individual soul itself—the answer is: No, because of impossibility.
That is to say, such a statement regarding the other—that is, something different from Brahman—is not found in the passage situated in the middle of the Dahara-vidyā.
This is not logical, because it is impossible; the previously mentioned qualities would be contradicted in the individual soul (jīva).

83. If [it is argued] that from the subsequent [text], namely from the words of Prajāpati, the individual soul (*jīva*) is understood as possessing qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), that statement is not correct. Rather, "one whose true nature has become manifest" means that the individual soul is one whose own essential nature has become revealed through the removal of concealment by attaining that [state] produced by the meditation upon the Supreme Brahman; this is what is stated in the words of Prajāpati. (It is not, however, [a state] characterized by freedom from sin by its very nature.)

84. Furthermore, the reference has another purpose—the reference indeed has another purpose: in the passage concerning the Dahara-vidyā, the introduction of the individual self (jīvātman) serves the purpose of demonstrating the supreme majesty of the Supreme Self, characterized by its power to manifest the true nature of the individual self; it does not, however, serve the purpose of establishing that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the individual self.

85. If it be argued that [the small ether is the individual soul] because of its being mentioned as small, that has already been answered: regarding the claim that "because of the mention of smallness"—that is, because a small dimension is declared in the scripture for that which is understood by the word *dahara* (small), therefore the individual soul alone, being of small dimension, is what is spoken of in the *dahara* passage—if this is said, it has been refuted here.

86. *Tadanukṛtes tasya ca tasya*: Because of the imitation of Him—that is, because of the very imitation of the Supreme Self who is by His own nature distinguished by such qualities as being free from sin—and indeed only through attaining equality with Him is there the manifestation of one's own true nature; (therefore, the small ether is the Supreme Self who is to be imitated by the individual soul, and He is certainly distinct from the individual soul, the imitator).

87. Furthermore, the imitation of that Supreme Self—the imitation residing in the individual soul in the form of attaining similarity with Him—is also recorded in Smṛti; for it is indeed stated in the Smṛti: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained My own nature."
22. The Section on the Measured (Pramitādhikaraṇam).

88. "Measured by the word alone, he is measured. The Person declared in the Śruti to be of the measure of a thumb is none other than the Supreme Self; this is known from the word alone—that is, from the very word that makes known his status as the Supreme Self, namely the scriptural statement: "The Lord of what has been and what is to be."

89. But with reference to the heart—because the scripture has human beings as its intended audience—it is measured as being the size of a thumb. That is to say, with reference to the heart—that specific location within the body called the "heart" (wherein the Supreme Self resides)—the designation "measured by a thumb" is made solely with the intention that the Supreme Self be manifested in that place for the sake of the worshipper. This is because the scripture prescribing the practice of meditation proceeds by taking the human worshipper as its subject;
and because the location of the heart in a human being corresponds in size to the thumb of that particular human being.
23. This concludes the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*).

90. *Taduparyapi bādarāyaṇaḥ sambhavāt*: That meditation on Brahman is possible even "above"—that is, among the gods and others who dwell in the worlds above humans—as Bādarāyaṇa, the teacher named Bādarāyaṇa, maintains. This is because the desire for liberation and the capacity [for it] are unimpeded even for the gods and others.

91. "If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding the action, we say no, because we observe the attainment of various states" (1.3.26) — [this refers to] the meditation of the gods and others.

If it is argued that there would be a contradiction—namely, the impossibility for a single embodied being to exist simultaneously in multiple distinct locations—if one accepts a body and sense organs that are exceptionally fit [for such action] during a ritual such as a sacrifice performed by many people at once—such a reflection is not appropriate, because we observe the simultaneous presence in many places through the assumption of multiple bodies by Saubhari and others, as heard in the Purāṇas and other texts.

92. If it is argued that there is a contradiction—namely, the consequence of accepting meanings not [otherwise] admitted, such as the meaninglessness or impermanence of words like "Indra" used in the Veda—because of the claim that these words are devoid of referents, this objection does not hold. Why? Because of their origin (*prabhava*) from those very words recited in the Veda; for we accept the creation of the gods Indra and others from the words "Indra" and so forth found in the Veda. This point is established by both perception and inference, as stated in the Veda: "By means of the Veda... [and so on].
This is established by the Śruti text, "He gave instruction," as well as by the Smṛti text, "In the beginning, He fashioned [the Vedas] from the words of the Veda itself."

93. For this very reason there is eternality; and because Prajāpati, the creator, creates everything by recollecting the forms of objects from the very words of the Veda, therefore there is indeed eternality. Thus, even though Vasiṣṭha and others are the authors of mantras and so forth, the eternality of the Veda remains intact.

94. Furthermore, because names and forms are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as is seen from both scripture and tradition. Even in the case of recurrence—that is, even when there is a new creation of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) following the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)—there is no contradiction because names and forms are identical. This means that among the objects to be created, the names and forms are exactly similar to the names and forms belonging to the objects of the previous creation; therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the eternity of the Vedas, for they lack the impermanence that would contradict their eternal nature.

The comprehension of this meaning [is obtained] from revelation—namely, from such scriptural texts as "He who in the beginning created Brahmā"—and also from traditional authority—namely, from such Smṛti passages as "Just as the seasonal signs [recur] according to the seasons. These serve as the indicators [of this truth].

25. The Section on the Honey [Vidyā] (Madhvadhikaraṇa). 95. *Jaimini* maintains that there is no entitlement [to these meditations] because of the impossibility [of it] in the case of the Honey and other [meditations]. Regarding the Honey and other [meditations]—that is, the meditations consisting of the Honey-Vidyā and so forth—there is no entitlement; namely, the absence of entitlement for conscious beings such as the Vasus who have already attained their respective stations. This is what the teacher named *Jaimini* believes, because of the impossibility—due to the fact that the Vasus and others, being the objects of meditation, cannot simultaneously be the meditators, since they have already attained the station of the Vasus and so forth.

Bādarāyaṇa—the venerable Bādarāyaṇa—considers that there indeed exists the qualification for the meditation on the Vasus and others; for (hi), even for those who have already attained the status of the Vasus and so forth, it is possible to attain the status of the Vasus and others in another kalpa, and through the contemplation of the identity of Brahman and the Self, their own selves can certainly become objects of meditation as well.

26. The Section on the Exclusion of Śūdras (Adhikaraṇa 98). The grief of this [Jānaśruti] is indicated by the hearing of that disregard and by his running toward him. For King Jānaśruti experienced *śuk*—that is, grief caused by the non-attainment of the knowledge of Brahman. This is indicated (*sūcyate*)—meaning it is inferred—from the hearing of that disregard, namely from hearing the words of disregard spoken by the swan immediately after which he ran toward the teacher who would instruct him in Brahman; for it is from this very grief that his status as a *śūdra* is indicated, not from being born into the *śūdra* caste.

99. And because of his attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya—since Jānaśruti, who desired to hear the knowledge of Brahman, is recognized as having attained the state of a Kṣatriya, that is, being born of the Kṣatriya caste—as indicated by the perception [of this fact] through two attributes peculiar to a Rājanya, namely, being a "great giver" (*bahudāyī*) and a "provider of much cooked food" (*bahupākya*), which signify his status as a lord of gifts and a donor of abundant prepared food, [it follows that] he was not born of the fourth caste.

100. "On account of the subsequent mention of Caitraratha [as a mark], there is the determination of the Kṣatriya status of this [Jānaśruti]—that is, an inferential conclusion regarding his being a Kṣatriya—based on the Kṣatriya named Abhipratārin, a descendant of Citraratha, who is mentioned later in the portion of the Upaniṣad connected with this very knowledge. (The fact that Abhipratārin was a descendant of Citraratha and a Kṣatriya) is established by the mark (*liṅga*), namely, the indicative evidence consisting in the association with the word *Kāpeya*."

101. Because of the reference to the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) and the mention of its absence [in the instructions on the knowledge of Brahman], [it is clear that] the one addressed as "O Śūdra" is not a member of the fourth caste. For, in the case of the twice-born, there is a reference to the *saṃskāra*—specifically the initiation rite (*upanayana-saṃskāra*) which is an auxiliary to the instruction—as presented in such sentences as "I shall lead you near"; whereas in the case of the Śūdra, there is a mention of the absence of that [rite], namely the lack of the initiation rite, as clearly stated in passages such as "And he does not deserve the sacramental rite. Therefore, the one addressed as "O Śūdra" is not one belonging to the fourth caste.

102. Furthermore, because [the teacher] proceeds [to teach] only when there is a determination of the absence of that [status]—namely, the determination (*nirdhāraṇa*) or ascertainment of the absence of being a member of the Śūdra class in the case of Jabālā’s son; for we observe such activity in the scriptural passage, "One who is not a Brāhmaṇa is not fit to speak this; bring fuel, my dear" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.4.5), which indicates that the instruction of knowledge is not established by scripture for one belonging to the Śūdra class.

Because of the prohibition of hearing, study, and the meaning [of the Veda]: since "hearing"—the grasping with the ear of the mass of syllables known as the Veda—is prohibited by the direct sense of the Śruti text, "Therefore, one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra"; and because, by the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutika-nyāya*), both "study"—which consists of the recitation following the utterance from the mouth of a teacher—and the "meaning," which is the performance of the study's purpose such as sacrifices and other rites, are also prohibited; [it follows that] a person of the Śūdra caste is not declared by the Śruti to be eligible for knowledge.

Furthermore, because there is an indicator in the form of a Smṛti prohibition—stated in the Smṛtis—of hearing the Veda, grasping the Veda, and performing its prescribed rites, it is known that one belonging to the Śūdra caste does not possess the qualification for the knowledge taught in the Veda.

The section on "Measured" (Pramitādhikaraṇa) 105: "Measured by the thumb"—the entity declared in scripture to be measured by the thumb (is the Supreme Self alone; not the individual soul), because of trembling—since it possesses the capacity to produce fear, which is the cause of the trembling of everything declared in scripture in the passage: "Whatever there is in this entire world, it trembles because of Prāṇa."

106. [The Supreme Self is] measured by the perception of light—the meaning established by scripture through the measurement by the thumb [is the Supreme Self, not the individual soul]—because of the perception of the connection with that Light which outshines all luminaries such as the sun and illumines all lights, as set forth in the scripture: "There the sun does not shine... by His light all this shines."
27. Section on the Designation as Being Something Else: 107.

*Ākāśa* [is the Supreme Self] because of the designation of being something else and so forth. The term *ākāśa* refers to the referent of the word *ākāśa* mentioned in the Śruti as the "conductor of name and form" (*nāmarūpanirvodṛtva*). [This is] the Supreme Self alone; it is neither the bound nor the liberated soul. This is because of the designation of being "something else" and so forth—namely, the state of being the conductor of name and form, as well as the state of being Brahman without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-brahmatva*), which are attributes not residing in the individual self (*pratyagātman*), but residing only in the Supreme Self who is other than the *jīva*. This is because it is clearly established by such Śruti passages as: "Verily, *ākāśa* is the conductor of name and form. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).

The fourth quarter: Just as the word "great" (*mahat*) [is used] in grammatical apposition [with Brahman], so too the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) in the passage "Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest" (*mahataḥ param avyaktam*) does not refer to the Pradhāna.

122. "By light" (*jyotiṣā*): for some, when food is absent—for the Kāṇvas, according to the remainder of the passage (*vākyaśeṣe*)—that is, when the word "food" (*anna*) is not present; by "light"—by the word "light" (*jyotiḥ*) occurring at the beginning of the passage, namely "The gods [know him] as the light of lights"—it is understood that [the five classes of beings] are the illuminating senses denoted by the term *pañcajana*. (An investigation into whether these are material elements is not the subject under discussion here.)

31. The Section on Being the Cause (Kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa) 123. And because of the mention [of Brahman] as the cause in the case of ether and so forth, according to how it was described. In the case of ether and so forth—i.e., in those passages marked by words such as "ether," beginning with "From the Self, ether was produced"—with respect to ether and the rest, it is precisely as the cause, as the instrumental reason, that [Brahman] is mentioned by us according to how it was described—that is, as being endowed with the nature of the universal Self and other attributes. (The Pradhāna, which is not of the nature of Brahman, is not the cause. [End of section] Vyapa-... [text fragment]

It is of the Supreme Brahman alone that has been declared [in the preceding section], because of the "drawing together" (samākarṣāt)—that is, because of the inclusion [of the term] by way of being the subject to which it refers. By the word "non-existent" (asat), it is Brahman itself in its state as the unmanifested causal condition that is expressed; it is not a doctrine asserting non-existence as the cause.
32. The Section Concerning the Denotation of the World (Jagadvācitvādhikaraṇam).

125. Because it denotes the world—because the word "karma" occurring in the Kauṣītaki passage, "Of whom this is the work" (*yasya vaitat karma*), is derived from the root *kṛ* meaning "to act," and thus denotes the created manifold universe; [therefore] the referent of the pronoun "he" (*sa*) in the phrase "He indeed is to be known" (*sa vai veditavyaḥ*) is taught as the Supreme Person alone, the creator of the entire world, who is to be known.

126. "If it be argued that [the one to be known] is not the Supreme Self because of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital air (mukhyaprāṇa)—that is, because of the mark of the individual soul in the form of being an enjoyer, as in 'The conscious self enjoys through these selves,' and because of the mark of the chief vital air in the form 'The vital air becomes onefold'—and therefore the one indicated by the words 'He indeed is to be known' is neither the Supreme Self but rather the individual soul or the vital air; if such an objection is raised, then that objection has been explained—that is, it has been specifically refuted in the *Pratardana-vidyā*."

"But for another purpose, Jaimini [says so], on account of the question and the explanation; and thus some [hold] as well. (Sūtra 1.4.18) "But for another purpose"—that is, the mention of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth by means of marks such as being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), is solely for the sake of establishing the existence of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who is distinct from that. This is shown by the question in the form of an inquiry: "O Bālāki, in whom did this person lie? and by the explanatory answer: "Then he becomes one with breath alone," and so forth. Thus says the teacher Jaimini.
Furthermore, moreover, some Vājasaneyins recite this very same thing clearly in this very manner.
Section 128: The Topic of the Consistency of the Sentence (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa).

Because of the consistency of the sentence—because the entire sentence, beginning with "By what should one know Him by whom all this is known? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), is consistent [only] with the Supreme Self through its own primary meaning—the Self indicated as the object to be seen in the passage "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen" is none other than the Supreme Self.

Āśmarathya [maintains] that there is a sign for the establishment of the proposition (1.4.20). Regarding the "proposition"—that is, the proposition that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all—for its "establishment"—meaning its accomplishment—there is a "sign"—namely, the indicator (that the Supreme Self is denoted by words expressing the individual self)—so says Āśmarathya, the teacher named Āśmarathya.

130. Auḍulomi maintains that [the identity of the individual soul with the Supreme Self] occurs because of the soul’s becoming such [as the Supreme Self] upon its departure—that is, when the soul, having abandoned the body and ascended upward, has perfected its means and attained the state of the Supreme Self; thus, [the scriptures] designate the Supreme Self by a word denoting the individual soul—this is the reason held by Auḍulomi, the teacher named Auḍulomi.

131. "On account of the abiding," says Kāśakṛtsna. Taking as the reason the abiding of the Supreme Self within the individual self as its inner self, as stated in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, the teacher named Kāśakṛtsna maintains this resolution: that [the Supreme Self] is denoted by those words among the Vedic texts which express the individual self.

135. Because of its being self-made—since the Self, which is Brahman itself, is the agent—and because of the teaching in the scripture, "It made itself by itself," which clearly indicates that it is both the material cause and the efficient cause.
Because of creation—both [the world and its cause] are Brahman alone in the form of the universe.

This is because of transformation: for Brahman, whose body consists of the subtle entities of consciousness and non-consciousness with undivided names and forms, there occurs a transformation into a state where the entities of consciousness and non-consciousness have gross, divided names and forms. This is taught in the Śruti: "The unmanifested existed; it was manifested through names and forms. (Modifications that are not ends of human purpose, being attributes, do not attach to the substantive, Brahman.)

137. For it is indeed sung as the source (*yoni*); Brahman is called the "source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*) and the "source of Brahman" (*brahmayoni*), and is thus declared in the Śruti as being the source. Therefore, Brahman is also the material cause (*prakṛti*), not merely the efficient cause.
The Second Chapter.

The first quarter [of the sūtra] is based on an indicator (*jñāpaka*): [in passages such as] "Earth desired" (*pṛthivy annavīt*) and "Waters indeed desired" (*āpo vā akāmayanta*), there is the treatment of the qualities of a conscious being with respect to Earth and so forth. However, this is a designation of the presiding deities (*abhimānivyapadeśaḥ*); that is, it is merely a designation of the qualities of consciousness belonging to the deities who preside over Earth and the rest, not [qualities] residing in Earth and the rest themselves.

144. But it is indeed observed—it is indeed observed—in the world that the state of being an effect is actually found even for things that are dissimilar to their cause (e.g., as worms, which are dissimilar to honey and other such substances, are born from them).

145. If it is argued that [the cause] is non-existent because it is a mere negation—[that is,] if one were to accept the proposition "the cause is different in nature from the effect," it would follow that "prior to production, the cause is non-existent"—this objection is not tenable because it is a mere negation. This is because the statement "but it is seen" aims solely at establishing the absence of a rule regarding identity between the cause and the effect by demonstrating the production of an effect that is different in nature from its cause.

146. "Because of the consequence that [the world] would be like that at the time of dissolution, it is inconsistent. Regarding "at the time of dissolution": whether at the time of the world's dissolution into Brahman, or at the time of its origination from Brahman, because of the consequence that it would be "like that"—that is, because defects such as the modifications belonging to the world and the absence of the supreme human goal would also accrue to Brahman—it is "inconsistent"; this means that by describing the world as the effect of Brahman, the Vedāntas are rendered inconsistent.

147. However, it is not the case that because of the existence of examples there arises the consequence of modification (*vikāra*) and so forth in Brahman, nor is there any consequence of the inconsistency of the Vedāntas; for examples do exist—namely, that even when a single entity undergoes two states, virtues and defects are restricted to those respective states alone, as in the example: "The man became a child, [and then] a youth."

148. And because of the defects in its own position—since even in the position that asserts Primordial Matter (pradhāna) as the cause, there exists the defect of inconsistency consisting in the expression of contradictory meanings—the Sāṃkhya position must indeed be abandoned.

149. Furthermore, because reasoning is not firmly established—due to the lack of a firm foundation for reasoning—the Sāṃkhya position, which is rooted in reasoning, should not be relied upon; rather, it is only the doctrine that Brahman is the cause, which is rooted in scripture, that should be accepted. 150.

If it is argued that "it must be established in another way," even so, there follows the consequence of non-release (*anirmokṣaprasaṅga*). "In another way" means: such that it is not sublated by counter-reasonings (*pratikūla-tarka*); [that is,] the primacy of *pradhāna* as the cause, as asserted by the Sāṃkhya, must be established by inference. If this is the objection—such a suspicion is also untenable; for even if it were established by inference in the form of a reasoning (*tarka*), there would still follow the consequence of non-release, which is the occurrence of the absence of distance from the defect known as the instability of reasoning (*tarkāpratiṣṭhitatva*).

39. Section on the Non-Acceptance by the Learned (Śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa). 151. "By this, those not accepted by the learned are also explained. By this—namely, by the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position which is not accepted by the Vedas—the remaining positions not accepted by the Vedas, such as those of Kaṇāda and others, are also to be understood as explained—that is, as refuted.

Because of its being endowed with the nature of non-conceptualization, and because of another scriptural passage—namely, the existence of another word that establishes existence, such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," which refers to that very same thing previously described as non-existent before creation.

157. "And like cloth, and like cloth"—just as that entity which previously bore the designation 'thread' is subsequently designated as 'cloth' by virtue of undergoing a particular state of the interweaving of threads, in exactly the same way, it is entirely appropriate for Brahman to be designated as 'non-existent' (asat) in its subtle state and as 'existent' (sat) in its gross state; thus, the effect is non-different from the cause. 158.

And just as the vital air (prāṇa) and so forth—meaning the elemental air functioning as the fivefold modifications consisting of prāṇa, apāna, and the rest—is non-different from the single causal air residing within the body, even so the world in its state as an effect, characterized by gross sentient and insentient entities, is indeed non-different from the reality in its causal state, which consists of Brahman characterized by subtle sentient and insentient entities.

163. "And as in the world, among gods and others"—that is, in their respective worlds, just as gods, gandharvas, and others possess the power to create objects required by themselves through their own volition, so too it is entirely logical that Brahman possesses the power to create everything through His own volition alone.

171. But it is like the play of the world; it is mere play—meaning that creation has the nature of being merely a pastime for [the Lord] who has all desires fulfilled. This is appropriate, just as in the case of a worldly king, even though his desires are fully satisfied, he engages in activities such as playing with a ball. 172.

"Regarding the charge of partiality and cruelty: [the objection is] that for the Supreme Brahman, who creates the world in the forms of gods, humans, and so forth, and abounds in pleasure and pain, there would follow an absence of equality toward all individual souls (*jīvātman*) as well as a lack of compassion for those who suffer. But this does not arise, because the inequality of creation is dependent upon [other factors]; specifically, it is due to the connection with the particular karma of each respective *kṣetrajña* (individual soul). Thus [it is said].
The joining of the bodies of the gods and others depends upon the respective karma of those individual souls; for the Śruti itself indeed demonstrates and makes this known.

173. "If it be argued that [the Lord's partiality] does not arise from the absence of action, we say no, because [the world] is beginningless; and this is both logical and observed. Regarding the phrase "from the absence of distinction" (*avibhāgāt*): since scripture declares that at the time prior to creation, the individual soul (*jīva*) was in a state of non-distinction with Brahman, one might argue—"Action" (*karma*), meaning the specific karma belonging to each individual soul which causes the unequal creation, cannot exist [prior to creation]. Such an objection is not tenable. Why? Because it is logical (*upapadyate*)—even though the souls and their respective karmas, which serve as the causes of inequality, existed prior to creation.

The scriptural statement regarding non-differentiation is appropriate solely on account of the absence of the differentiation of name and form. Because of beginninglessness—since the existence of both the individual souls and their karmas is likewise not first in time—and because it is indeed perceived through such scriptural texts as "It is neither born nor does it die," the beginninglessness of the individual souls is known.

174. And because all attributes are possible: For this reason as well—that all attributes, such as omniscience and others, which are necessary for the governance of the entire world and which are impossible in cases such as *pradhāna* or atoms, are compatible with the Supreme Brahman—the Supreme Brahman alone is the cause of the world.
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter.

176. "If [it is argued] that it is like milk and water"—if it is said that, just as in the case of milk and water, the activity of *pradhāna* occurs even without being presided over by a conscious being, this is not impossible; for even in the case of milk and water, there exists an activity consisting of a transformation suited to the effect, which occurs only when they are presided over by a conscious, intelligent agent (*prājña*).

"And because of the non-continuity of the distinction, and because of independence" (2-2-3). "Because of independence"—that is, [if the Pradhāna were the cause] in its solitary state, because the Pradhāna lacks dependence on a conscious being—and "because of the non-continuity of the distinction": because it would follow that there is no persistence in the state of dissolution (pralaya), which is the state following the period of creation; therefore, the Pradhāna is not the cause.

And because [transformation] does not occur elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth. Just as grass, water, and the like undergo transformation into the form of milk and so on even without being presided over by a conscious agent, [one might argue that] the transformation of the *pradhāna* into the form of the world is likewise possible without being presided over by a conscious agent—this is not tenable. Why? Because it does not occur elsewhere; that is, in the case of non-living things such as jars and the like, there is an absence of the transformation of grass, water, and so forth into the form of milk and the like.

179.
