If it is argued that [the Pradhāna acts] "like a man and a stone"—that is, just as a man who lacks the power of locomotion but possesses the power of vision causes a blind man to engage in walking by his mere proximity, and just as a magnet causes iron to move by its mere proximity—so too the Pradhāna causes activity in the Puruṣa; even such a reflection is not tenable. Why? Because even by way of the analogy with the man and the magnet, [it is not so].

(On account of the impossibility of activity in the Pradhāna) 180. And because of the impossibility of being a principal [member] (2-2-6)—that is, because of the impossibility of "being a principal" (aṅgitva), which is based on superiority and consists in being related to subordinate members (aṅga), or being that which is benefited—and because it is impossible for this to exist in the single Pradhāna when it is in the state of equilibrium at the time of dissolution; and also for the reason that [such a relationship] cannot occur during the state when the cause is not present, (the status of the Pradhāna as the cause of the world is not tenable).

181. Furthermore, in the case of inference based on a different [mode], due to the absence of the power of cognition: "in a different manner" means by following a mode distinct from the defective one; and "even in the case of inference"—that is, even in the primary inference—"due to the absence of the power of cognition," meaning because the capacity for being a cognizer is impossible in the case of *pradhāna*, the status of *pradhāna* as an independent cause of the world is not at all possible.

182. "Even if it is accepted, because of the absence of a purpose" (2-2-8). Even if there is acceptance—that is, even if one grants the existence of the entity called *pradhāna*—there is an absence of a purpose; for it is impossible to establish the two purposes consisting of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) in a changeless *puruṣa*. (Therefore, the *pradhāna* cannot be established through inference.)
183. Furthermore, it is inconsistent because of contradiction; that is, because of speaking in mutual opposition, the Sāṃkhya doctrine is not correct—it is inconsistent.
47. The Topic on the Great and the Long (Mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa).

184. "Or else, like the great and the long, from the short and the spherical"—that is, from the dyads and atoms acting as causes, just as the production of dyads and triads occurs like that of the great and the long; or rather, another object of knowledge accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas is simply inconsistent, being devoid of logical justification.

In either case, there is no such thing as *karman*. Regarding that which is accepted as the producer of action—*adṛṣṭa* (the unseen merit/demerit)—whether it resides in the atoms (*aṇu*) or in the individual soul (*jīva*), the visible action consisting of motion (*spanda*) cannot possibly be caused by *adṛṣṭa*. Therefore, because it is impossible for *adṛṣṭa*, whether residing in the atoms or in the self, to be the cause of action, there is its absence; that is, there is an absence of the prior necessity of atom-residing action for the origination of the world.
In either case— [namely,] because action in atoms is occasional (kādācitkatayā)—

And because of the acceptance of inherence, due to parity, there is an infinite regress; for even because of the acceptance of a relation called "inherence" (as the means of accounting for the cognition of things qualified by universals, qualities, etc.), the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is illogical and devoid of justification. This is so because of parity—since it would be equally necessary to accept another inherence defined by the first inherence (to account for the cognition of "the cloth is inherent")—and because of the resulting infinite regress (if such further relations were accepted).

187. Furthermore, because [inherence] exists eternally, and because it exists eternally—due to the perpetual existence of that which is called "eternal relation" (namely, inherence)—it follows that [the atoms] would also be eternal by virtue of their relationship (since they are related through it). Thus, the description of atoms as the cause [of the world] is inconsistent; it is utterly devoid of logical justification.

188. "And because of possessing form and so forth, there would be the opposite [of permanence], since they are seen to possess form and so forth. Because it is admitted that atoms possess form, taste, and so forth, the opposite would follow for them: namely, impermanence—which is the opposite of permanence—and possession of parts—which is the opposite of partlessness. This is because, in the case of things such as jars which possess form and so forth, both impermanence and possession of parts are observed.

And because there are faults in both cases—since in both cases, whether atoms lack qualities such as color and so forth or possess them, the faults remain unrefuted: namely, the absence of the principle that the qualities of an effect must be preceded by the qualities of their cause, and the fault of [atoms] being non-eternal; therefore, the description of atoms as the cause [of the world] is indeed inconsistent.

190. And because it is not accepted [by the learned Vaidikas] in any respect, there is absolute disregard for it—due to its being unaccepted by the learned followers of the Vedas even in any part [of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine], there is absolute disregard—that is, a total lack of anything to be expected from it in every way by those seeking the supreme good; it is simply to be ignored.

48. The section on the aggregate (*samudāya-adhikaraṇam*): Even in the case of that which is caused by both, there is no attainment of that [aggregate]; that is, even in the case of what is intended to have atoms as its cause, as well as in what is intended to have earth and the other elements as its cause—in the aggregate of the elements such as earth, and likewise in the aggregate of the body, sense organs, and so forth—there is no attainment of that, meaning the aggregate-status is not established; (because it is admitted that all things are momentary). || 192 ||

If it is argued that [the world] is established because of mutual conditionality—that is, because of the mutual relationship of cause and effect between ignorance (*avidyā*), passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth, and thus all worldly transactions and the like are established as uncontradicted and complete—this objection is not tenable. It does not hold, because there is no basis for the state of being a composite (*saṅghātabhāva*). Since ignorance—which consists of erroneous cognition—is incapable of being the cause for the aggregation of earth and the other elements, the very existence of such a composite is unproven.

And because of recognition—by the force of re-cognition in the form "this is that very same thing" (which establishes stability, contradicting momentariness)—the doctrine of momentariness favored by the Buddhists is indeed untenable.

199. "Because it is not observed that [there is a transition] from the non-existent"—it is not the case that there is a transition of a property (or of a substratum) that has perished without leaving a trace; for such a thing is entirely impossible, because it has never been observed or perceived anywhere.

200. And thus there would be accomplishment even for those who are indifferent: if the momentariness of all things is accepted, then accomplishment—meaning the fulfillment of all goals pertaining to this world and the next—would occur even for those who are indifferent, that is, for persons who exert no effort. (Therefore, the doctrine of both the Sautrāntikas and the Vaibhāṣikas is indeed inconsistent.)

49. The Topic of Apprehension (Upalabdhyadhikaraṇa) 201. "Non-existence [is not possible], because of apprehension. Non-existence—that is, the non-reality of external objects other than cognition—cannot be accepted, because of apprehension; for an object such as a jar that has become the content of cognition is seen through direct perception and thus cannot be denied.

202. And because of dissimilarity, it is not as in the case of dreams and the like; that is, just as in the case of dream-cognitions, it is not possible for waking cognitions to have unreal objects. This is because of dissimilarity—that is, due to the difference between dream-cognitions and waking cognitions consisting in the absence of defects in the causes and the absence of subverting cognitions [in the latter]. Therefore, waking cognitions have only real objects.

203. There is no existence, because it is not perceived. "Existence"—that is, the being of cognition alone, devoid of an object—is not possible, because it is not perceived; that is, because there is no experience of the existence of a cognition that is neither an agent nor possesses an object.

206. And thus, there is a partiality of the self (*ātmākātsyam*); for just as there is the admission of contradictory properties in one [locus], so too, in the case of the partiality of the self, it would follow that the living self (*jīvātman*) is incomplete. [For according to the Jaina view,] it is held that the living self has a size equal to each respective body throughout the entire body; this, however, is not logical.

207. Nor can there be non-contradiction even through the theory of modal succession (*paryāya*), because of [the necessity of admitting] transformation and so forth. Even by accepting a diversity of dimensions—consisting of contraction and expansion—within the self at different times through modal succession, the absence of non-co-referentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) cannot be established; for it is simply impossible to avoid the transformations consisting of change (*pariṇāma*) and the defects consequent upon them. 208.

Because of the permanence of both at the final state, there is no distinction; and because of the permanence of both—the fact that the dimension of the individual soul (*jīva*) remains undestroyed in the state of liberation—and because of the permanence of both—the very indestructibility of the soul and its dimension—there is no distinction, meaning that the difference in dimension between the state of liberation and the state preceding it is not established. (Thus, the doctrine of the Ārhatas is indeed untenable.)
Non-contradiction [of the two sizes] due to transformation and so forth.

Section 52: On Paśupati. Regarding the Lord (pati)—that is, the doctrine of Paśupati—it is not to be respected because of its inconsistency; that is, because it is improper, being characterized by a realization of principles and conduct contrary to the Vedas.

And because of the impossibility of superintendence (*adhiṣṭhāna*); that is, because it is impossible for the Pradhāna—the material cause—to abide by being superintended [by an agent], and because such superintendence is also untenable in the case of a bodiless Lord (*īśvara*), [the doctrine of Paśupati is inconsistent].

211. "If it is argued that [the Lord's control] is like that of an instrument—[that is,] if it is claimed that just as the bodiless *kṣetrajña* (individual soul) presides over its own instruments and body, so too is the presiding over *prakṛti* by the bodiless Paśupati logical—this resolution is not tenable. Why? Because of enjoyment and so forth; for if that were the case, then just as the individual soul experiences the pleasure and pain that are the fruits of merit and demerit, enjoyment and other such states would necessarily follow for Paśupati as well."

(2-2-38) "Either finitude or non-omniscience [would follow]. Finitude—[that is, even for Paśupati,] if merit and demerit are admitted, he too would be subject to creation and dissolution—or else non-omniscience, that is, the absence of omniscience, would necessarily result; thus the doctrine of Paśupati is indeed inconsistent.

53. The Section on the Impossibility of Origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa). 213. Because of the impossibility of origination—that is, because of the impossibility of the origination of the individual soul as taught in the Pāñcarātra Āgama—due to its inconsistency [with scripture], since the individual soul is established by the Śruti as being devoid of both origination and destruction; [therefore, the Pāñcarātra which teaches the origination of the soul is not an authoritative means of knowledge].

Furthermore, an instrument is not the cause of the agent; that is, the mind, which serves as the instrument for knowledge and so forth, does not arise from the agent—the living self (jīva). Thus, the Pāñcarātra scripture, which asserts the production of the mind from the living self, is not authoritative.

215. Or, if consciousness and so forth exist, there is no negation of that: if it is established that Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman, which consists of pure consciousness, then there is no negation of that—that is, the negation of the authority of the Pāñcarātra (which teaches the origination of Brahman in the form of voluntary incarnations) is not at all established.

216. And because of contradiction—(even in this Pāñcarātra), since the production of the individual soul (*jīva*) is specifically prohibited, [the Pāñcarātra] does not propound a meaning contrary to the Vedas; therefore, there is no refutation of the authority of the Pāñcarātra. Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter.
222. From those Vedic statements which establish that before creation there was only the one Brahman, it is determined that space is an effect.

223. "But as far as there is modification, so far there is division, as in the world. That is to say, for all things that have become modifications, their division—that is, their origination from Brahman alone—is like in the world; just as in worldly transactions, even if some part is not explicitly stated by words, it is established by implication (artha), so it is established here by implication alone.

224. By this, Mātariśvan is explained; by this very same reasoning that establishes the origin of ether, Mātariśvan—that is, air—is also explained, meaning it is established as having an origin and a substratum.

225. "But the non-existence [of the effect] is due to the impossibility of the existence [of the cause]; that is, the non-existence of the existent—that which is denoted by the word 'existent,' namely Brahman itself—is established precisely because of the impossibility [otherwise] of the proposition that through the knowledge of one [thing], there is the knowledge of everything other than Brahman. This is proven solely by the fact that such a proposition would otherwise be untenable.
[The objection of] impossibility [is refuted].

55. Section on Fire (Tejo'dhikaraṇa) 226. Fire arises from that [air], for so the scripture declares. Fire is light; it is produced, for the Śruti clearly states: "Its production is from air, from fire."
Therefore, he indeed says "from air alone" in the words, "From air, fire."
227. Water [originates] from that—namely, from fire alone; for thus indeed the Śruti declares: "The production of water is from fire."
Water—water is produced;

it is said, "From fire, water" (2.3.10). Earth—the earth-element also is produced from water alone; for thus the Śruti describes the very production of earth from water, saying, "From water, earth" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).

229. [The word "earth" refers to the gross element earth] because of the context (adhikāra), the form (rūpa), another scriptural passage (śabdāntara), and an indicative mark (jñāpaka). Context: Because the subject matter under discussion is the creation of the great elements (mahābhūta-sṛṣṭi). Form: Because of the mention of the black color belonging to the earth within the category of the great elements. Another scriptural passage: Because in the same section, in the statement "from water, earth," the word "earth" is heard in place of the word "food" (anna). Indicative mark: [This is known from the fact that] in passages such as "they created food" (tā annamasṛjanta), the meaning of the word "food" is indeed the earth itself.

"But from the meditation on Him alone, on account of His characteristic mark; from His characteristic mark—that is, from the attribute consisting of the volition regarding creation in the form 'May I become many,' which serves as the unique indicator of His being the Supreme Self—it is determined that He alone—the Supreme Self having fire and the other elements as His body—is the cause of those respective subsequent elements (and not merely those elements themselves)."

231. However, the reverse order is also logically consistent for this reason: because the Supreme Self alone is the material cause through those respective elements, the reverse order—the sequence stated in the scripture beginning with "From Him is born the vital breath" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.3)—is also established and rendered consistent.

If it is argued that consciousness and the mind arise sequentially between [the elements and the breath] because of their respective signs, we say no, because there is no distinction [in the text]. "Between" means in the interval between the elements and the breath; "consciousness and the mind" refers to the sense organs and the mind arising sequentially—that is, in a temporal succession established by tradition.

If it is argued that the passage beginning with "From this, the vital breath is born" does not teach that [the creation] proceeds from Brahman without mediation—on the grounds of its indicative mark (liṅga), namely the recognition of the sequence of elemental creation found in the co-reading of ether and so forth (as understood from another Śruti text) such as "Ether, air," etc.—this statement is certainly not tenable. For there is no distinction; since the teaching that Brahman is the cause of the production of the vital breath, mind, and so on is equal [to the case of the elements], it is improper to abandon that [teaching of non-mediation].

233. But the designation [of Brahman] based on the moving and the non-moving would be non-figurative, because it exists when they exist. "Based on the moving and the non-moving" means having as its denotable objects things consisting of the mobile and the immobile. "That designation"—the application of various words denoting [entities] up to Brahman—"would be non-figurative," meaning it would indeed be primary and not metaphorical with respect to Brahman; "because it exists when they exist," that is, because it occurs immediately after the Supreme Self has entered into the moving and non-moving beings as their inner ruler (*antaryāmin*).
Because of the scriptural statement regarding going, "All go," and because the coming back is also established by scripture in the passage, "From that world he returns again," [the soul must return].

237. And by its own self in the two subsequent [passages]—that is, in the two scriptural passages concerning going and returning that follow immediately after the departure from the body—it must be carried out by its own nature alone; therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the substratum of going and returning, is indeed atomic (*aṇu*) and not all-pervading (*vibhu*).

238. "If it be argued that [the Self] cannot be atomic because of scriptural texts to that effect—[that is,] the Self, namely the individual soul (*jīva*), ought not to possess the dimension of an atom (*aṇu*) because of scriptural texts to the contrary; for in passages such as 'The Self is great,' a magnitude (*mahattva*) is heard which is opposed to atomicity—if this is said, such a statement is indeed not logical, because of the context of another [subject]; for, having introduced the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is other than the individual soul and so forth, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is declared."

239. Furthermore, by its own term and by its measurement, the self—the *jīva*—is atomic (*aṇu*), meaning it possesses the dimension of an atom. This is because of its own term and its measurement: first, by the word "atom" (*aṇu*) which directly denotes the dimension of an atom in the passage, "This atomic self"; and second, by the explicit clarification of its having a dimension equal to that [of an atom], after separately pointing out a thing of atomic size in the form of the point of an awl, in the passage, "The smallest is of the measure of the point of an awl."

240. *Avirodhaścandanavat* ("Non-contradiction like sandalwood"): Just as sandalwood, though situated in only one part of the body, produces refreshing joy throughout the entire body, so too—non-contradiction (*avirodha*)—there is no contradiction in the Self, though atomic and situated in only one part of the body, being the experiencer of pleasure and other sensations throughout all limbs by means of its own attribute, knowledge (*jñāna*). (This is to be reflected upon.)

241. If it be argued that [the analogy of sandalwood paste does not apply] because of the difference in location (*avasthitivaiśeṣyāt*), we say no, because [the soul's location] is accepted; for the difference in location—namely, the difference between the soul’s location and the location of sandalwood paste in a specific part of the body—exists, and thus the comparison of the soul to sandalwood paste is not tenable. If this is thought, such reflection is indeed not consistent, because it is accepted that the soul resides in a specific part of the body; for it is clearly stated in the scripture, "The light within the heart" (*hṛdyantajyotiḥ*), that the individual soul (*jīva*) is situated in the region of the heart.

242. Or [the soul appears to occupy the whole body] because of its quality, like light. Just as the radiance of gems such as the sun-gem (sūryakānta) pervades many locations, so too, by means of its own attribute—namely, knowledge which pervades the entire body (and serves as the instrument)—the self, though residing in one part of the body, becomes connected with the whole body.

243. There is a distinction (*vyatireka*), as shown by the example of fragrance (*gandhavat*). Just as the fragrance, which is a quality (*guṇa*) of the earth, must be admitted to be distinct from the earth itself, so too must the nature of knowledge—which is an attribute of the Self—be accepted as distinct from the Self. Thus, scripture clearly establishes this very difference in essential nature based on the relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), in such forms as: "This person indeed knows" (*jānāty evāyam puruṣaḥ*).

244. Because of the separate instruction: having pointed out the Self and the knowledge resting upon it individually by means of their respective designating words, because of the instruction in the Śruti, "of the knower" and "of the known," [the distinction between the knower and the knowledge is established].

245. But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated by that term, as in the case of the Intelligent One (*prājña*). Because its essence consists of those qualities—that is, because the individual self (*jīvātman*) possesses the quality known as knowledge (*jñāna*), which is its primary attribute—it is appropriate for the self to be referred to by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the scriptures; (this is not, however, due to the non-difference between the knower and the act of knowing). As in the case of the Intelligent One—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—it is called "bliss" (*ānanda*) because the quality consisting of bliss is predominant.

Thus, because of the predominance of the attribute of knowledge, there is usage such as "truth is knowledge," as if [knowledge were the essence]. And because it persists as long as the self exists, there is no fault, since that is observed: because the attribute whose nature is knowledge exists invariably throughout the existence of the self; and also because the self is self-luminous, there is no fault—that is, the absence of the defect caused by designating the substratum, the individual soul (*jīva*), by the word "knowledge" which denotes its attribute. This is because that [absence of fault] is observed.

For it is observed in the world that the application of words such as "cow" occurs invariably with respect to individual subjects like "the broken-horned one," which are the substrata for properties such as "cowness" existing in the present.

247. Because of the possibility of manifestation for that which exists, like virility and so forth: [this means] because of the possibility of manifestation—merely reaching a state of being manifest at the time of contact with the senses—for this quality consisting of knowledge, which exists without deviation in the Self throughout all states such as waking and the rest; "like virility and so forth" means just as the seventh constituent (*dhātu*), though present from birth within the body composed of the seven constituents, is manifested only in youth. (Therefore, knowledge is not an adventitious quality of the Self.)

248. Otherwise—by the opposite of what has been stated, namely, if one accepts that the self is pure consciousness and that it exists everywhere—there follows the consequence of either perpetual perception or non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other. That is to say, if these two were accepted, there would result the consequence of both perception and non-perception occurring eternally and simultaneously; or else, there would result the restriction of either the self being invariably perceived alone, or invariably unperceived alone.

58. The Topic of the Agent (Kartṛ-adhikaraṇa) 249. There is an agent; because the scriptures have purpose. The agent—the Self—is indeed possessed of agency (and must be admitted not to be devoid of agency as in the Sāṃkhya system), because the scriptures have purpose. For it must necessarily be maintained that the scriptures—which enjoin activities pertaining to the three aims of life (trivarga) such as the worship of deities, as well as those leading to liberation (apavarga)—possess a meaningful purpose.

250. [The Self is] the agent because of appropriation and because of the teaching of movement. The Self is indeed possessed of agency: because of appropriation—that is, because of the indicative evidence in the Śruti of the teaching that the Self is the grasper of the senses; and likewise because of the teaching of movement—that is, because of the indicative evidence in the Śruti of the teaching that the Self is the agent of moving about within the body.

251. Furthermore, because of the designation [of agency] in action—and provided there is no reversal of the instruction—[it follows that] the self is the agent. Since the designation of the individual soul (jīvātman) as the agent with respect to sacrificial action is clearly expressed in the scriptural text, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice," this serves as a proof that the self—the individual soul—is indeed the agent, possessing the quality of agency.

If, however, it is argued that by the word "vijñāna" (consciousness) only the intellect (*buddhi*) in the form of the internal organ is meant and not the Self (*ātman*), then the following response must be considered: there would have been a reversal of the grammatical indication; that is, in the Śruti, instead of the word "vijñāna" being in the nominative case, it would have been indicated in the instrumental case.

252. The argument regarding the lack of restriction, like perception: (If, without accepting the agency of the Self, one were to attribute agency to Pradhāna alone as common to all, then) it would follow that there is no restriction, just as in the case of perception—given the admission that the Self is omnipresent, just as the perception of the Self is [universal], there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of any rule such as: "this person alone is the enjoyer of pleasure and other fruits of action arising from karma; not the other."

253. *Śakti-viparyayāt* (2-3-37) — (If agency is admitted to belong to the intellect alone: because of the reversal of capacity—namely, the undesirable consequence of the loss of the Self’s capacity for being the enjoyer (since it is impossible for agency and enjoyership to reside in different substrata)—the Self, that is, the living soul (*jīva*), is the agent, the locus of agency.

Furthermore, due to the absence of *samādhi*—that is, because of the absence of that knowledge of the Self as distinct from *prakṛti*, which takes the form "I am other than *prakṛti*" and is accepted by the Sāṃkhyas as the means to liberation (*mokṣa*)—there would follow the impossibility of a locus [for such knowledge]. Consequently, even the agency involved in such reflection does not reside in the Self, since the notion of being "other than *prakṛti*" is sublated in *prakṛti* itself. Therefore, the *ātman*—the individual soul—is the agent, the substratum of agency.

254–255. Just as a carpenter is "in both ways"—that is, a woodworker who is equipped with the tools for carving—and just as he performs the carving when there is a desire to do so, but does not perform it otherwise, thus possessing both modes; so too the Self—the living being (*jīva*) who possesses the instruments such as speech—is "in both ways": when there is volition (*saṅkalpa*), it possesses agency, and in its absence, it lacks it. Thus, it possesses both agency and its absence (and therefore, agency is not invariably constant).

59. The Topic of Dependence on Another (Parāyattādhikaraṇam). 256. But [the agency] is from another, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. That is to say, the agency residing in the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is from another—from the Supreme Brahman who exists as the controller. (The meaning is that it is dependent solely upon the Supreme Self and not entirely under its own control. This is because of the scriptural statement: "He has entered within, the ruler of people," which declares that the quality of being the ruler belongs to the Supreme alone.

257. But [the Lord] is dependent upon the effort performed [by the individual soul], because otherwise scriptural injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless, and so forth. "The Supreme One" refers to the Paramātman. "But dependent upon the effort performed" means that He is the sole impeller while observing as a causal factor the exertion—the effort made by the individual soul—which serves as the primary cause for initial activity. This is because of the necessity that scriptural injunctions and prohibitions found in the Śāstras not be rendered meaningless; and likewise, because of the Lord's own acts of restraint and grace.

And because of the lack of continuity, there is no confusion; that is, because there is no all-pervading connection among the individual souls—which, being atomic, are distinct due to their difference in bodies—there is no confusion [of experiences], meaning no mixing of enjoyments with the omnipresent Supreme Self which is connected to everything by its pervasiveness. (Therefore, the soul is indeed a part of Brahman, but not Brahman itself.)

265. "And only an appearance, and only an appearance"—this refers to that which is stated as the cause for the concealment of the true nature of the supreme Brahman by ignorance (*avidyā*) and for the conceptualization of its state as a living soul (*jīva*); in reality, it is not a cause, but is indeed defective, and such a conceptualization contradicts the scriptural texts concerning [Brahman's] faultlessness. (Therefore, the *jīva* is indeed a part of Brahman; it is not Brahman itself.)

266. *Adṛṣṭāniyamāt* (2-3-50). Because of the lack of a regulating principle for unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), that is, because it is impossible to state a regulating principle of unseen merit within the one undivided Brahman itself to determine experience, the defects produced by ignorance would be unavoidable for Brahman; [therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is merely a part of Brahman, not Brahman itself].

267. "And likewise in the case of intentions and so forth" (2-3-51). And likewise in the case of intentions and so forth—meaning even in the case of volitions and the like which have been stated to be caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa)—it is thus unavoidable that there would be an absence of any restrictive principle regarding the non-restriction of the unseen in Brahman; therefore, there is simply an absence of a regulator for defects [in Brahman] (hence the individual soul is merely a part of Brahman, not Brahman itself).

268. If it is argued that [the distinction between the two] is due to a difference in location, we say no, because there is no internal division of location. For when Brahman exists in the state of a jīva as imagined through ignorance, there is the location of Brahman as conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and there is the location of Brahman as unconditioned by them.

If it is argued that the regulation of experience is possible because a distinction between spatial locations is admitted, such a conception is not tenable. It serves no purpose, because due to the inclusion [of all parts], when a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) moves to another place, even a location of Brahman that was previously unconditioned becomes a location of Brahman that is conditioned. Since there is thus an absence of any regulating factor consisting of a distinction between locations, there would be an absence of the regulation of experience itself. Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a part of Brahman, but it is not Brahman itself.
2-3-50 [End of Sūtra]. Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter.

270. Because of the impossibility [of the primary sense] and because of its being heard prior to that, the term "prāṇāḥ" (breaths) is figurative. In the word "prāṇāḥ," which refers to the Supreme Self—the cause of the animation of all—there is a scriptural mention of the plural number; this is metaphorical because it is impossible, since the primary plurality is contradicted in the Supreme Self existing prior to creation, and because of its being heard prior to that—that is, precisely because of the scriptural statement that He exists prior to the time of creation.

"Because speech is preceded by that" (2.4.3). "Speech"—that is, name, which is distinct from the Supreme Self—"because it is preceded by that," meaning because it is preceded by the creation of ether and the other elements. Therefore, he who is designated by the word "prāṇa" is indeed the Supreme Self alone.

It is indeed an instrument of the individual soul (jīva), because of its being taught together with them and other such reasons—namely, because it is taught as an instrument of the soul through its association with the eyes and other organs, and because it is specifically designated by the term "chief vital breath" (mukhyaprāṇa) as an indicator.

278. "And because it is without organs, there is no defect; for thus Scripture shows" (2-4-10). Because this supreme vital breath (*prāṇa*) is "without organs"—that is, without instruments of action (the defect being raised on the grounds that it lacks the specific activity consisting of service toward the individual soul)—no defect arises, namely the defect of not belonging to the same class as the eyes and other sense organs. For, indeed, Scripture itself teaches this by demonstrating its very activity in the form of the specific service consisting of sustaining the body and the senses, through such passages as, "When he departs... and so forth.

279. The chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), which possesses five functions, is designated as "mind" (*manovat*). That is, the chief vital breath—which has five functions, meaning it possesses the fivefold set of names dependent upon the fivefold functions such as *prāṇa* and so forth—is designated and pointed out in the scriptures (*śruti*). Just as the single mind is clearly indicated in the scripture by various names such as "desire" (*kāma*) and "volition" (*saṅkalpa*) due to its different functions—according to the text, "Desire, volition..."—in the same manner [the chief vital breath is designated as mind].
All is mind alone.

Section 65: The Topic of the Subtlety and Preeminence [of Prāṇa]. And this principal vital breath (prāṇa) is both subtle and preeminent; it is subtle—possessing an atomic dimension like the sense organs—because of the scriptural mention of its movement, such as its departure [from the body] and so forth.
66. The Section Concerning the Presiding over Light and Other Elements (Jyotirādyadhiṣṭhānādhikaraṇam).

But the presiding over light and other elements is by him who possesses the vital breath, because of the scriptural statement regarding him who possesses the vital breath; that is, the agency consisting in the directing of the deities of fire and so forth toward their respective functions within the sense organs is by him who possesses the vital breath—the individual soul—yet it occurs solely through the volition of that Supreme Person, because of the scriptural statement, that is, from the sacred teaching which establishes dependence upon His volition.

And because that [pervasion] is eternal— since the state of being presided over by the Supreme Self is eternal for all things, whether conscious or unconscious— and because it is necessarily and unavoidably fixed, the stated meaning alone is correct.

67. Section on the Senses (Indriyādhikaraṇa). 283. "They are the senses because they are designated as such, except for the Best. Except for the Best—the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*)—those which exist and are denoted by the word "breaths" (*prāṇa*), they are indeed the senses; they possess the designation "senses" because of that very designation, as in the scriptural passage: "They all became his form" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.21). 282.

284. Because of the scriptural mention of distinction (*bhedaśruti*)—since the distinction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the mind and the senses is established in the scripture, "From this [Self] are born the breath, the mind, and all the senses"—and because of its difference in nature (*vailakṣaṇya*), as a function distinct from the functions of the senses is observed in the vital breaths, these [others] are indeed the vital breaths distinct from the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*); they alone are the "senses" (*indriyāṇi*), denoted by the term "sense," (but not the chief vital breath).

68. The Section on the Formation of Names and Forms (Saṃjñāmūrtikḷptyadhikaraṇam). But the formation of names and forms belongs to Him who effects the tripartition, because of the scriptural teaching. The "formation of names and forms" consists of the evolution of individual entities characterized by the differentiation of name and form; this belongs specifically to the Supreme Self, who is the accomplisher of the action consisting of tripartition—that is, the one who effects the tripartition—and not to the four-faced Brahmā. This is because of the scriptural teaching: for in the Śruti, we observe that the intention expressed as "I shall differentiate name and form" follows immediately after the resolve, "Let me make each one threefold. Thus, it is taught that the act of naming and shaping belongs to the Supreme Lord alone.

286. Flesh and so forth are earthly; likewise for the other two, according to the respective scriptural statements. Following the Vedic statement, "Food, when eaten, becomes threefold," flesh—which is distinct from feces, the gross product—and the subtle mind as well, are both earthly—that is, composed of earth. For the other two cases as well—namely, the statements "Water, when drunk" and "Fire, when consumed"—it is exactly the same.

287. "But on account of its predominance, there is that designation; indeed, on account of its predominance. Because even for each individual element, there exists a state of predominance, there is "that designation"—namely, the distinct verbal designations found in the Vedic texts for food and the other elements.
—The Fourth Quarter—(Thus ends the Second Chapter) 289.

"But because of consisting of three, because of abundance, and because of consisting of the triad"—because, through the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), water consists of the nature of the three elements; and "because of abundance," that is, also due to the preponderance of water (as in the passage beginning with "In the fifth oblation, the waters [are offered]," where all [elements] are designated by the word "water").

And because of the departure of the vital breaths—that is, the senses—and because of the scriptural statement that "the vital breath departs after [the soul]," which teaches that it moves along with the departing living self (jīva), the jīva moves from one body to another only while being enveloped and conjoined with the subtle elements that have attained the state of being a body.

291. If it be argued that [the scripture] does not teach the departure [of the senses], because the scriptural mention of their going to fire and so forth is figurative—the scriptural mention of the senses such as speech going to fire and so forth, as in "Speech merges into fire" (*agniṃ vāgapyeti*), refers to the dissolution of the senses in the form of speech etc. into fire and so forth; therefore, the scriptural mention of the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) along with the soul regarding the senses is not primary, but must be interpreted otherwise—if this is said, it is not tenable. Why? Because it is figurative; for the words "speech" and so forth are used metaphorically to denote the deities presiding over speech and the other senses.

292. If it be argued that [the waters] are not mentioned in the first [instance], we say no; for they are indeed established by reason. In the first instance—that is, in the *pañcāgni-vidyā* (knowledge of the five fires), concerning the oblation whose locus is the fire consisting of the heavenly world—the waters are not heard of as the object of the oblation, because they are not recited in the scripture as such (it would not be easy to say that "the waters go forth mixed with other elements"). If this is argued, we say no; this statement is not tenable, for it is precisely those waters (which are denoted by the term *śraddhā*, faith, when offered into the heavenly world).
Because, in providing an answer to an objection, it must be established that the response is consistent with the question only when that [explanation] is indeed the case.

293. If it is argued that [the soul does not go] because it is not heard [in scripture], we say no; for there is the recognition of those who perform sacrifices and other rites. Regarding the claim that "because it is not heard"—that is, because the scripture does not state that the soul goes enveloped by water (*adbhiḥ saṃpariṣvakta*) when it speaks of the going of water alone—it follows that "it is difficult to say that the soul goes. This statement is not tenable, because there is the recognition of those who perform sacrifices and other rites—that is, of souls who have performed optional acts such as sacrifice and charity—within the scriptural passage. Thus, the word "water" (*ap*) denotes the soul as joined with water, and not the water alone.

294. Or [the statement that they are] "enjoyed" is figurative because they do not know the Self; for scripture shows this—(the statement that those who have gone by the path of smoke are "enjoyed" by the gods) is merely figurative (intended to show that they serve as instruments for the gods), because they do not know the Self—for those who perform only sacrifices and the like, without the mode of service to the Supreme Person, there is an absence of knowledge of the Self. For scripture shows this in the passage: "As a beast, so is he to the gods," which makes known precisely their status as instruments for the gods.

**Topic 295: On the Departure of One Possessing Residual Karma.** When there is the exhaustion of performed karma through its fruition, the conscious soul departs from heaven and other realms "as it came" and also "not so," possessing residual karma—that is, possessing the remainder of karma not yet experienced. This is understood from both direct observation (*dṛṣṭa*) and scripture (*smṛti*), that is, from *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. **Kṛtātyayādhikaraṇam:** When there is the exhaustion (*atyaya*) of what was performed (*kṛta*), meaning when previous karmas are destroyed by experience, the conscious being (*cetanaḥ*) possesses residual karma (*anuśayavān*), i.e., possesses the karma remaining after what has been enjoyed. It returns "as it came" (*yathetam*)—by the same manner of ascent—and also "not so" (*anevam*)—by a different manner. This is known from *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

296. If it be argued that [the attainment of specific births such as pleasant ones] is due to conduct (*caraṇa*) alone—and not from residual karma (*anuśaya*), i.e., the remainder of performed actions—Kārṣṇājini maintains that this statement is not correct. He holds that the scriptural text "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) is intended as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of making known the nature of one's meritorious and sinful karma. Thus, the teacher named Kārṣṇājini considers that the scripture is directed toward revealing the character of merit and demerit.

297. If it be argued that there is pointlessness—[that is,] if it be argued that since merit and demerit alone are the motivators for attaining specific wombs, then good conduct (*sadācāra*) is fruitless—such a doubt is not appropriate, because [good conduct] is required by those [actions]; for meritorious actions depend upon good conduct. Thus, there is no pointlessness of conduct. 298.

But Bādari holds that it is merit and demerit alone; namely, Bādari—the teacher named Bādari—considers that "merit and demerit" alone, i.e., virtue and vice, are what is denoted by the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*).
Section 71: The Topic of Those Who Perform Unrighteous Acts and the Like.

It is also heard in the Śruti that those who perform unrighteous acts and the like—even sinners who do not perform sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) or works of public utility (*pūrta*)—go to the moon; indeed, the Śruti teaches that they all go to the moon alone. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.3: "All of them go to the moon.")

300. However, having experienced ascent and descent in Saṃyamana, because their destination is seen; "ascent and descent" means that for those who perform undesirable acts (sinners), there is an ascent to the moon and a descent from it. This occurs in Saṃyamana—a region within the jurisdiction of Yama—only after experiencing, that is, after attaining the perception of the fruits of their sins. This is because their destination is observed, as established by the Vedic text: "The abode of Yama is the meeting place of men" (Vaivasvataṃ saṅgamanaṃ janānām).
Furthermore, the great sages such as Parāśara and others remember and declare in their Smṛtis that all these [sinners] go under the power of Yama, thereby making known the attainment of Yama’s abode.
302. Even the seven—namely, even the seven hells beginning with Raurava—the sages remember and teach in the Smṛtis as the destinations for sinners.

303. Even there, there is no contradiction because of his agency; even there—in the seven worlds called hells, such as Raurava and the rest—because of his agency, that is, because one goes only by Yama’s command, there is no contradiction with the scriptural statements indicating the attainment of Yama’s abode.

304. Regarding the phrase "of knowledge and action" (*vidyā-karmaṇoḥ*): because these two are the subject under discussion—namely, that the journey to Brahman by way of the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) is the fruit of knowledge, and the journey to the moon by way of the path of smoke (*dhūma-ādi*) is the fruit of rites such as sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭā-pūrta*)—and because they have been presented as such in this context, it is understood that for those devoid of both knowledge and action, namely the sinful, neither the journey to Brahman nor the journey to the moon is possible.

305. "Not in the third, because it is so perceived": in the third—that is, at the commencement of the body for those evil-doers designated as belonging to the third place—there is no dependence on the fifth oblation; this is because it is so perceived, as seen in the Śruti passage: "Therefore that world is not filled."

306. Furthermore, it is recorded in common worldly tradition—and indeed in the tradition of the learned (śiṣṭa)—that even for those of meritorious deeds such as Draupadī and others, the requirement of the fifth libation at the commencement of a new body is not observed; this is indeed recorded in the Mahābhārata and other texts.

307. And because it is observed [that for sweat-born and sprout-born beings there is no requirement for the fifth oblation at the commencement of the body], and because of the indicative evidence from the fact that the scripture recites: "There are only three kinds of seeds: the egg-born, the viviparous, and the sprout-born."

308. The inclusion of the third term, "born of moisture" (*svedaja*), within the category of "born of decay" (*saṃśokaja*)—that is, by the third term "born from a sprout" (*udbhijja*)—is an inclusion; therefore, even those born of moisture are indeed mentioned in the Veda. (Consequently, for those who are exclusively sinful, neither the ascent to nor the descent from the moon is possible.)

In the case of the bodies of rice and so forth, there is for the descending souls merely a state of contact—as previously [stated] regarding the sequence from space up to the clouds—because of the scriptural statement, which speaks only of their becoming those [beings] (meaning that since no karma serving as the cause of experience is mentioned, there is no experience delimited by the bodies of rice and so forth).

312. If it be argued that [the fruit] is impure—[that is,] that the fruit such as heaven produced by sacrifices and the like is mixed with impurity because it is produced by the injury to animals (and therefore becomes a cause for an impure birth in rice and so forth)—such a doubt is not inconsistent, because of the Word; that is, because of the Vedic word such as "Indeed, you are not slain, nor do you suffer harm," which makes known the absence of the nature of injury.

313. "Then the union with those who emit semen" (retassigyoga): this occurs immediately thereafter. "Union with those who emit semen" refers to the connection of the descending souls—already mixed with food—with embodied beings who emit semen; just as that is a mere conjunction, so too the union with rice and other grains is merely a connection.
314. From the womb comes the body: for the individual soul (jīva) descending from the higher realms, the state of possessing a body occurs immediately upon reaching a womb, but not prior to that.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter.

318. "But [the self] is concealed by meditation upon the Supreme; for from that indeed come its bondage and the opposite. By meditation upon the Supreme—that is, solely through the volition of the Supreme Person—the innate form of this individual soul (jīva) is concealed; it is covered by the beginningless stream of karma due to its state of transgression. For from that very volition of the Supreme Person, the bondage and the opposite of this individual soul—namely, transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) and liberation (apavarga)—are declared in the Śruti.

319. Furthermore, that very connection with concealment belonging to the individual self (*jīvātman*) arises from its conjunction with the body—that is, with the insentient (*acit*) transformed into the forms of gods and so forth, as well as with the insentient in its subtle state, which is incapable of being divided into name and form; [this occurs] through the contact [between them] during the periods of creation and dissolution.

For it is indicated by scripture, and those who know it declare this: because the "intermediate state" (sandhya)—that which is denoted by the word *sandhya*, namely dream—is not merely an object of experience for a particular individual, but is also an indicator (*sūcaka*) of future auspicious and inauspicious events; this is known from scripture, such as: "He sees a woman in his dreams," and from the fact that those who know it—the experts in the science of dreams (*svapnādhyāyavidaḥ*)—also declare this very same point, as stated in the scripture: "One should understand [the dream] in this way. (320)
They say: (all this is only consistent if the Lord himself is the creator of the objects of dreams).
Section 78.

324. In the state of fainting (mugdha), there is a half-attainment [of death], because it remains as the only alternative. In a person who has fainted—that is, one who is unconscious—the state present is "half-attainment," which is indeed half-death; this is because, by process of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), it is a specific state distinct from the states consisting of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death.

And it says "only that, only that"—meaning "only so much," namely, it declares "Brahman is of the nature of knowledge" and conveys this through the statement "Truth, Knowledge. (It does not, however, deny Brahman's being a mine of auspicious qualities. Therefore, Brahman indeed possesses both characteristics.

Furthermore, it is shown that Brahman possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva), as it is both taught [in scripture] and remembered. A multitude of Vedāntic passages clearly establish this, such as: "Brahman is partless, faultless, and stainless," and "Knowledge, power, and action are His very nature. It is also recorded in Smṛti: "He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds"—thus, even in Smṛti, the dual characteristic of Brahman is set forth.
