332. For this very reason, there is a comparison with the sun and so forth; for this very reason—namely, because Brahman possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva) and is thus entirely free from even a trace of defects caused by its location in earth and other elements—it is like the sun and so forth, i.e., like the solar disc reflected in water, mirrors, and the like. Thus, a description of similarity is made in the scriptures through such comparisons as, "Like the sun in various receptacles of water."

Because it is not perceived like water, there is no such similarity—namely, the likeness to the reflection of the sun and so forth; this is not possible, because, as in the case of the solar disc which does not actually exist in water, there is a lack of perception due precisely to the absence of such perception. (For the Supreme Self is indeed perceived in the earth and other elements while actually existing therein.)

334. [The Supreme Self] does not partake of increase or decrease because it is contained within [all things], because both [illustrations] are consistent, and because such is seen. Regarding "because it is contained within": since the Supreme Self merely abides within the modifications of earth and other elements, it does not follow that the Supreme Self partakes of the growth and decay—that is, the increase and decrease—found in those modified objects. This is because both [illustrations] are consistent; for this description must be made in order to maintain the harmony of the two examples—the space within a jar and the sun reflected in a vessel of water. Thus, there is similarity only in the intended aspect.

Furthermore, it is because of observation—in instances such as "The boy is like a lion," we observe that the demonstration of similarity pertains only to aspects such as valor, as evidenced by the explanatory sentences used to justify the simile.

333. 335. "For [the scripture] negates only what has been introduced; thereafter it speaks further. That is to say: because there is a limitation consisting in the specific qualities previously introduced—namely, the nature of having form and being formless—the Śruti negates only that much with the words "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Thereafter, it also speaks of a connection with qualities superior to that, as the Śruti indeed establishes through such passages as "for from this... (*na hy etasmāt...*) and so forth.

For it says that this is unmanifest—that Brahman is unmanifest, meaning not known through other means of valid cognition; for indeed, the Śruti itself speaks firmly: "His form does not stand within the range of vision."

337. Furthermore, regarding its realization through both perception and inference: "In the case of *saṃrādhana*—that is, when worship characterized by perfect love and devotion is performed, and only when such meditation is practiced—is that Brahman directly realized; not otherwise.

This is made known by perception through such scriptural testimony (*śruti*) as, "The Self is not to be obtained... but He is obtainable by whomsoever He chooses" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.3), and by inference through such traditional scripture (*smṛti*) as, "But by unswerving devotion He can be known" (Bhagavad Gītā 11.54).
81. Parādhikaraṇa:

344. But [there is] something higher than that, on account of the designations of measurement, connection, and difference. Therefore—from this Supreme Brahman, which has been determined as the ultimate cause from the beginning of the scripture up to this point—there exists some reality that is even higher (param), meaning more excellent.

Because of the designation as a "bridge"—since, by first designating the Supreme Self as a bridge in the passage, "Having crossed this bridge," it is made known that He is to be crossed; because of the designation of measurement—since, by first designating Brahman as consisting of four feet in the passage, "Brahman has four feet," it is made known that there exists another immeasurable reality; and because of the designation of relationship—with the individual self.

Because the statement, "He is the bridge to immortality," describes the Lord as the one who causes [the soul] to reach another state that is to be attained; because it establishes a relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) characterized by the Lord being the means for the soul to attain the immortality that is to be reached; and because of the designation of difference—since the designation of difference in any object other than the all-pervading Reality is indicated throughout by such passages as, "That which is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).

345. On account of similarity: the designation of a "bridge" (*setu*) for the Supreme Self—as in the expression "He is the bridge"—is due to similarity alone, namely, because of its nature as a support (*vidhṛti*). This is because it possesses a likeness to a bridge in that it maintains the essential nature of all things without confusion.

346. [The designation of measurement] is for the sake of meditation, like the "feet. Regarding the designation of measurement—such as in the passage, "Brahman has four feet" and so forth—the conventional usage of Brahman being measured by some specific dimension is for the sake of meditation (*buddhy-artha*), like the "feet," just as in the case of the indivisible Brahman, speech and the other [senses] are conventionally designated as "feet" in passages such as "Speech is a foot. This is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana-phalaka*), and not for the purpose of indicating actual limitation (*paricchinna-tva*).

347. The designation of measurement [is due] to the distinction of location, as in the case of light and so forth: the designation of the indivisible and complete Supreme Self as being limited arises from the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of specific locations such as speech and so forth—that is, from the connection with specific locations such as speech and so forth—just as in the case of light and so forth; for example, although space and light are pervasive everywhere, they are connected with specific locations such as windows or jars, and it is just like that.

348. And because it is logical (*upapatteśca*). (The designation of a relationship—consisting of the state of being the goal and the means of attainment—as expressed in the phrase "This is the bridge to immortality," which is intended to indicate distinctness,) is also justified because it is logical; for it is possible within a single entity itself, without contradiction, as indicated by the scriptural text "Whomever He chooses" (*yamevaiṣa vṛṇute*), since [the self] can be the means of attainment for itself. Therefore, that [designation] does not indicate distinctness.

349. Likewise, because of the negation of another. Because of the negation of another—that is, of anything superior to Brahman established as the cause of the world—through the communication of its non-existence in such passages as, "There is nothing higher than which there is another," and so forth; likewise, it is correctly understood that "there is nothing higher than Brahman; Brahman alone is supreme."

350. By this [scriptural evidence], its omnipresence is established from words such as "pervasion" (*āyāma*). By this—the Supreme Brahman—its omnipresence, that is, the state of pervading the entire universe, is known from scriptural passages expressing universal pervasion, such as "All this is filled by this Puruṣa," as well as from statements such as "Brahman alone is all this."
Regarding the phrase "codanādeḥ": *codanā* refers to injunctions, conjunctions, forms, and names; *aviśeṣāt* means because of their being identical or equal.

356. If it is argued that [the identity of the meditations] does not hold because of differences—even in a single [meditation], there is a difference due to the repetition of the same text without distinction, whereby a difference is understood; thus, there is no unity among the Dahara and other meditations—if this is said, such a statement is not correct. For even in a single meditation—one that is not disputed as being one—there is a difference due to the difference among the perceivers (since the purposeful repetition of the same text in different recensions does not necessitate a difference in the meditation).

357. Because of the nature of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), its inclusion in the *samācāra* (traditional conduct), and because it is a qualification [for Vedic study], there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding *svādhyāya*, as in the case of the *sava* sacrifice. That is to say, for the sake of establishing that very nature—namely, for the sake of establishing the possession of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by study—there is this restriction: among the followers of the Atharvaveda, there is a rule for students regarding a specific vow (*vrata*) consisting of carrying a vessel of glowing coals on the head, which serves as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to their study.

There is no restriction regarding those who worship [the teacher], because it is prescribed in the *Samācāra*—a specific Atharvaṇa text so named—and because of the qualification [implied] by the mention of the "Vedic vow" (*vedavrata*), which introduces the "head-vow" (*śirovrata*) (as indicated by the word "and," *ca*); furthermore, it is known from the statement at the end of the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, "One who has not performed this vow should not study," that the performance of the vow is a necessary rule for the commencement of study. Likewise, as in the case of the *savana*s—the oblations related to the single fire (*aikāgni*) of the Atharvaṇikas—it is understood that knowledge does not differ on account of such specific rules.

358. And it is shown—(the Śruti [shows] that meditation is the same across all Vedāntas)—and the Taittirīya Śruti also clearly reveals this in the form: "The Self... that is to be meditated upon. Thus it is demonstrated.

359. There is a synthesis (upasaṃhāra) because the purpose is non-different, as in the case of the supplementary parts of injunctions; and since the meditation on the "small ether" (dahara) and others is identical across all Vedāntas—possessing unity and being the same in each respective meditation—the synthesis must be performed, which means that the qualities heard in one Vedānta text as attributes of the object of meditation must be accepted as delimiters of that very object. This is because the purpose, consisting of spiritual benefit, is uniform, just like the qualities enjoined in various meditations as supplementary parts of those specific injunctions.

Or rather, it is not so, because of the difference in context, as in the case of the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) and other such instances; nor is it appropriate to establish the identity of the knowledge by making the lack of distinction the reason, for that is simply not consistent due to the difference in context—namely, that while there is meditation on the *udgītha* introduced by the *praṇava* which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*, and meditation on the *praṇava* itself, there is also meditation on the entire *udgītha* introduced without mentioning the *praṇava*, which is not meditation on the *praṇava*.

However, [the meditation] belongs to the *udgītha* alone; thus, because of the difference in the *prastāva*, there is indeed a difference in the nature of the meditations, and so there is no identity of meditation—just as in the case of the "higher than the high" (*parovarīyastva*) and other qualities. For example, within the very same *udgītha* meditation contained in a single recensional branch (*śākhā*), although there is no difference in the fact that both are meditations on the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is a distinction due to the difference in form: in one place, there is the injunction to view the *praṇava* (which is a part of the *udgītha*) as the golden person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*), while elsewhere there is the injunction to view it as qualified by qualities such as being "higher than the high. In the same way, a distinction must be stated here as well, because of the specific difference in form.

If it is argued that because they share a common name, it has been stated—and indeed we have already described—that there is non-difference between the two meditations on the *udgītha* as enjoined, based on the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) of their having the single name "Udgītha-vidyā," such a doubt is not at all tenable; for even in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra* and the monthly *agnihotra* belonging to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), where there is a difference in what is enjoined, the unity of name as "Agnihotra" nevertheless exists—it certainly persists.

363. *Vyāpteśca samañjasam*. Because of the pervasion—since the syllable *praṇava* alone is the object of meditation at the beginning as well as at the end of the Udgītha-knowledge sections in the first prapāṭhaka of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—it is most appropriate that even the word "Udgītha" occurring in the middle passage, "The gods took up the Udgītha," refers specifically to the *praṇava*.

For even though specific features such as the head, wings, and tail are mutually distinct, they are nonetheless included within the very nature of Brahman; consequently, increase and decrease—namely, growth and diminution—would follow [as applying] even to the nature of Brahman itself, which would contradict the Śruti.

367. But the others, however, on account of the identity of the object—“the others,” that is, attributes such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth which define the very nature of Brahman, must indeed be combined in all meditations (*vidyās*), because of the identity of the object; for the object, which is the form of Brahman to be meditated upon, is the same in all meditations.

368. "For the purpose of meditation, because there is no other purpose" (referring to the figurative descriptions such as having the beloved as the head). "For the purpose of meditation" means solely for the sake of accomplishing constant reflection (*anucintana*); "because there is no other purpose" means due to the absence of any purpose other than the ascent of [the object] into the intellect (*buddhi*) which is useful for such reflection.

369. Furthermore, because of the word "Self" (ātman)—that is, from the designation "another inner Self consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) applied to that which is to be meditated upon as having "joy for its head" and so forth—it is known that [the attributes] such as "having joy for its head" are not qualities intended to define the essential nature of Brahman; rather, they are solely for the purpose of contemplation.
Regarding the phrase "rūpite" (in the passage concerning the one who is embodied),

the term "grasping of the Self" (*ātmagṛhīti*) means that by the word "Self," only the Supreme Self is grasped, just as in other instances— such as "The Self, indeed, was this alone in the beginning"— where the Supreme Self is grasped by various other words for "Self"; this is established on account of what follows, namely, the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
This is because of the indicative evidence from the subsequent passage beginning with "He desired."

371. If it be argued that [the word "Self" refers to the individual self] because of its recurrence (*anvaya*); that is, because of the recurrence of the word "Self" even with respect to non-Selves (in the passages concerning the *prāṇamaya* and so forth)—[and thus the subsequent passage does not establish that the word "Self" refers to the Supreme Self]—such a doubt is indeed not tenable, because of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). For it is established by the restriction that throughout this context, by the word "Self," only the Supreme Self is intended; thus, the fact that the subsequent passage serves as the indicator for that meaning is indeed proven.

88. *Samānādhikaraṇam* (373). "And likewise, because of identity. And likewise—just as in the *Agnirahasya*, so too in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: when the qualities of the object of meditation, such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, are identical and non-different; and because of that non-difference—that is, because the additional qualities such as "mastery" (*vaśitva*) are not distinct from "truthfulness of resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—there is no difference in form, and thus the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is one and the same despite its recitation in both places.
89. Section on Connection (Sambandhādhikaraṇa).

374. "In the same way elsewhere also, because of the connection. Just as there is identity of knowledge when the object of meditation—qualified by identical attributes—is the same, so it is "elsewhere also"—that is, even in the case of Brahman as the object of meditation residing in both the eye and the sun—it is so "because of the connection," namely, because the one and the same true Brahman is connected with the two locations called the eye and the sun. (Since there is no difference in form, there is also no difference in the knowledge; therefore, the two names "Day" and "I" are to be combined without restriction in both meditations.)

375. Or rather, because of the distinction—(since there is unity of knowledge, the combination of both names [the eye and the sun] every day) is not possible; this is because of the distinction—the clear perception of a difference in the nature of the objects to be reached, consisting of the locations of the eye and the sun, which serves as the differentiator of the two knowledges.

376. And the Śruti clearly demonstrates—indeed, it repeatedly shows—that there is no mutual combination of qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra) between the two Brahmans to be meditated upon, namely that based on the eye and that based on the sun. This is evident from the transference of form expressed in the words, "The form of this one is the very same as the form of that one. Therefore, there is indeed a difference between these two meditations (vidyābheda).

And in such a "human science" (*puruṣavidyā*) as "The sacrifice is the *bāhu*," there is indeed a difference in the sciences based on the difference in form; for the forms of the sacrificer, his wife, and so forth, as well as the *savana*s and other elements mentioned in other recensions—that is, not being recorded or taught in those other branches—are absent [in this one].
92. Section on Piercing and so forth (Vedhādyadhikaraṇam).

379. Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing and so forth, the mantras recited at the commencement of study are indeed auxiliary to the act of study itself, and not auxiliary to the meditative knowledge (vidyā); for there is a clear distinction between the purposes mentioned in such passages as "Piercing the bright [eye], piercing the heart," which consist of the rending of the enemy's strength and heart, and those purposes related to the study itself found in mantras such as "May Mitra be auspicious to us. This distinction remains firmly established even regarding the purposes connected to the study.

Because there is no remainder of enjoyment whatsoever to be crossed over, others—the Chandogas—read it in exactly the manner described: "For him, the delay is only so long as he is not released; then he shall be united. Thus they recite.

382. "According to one's wish, because there is no contradiction between the two"—that is, having considered the absence of contradiction between the two scriptural passages, namely, "Having shaken off evil as a horse shakes its hair" and "For him, the delay is only so long," one may, according to one's wish—that is, in accordance with what is desired—connect the phrase "he shakes off his good and evil deeds" (to the section following the statement "this path of the gods"). [It should be joined before the sentence "this path of the gods"].

383. *Gater arthavattvam ubhayathā; anyathā hi virodhaḥ*. Regarding "the journey" (*gati*): because of the scriptural teaching that the knower travels by the path of the gods (*devayāna*), its "purposefulness" (*arthavattva*)—that is, its being endowed with a specific utility—is appropriate only if the exhaustion of karma is accepted in two ways: both at the time of separation from the body and while on the way. Otherwise, if one were to accept the exhaustion of all karma only at the moment of separation from the body, there would indeed be a contradiction; for a conflict with the scriptural teaching of the journey by the path of the gods would necessarily result.

384. [The ascent] is established because of the perception of that which is characterized by such [results], as in the case of the world; (even otherwise—that is, even if all *karmas* were exhausted at the very moment of separation from the body)—it is established (that the procedure for traveling by the path of the gods for those attending upon the Blessed One is indeed consistent) because of the perception of that which is characterized by such [results]—namely, of a state of being attainable not through *karman*—since it is understood in that regard from such scriptural texts as "He becomes his own lord" (*sa svarāḍ bhavati*), just as in the case of the world—as in the case of a person who attends upon a king seen in the world.
Just as there is the possibility of even unthought-of enjoyments occurring without being common to ordinary persons, so it is in this case.

385. "The abiding of those who hold office lasts as long as their office."—For even those who possess knowledge, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, who have attained specific offices by means of specific actions, their "abiding" (*avasthiti*) lasts "as long as their office" (*yāvadadhikāram*), that is, until the completion of the office obtained through action; it is simply remaining in office, and not the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi-gati*) immediately after the fall of the body.

95. Section on Non-Restriction (Aniyamādhikaraṇa). 386. There is no restriction; there is no contradiction for all, because of scripture and inference. For all—meaning even for those devoted to every kind of meditation, such as the Upakośala-vidyā and others—the path beginning with light (arcirādigati) exists. Therefore, there is no restriction—that is, an absence of the rule that it belongs only to those devoted to the Upakośala-vidyā. And this being so, there is no contradiction—that is, an absence of conflict—with both scripture and inference: namely, with the scriptural text beginning "And those who in the forest... and with the Smṛti text beginning "From here, by day, during the bright fortnight... and so forth.

Regarding the cognitions characterized by the aforementioned modes of attributes, their inclusion must indeed be effected within all the meditations (*vidyās*), both through the general and the specific: because the Brahman who is the object of meditation is one and the same in all meditations, and because all those cognitions are subsumed within the contemplation of Brahman. This is like the *aupasada*—that is, like the mantra that is an auxiliary part of the rite called *upasad*; for since qualities follow the principal, and because that [mantra] is recited in the Sāmaveda, [the rule] "one chants the Sāman loudly" applies.

Although loudness (*uccaiḥ*) is required for what has been thus stated, just as the low tone (*upāṃśu*) prescribed by the rule "the Yajus is recited in a low voice" applies because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *Upasad* rite of the Yajurveda, so too is the principle that qualities must follow the primary matter (*guṇānāṃ pradhānānuvartitvam*) stated; this is clarified in the Karma-kāṇḍa of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā under the sūtra "In case of conflict between the subordinate and the principal" (*guṇamukhyavyatikrame*).
Regarding the notions of the syllable— those notions pertaining to the syllable as the Supreme Brahman, such as "neither gross nor subtle" and so forth.

"Because of this much being enjoined"—that is, "only this much" (is to be meditated upon as connected with Brahman in all branches of knowledge); because of its being enjoined—that is, because of the mental reflection directed toward Brahman—due to the reason that it consists in the meditation upon Brahman (the meaning is: only so much is to be meditated upon as, without which the meditation upon Brahman itself cannot be accomplished).

388. 97. The Section on Being Internal: If it be argued that, as in the case of the group of elements (*bhūtagrāma*), there is no possibility of difference from one's own self because of being internal, we say no; for it is like the instruction [in the *Upastipraśna*]: "That Self which is within all" (*ya ātmā sarvāntaraḥ*). To him who asked thus regarding the Self that is within all, [the answer is given: "This is your Self that is within all. (*eṣa ta ātmā sarvāntaraḥ*)

In this reply, the designation [of the Self] is made as being within all; it concerns the individual self (*jīvātman*) who is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of the insentient beings denoted by the term "the aggregate of beings" (*bhūtagrāma*), and not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Otherwise, if it were concerned with the Supreme Self, there would be an inconsistency—an incongruity—regarding the two subsequent answers: "He who breathes by means of breath" and "He who is beyond hunger, thirst, and so forth," for these would not apply to the Brahman that is the object of meditation (*upāsya*).

If it is argued that [the repetition is] due to oneness—such reflection is indeed not appropriate, as it is in the case of instruction; for just as in the instruction concerning the Knowledge of Being (sadvidyā) directed toward Śvetaketu, there was a repetition of the question, "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further," so too here, a difference in the responses is what is logically consistent.

390. There is an exchange [of attributes], because they distinguish [the Self] as they do the other [Brahman]; for [the words of Yājñavalkya] distinguish [the inner Self] by making it understood as distinct from the individual self through attributes such as being the cause of the life of all living beings and being beyond hunger and so forth; therefore, there is an exchange.

—(Regarding the two Brāhmaṇas: there must be a mutual combination of the attributes, as in the other case—just as in the other Sadvidyā, all the attributes found in every answer are combined everywhere (and therefore, there is no difference in the knowledge here).

391. For that very [deity] is indeed "Truth" and so forth; for "that very one"—the supreme deity denoted by the word *sat* (Being), which is consistently referred to in all [sections] by the words "That is Truth, That is the Self"—is also characterized by attributes such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) and the rest (which persist throughout all nine sections and thus indicate the non-difference of the object of meditation). Therefore, the example stated in the preceding sūtra ("like the others") is perfectly well-established.

98. Section on Desire and the Like (Kāmādyadhikaraṇam). 392. *Kāmādītaratra tatra cāyatanādibhyaḥ* (3.3.38). "In the other [text] and there" means that in both the Vājasaneyaka and the Chāndogya, Brahman alone—characterized by "desire and the like," such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth—is the object of meditation in the Dahara-vidyā. This is because of the grounds of the heart as the abode (*hṛdayāyatanatva*), the possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), and specific forms of mastery (*vaiśvaryādi*). [This is established] through the recognition of the identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikyapratyabhijñāna*), which serves as the indicator. 393.

"Non-exclusion due to emphasis": because of the emphasis—namely, because qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*), which are accessible through scripture alone, are repeatedly taught with respect regarding Brahman—there is "non-exclusion," meaning that the qualities of Brahman mentioned in the *dahara-vidyā* and other contexts are not to be considered negated.

394. "Because of that statement when [the state] has arrived"—"when it has arrived" means when one has attained Brahman; "because of that," meaning for the very reason of attaining Brahman, "because of that statement," since the scripture declares that one may act according to desire in all worlds [it follows that meditation on the qualified Brahman does not bestow worldly results].

Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*); for this section (*anuvāka*) is intent upon determining the Supreme Reality as the object of worship for all higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). Indeed, that [indicative mark] is more powerful than the authority of syntactical connection (*vākya*); moreover, the superior strength of the indicative mark over syntactical connection has been correctly established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* in the discussion beginning with "Direct Assertion, Indicative Mark, Syntactical Connection" (*śrutiliṅgavākya*).
102. Topic on Prior Alternatives.

398. *Pūrvavikalpaḥ prakaraṇāt syāt kriyā mānasavat* (3.3.34). [The fire-altar consisting of mind (*manas*) and so forth, mentioned in the *Vājasaneyaka-rahasya*, though to be accomplished by the mind,] must be an action—it must necessarily enter into a sacrifice consisting of action; it does not enter into a sacrifice consisting of knowledge, because of the context—the context being that of a sacrificial accessory consisting of action, namely the altar built with bricks.

Because this *manascit* and so forth is proximate to what was previously mentioned, there is an alternative view (*pūrvavikalpa*): this *manascit* and so forth is to be treated as an alternative to the fire-altar built of bricks (*iṣṭakacitāgni*) which was introduced earlier. It is like the "mental" (*mānasa*) cup—a specific type of vessel mentioned in the context of the tenth day of the twelve-day sacrifice, known as the *Avivākya*, because it is devoid of various recitations; since its nature is produced by the mind, it is designated by the word "mental," and just as that [cup] enters into the essence of the ritual action, so too does this [fire-altar].
(This illustration applies to the fact that even that which consists of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*) may enter into the nature of ritual action.)

399. And because of the extension (*atideśa*), there is an option (*vikalpa*) with the previously mentioned fire built of bricks; for it is established that the function of the fire built of bricks is extended (*atidiśyamāna*) to each individual fire among those consisting of mind (*manaścita*) and so forth. (Indeed, only equals are subject to option. Therefore, [the fire consisting of mind and so forth] would be an action—it would consist of action alone.

But it is indeed of the nature of knowledge (vidhā), because of the specific determination and because of the scriptural vision. The fire-altars consisting of mind and so forth enter only into a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (vidyāmaya-kratu), not into a sacrifice consisting of ritual action (kriyāmaya-kratu). This is because of the specific determination in the text, "These, indeed, are built of knowledge alone," which makes known the determination that they are to be accomplished through knowledge; and because of the scriptural vision in the statement, "It was made consisting of mind."

401. Furthermore, there is no sublation because of the superior strength of direct assertion (*śruti*) and the rest; that is, because of the greater strength of direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*) over context (*prakaraṇa*), there is no sublation. Thus, the nature of being composed of knowledge (*vidyārūpatva*), which is established by the direct assertion "These indeed are piled up by knowledge," is not sublated by the context of being piled with bricks—which indicates they consist of ritual action—therefore, they consist solely of knowledge.

402. From the "accessories" (anubandha) and so forth, [the distinction is established] just as the distinctness of other cognitions is seen; this has been stated regarding the "other cognitions"—namely, those known by names such as the "Small" (dahara) and others—just as their difference is established through the various characteristics heard here and there that indicate difference, so too from the "accessories" and so forth, which consist precisely of the mental elements employed in sacrifice.

From the *graha-stotra* treatises, as well as from the indicative marks (*liṅga*), syntactical connections (*vākya*), and other such indicators, the distinctness—the difference—of the "mind-altar" (*manaścita*) and so forth from the ritual consisting of action is understood; thus, a rule for a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu-vidhi*) must be postulated here.

And it has been observed that even in a sentence resembling an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), an injunction (*vidhi*) is postulated; this is well known from Vedic passages such as "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yadeva vidyayā karoti*). Thus, it is established in the *Karmamīmāṃsā-sūtra*—"But [these] statements [are injunctions], because they convey something not previously known" (*vacanāni tvapūrvatvāt*)—that the postulation of an injunction is stated even in a sentence that has the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*).
403. Nor is there attainment of the world through similarity, for even from similarity there is no perception [of it], just as in the case of death.

Regarding the statement, "This is that Death, who is this person in this orb," since the extension of the nature of Death to the person in the orb is observed even through the mere connection with a common attribute consisting of the power of destruction (*saṃhartṛtva*), there is no extension of specific attributes such as the entry into a ritual consisting of action; for just as in the case of Death, the quality of being the destroyer of all—which exists in Death—is indeed extended there, so too here, the fruitfulness of the "mind-altars" (*manascit*) and so forth is [extended] just like that of the "brick-altars" (*iṣṭakacita*).

Regarding the term "extended application" (atideśa): it is not the case that there is an attainment of the world of mortals; for the attainment of the world of death by the person within the mandala is certainly not obtained through extended application.

404. "And by the subsequent [text], and because of abundance, there is a connection with the subsequent. By the subsequent Brāhmaṇa beginning with "This indeed is the world," the subsequent—that is, the immediately following—text, which consists of words denoting the "mind-altar" (manaścit) and so forth, is understood to possess that same nature; namely, the character of teaching a knowledge-based (vidyāmaya) construction. Furthermore, the "connection"—the joining of the mind-altars and other such things to be accomplished through knowledge within the context of ritual action—is due to "abundance," that is, the predominance of the constituent parts of the fire-altar (agnyaṅga) within the context of ritual action.

103. The section concerning existence in the body (Sūtras 51–52). 405. "Because [the self] exists in the body" (eka ātmanaḥ śarīre bhāvāt). Because the self—the inner self (*pratyagātman*), the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the meditator—exists in the body, that is, within the physical frame; therefore, some proponents of the prima facie view (or those studying the *Pañcāgni-vidyā* chapter) maintain that at the time of meditation, one's own essential nature must be contemplated as characterized precisely by agency, enjoyership, and so forth. 406.

The distinction [of the Self] exists because it arises when that [meditation] is present, but not like [the attributes of] perception—namely, for the *ātman*, the inner self who is the meditator. The distinction is that which exists in the liberated state, distinct from the transmigratory state, free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), and characterized by such qualities as being "devoid of sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*); this very form is what is to be meditated upon. However, the form existing while one is in the body is not at all to be contemplated. This is because the liberated, distinct true nature is attained only when that meditation is present—that is, when such meditation exists. Thus, [the distinction is established].
Like the attainment [of the goal]: just as one who is steadfast in the contemplation of Brahman as it truly exists attains the direct realization of the nature of Brahman.

104. The Section on the Meditations Connected with the Subsidiary Parts (*Aṅgāvabaddhādhikaraṇa*). "But the meditations connected with the subsidiary parts (*aṅgāvabaddha*) belong to all the branches, for they are connected with each Veda. The meditations connected with the subsidiary parts—namely those resting upon the *udgītha* and other such parts which are themselves subsidiary—are not restricted to specific branches; rather, because they are connected solely with the subsidiary part itself by the direct statement of scripture (*śruti*), they must apply to all branches within every Veda."

Or, as with the mantras and so forth, there is no contradiction; or, "as with the mantras and so forth" means that just as there is no contradiction when mantras prescribed in one Vedic recension (śākhā) as auxiliary elements of a sacrifice are connected to a different recension that lacks the recitation of those specific mantras, so too there is an absence of contradiction even when meditations on the *udgītha* and other such elements are associated with a different recension.

105. The Section on the Superiority of the Whole (Bhūmajyāyastvādhikaraṇa). Regarding the Whole (bhūman): [The Sūtra states] "The superiority of the Whole, like that of a sacrifice; for thus it shows [in the context of knowledge]. This means that the superiority—meaning excellence and authoritative validity—belongs to the meditation on the whole, and not to the meditation on the parts.

Because the unity of the sentence is understood—just as in the case of the *ṛtu* sacrifice: regarding the sacrifice enjoined by the text, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," the statement, "When it consists of eight potsherds," is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a portion thereof; likewise, here too, there is only a restatement of a single part of the meditation on the Head and so forth, and not an injunction for separate meditations.
For the scripture clearly demonstrates this, showing both the meditation on the whole and the harmfulness of the separate meditations in such passages as, "Your head would have fallen off."

106. The Section on the Difference of Words, etc. (Śabdādibhedādhikaraṇam): The meditations (*vidyās*)—such as the meditation on the True (*sadvidyā*), the meditation on the Small (*daharavidyā*), and others—which consist of worship, are to be understood as distinct by means of various words; that is, they are "distinct" because their essential natures are mutually different due to the difference of words and so forth. This is because we observe distinct differences in the means of injunction, such as the use of different words and other factors. (Therefore, even though the object of worship may be one and the same, the meditations themselves are indeed distinct.
107. The Section on Option (Vikalpādhikaraṇam).

411. *Vikalpa* (option): Because the fruit is not distinct, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the various knowledges such as the *Sadvidyā* and others, which have the attainment of Brahman as their fruit; that is, a single person must practice only one of them according to a fixed rule, and not all together (*samuccaya*), because the fruit is not distinct—since there is no difference in Brahman, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss unconditioned by space, time, or form, as it is experienced by the person through perfected meditation which constitutes the fruit of knowledge—or rather, because the knowledges result in a single experience of non-distinct Brahman.

412. But the optional [vidyās] may either be combined or not, because of the absence of the previous reason. "But the optional"—that is, those vidyās which have fruits other than the attainment of Brahman—may be combined (*samuccīyeran*), meaning they may coexist in a single person according to one's desire (*yathākāmam*, *yatheṣṭam*); or they may be treated as alternatives (*vikalpyeran*). This is because of the absence of the previous reason: namely, because their fruit is not of an unlimited nature (the meaning is that while combination is possible among rites with optional fruits when there is a desire for a greater abundance of results, it is not so here).

413. The status of being a constituent part according to its substratum (*yathāśrayabhāvādhikaraṇa*). Regarding the "constituent parts" (*aṅgeṣu*)—that is, regarding the constituent parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*) such as the *udgītha*—the meditations (*upāsanā*) that exist by depending upon them possess the status of being constituent parts according to their substratum; that is, they possess the status of being constituent parts of the ritual action just like the *udgītha* and so forth which serve as their substrata. Therefore, the employment of the *udgītha* must necessarily be performed.

414. And because of the teaching of the learned—meaning from the injunction "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," which serves as an indicator—it follows that for those meditations based on the *udgītha* and so forth, their status as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is not contradicted, just as it is for their own substrates; thus, the employment of the *udgītha* and so forth is mandatory.

Because of the restoration (*samāhāra*). The knowledge of the *udgītha* must necessarily be accomplished because of the restoration—namely, the restoration (*samādhāna*), which is the removal of that defect [of a faulty *udgītha*], as indicated by the scriptural statement: "Even from the seat of the *hotṛ*, he indeed restores a poorly sung *udgītha*" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 1.5.5), where the restoration occurs through the knowledge of the oneness of the *udgītha* and the *praṇava* performed by the *hotṛ* when the knowledge performed by the *udgātṛ* has failed.

415–416. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of the quality—namely, the commonality of the *praṇava*, which possesses the quality of being an object of meditation for the purpose of meditation—and because of the evidence that it occurs generally in the acts of calling (*āśrāvaṇa*), reciting (*śaṃsana*), and chanting (*udgāna*) due to its being heard in such passages as "By this [syllable] the threefold knowledge proceeds," [the inclusion of the *udgītha* and so forth as auxiliary parts of ritual action is mandatory]. 417.

Or rather, there is no such rule; for there is no scriptural statement of their coexistence. That is to say, there is certainly no rule for the inclusion of meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth as constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice, because there is no scriptural establishment (*aśruteḥ*) of their coexistence—that is, their status as constituents (*aṅgatva*) with respect to the sacrifice. This is because their status as constituents is understood from such passages as "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yadeva vidyayā karoti*) to be with respect to the fruit pertaining to the sacrifice—namely, the state of being more powerful (*vīryavattaratva*)—and not as a constituent part of the sacrifice itself.

418. And because of the observation—namely, because it is observed that the protection of all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is prescribed in the Veda—it follows that there is indeed no restrictive rule regarding knowledge being dependent upon the Udgātṛ priest.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter.
The teacher named Bādarāyaṇa maintains this view—that such a meaning is understood from the scriptural word beginning with "The knower becomes immortal here"—as derived from the Śruti.

420. "Because it is a subordinate element (śeṣa), it is a statement of human purpose (puruṣārthavāda), as in the case of other [rites]"; thus says Jaimini. Because knowledge (vidyā) is a subordinate element of the ritual (kratu) by being an auxiliary to the action through its function as a refinement of the agent (kartṛ-saṃskāra), just as in the case of other things—namely, substances, refinements, and actions—the statement "human purpose is achieved through knowledge" is merely a *puruṣārthavāda*; that is, it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to glorify knowledge. This is the view held by the teacher named Jaimini.

421. Because of the observation of conduct—that is, because of the observation of the conduct of those who know Brahman, which consists primarily of ritual action, as it is found among Aśvapati, Janaka, and others, and is made known through the Śrutis and Smṛtis—action is indeed a limb of knowledge; action is not a limb of wisdom.

422. From that scriptural statement—that is, from the scripture [itself]—the fact that knowledge is a subsidiary part of ritual action is understood from the scriptural evidence consisting of the instrumental case-ending in the word "vidyayā" (by means of knowledge) in the passage "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yadeva vidyayā karoti*), which indicates its application (*viniyoga*) to the action denoted by the word "performs."

423. From the statement "from simultaneous undertaking, from simultaneous undertaking"—since the scripture declares that knowledge and action both undertake the same person as their substrate in the words "knowledge and action both undertake him" (*taṃ vidyā karmaṇī samanvārabhete*), it follows that knowledge, being in grammatical apposition with action, is indeed an auxiliary to action.

428. [The scriptural passage] "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10) is not universal; that is, it does not pertain to all forms of knowledge, but rather pertains only to the Udgītha-knowledge. Thus, by this scripture, the status of knowledge as an auxiliary to ritual action is not established.

429. "The division is like that of a hundred": this refers to the separate existence within a single person of knowledge and action, which have not yet entered into the relationship of subordinate and principal. This is stated in the passage, "Knowledge and action both follow him. And that division is "like a hundred"—just as when a man who sells both land and jewels has an inheritance of two hundred, there is a division such that one hundred is for the land and one hundred is for the jewels; so too [is this division established].

For one who possesses merely the study [of the Veda]—that is, for one who has simply grasped the mass of syllables according to the rules, because the performance of ritual action is enjoined by the scriptural text "Having studied the Veda"—the view of Bādarāyaṇa alone is correct, namely that "knowledge is not an auxiliary part of ritual action. (Indeed, knowledge is certainly not mere study; rather, it is something entirely different, consisting of the mental state of recollection.)

431. *Nāviśeṣāt* (3-4-13). [The injunction in the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*, "Performing actions here indeed," which prescribes the performance of ritual acts for as long as one lives] does not refer to those rites that are independent subsidiaries of knowledge (*vidyā*) and serve as means to attain desired fruits (*kāmyaphala*). Why? Because there is no distinction; that is, because there is no specific reason (*viśiṣṭahetu*) to indicate such a specific meaning. [Even if the general rule of performing rites—expressed as "performing actions indeed"—is intended to refer to specific rites that act as auxiliaries to the arising of knowledge, the injunction... 430.
Because [the alternative] would be purposeless; for there is no determining factor [to restrict the application] when it comes to being the object of a specific independent action.

432. [The statement] "or permission for the sake of praise" means that, regarding the knowledge under discussion, permission—namely, the authorization to perform actions while one is performing them (as in the text, "Performing actions here indeed")—is granted for the purpose of producing the cognition of their excellence. And this excellence consists in the fact that even those actions which are by nature entangled [with defects] become free from such entanglement when they are accompanied by the knowledge under discussion. Therefore, it follows that knowledge is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action.

433. Furthermore, some—the Vājasaneyins—[state] that by one's own will (*kāmakāreṇa*), that is, solely by desire, [one may renounce]; they read [the text] beginning with "What shall we do with offspring? [referring to the renunciation of the householder stage and the duties of the domestic life]. For a limb [of the sacrifice] is never to be abandoned [in that manner]. Therefore, knowledge is not a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*). 434.

And "destruction" (upamarda)—that is, the destruction of all karma through knowledge consisting of meditation—some, namely the followers of the Atharva Veda, study: "His karmas are exhausted when He is seen. (For it is not logical that the principal [the Self] should be destroyed by its subordinate part; thus, knowledge is not a subordinate part of ritual action.)

435. And [the conclusion holds] regarding those whose vital energy is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*), for in scripture—namely, in the words "and among those whose vital energy is drawn upward"—it is heard that this applies to the stages of life of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*). Since the knowledge of Brahman is seen there and since rituals such as the *agnihotra* are absent in those stages, knowledge is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action;

for the performance of subordinate parts is not possible without the principal (*aṅgin*). Indeed, the stages of life of wandering mendicants whose vital energy is drawn upward do exist; for this is so because it is heard in the Upaniṣadic scripture in such words as, "It is precisely these wandering mendicants... and so forth.

436. Jaimini [holds that there is] a mere reference (*parāmarśa*), because there is no injunction; for he censures [it], since there is no injunction. (Regarding such passages as) "There are three branches of duty: sacrifice, study, and charity," and so forth—the teacher named Jaimini considers that the stage of life (*āśrama*) of wandering mendicants (*pravrajita*) is not prescribed [as an obligatory rule]; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the mendicant stage in the Śruti for the purpose of praising meditation (*upāsana*), and not an injunction.

For—since—the scriptural statement, "He who causes the sacred fire to be extinguished is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods," censures the condition of those who have abandoned the sacred fires.

437. Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the other stages of life] are to be practiced, because of the scriptural statement of equality. "To be practiced" means that, like the householder's stage (gṛhasthāśrama), the other stages of life (āśramāntara) are also to be followed; this is what the venerable Vyāsa, namely Bādarāyaṇa, maintains, because of the scriptural statement of equality—that is, because the other stages of life are mentioned with the same form as the householder's stage.

438. [The passage beginning with] "The injunction regarding the aggregates of dharma" (*vidhirvā dhāraṇavat vidhirvā*) means that for all stages of life (*āśrama*), there is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), and not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) of anything. This is like the case of "wearing" (*dhāraṇa*); even though the sentence "For he wears [the sacred thread] above, for the gods" (*upari hi devebhyo dhārayati*) is of the nature of a restatement, the aspect of wearing is accepted as being an injunction. Therefore, by these arguments, it is established that "the human goal [is attained] from knowledge alone."

If it is argued that these [stories] are useful only for the recitation of the *pāriplava* and not for the purpose of the injunctions regarding knowledge (*vidyā-vidhi*), such a possibility is not appropriate, because they have been specifically distinguished; that is, the stories of Manu and others have been explicitly stated to be for the purpose of the *pāriplava* recitation.

442. And likewise, because they are connected as parts of a single sentence—just as in cases such as "Ghee is indeed brilliance" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*) or "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*), and similarly in the narratives of Yājñavalkya and others, because they are syntactically linked as a single unit with injunctions such as "The Self, verily, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*)—none of these narratives are intended for the *pāriplava* recitations; rather, they serve solely the purpose of the injunctions regarding knowledge (*vidyā*).
It is not so, however, because that meaning—the eating of all things—is revealed by the Śruti to Akrāyaṇa, who was named Uṣasti, only in such a state, and not as something always to be seen.

And because there is no contradiction—since it is only when this is so that one can avoid contradicting the scriptural passage establishing the purity of food, namely, "When food is pure, the being is purified. This is also for the reason [of avoiding such contradiction].

Furthermore, even when life is at stake—that is, when there is the imminent danger of losing one's life—the permission to eat all kinds of food is recorded in the Smṛti as an unrestricted authorization to consume any food whatsoever. This is made clear by the Smṛti text: "He who, having fallen into a state where his life is in peril, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by sin."

Because there is this scriptural statement regarding acting according to one's desire, permission for all food is granted only in the event of danger to life; for this very reason, when not acting according to one's desire—that is, when there is a prohibition against acting according to one's own will—a scriptural statement is also seen, such as "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa does not drink liquor."
Section 116: On Being Enjoined (Vihitatvādhikaraṇam).

450. And because it is enjoined, even the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must be performed. Because they are indeed enjoined by such scriptural texts as, "The Agnihotra is to be performed for as long as one lives," the duties of the stages of life—such as sacrifices and the like—which are prescribed for those belonging solely to a particular stage of life, must certainly be practiced even by one who is qualified for knowledge (vidyā).

451. And by way of being auxiliaries—relying on the fact that sacrificial rites and the like serve as auxiliaries for the arising of knowledge—even so, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma), namely the sacrifices and other rites prescribed for those belonging solely to a stage of life, must indeed be performed. 452. In every respect, they are the same because of the twofold indicative mark—in every respect, even when performed for the sake of knowledge as well as for the sake of the stage of life, they are the very same acts performed.

Sacrifices and the like are indeed non-different [in essence]—they do not possess a difference in their own nature caused by a difference in their intended objects (uddeśya)—because of the evidence of both genders; that is, because there is recognition through the very same word, such as "Agnihotra," in both cases. And it shows non-overpowering: even when knowledge arises, there is no overpowering by more powerful evil deeds.

This scripture—“By dharma one dispels evil”—clearly demonstrates that even for a person performing rites such as sacrifices, there may exist an obstacle [to liberation]; therefore, even by one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*), the duty prescribed for those in the stages of life (*āśrama*) must indeed be performed.

455. Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti that even for those who do not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin), there is the attainment of knowledge; for it is taught in such Smṛti passages as, "A Brāhmaṇa may attain perfection even by means of silent recitation (japya). (Therefore, the eligibility of even those outside the stages of life for the knowledge of Brahman is unimpeded.)

And there is a special favor by way of distinction: through the specific dharma of the stages of life (*āśrama*) consisting of non-restricted austerity, celibacy, and so forth; and there is also the assistance to knowledge for those not belonging to a stage of life (*anāśramin*), as stated in the scripture, "One should seek the Self through austerity" (*tapasā ātmānamanvicchet*); therefore, even for those in the intermediate state (*antarāla*)—that is, for those not belonging to a stage of life—there is approval for knowledge.

457. Therefore, the other is superior, both because of the scriptural indication (*liṅga*) and because of [the Smṛti]. "Therefore"—that is, in comparison with the state of being without an *āśrama*—the "other," namely the state of belonging to an *āśrama*, is superior, due to its excellence consisting in the greater abundance of dharma; and also because of the scriptural indication, such as the existence of Smṛti texts stating, "One should not remain without an *āśrama*," and so forth.

They are indeed excluded from the outside world— on account of the aforementioned traditional teaching regarding their downfall, and on account of conduct, which consists of the avoidance of those who have fallen away, as well as the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas).

121. The Section on Non-Manifestation (Anāviṣkārādhikaraṇa). 467. "Not manifesting [his wisdom], because of the connection. "Not manifesting" means assuming the nature of a child, which consists in not displaying the greatness of oneself that has been acquired through scholarship; [the wise person] should so abide. This is because of the "connection"—that is, because such a state of non-manifestation is possible in a wise person as being compatible with the connection to knowledge, according to the injunction: "Having become disillusioned with scholarship, one should abide in childhood. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.4) Thus, it is precisely this non-manifestation that is appropriate for the wise person.

The meaning that constitutes the intended purport of the scripture (namely, that "knowing" is synonymous with "meditation") is established on the basis of instruction; for in a statement primarily concerned with teaching the means to liberation, the verbal root *vid* is employed as a synonym for meditation.

471. Also from indicative marks (*liṅga*): the meaning of the scripture is that [the knowledge which is the means to liberation] must be practiced many times through repetition (*paunaḥpunya*) and continuity (*nairantarya*). This is also known from indicative marks such as the scriptural tradition (*smṛti*) stating: "And a continuous flow of cognition having that form, free from longing for anything else—that is meditation (*dhyāna*)," and so forth.

477. And from [the rule regarding] meditation (*dhyāna*)—[referring to the worship enjoined by the injunction "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)]—because such meditation consists of one-pointed reflection uninterrupted by heterogeneous cognitions, one should perform it while sitting alone.

478. "With reference to immobility and [the state of] being immobile"—this refers to the very state of remaining unshakable in the person who meditates (*dhyātṛ*). With reference to—that is, with intent toward—even insentient things such as mountains, designations are seen such as "the mountains seem to be meditating. (In order to achieve the physical state of immobility conducive to meditation, one should practice meditation while sitting alone.)

479. And the sages remember that it is proper for a person to practice meditation while remaining seated; they also make this known through such Smṛti texts as, "Having sat down on a seat, one should apply oneself to yoga."

Wherever there is one-pointedness, there [meditation should be performed], because there is no distinction. One-pointedness is the mind’s state of being fixed upon a single auspicious object. "Wherever"—meaning in whatever place or at whatever time it is accomplished—"there"—in that very place and at that very time—the lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) should perform meditation. This is because there is no distinction; for in the Śrutis and other scriptures regarding the practice of yoga, no specific restriction of place or time is heard apart from one-pointedness. 129. Section on Until Death (Āprayāṇādhikaraṇa). 480.

"Until the departure, for it is seen even there"—that is, the meditation being performed by the practitioner must be done daily until the departure, meaning until the separation from the body; for it is seen that even during the intervening period from the commencement of the worship until the limit of the separation from the body, the duty to perform meditation daily is ordained by the scripture: "He, indeed, living thus as long as he lives."

481. 130. The Topic of the Attainment of That [Knowledge]. 482. Upon the attainment of that, there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the designation thereof. When there is the attainment (*prāpti*) of knowledge (*vidyā*)—which, in meditation (*dhyāna*), has a form identical to the vision [of reality]—there occurs, respectively, the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of subsequent and prior sins: the non-clinging, which is the absence of being tainted, and the destruction, which is the dissolution of the essential nature of the mass of evil deeds belonging to the period before and after the accomplishment of knowledge. This is because of the scriptural designation: "In one who knows thus, evil action does not cling," and "Thus, for him, all... [sins are destroyed].
And because the scripture clearly states both non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) in the passage, "The evils are consumed.
131. The Section on the Other (Itarādhikaraṇa).

483. For the other as well, there is likewise non-clinging; but upon falling away, it is thus—by the very same reasoning already stated, for the "other" as well—that is, for merit (*puṇya*) also, there is non-clinging, meaning the absence of any stain when knowledge is attained, and its destruction occurs, because that is so designated in scripture.
This is because it is clearly stated in those two [passages]: "He shakes off good and evil deeds," and "All evils turn back from him";
however, upon the fall—that is, when the body falls—immediately thereafter, there is the destruction of that merit which was conducive to longevity, food, and so forth.

132. Section on Actions Not Yet Begun (Anārabdhakāryādhikaraṇa). However, only those previous merits and demerits whose effects have not yet begun—that is, those which existed prior to the arising of knowledge and had not yet commenced the production of their results—attain destruction; this alone is certain. This is because of the scriptural statement regarding the limit of that [destruction]: "until I am released," which establishes that the limit is the liberation from the body.
The Second Quarter (Pāda):

494. "Because [the scriptures] show that it does not [dissolve] into one alone; for the vital breath (prāṇa) conjoined with the individual soul (jīva) does not merge into one—namely, into fire alone when unmixed with other elements—for both Śruti and Smṛti demonstrate this. They clarify that each single element, when unmixed with the others, lacks the capacity to produce its own specific effect, as in the passage, 'The threefold, the threefold' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.3), and likewise, '[We] were unable [to create] without a combination' (Mahābhārata)."

If it be argued that [the soul does not depart] because of the prohibition [of departure], we say no; for some [scriptures] clearly state [it departs] from the embodied one. (The meaning stated by these many sūtras has been refuted. If it is argued that this is so because of the prohibition—namely, that the absence of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) from the knower of reality is made known by the scriptural text, "His vital breaths do not depart"—we reply: such a doubt is not at all consistent. This is because the prohibition refers precisely to the departure of the vital breaths from the "embodied one" (*śārīra*), that is, from the individual soul (*jīva*) itself (and not from the physical body), as is established by the negation in the passage, "His vital breaths [do not depart]."
For this reason, according to some—namely the followers of the Mādhyandina recension—in the reading "the vital breaths do not depart from him," this meaning is clearly and explicitly understood.

501. Furthermore, it is recorded in tradition that even for the wise man there is an exit through the cranial channel; this is clearly established by the Smṛti text: "One among them stands erect, and he goes upwards. Therefore, until the commencement of death—that is, prior to entering the channel—the path is the same for both the wise and the ignorant; their departure is of one and the same form.

143. Section on Following the Rays (Raśmyanusārādhikaraṇa). 505. Following the Rays (4.2.17): [The knower] having departed through the hundred-and-first vein at the crown of the head, follows the rays—meaning that according to the method stated in the scripture, "Then by these very rays he ascends upwards," he possesses the means of travel by following the rays of the sun at any time whatsoever, whether by day or by night, and thus attains the higher station.

144. *Niśādhikaraṇam*. If it be argued that [liberation] does not occur at night—[that is,] if one objects: "Because death during the night is prohibited, the attainment of Brahman is not possible for the wise man who dies at night"—such a doubt is indeed not consistent, because the connection [of the soul with the fruit] persists as long as the body lasts; for the karma that has begun to yield its fruit remains connected [to the soul] for the duration of the bodily existence. Furthermore, the scripture itself indicates [this] regarding the night: [it shows that there is no obstacle to the attainment of Brahman even when death occurs at night]. Thus, the attainment of Brahman is possible.
