147. The Section on Air (Vāyvadhikaraṇa). 510. From the Year, Air [is to be placed] because of the general and the specific. After the year on the path beginning with light, one should place air alone; "because of the general and the specific"—that is, by way of generality through the general term "the world of the gods," and (likewise) by way of specificity through the specific term "air" for that very same entity, since it must be understood that the single [entity] is designated in various places by these respective terms.

516. "Designation by proximity" means designation based on proximity—(referring to the *brahman* as the goal without specifying it as the Supreme Brahman, but indicating the goal of the Supreme Brahman): "He leads them to Brahman. This use of the neuter term for designation is due solely to its being in close proximity to the *brahman* consisting of Hiraṇyagarbha, based on the fact that it is an immediate effect of the Supreme Brahman.

517. "At the dissolution of the effect, together with its presiding deity, [he attains] that which is beyond this, because it is so stated" (4.3.2). Regarding the "effect"—the world of Hiraṇyagarbha, which is to be created—at its "dissolution," i.e., at its end; "together with its presiding deity"—along with Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the superintendent of the world of Brahman and whose office has terminated; "beyond this"—the world of the Supreme Brahman, which is superior or higher than the world of Brahman (he attains), "because it is so stated" in the Śruti: "But they, in the world of Brahman, at the time of their final end... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1).
Because it is established by the indicative mark of the attainment of immortality and the non-return [to saṃsāra].

518. And on account of Smṛti (4.3.10): [The meaning is that] the worshiper of the effected Brahman (kāryabrahma) attains the supreme state along with Hiraṇyagarbha; this is understood from the authority of Smṛti as well, from the statement: "All those, together with Brahmā, enter the supreme state. 519.

"But Jaimini [holds that it leads] the person who meditates on the Supreme Brahman, because of the primary sense."—The group of conductors, beginning with Light (*arcis*), is the "conductor" (*ātivāhika*); [it leads him] because of the primary sense, for the word "Brahman" has its primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) only to the Supreme Brahman, as it possesses a non-metaphorical application (*anupacaritavṛttikatvāt*). Thus thinks the teacher named Jaimini.

And because of the scriptural evidence that [the group of deities] leads those who meditate on Brahman from one stage to the next—namely, from the authority of the Śruti text, "Having reached the highest light... he emerges"—[this conclusion] becomes firm. || 521 ||

Furthermore, "intention" (*pratyabhisandhi*) does not mean an intention directed toward the effect—such as the mental reflection expressed in "I enter the assembly hall and the dwelling of Prajāpati"—nor is it an intention regarding the effect, namely Hiraṇyagarbha; for the word *prajāpati* has its primary meaning in the Supreme Self alone, according to the scriptural principle "the Lord of the universe."

520. 522. "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that the group of conducting deities] leads those who do not rely on symbols (apratīkālambana), because there are defects in both cases, and because of their resolve (tatkratu). That is to say, it leads those other than those who rely on symbols—namely, all classes of sentient and insentient beings from the name (nāman) up to the individual self (pratyagātman) as designated by the word "vital breath" (prāṇa)—whether they meditate upon them through the vision of Brahman (brahmadṛṣṭi) or in their own nature; excluding these, it leads those such as the knowers of the five fires (pañcāgnividaḥ) and the worshippers of the Supreme Brahman. Thus, the group of conducting deities (ātivāhika-gaṇa) causes them to reach the supreme state (paraṃ padam).

Regarding this point, Bādarāyaṇa—the teacher named Bādarāyaṇa—holds the following view: because there would be a defect in both positions—that of leading those who meditate on the "effect" (kārya) and that of leading those who meditate on the "supreme light" (paraṃ jyotiḥ)—there would result the flaw of contradicting all the Upaniṣads; furthermore, the principle of "the nature of one's resolve" (tatkratu-nyāya), as stated in the scripture, "According to one's resolve in this world," would be contradicted.

And he shows both the distinction and the specific excellence—even the distinction of limited fruits for those who take hold of symbols (pratīka)—as the scripture, beginning with "As far as the reach of Name," clearly establishes.
Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter.

The individual soul (*jīva*), with its concealment removed, manifests through attributes such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, which are established by scripture as belonging to Brahman—that is, as being related to Brahman—on account of the "introduction" (*upanyāsa*) and other reasons; for those very qualities of Brahman are introduced in scripture as qualities of the *jīva*, and because specific activities such as eating (*jakṣaṇa*) and so forth, which are prompted by the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), are likewise mentioned. This is the view of Jaimini—the teacher named Jaimini.

529. "By means of pure consciousness alone, because it has that as its essence," says Auḍulomi. "By means of pure consciousness alone"—that is, by its own nature consisting of pure sentience (the individual soul manifests); "because it has that as its essence"—because this inner self has the nature of being solely consciousness, as stated in the passage, "He is indeed a mass of consciousness. It is with this intention that the teacher named Auḍulomi holds this view.

(530) Even so, Bādarāyaṇa maintains there is no contradiction because of the introductory statement and because of the prior existence [of those qualities]. "Even so"—that is, even though there is the state of being a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*)—because of the introductory statement consisting of the Upaniṣadic declaration, "The Self which is free from evil," and so forth; and because of the prior existence—that is, because the previously mentioned qualities such as being free from evil also exist in the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—Bādarāyaṇa, the venerable teacher named Bādarāyaṇa, maintains that there is no contradiction, meaning that there is no resulting lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the states of being a mass of consciousness and being free from evil.

535. Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] it is of both kinds, like the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). "Like the twelve-day sacrifice" means: because of the difference in resolve (*saṅkalpa*) from the injunction "They should undertake the twelve-day sacrifice if they desire prosperity" (*dvādaśāham ṛddhikāmā upeyuḥ*), which uses the verb *upaiti* (they undertake), it has the nature of a *sattra*; and because of the difference in resolve from the injunction "One should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the twelve-day sacrifice" (*dvādaśāhena prajākāmaṃ yājayet*), which uses the verb *yajati* (he sacrifices), it has the nature of an *ahīna*. Thus, it is of both kinds—[and this applies] even to the liberated self (*muktātman*).
The state of possessing both modes—having a body and being bodiless—is established solely from the cause of the liberated one's volition; thus, the teacher named Bādarāyaṇa maintains this view.

536. "Because [experience] is possible even in the absence of a body, as in the case of the twilight state"—that is, in the absence of a body, meaning in the lack of the instruments such as the body and senses created by one's own volition, experience is possible "like the twilight state," i.e., like in a dream; for the accomplishment of enjoyment occurs through the very instruments such as the body created by the Supreme Person, which are perceivable solely by each respective individual. (Even though the individual soul possesses true volition, it may not create the instruments for its own enjoyment.)

537. *Bhāve jāgradvat*—(4-4-14). "In the state of existence" (*bhāve*) means when the instruments such as the body created by one's own volition exist; "like one in the waking state" (*jāgradvat*) means like a person situated in the condition of wakefulness, [he experiences enjoyment].

5.38. "Like a lamp" refers to entry (*āveśa*); for it demonstrates [this] like a lamp: just as a lamp situated in one place appears, by its own radiance, to enter many places, so too is entry possible—the pervasion of the Self, though residing in one place, throughout all bodies by means of knowledge which is of the nature of its own radiance, according to its resolve. It demonstrates that very manner; indeed, the Śruti clarifies this: "As the tip of a hair... up to "...is capable of infinity. Thus, it is clearly established.

[The statement] "dependent on either deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) or death (*sampatti*), for it is made manifest" means: regarding either of the two states—deep sleep (*suṣupti*) or death (*maraṇa*)—it has been set forth; for indeed, this very point has been clarified by the scripture beginning with "Verily, he does not [know]," and so forth (but here there is no investigation into the state of liberation).
156. The Topic of the Exclusion of Worldly Activity (Jagadvyāpāravajadhikaraṇa).

540. "Excluding worldly activity, because of the context and because of non-proximity" (the sovereignty of the liberated one whose true nature has become manifest). "Excluding worldly activity"—that is, excluding the regulation of the nature, maintenance, and specific functions of all sentient and insentient beings; it is only other than that, consisting solely of the unmediated experience of Brahman.

Because of the context—inasmuch as in all instances, such as the world-activity and so forth, the Supreme Brahman alone is introduced and discussed in the Śruti and other texts—and because of the lack of proximity—since there is no mention whatsoever of the liberated soul (mukta) in any Śruti within the context of the world-activity; this too serves as an indicator.

541. If it be argued that [the liberated soul possesses worldly functions] because of direct instruction—[we reply] no, because of the mention of those situated in the spheres of authority. For there is a clear teaching regarding the worldly activity of the liberated self through direct perception, namely by means of scripture (śruti) such as: "He leads these worlds and all objects of desire. [This refers to those who hold office.]

If it is argued that because [the Lord] makes [them] known, the statement "excluding the activity of the world" (*jagadvyāpāravarjam*) is not tenable—such an objection is not correct, because of the mention of those situated in the presiding circle (*ādhikārika-maṇḍala*). For it is stated in scripture that for Hiraṇyagarbha and others, who are appointed by the Blessed One to the office of governing the worlds, there is only the experience of those enjoyments existing within the worlds; the possibility of their performing the activity of the entire world does not arise. 542.

And likewise, it speaks of the state as being "beyond transformation" (*vikārāvarti*); for the Supreme Brahman, which is free from all transformations and endowed with its manifestations, is experienced by the liberated conscious self. Indeed, by virtue of being the experiencer, scripture clarifies the abiding of the liberated soul in the changeless, unsurpassed bliss of the Supreme Brahman through such passages as: "He finds the fearless foundation," and "Having attained [it], he becomes blissful. Thus, it speaks of that state.

543. Furthermore, both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)—that is, both *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—demonstrate and clarify this very point: "The activity of the world is not common to the Supreme Person. 544. Also, because of the mark of equality only in respect to enjoyment (*bhoga*), that is, only in the enjoyment consisting of the experience of the nature of Brahman; and because of the evidence consisting of the teaching of the soul's equality with the Supreme Self in the state of liberation, [it is determined that the liberated one's sovereignty excludes the activity of the world and so forth].

545. "Non-return, non-return, non-return—on account of the Word. Non-return means the non-re-entry into the wheel of saṃsāra, which is exceedingly fraught with calamities such as birth, disease, old age, misfortune, and death; this is determined on account of the Word—that is, from the Word consisting of Śruti and Smṛti, such as: "They do not return to the whirlpool," "He does not return again," and "Rebirth is no longer found. May all be auspicious!

May this auspicious exposition of the meaning of the words of the *Śārīraka-sūtras*, composed by the learned Rāmabhadra—son of Ātreya Śrī Śrīnivāsa Rāghavācārya and born of the lineage of Ṛtunātha—for the retention of students, be for the delight of Lord Hari.

In the first chapter, thirty-five principles (nyāyas) were declared; in the second chapter, concerning the definitions (lakṣaṇas), thirty-three principles are proclaimed. In the third definition, however, fifty-five are declared; likewise, in the fourth definition, thirty-three principles are recorded.
In the fifth [chapter], the Smṛtipāda, thirty-six sūtras are considered; in the sixth, the Tarkapāda, forty-two are considered. (14)

In the seventh chapter, however, on the "Sky-foot" (viyatpāda), fifty-two [sūtras] are recorded; in the eighth, on the "Vital-breath-foot" (prāṇapāda), there are nineteen sūtras less twenty [i.e., nine]; in the ninth, on the "Dispassion-foot" (vairāgyapāda), there are twenty-seven sūtras; and in the tenth, on the "Two-characteristics-foot" (dviliṅgapāda), forty are proclaimed.
In the eleventh [chapter], there are sixty-four verses concerning the withdrawal of the qualities; in the twelfth chapter, the "Limbs" (Aṅga), the fifty-fold wheel is taught.
In this quarter known as *Āvṛtti*, there are nineteen sūtras; in the quarter known as *Utkrānti*, twenty sūtras are stated;
and in the fifteenth quarter, *Gati*, there are fifteen sūtras.
In the final quarter, known as "Liberation," twenty-two sūtras are considered to be present. || 19 ||
This enumeration of the chapters, sections, and sūtras has been determined according to the tradition in the venerable Rāmānuja school. 20.

The Essence of the Meaning of the Sixteen Chapters of the Śārīraka: 3. The Form to be Known; the meaning of the chapters.
The feet [are] Bhadra-sūkta.
156. Indicating the Essential Meaning of the Chapters—3:
The Subjects of the Chapters and the Qualities They Expound.

In passages such as "They arise from space alone," the space mentioned as the object of meditation is the Supreme Self alone, not the elemental space (bhūtākāśa). In statements such as "The Lord, whose nature is unconditioned luminosity," and "They enter into Prāṇa alone," the Prāṇa mentioned as the object of meditation is the Supreme Self alone, not the well-known vital breath.
Saṃ-saṃ is the name of the section;
su-saṃ is the section on space (ākāśa).
9. Section on Prāṇa:

The Lord, who is the vitalizer of the universe—which is characterized by the distinction between those endowed with breath and those without breath—is indeed the Supreme Person who is to be meditated upon as light in passages such as "The light beyond heaven"; it is not light in the form of the sun or other luminaries.
10.10 The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa), Sūtras 25–28: "The Lord is divine radiance."

In the passage beginning with "I am the vital breath (prāṇa), the conscious self (prajñātman)," the entity denoted by the words "Indra" and "prāṇa" as the object of meditation is none other than the Supreme Self (paramātman) embodied therein, and not merely Indra or others.
This concludes the section on Indra and Prāṇa (Sūtras 29–32).
11.11 "The Lord is the inner self of Prāṇa, Indra, and so forth":
the subject matter of this section and the qualities to be established therein.

"He who is within the earth... the inner controller, the immortal"—thus described, the inner controller of all is indeed the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), not the individual soul (jīva) which presides over the body. In the passages "Śrīnivāsa whose body is the entire universe" and "by which that Imperishable is attained," the status of being denoted by the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable) belongs to Brahman alone, not to the Pradhāna, the individual soul, or others. "Śrīnivāsa, whose limbs are composed of imagined fires and other elements."
Saṃ saṃ, the name of the legal category (adhikaraṇa) 1.
Sūtra-saṃgraha 4: Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa), Sūtras 19–21;
Section on the Qualities of Being Invisible and so forth (Adṛśyatvādiguṇa-adhikaraṇa), Sūtras 22–24.

Section 176, Part 6: The Section on Vaiśvānara (Sūtras 25–33). Regarding the statement "one meditates upon Vaiśvānara," the Vaiśvānara who is the object of meditation is indeed the Supreme Brahman; it is not the digestive fire within the body or any other such entity.

Śrīnivāsa is the object of the intellect of Vaiśvānara, who begins with the heavenly world; the meanings and qualities expounded therein are such that the Puruṣa, measured by the size of a thumb as stated in the passage, "The Puruṣa of the size of a thumb... dwells in the heart," is indeed the Supreme Self (Paramātman) alone, and not the individual soul (jīva) subject to karma. "The Lord is the controller of all through His state of being measured by the heart."

25–29. The section concerning the eligibility of even the gods for meditations aimed at goals such as liberation, as taught in all the Śrutis, exists indeed for them as well. "The Lord is to be meditated upon by the gods and others"—this is the name of the *adhikaraṇa* (sūtra collection).
Sūtra-saṃgraha.
23.6 The Section on Measuring (praminādhikaraṇa) 23–24 24.7 The Section on Deities (devatādhikaraṇa)

In the Madhuvidyā and other such meditations, as stated in passages beginning with "This indeed is the honey of the gods," there is certainly eligibility even for those who have attained the status of the Vasus and others; for [it is said]: "The Lord is to be served by the Vasus and other deities as their own self. (Sūtra 3.3.25). This concludes the section on the intermediate state (madhya-adhikaraṇa), sūtras 30–32.

The nature of the years, the rivers, and those who indeed dwell within them has been described; now hear again this summary. O Brahmin, from that body of Viṣṇu which was water, the earth emerged in the form of a lotus, endowed with mountains, oceans, and the rest.

The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu, the forests, the mountains, and the directions are Viṣṇu; the rivers and the oceans—he alone is everything that exists and that does not exist, O best of brahmins. Since the Blessed One is the very nature of knowledge, he possesses an infinite form and is not a material object; therefore, know that the distinctions such as mountains and the like are merely the manifestations of consciousness. When all karma has been exhausted, his own pure form is revealed as knowledge from which all defects have been cast away.

For then the fruits of the tree of volition arise; there are no real distinctions among things in reality. Is there any entity anywhere—whether at the beginning, middle, or end—that is devoid of change and remains eternally of one form?
O twice-born, that which repeatedly undergoes alteration is not truly so; for how can there be any reality in that?
The earth becomes a jar; from the jar, shards; from the shards, powdered dust; and from that, atoms.
This sequence is perceived by people whose certainty regarding the self is stilled by their own karma. Tell me, what is the real substance here?
"Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of objects whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, that exists apart from consciousness.
Consciousness alone is accepted as manifold, being divided by various minds according to the distinctions of their own respective karmas."

His knowledge is pure and stainless, eternal, and free from all greed and other passions; it is devoid of attachment. He is the one, eternally singular, supreme, and highest Lord, that Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists. (2.12.44) 13.

Thus, true devotion has been described by me, as well as knowledge which is truth, while everything else is untruth. Furthermore, that which consists of the threefold path of action (*tri-karma-patha*), resting upon the worlds, has also been told to you: sacrifice, the sacrificial animal, the fire, the entire assembly of priests, Soma, the gods, and desire consisting of heaven—this is seen as the path based on ritual action (*karma-āśrita-mārga*). The earth and other realms, as well as the enjoyments therein, are the fruits of those [actions]. And this world-system (*bhuvana-gata*) which I have described to you, one who is subject to karma indeed wanders everywhere within it.
Having thus known that which is certain, immovable, and eternally uniform in nature, one should act so that one enters Vāsudeva by means of that [knowledge].
"Why does she speak by means of reasons, saying 'I myself am speech'? Therefore, it is not appropriate to say of her, 'She drinks and eats.'"
Since this body, characterized by a head, hands, and so forth,
is distinct from the person, O King, whereupon do I apply this designation "I"?
O best of kings, if there were anyone else superior to me,
then it would be appropriate to say, "This one is I, and that one is another."
Since the One Person is established within all bodies, then who indeed are you? "I am he"—such speech is futile.
"You are the king, this is the palanquin, we are the bearers going before you, and this is your world; yet, O King, all this that is said is not real."

"Man, woman, cow, goat, horse, elephant, bird, and tree—this worldly designation applied to bodies should be understood as having karma for its cause. O King, the soul is neither god, nor man, nor beast, nor tree; these differences in bodily form have their origin in karma."

O King, that which is called "king" in the world, as well as the king’s soldiers and so forth, and whatever else exists in this manner—none of that consists of real conceptualization (*saṃkalpanā*). But what, O King, is that thing which does not indeed assume another name even after the lapse of time—a name arising from transformation and the like? That alone is a real entity (*vastu*).

"You are the king of the entire world; you are the son of your father, the enemy of your foe, the husband of your wife, and the father of your son. O King, whom among these may I call 'you'? Is this head you, or is it your neck, or likewise your belly? Or is it your feet and so forth? Indeed, which of these is truly 'you', O Lord of the Earth?"
"O King, you exist as something distinct from all your constituent parts. O Ruler of the Earth, becoming skillful in this regard, reflect upon the question: 'Who am I?
Since reality is established in this way, it is improper for me to speak of 'I'."
O King, how can that which is to be accomplished by means of separation be possible?

That by which something is perceived—being free from defects, pure, supreme, stainless, and of a single nature—is either seen or realized; that is knowledge, and what is other than that is said to be ignorance.
O King, the support of the mind is Brahman, which is twofold by its very nature:
it is both embodied and unembodied, as well as supreme and non-supreme.
O King, understand that this entire universe consists of three kinds of cultivation (*bhāvanā*):
that called Brahman, that known as action (*karman*), and likewise that which is of the nature of both.
Indeed, one is of the nature of the state of action, while the other is of the nature of the state of Brahman.
Likewise, there is another threefold cultivation of existence which is of a dual nature.
"Those such as Sanandana and others who are endowed with the contemplation of Brahman,
while others, from the gods down to the most excellent of immobile beings, are characterized by the contemplation of karma."
And among those such as Hiraṇyagarbha, who are endowed with awakening and authority, there exists a twofold cultivation of being consisting of both Brahman and action.
As long as all the specific cognitions and activities remain unexhausted,
this entire universe and that which is beyond it appear divided by the perception of duality to men.
That knowledge which is designated as Brahman is that in which all distinctions have subsided, which is pure existence alone, beyond the reach of speech, and self-cognizable.
And because it is concealed by that [power], O King, the power known as the *kṣetrajña* is perceived with varying degrees of clarity among all living beings.
That [sin] is very slight among those without breath; it is greater among stationary beings (sthāvara);
it is even greater than that among reptiles, and indeed exceedingly great among winged creatures.
From birds, wild animals are superior; from them, domestic animals are superior by virtue of that power;
and from domestic animals, human beings are far more powerful, being manifested through the power of the Puruṣa.
O King, even superior to them were the deities such as the Nāgas, Garuḍas, and Yakṣas.
Śakra is superior to all the gods, and Prajāpati is superior to him;
Hiraṇyagarbha is even superior to that, being characterized by the power of the Supreme Person (Puṃs).
O King, all these forms without exception are his very forms,
because they are joined with his power, just as [all things] are joined with space.
O Mahāmati, the second [form] is that which is to be meditated upon by the yogi, known as Viṣṇu;
it is the formless aspect of Brahman, which is called "Being" (sat) by the wise. O King, all these powers of the rays are established therein;
it is that other great form of Hari, which is both the universal form and yet devoid of form.
O Lord of Men, He manifests all forms of power—
gods, animals, humans, and so forth— endowed with activity, by His own divine play.
For the benefit of the worlds, that activity of the immeasurable one is not caused by karma; it is all-pervading and characterized by being unimpeded.
O King, that form of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa) should be meditated upon by one engaged in yoga for the sake of purifying the self and for the destruction of all sins.

Just as a fire with undiminished flames, aided by the wind, consumes dry grass, so too Viṣṇu, when established in the mind, burns away all the impurities of yogis. Therefore, one should effect the steady abiding of the mind upon that which is the substratum of all powers; this indeed is to be known as pure *dhāraṇā*.
"O King, for the yogin whose mind has a pure substratum, who is omnipresent and of an immovable nature, and who has transcended the cultivation of the three states of existence, there is liberation."
But others, O tiger among men, who are the objects of mental reliance—
such as the gods and the rest— are all impure, for they have their origin in karma.
The embodied form of the Blessed One is free from attachment to all supports;
this indeed is declared to be *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is fixed.
O lord of men, whatever form of Hari’s embodiment is to be meditated upon—
Therefore, O gentle one, it is not logical that there should be no support for the stream of concentration. [He was] with a serene countenance, beautiful eyes like lotus petals,
lovely cheeks, and a radiant, broad forehead.
Adorned with beautiful earrings resting as far as his ears,
he had a neck like a conch shell and a very broad chest marked with the Śrīvatsa.
“Then, the wise man [should visualize the deity] with a belly bent by three folds and a navel,
yet devoid of the conch, mace, discus, Śārṅga bow, and other [emblems].”
One should meditate upon the Blessed One, peaceful and holding a rosary.
When that concentration has become stable in that state,
one should then meditate upon [the deity] as being devoid of head-ornaments, armlets, and facial decorations.
Then, the wise one should indeed mentally focus upon that deity as a single limb; thereafter, he should become intent on meditative concentration upon the whole composed of those limbs.
O King, that meditative absorption (dhyāna) is accomplished through six initial factors: it is a single continuum characterized by that [object], free from longing for anything else,
and consists of the apprehension of the very nature of that [object] itself, devoid of conceptual construction.
That which is to be accomplished through mental meditation by means of the mind is designated as *samādhi*.
O King, consciousness is that which attains the supreme Brahman as its object;
likewise, the Self is that which is to be attained once all residual mental impressions have been extinguished.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the agent, and knowledge is his instrument (O twice-born one). Having accomplished the task of liberation by means of that [knowledge], he indeed desists once his purpose has been fulfilled.
Having attained the state of being that very essence, he then becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
for any difference would be produced by ignorance.
When the knowledge that produces the sense of duality has gone to absolute destruction,
who will create the non-existent distinction between the self and Brahman?
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman.

11. That [devotee] intent on liberation is of two kinds, distinguished as the *bhakta* (the devotee) and the *prapanna* (the one who has sought refuge). The *prapanna* is further divided into two types: the *ekāntin* (the exclusive devotee) and the *paramaikāntin* (the supreme exclusive devotee). || 9 || The *paramaikāntin* is described as being of two kinds: the *dṛpta* (the haughty) and the *ārta* (the distressed). The Lord (*īśvara*) is divided into five forms according to the distinctions of the *para* (the supreme), the *vyūha* (the manifestations), and so forth. || 10 || The *para* (supreme form) is one, while the *vyūha* consists of four, namely Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, according to their respective divisions. || 11 ||

The Matsya and other [incarnations] are proclaimed to be infinite manifestations (*vibhava*). The Lord as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*), however, resides within every body. His incarnations (*avatāra*) are situated in Śrīraṅga, Veṅkaṭādri, and other such places. Keśava and the others are declared by the knowers of reality to be further manifestations (*vyūha*).
Sattva, rajas, tamas, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, conjunction, and power—thus the non-material substance (*adravya*) is considered to be tenfold.
This [perception] is seen to be both dependent on the sense organs and independent of them.

It is considered to be of two kinds: that which is independent and self-established, or that which is divine. However, the perception born of yoga is self-established, while the other is born from the grace of a master. The wise declare that all of this is mundane (arvācīna), whereas the knowledge of the eternally liberated Lord is called super-mundane (anarvācīna).

Memory is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), for it arises from a prior experience (22). When the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is awakened by means such as similarity, perception, or reflection, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—like memory—is also included within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) (23). Even intuition (*pratibhā*) residing in holy persons is accepted here as being included in this very category.
As Yāmuna stated: "All cognition is in accordance with reality" (24). Furthermore, the absence of a jar on the ground is nothing other than the nature of the ground itself.
The prior non-existence of a clay pot is its destruction, which consists of the potsherds. Indeed, it is the unique property of a thing that is denoted by the word "difference" (bheda).

In some cases, the cognition of being a counter-correlate (pratiyogitva) is produced merely by the inherent nature of words. The consciousness of the internal organ, through its modification and the object, becomes equalized with consciousness; thus arisen, it produces direct perception (sākṣātkāra).
All such statements as these, propounded by others, are not accepted here;
neither generality (sāmānya), nor inherence (samavāya), nor particularity (viśeṣa) is accepted here. || 28 ||

The conception of number as a separate category from the qualities, and the classification of the group of qualities, are all in contradiction with the author of the Sūtras and shall therefore be refuted. (29)
Thus concludes the examination of direct perception.

Pervasion (vyāpti) is said to be the non-occurrence [of the probans] in the locus of the absence of the probandum. The cognition that the pervaded [probans] occurs in the subject (pakṣa) bears the name "ascertainment" (parāmarśa). (2)

The resulting cognition regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), which consists of the object to be proven (*sādhya*), is considered to be inference (*anumiti*). Through a single cognition characterized by extensive concomitance (*bhūyiṣṭhasāhacarya*), the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises. (3) In that context, the *sapakṣa* is that in which the *sādhya* has been previously ascertained; the *pakṣa* is that in which the *sādhya* is suspected; and the *vipakṣa* is that which possesses the absence of that [sādhya]. (4) Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is of two types: positive (*anvayin*) and negative (*vyatirekin*). There are five fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) that are not effective as proofs: the deviant (*vyabhicārin*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the unestablished (*asiddha*), the counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣaka*), and the sublated (*bādhita*). (5)
Thus has the detailed exposition of inference for oneself been described. For the sake of inference for others, there is the *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) produced by *nyāya* (formal reasoning);
and *nyāya* consists of five members of the argumentative statement, beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).

The thesis is the statement of that which is to be proven; the reason is considered to be the statement of that [thesis]. The example would be the citation of an instance preceded by the application of the logical connection. (8)
The cognition that the pervaded [probans] resides in the subject is considered the application (upanaya); furthermore, the statement of conclusion is the final summation (nigamana). || 9 ||
Thus concludes the exposition of inference.

Because it designates both action (*karman*) and Brahman, it consists of two parts: the first part is devoted to action, while the latter pertains to the domain of Brahman. (3) Due to the unity of these preceding and subsequent expositions, there is a single scripture; even though there is a division into chapters, the oneness of the scripture is not contradicted. (4) It is perceived as threefold in nature—consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras. A mantra is that which makes known the meaning to be performed, while an *arthavāda* is "that which praises" (*agīḥ*). (5)

That which incites activity is an injunction (*vidhi*); it is the sentence that prompts action. It is threefold, distinguished as *apūrva*, *niyama*, and *parisaṅkhyā*. || 6 || These are considered to be manifold: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Their essential natures and definitions should be understood according to other systems (*nayāntara*). || 7 || Prosody (*chandas*), Ritual Procedure (*kalpa*), Phonetics (*śikṣā*), Etymology (*nirukta*), Astronomy (*jyautiṣa*), and Grammar (*vyākṛti*)—these are declared to be the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the Veda. || 8 ||

The *chandas* [Veda] beginning with the *anuṣṭubh* [metres], the *kalpa* which makes known the *śrauta* rituals and so forth, the *śikṣā* which determines the phonemes, and the *nirukta* which makes known the meanings of words. || 9 ||

For determining the time for performance and so forth, astronomy is authoritative; for correct grammar, it is grammar; thus, the status of authority resides in the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs.
The authority of the Smṛtis and other texts is declared on the basis of this [Veda];
whatever is contrary to this cannot attain the status of valid knowledge. (11)
This [set of conditions], beginning with expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), is the sole cause of verbal cognition; its investigation has been summarized here by one fearing excessive prolixity in the text. (12)
That word is considered to be of two kinds, by way of being primary (mukhya) or secondary (pacārika).
Denotation (abhidhā) is the primary function (mukhyavṛtti), while the other function is secondary (upacārikī). (13)
Words denoting the body function by referring to the embodied one; it will be stated that Hari is the denotable object of all words. (14)
Thus concludes the investigation of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition.
The eye grasps only form; the skin is the cause for grasping touch;
the nose grasps odor; and the tongue illuminates taste. (10)
The connection between these [objects] and their spheres is proclaimed to be conjunction (saṃyoga) and so forth.
The organs of action are considered to be those whose single capacity consists in utterance and other such functions. (11)
It is fivefold, distinguished as speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ.
Speech is the cause for the utterance of phonemes; the hand is the instrument for crafts and the like. (12)
The foot is the cause of movement; the anus effects the discharge of waste;

and the generative organ is considered the cause of supreme bliss for both men and women. (13) Furthermore, from the ego characterized by *rajas* arises activity (*kriyā*), while from the ego characterized by *tamas* arise the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as sound, which are the causes of the gross elements. (14) They say that the "subtle element" (*tanmātra*) is a substance consisting of the specific prior state of the gross elements alone, existing as a single subtle essence; these are fivefold, corresponding to the five elements. (15)

The pentad of subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with sound, is associated as the substratum [of the gross elements]. Among the gross elements, the subtle element of sound is the primary material cause; likewise are the subtle elements of touch, form, taste, and smell. These constitute the origins of ether, air, fire, water, and earth respectively. (16–17)
The five elements are now described as being of the nature of the subtle elements (tanmātra); they represent the primordial state situated between the two forms of tamasic ego. (18)
From this [tanmātra], the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), space (*viyat*) is produced in the same manner.

Space itself, by means of its solar form, is designated as the "directions" (*diś*). That substance which is well-combined in the intermediate state between space and air is the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*); from that, air (*vāyu*) is produced in due order. The substance which possesses the intermediate state between air and fire is called the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*); from that, [fire] is produced in due order.

The substance consisting of fire (*tejas*) combined with the intermediate state [of sound] is called the subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*); from this, indeed, water is born. (22) The substance consisting of water and earth combined with the intermediate state is called the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*); from this, that earth arises. (23) The first [subtle element] possesses sound; the others are said to possess sound and touch. The third [subtle element] possesses form, sound, and touch, and the fourth likewise. (24) The fifth [subtle element] is endowed with form, sound, touch, and taste, and has smell as its predominant quality. Thus are described the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the five gross elements (*bhūta*). (25)

Thus, the twenty-fourfold enumeration of the distinctions, beginning with *prakṛti*, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and the great principle (*mahat*), has been well-determined. Having created the elements, the Blessed One divided each one into two;
having made one part into one, He divided the other into four. (26–27)
He joined those portions, which had been arranged fourfold, with their respective parts; by means of his own portions augmented by a fourth part each, he brought forth the five elements.

Although all other elements were present as constituent parts, because of the predominance of its own respective part, the designations "earth," "water," "fire," "air," and "space" came into being in the world. (29)
The Śruti indicates that this quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) is analogous to the process by which the Mahat and Ahaṃkāra are rendered sevenfold through the elements.
The five elements, the unmanifest, the Great Principle (mahat), and the ego (ahaṃkṛti)—
these are the material causes of the body and the sense organs for every individual soul.
Indeed, various other things may adorn the body for eon after eon; yet that which is governed by consciousness alone is truly called the "body. (32)
The body is of two kinds, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal; O Blessed One, that which belongs to the eternal sūris is indeed eternal and innate.
That which is impermanent is also twofold, according to whether it is produced by karma or not produced by karma. That which is not produced by karma is fashioned by the will of the Lord and others.
And that [action] is performed through hatred, as well as accompanied by one's own will. 34.

And there is that which is produced by karma, as in the case of Saubhari and others; this is the first [type]. The second [type] belongs to those such as ourselves. Furthermore, it is twofold in general:
stationary (sthāvara) and moving (jaṅgama); the stationary is considered to be stones and the like.

The mobile (jaṅgama) is said to be of two kinds: born from a womb (yonija) and not born from a womb (ayonija). That which is born from a womb is divided into gods, humans, animals, and so forth. The non-womb-born is known as that which arises from sprouts (udbhijja), sweat (svedaja), eggs (aṇḍaja), and hell-beings (nārakīya). Thus, it is traditionally held that the quintuplicated elements (pañcīkṛtāni) possess the capacity to produce the cosmic egg (aṇḍa). Prior to the production of the egg, there is the primary creation (pūrvasṛṣṭi); thereafter, creation is considered to be twofold according to the Vedānta: the collective (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi). From the unmanifest (avyakta) onwards, a state distinct from itself, such as the Great Principle (mahat), is accepted; if there were a state of a different genus, it would be called a different darkness (tamas).
Thus, [it is composed] of those named the unmanifest (avyakta), mahat, ahaṃkāra, and the sense organs.
The subtle elements (tanmātras) are thus the principles (tattvas); they became twenty-four in number.
This entire Jambūdvīpa is surrounded by the salt ocean;
beyond that, Lakṣadvīpa is encircled by the sugarcane sea;
and thereafter, Śālmalidvīpa is surrounded by the wine ocean.
Beyond that is Kuśadvīpa, which is surrounded by an ocean of clarified butter.
Beyond that is Krauñcadvīpa, which is surrounded by the ocean of curd.
Then Śākadvīpa is surrounded by the Ocean of Milk. || 47 ||
Puṣkaradvīpa is surrounded on all sides by a pure ocean;
all of this is upon a golden ground, and beyond that is the Valaya mountain range.
Enveloped in darkness, he too, as well as [the world] by the waters of the womb—thus there would be a single egg, both above and below the earth. (49)
Such are the infinite eggs of the Great Hari, described in sequence in the Purāṇas as being like bubbles upon the water. (50)
Thus concludes the examination of primordial nature (prakṛti).

But this [time] does not depend upon time within the eternal manifestation (nityavibhūti); rather, it is time that serves as the equipment for the sport (krīḍā) of the Supreme Self. The dissolutions—whether eternal, occasional, or elemental—are caused by time. Thus has been explained the description of the true nature of time.
Thus ends the fifth [section], the Determination of Time.

Indeed, when [the Lord] becomes inclined toward grace (*prasāda*), [His powers] become manifest; and that manifestation of His is understood to be dependent upon His will. (9) Enough with the question, "How can there be contact with an ordinary body for one who is beyond the ordinary? For such [contact] is frequently seen in the incarnations (*avatāra*) of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. (10) Those qualities such as brilliance (*ojas*) which exist in Hari’s divine and auspicious form (*divyamaṅgalavigraha*), you should understand them through an investigation of the *Gadyatraya*. (11)

As for the statement seen regarding the bodilessness of the liberated ones, that refers to the absence of connection with a body produced by karma. O Śrīnātha, our teachers and others who follow the Vedānta have described Your divine and auspicious form according to the sequence stated in the Purāṇas.
For thus the mind creates consciousness, the sword of volition, and the garland of its concealment; the elements, through their own qualities, do not perceive the pair of actions.

O Lord of Kamalā, the wise say that Your ten cavities are the Cāṇūra demon, the Kaustubha gem is the individual soul (jīva), the Śrīvatsa mark is primordial matter (pradhāna), and Your mace is the Great Principle (mahat).
Thus it is said.

Therein, worshipped by Vimala and others with chowries in their hands, shines an eight-petaled lotus; there resides Śeṣa, whose nature is intellect. Therein, consisting of bliss, directly beyond the reach of all words, he shines in the form of Nārāyaṇa as a wondrous light.
|| Exposition of Eternal Glory || 6 ||

The Lord, being well-pleased by devotion and surrender, is the bestower of liberation; therefore, devotion and surrender are indeed the supreme causes of liberation. Those who practice Karma-yoga and Jñāna-yoga have declared that these are the means for attaining devotion. Ritual action performed without attachment to its fruits as a form of worship toward the Lord, and meditation upon Him once the internal organ has been purified, constitute Jñāna-yoga.
Whether directly or otherwise, these two serve as the cause for devotion.

This eight-limbed yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga), having been produced by means of discernment (viveka) and the other [limbs], becomes uninterrupted continuity of remembrance and attains the form of direct perception.
At the time of the conclusion of each respective body,
this very instrumental devotion (sādhanabhakti), which is subject to transformation, is considered to be accompanied by the limb of surrender (prapatti).
But the enjoyment of the fruit arises from the grace of the Lord;
for this very reason, Hari directly attains the state of being the perfected means.
Now follows the definition of the living being (jīva). || 8 ||
In that state, consciousness is said to be the defining characteristic of the living being (*jīva*). And that [consciousness] is considered to be distinct from the body, the senses, and so forth.
Although the *jīva* is atomic in size, its experience of manifold objects is traditionally taught;
for that purpose, the pervasion by consciousness—which is its essential attribute (*dharma*)—is necessary.
Because of the connection with the recollection of objects previously experienced.
It is eternal, distinct in each body, and designated by such terms as "the enjoyer" and so forth. (3)
In relation to its material nature, the embodied soul is the body; in relation to its glory, it is the possessor of the body.
Its self-luminosity is taught by direct perception and scripture.
Even for one who is minute, there is the apprehension of results occurring in other locations.
They declared that even the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by karma arises from consciousness.

The individual soul (jīva) is considered to be of three kinds: bound, liberated, and eternal. From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, those joined to the cycle of transmigration are "bound. Those who are proficient in the aims of the three goals of life (the three vargas) but do not desire liberation are called "those seeking enjoyment" (avubhukṣu). Among them, those devoted to wealth and pleasure are "those who identify with the embodied self" (sadehātmābhimānin).
Even having attained the supreme state of isolation (*kaivalya*) by traveling along the path of light,
one remains as if in some corner, like a woman abandoned by her lover; this kind of isolation is approved only by certain noble ones (*āryas*).
It is established that these [schools] do not consider liberation to be for us. || 12 ||
"Devotees" (bhaktāḥ) are those who, by means of the very devotion previously described, desire the attainment of liberation;
it is clear that in the *Apaśūdranaya* [the section concerning non-Śūdras], Śūdras have no entitlement to such devotion.
